text:
3
RICE TARIFFICATION LAW
What is the Rice Tariffication Act or Republic Act (RA) 11203?
The Rice Tariffication Act amends the Agricultural Tariffication Act of 1996
(RA 8178). The law replaces the system of quantitative restriction (QR) on rice
importation with a purely tariff system.
Why are we shifting to a tariff system?
For one, limiting the supply of goods in the market results in higher prices. This
is what the country experienced several times when the decision to import rice is
left to a political process. Political leaders are always subjected to public opinion
whenever they allow rice imports resulting in either low volume of imported rice
or delayed importation. These results in price spikes. With the use of tariffs, rice
importation becomes a business decision, which responds to changes in market
demand. The use of tariffs also generates revenues for the government that can
be used in development projects.
Second, it is our commitment to the World Trade Organization (WTO) to replace all
QRs imposed on agricultural products into tariffs since 1995. We have allowed the
tariffication of all other agricultural products, except rice.
In 2005, the Philippines requested for an extension of the QR until 2012. After it
lapsed, the Philippines again requested for a waiver to extend. The final extension
was approved until June 30, 2017. To fully comply with our commitment, we need
to harmonize our domestic law with our international agreement; hence, the
passage of RA 11203.
What is the difference between QRs and tariffs?
Both QRs and tariffs aim to protect the local industry from competition by limiting
the entry of imported goods. QRs refer to the allowable amount or quantity of
goods that may be imported into the country, while tariffs refer to taxes or duties
imposed on imported goods.
BASICS OF THE LAW

4
What is the minimum access volume (MAV)?
MAV refers to the volume or quantity of a specific agricultural commodity that may
be imported with a lower tariff as committed by the Philippines to WTO.
What is the current MAV for rice?
RA 11203 reverts the MAV for rice to 350,000 metric tons (mt) from 805,200mt
when the waiver was still in effect.
What is the timeline for this reform?
Year 	Milestone
1995 	Upon joining the WTO, the Philippines secured a “Special Treatment”
for rice under Annex 5 of the WTO Agreement on Agriculture. The Spe-
cial Treatment allowed the country to retain its QR on rice for 10 years
(1995-2005).
1996 	Except for rice, all existing QRs on agricultural products were converted
into tariffs with the passage of RA 8178.
2005 	The Philippines requested for an extension of the QR up to 2012 sub-
ject to the following concessions:
a. 	Increase in MAV from 119,460mt to 350,000mt
b. 	In-Quota Tariff reduced from 50 to 40%
c. 	Other non-tariff concessions (e.g., meat products)
2012 	The Philippines requested for a “Waiver” to again extend the QR on rice
up to June 30, 2017, subject to the following concessions:
a. 	Increase the MAV from 350,000mt to 805,200mt
b. 	In-Quota Tariff lowered from 40 to 35%
c. 	Other non-tariff concessions (e.g., lower tariff rates for meat
products, peas, and potatoes)
2017 	Philippines allows “Waiver” to lapse; thereby, increasing pressure for it
to fulfill WTO obligation to finally shift from QRs on rice to tariff.
2019 	QRs on rice to be converted into tariffs with passage of RA 11203.

5
RICE TARIFFICATION LAW
What are the key components of RA 11203?
• 	Allows the private sector to freely import rice subject to a tariff.
• 	Removes the regulatory and import licensing functions of the National Food
Authority (NFA).
• 	Requires importers to obtain Sanitary and Phytosanitary Import Clearance
(SPSIC) to be issued by the Department of Agriculture - Bureau of Plant
Industry (DA-BPI) to protect our agriculture and consumers from diseases,
pests, or contaminants.
• 	Reduces the mandate of the NFA to emergency buffer stocking of rice that
will be sourced solely from local farmers.
• 	Shifts to a purely tariff system with the following rates:
– 35% if rice is imported within ASEAN
– 40% if within the MAV of 350,000mt for imports coming from countries
outside of ASEAN
– 180% if above the MAV and from non-ASEAN countries
• 	Creates the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (RCEF) or Rice Fund
with a P10 billion annual appropriation for the next six years to be allocated
and disbursed as follows:
– Rice farm machinery and equipment (50%) - will be released to and
implemented by the Philippine Center for Postharvest Development and
Mechanization (PhilMech)
– Rice seed development, propagation, and promotion (30%) - will be
released to and implemented by the Philippine Rice Research Institute
(PhilRice)
– Expanded rice credit assistance (10%) - will be made available in the form
of a credit facility with minimal interest rates and minimum collateral
requirements to rice farmers and cooperatives to be managed equally by
the Land Bank of the Philippines (LBP) and the Development Bank of the
Philippines (DBP)
– Rice extension services (10%) – will be made available for extension
services provided by the PhilMech, PhilRice, Agricultural Training Institute
(ATI), and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA).
• 	Tariff revenues in excess of the P10 billion annual appropriation will be
earmarked for the following:
– Rice farmer financial assistance
– Titling of agricultural rice lands
– Expanding crop insurance program on rice
– Crop diversification program

6
Will the Rice Fund replace the other assistance provided to rice farmers?
No. The Rice Fund is on top of regular funds of the Department of Agriculture used
in programs and assistance for rice farmers such as the National Rice Program.
What are required of importers under RA 11203?
The only requirement to import rice under the reform is the SPSIC issued by
DA-BPI. Import licensing is no longer required, but importers of rice shall register
with the BPI and be part of the DA Trade System Registration Procedure. The BPI
is mandated to regularly publish and update in its website the list of importers
issued with SPSIC, including the volume of imports.
How long will it take to obtain an SPSIC?
The law mandates that the application for the issuance of the SPSIC shall be acted
upon within seven calendar days. The BPI is required to communicate in writing
any incomplete application or non-compliance to SPSIC requirements before the
seven-day period ends. The failure of the BPI to respond to the applicant shall
mean automatic approval of the SPSIC application.
While tariff revenues are yet to be realized, are there available funds now to
mitigate the impact on rice farmers during the transition?
In December 2018, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) already
released P5 billion to DA on top of its 2019 budget for National Rice Program to
assist farmers in facing the possible adverse effects of lifting the rice QR. This is
in addition to the P10 billion annual appropriation for the Rice Competitiveness
Enhancement Fund (RCEF) or Rice Fund that will help farmers transition to a new
rice regime.
What is the primary role of NFA under RA 11203?
NFA is mandated to maintain the country’s emergency buffer stock that it will
source solely from local farmers and farmer cooperatives.

7
RICE TARIFFICATION LAW
How much rice will NFA keep as buffer stock for emergency?
Based on its mandate, NFA will adopt an optimal level of rice inventory enough
to accommodate 15-30 days of national rice consumption. This is equivalent to
around 480,000-960,000mt of rice. The implementing rules and regulations (IRR) of
RA 11203 will determine the required level of inventory.
Will the NFA’s buffer stock be released only for disaster relief operations?
The NFA’s buffer stock is primarily for emergency distribution in support of
disaster relief programs. If, however, there are no calamities, the NFA can regularly
replenish the inventory and sell to avoid spoilage.
ISSUES WITH THE PREVIOUS SYSTEM
The rice sector remains weak despite the QRs since 1995. This weakness is
manifested in the following:
• 	High-price of rice: More than 100 million Filipinos pay two-three higher than
the citizens in our neighboring countries. In 2018, Filipinos paid an average
of P45/kg for well-milled rice while neighboring Thais paid only P22/kg and
Vietnamese even less. Food and nutrition security for the Filipinos requires
that our nation’s staple is accessible to all at affordable prices.
• 	Elevated inflation: In 2018, rice was the number one driver of high
inflation, contributing one full percentage point to 2018 inflation at its peak.
High rice price brings hardship, especially to poor households spending
around 20% of their family budget on rice. By spending less for the same
amount of rice, poor households could then increase expenditures on other
items, especially on education. With rice tariffication implemented, the
Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas expects inflation to fall by 0.6 percentage points,
placing 2019 inflation within the government’s target range of 2-4%.
• 	Lower real income for small farmers: Around 1.6 million (55%) of 2.9 million
rice farming households are smallholders, planting less than one hectare,
and most of them are net consumers of rice. While they may gain from
higher prices during harvest, they buy expensive rice during the rest of the
year; thereby, reducing their real income.

8
• 	Reduced employment opportunities: The high price of rice has put undue
pressure on the minimum wage rate over the decades, increasing labor cost
and making manufacturing uncompetitive. Other countries in the region
developed a strong labor-intensive manufacturing sector by keeping food
prices low.
• 	Massive government debt: As of December 2018, the subsidy to NFA has
cost taxpayers P140.5 billion in outstanding debt, and the NFA continues to
request for additional P7 billion per year for its annual procurement. This is a
significant burden on taxpayers and all Filipinos, especially the poor who are
deprived of social services while paying high rice prices. Allowing the private
sector to handle importation will address these problems and free up public
funds for other purposes.
How is rice tariffication pro-consumer?
Over 100 million Filipino consumers, including majority of the rice farmers that are
net consumers of rice, will benefit from the lower rice prices due to tariffication.
The BSP and NEDA estimate that rice prices will drop by P2-7/kg under a tariffied
regime. This will slow down inflation by 0.6 percentage point; thereby, helping the
country achieve the target inflation of 2-4%.
How is rice tariffication pro-farmer?
Rice tariffication is a win-win for rice farmers because they will have access to
cheap, affordable, and high-quality rice and receive government support to
improve their productivity through the Rice Fund. Around 1.1 million of 2.9 million
rice farmers and farm workers are smallholders, planting less than one hectare,
and most of them are net consumers of rice. They may gain from higher prices
during harvest, but they would buy expensive rice during the rest of the year. An
estimated 4.5 million non-rice farmers and farm workers will also benefit from the
lower price of rice.
BENEFITS OF RICE TARIFFICATION

9
RICE TARIFFICATION LAW
How is rice tariffication pro-tax payer?
As of December 2018, the subsidy to NFA has cost taxpayers P140.5 billion in
outstanding debt. This debt is paid for by taxpayers and the poor who are deprived
of social services while paying for high rice prices.
How is rice tariffication pro-worker?
Workers will see their real income increase. In the past, the high price of rice has
put undue pressure on the minimum wage rate over the decades, increasing labor
costs and making manufacturing uncompetitive.
Other countries in the region developed a strong labor-intensive manufacturing
sector by keeping food prices; and thus, nominal minimum wages, low.
How is rice tariffication pro-children?
One in three Filipino children below 5 years old are stunted based on the National
Nutrition Survey. This is equivalent to 4.2 million children who will be able to enjoy
better nutrition as the country’s staple becomes more affordable.
How is rice tariffication pro-poor?
Lower rice prices will significantly improve society welfare as rice accounts for 20%
of a poor household’s consumption. Food security requires that our nation’s food
staple is available, accessible, and affordable at all times, and not force the poor to
pay double when they can pay half.

10
NOTES

Rice Production Manual
Rice production Manual – Produced by the International Rice Research Institute
(IRRI) under Creative Commons.
Farm Power
Rationale
Farm power is one of the most expensive and critical inputs when growing
a rice crop. All operations require a certain amount of power and often the
success of a crop is dependent on the ability to get the task completed on
time. In the past much of the power used on farm came from human inputs
but with much of the rural labor force now moved to cities, farmers are
becoming more dependent on machines to complete tillage, planting and
harvesting operations.
Objectives
At the end of this lesson participants will:
 	Have an understanding of the different power sources used in rice
farming
 	Identify the control levers for different types of tractors
 	Conduct a preliminary maintenance check before starting a tractor.
 	Have a basic understanding of how to safely operate a tractor
Key Activity
This lesson introduces the concept of farm power and the different types of
power sources. It also provides hands on experience in basic tractor
maintenance and operation.

Farm Power
Rice production Manual – Produced by the International Rice Research Institute
(IRRI) under Creative Commons.
Farm Power
1. Introduction
Farm power is one of the most expensive and
critical inputs when growing a rice crop. All
operations require a certain amount of power
and often the success of the crop depends on
the ability to get the task completed on time.
In the past much of the power used on farm
came from human inputs but with much of
the rural labor force now moved to cities,
farmers are becoming more dependent on
machines to complete tillage, planting and
harvesting operations. Humans, animals and
machines are all used as sources of power in
agriculture production.
When undertaking different operations on a farm, a certain amount of work/energy is
required to complete the task. When this work is undertaken over time, it is then called
power. Power or the rate of doing work can be expressed as horsepower (hp) or
Kilowatt (kW). One horsepower is equivalent to 0.75 Kilowatt. Often it takes the same
amount of energy to complete a task and as the table shows, time is the major variable.

Farm Power
Rice production Manual – Produced by the International Rice Research Institute
(IRRI) under Creative Commons.
2. Human Power
Many tasks on farm are still undertaken using people as the power source.
Manual tasks undertaken and time
required include:
 	Land preparation (120‐160 days /ha)
 	Plant establishment (25‐35 days/ha)
 	Weeding (30‐40 days/ha)l,
 	Crops harvesting and transporting (30‐
40days /ha)
 	Transport. (5‐10days)
In some instances manual labor is still
more efficient and precise than machine.
Many countries are now suffering from
rural labor shortages and have had to
develop and use machines to complete tasks on time. In Africa between 80‐90% of all
farm tasks are still done manually.
3. Animal power
Animals are still widely used as the major power source in many countries. Land
preparation, weed management, crop threshing and transport are undertaken using
animal power. Oxen and caribou or buffalo are the most popular animal power source
for agricultural practices although horses, donkeys, mules and camels are used in many
countries for transportation. Caribou/buffalo are considered to be hardier and stronger
than oxen. Oxen are normally used in pairs while buffalo are often used singularly. In
Africa, between 10‐15% of tasks are undertaken using animals
The advantages of using animals include they are
cheap to maintain, have a multipurpose use for
meat and milk, are self‐replacement and produce
manure.
The disadvantage of using animals include: they
have limited daily working hours ,animals need
feeding and protection against pests and disease,
they are slow, a high man/power ratio is needed,
they have limited range of working conditions
and they require training.
One animal will take approximately 10‐12 days to
plough 1 hectare and cost up to $US 500 each.

Farm Power
Rice production Manual – Produced by the International Rice Research Institute
(IRRI) under Creative Commons.
4. Engine powered tractors
There are 3 broad groups of engine powered tractors used for rice production. These
are 2 wheel tractors, 4 wheel tractors and track laying tractors.
Two wheel tractors (also called walking tractor, iron or steel buffalo, hand tractor)
Two wheel tractors are used in many rice
producing countries. These tractors have a
forward mounted engine which is counter
balanced by the equipment attached behind
the 	two 	drive 	wheels 	and 	the 	operator
walking behind.
They are 	normally 	powered by 6‐12 kW
gasoline or diesel engines and are fitted with
either rubber tires or steel cage wheels.
Rubber tires are commonly used when dry
land plowing and for transportation. Cage
wheels are necessary for all wet workings. Most makes incorporate an independent
drive clutch as well as individual steering clutches or brakes. Three forwards and one
reverse working gear are most common.
Two wheel tractors are used for land preparation, which includes plowing and land
leveling, transportation and pumping water. The attachments used with 2 wheel
tractors are the moldboard plough, the disc plough, harrows, and rotovator.
The advantages of two wheel tractors are:
 	Multi purpose vehicle especially for
transport
 	Operate in harder conditions than
animals or humans
 	Operate in both wet and dry
conditions
 	Fairly simple mechanical design
Disadvantage
 	Cost of owning and operating
 	Operators fatigue, although rides on versions are now available.
The cost of a 9 kW (12 hp) walking tractor range from $US110 to $US270 per engine
kW, depending on the make of the engine and location. Two wheel tractors in Africa
are nearly double the price in Asia. One 9 kW walking tractor, with two operators, is
capable of plowing 1 ha / day. While fuel usage depends on engine size and working
conditions, fuel consumption will range from 2‐5 liters per hour.

Farm Power
Rice production Manual – Produced by the International Rice Research Institute
(IRRI) under Creative Commons.
Four wheel tractors
Four‐wheel tractors can be divided into 3 categories; two wheel drive, front wheel assist
or unequal four wheel drive and equal four wheel drive tractors. Each one of these
tractors has different tire configurations and different ballast requirements.
Two Wheel Drive tractors (2WD) are
the most commonly used tractors in
dry or upland farming situations and
for transportation. They range in size
from 4‐150 kW and require 75%‐ 80%
of the weight distributed over the rear
axle 	to 	maximize 	traction. 	These
tractors are capable of delivering 45‐
50% of their rated engine power at
the drawbar.
The advantage of this type of tractor
over other 4 wheel tractors is:
 	Smaller turning circle,
 	Simplicity of design,
 	Fewer mechanical parts, and
 	Lower purchase price.
The major disadvantage is the inability to work in very wet and muddy conditions.
When these tractors are used in a wet farming situation they will require cage wheels
attachments to the rear drive for traction. O
Front Wheel Assist or Unequal Four Wheel Drive (FWA)
are the most popular 4 wheel tractor used in rice
production in Asia and Africa. These tractors range in
size from 15‐180 kW and are capable of delivering
between 50‐55% of the rated power at the drawbar.
The front drive tires, whilst larger than two wheel drive
front tires, are smaller than the rear tires. These
tractors require 40% of the weight over the front axle
and 60% over the rear axle to maximize traction As all
four wheels turn simultaneously, the front and rear
tires must travel at the same speed. Because the front
tire is generally 30% smaller than the rear tire it must
turn at least 30% faster. Tire pressures must also be set
and maintained correctly(18psi front‐14psi rear) Front wheel drive should be used at all
times when the tractor is working in the field. If not at least 10% efficiency will be lost.

Farm Power
Rice production Manual – Produced by the International Rice Research Institute
(IRRI) under Creative Commons.
The major advantage of a FWA tractor is that it can deliver 10% more power to the
ground for the same fuel consumption, and has much better traction and flotation
capabilities than 2 wheel tractors of the same size. These tractors normally cost about
10‐15% more than the same size 2‐wheel drive tractor. A major disadvantage is that
this tractor type has more mechanical failures, displays unequal tire wear front to rear
and may be less maneuverable than a 2 wheel drive tractor.
Other Types of tractors
Equal Four Wheel Drive tractors (4WD) have all four tires of equal size and range in size
from 25‐ 450kW. Irrespective of size, these tractors should be ballasted with 60% of the
weight distributed over the front axle and 40% over the rear axle. This tractor type has
the greatest power to weight ratio and can deliver between 55‐60% of power at the
drawbar. Very few of these tractors are used in rice production in Asia or Africa because
of their large size, greater turning radius and high purchase price
Track laying tractors. (Chain tractor, crawler, Caterpillar)
Agricultural track layers range in size
from 15 ‐ 250 kW. 	Tracks can be
made from rubber or steel and vary in
width depending on the application.
Weight 	distribution 	for 	agricultural
purposes is different from that for
industrial use. Because the load is
applied to the rear of these tractors,
weight distribution should be similar
to that for an equal 4 wheel drive
tractors. 	These tractors can deliver
between 	60‐65% 	of 	their 	engine
power at the drawbar and are most efficient where flotation is a problem.
Tracklayers have been imported into many rice growing countries but their major use
has been in industrial and forestry regions. Very few are used in rice farming as they
have high purchase price, high repair and maintenance costs and are not efficient when
working in smaller paddy fields or water.

Service Guide 	5
The development in agriculture in the recent years has seen the declining role
of draft carabaos, more particularly in the intensively farmed, irrigated areas
and an increasing trend in farm mechanization. But while this substitution
takes place in some specific farming communities, the role of draft carabaos
in the rain-fed and hilly agricultural land has not diminished. In fact, the need
for draft carabaos may remain high in irrigated areas for some specifi c farm
activities for many years to come.
In the light of the need to improve productivity of the carabaos not only in
terms of draft but more importantly for milk and meat to increase income,
nutrition, and the general well-being of farmers, the implementation of the
national carabao development program becomes an important component
of the overall national strategies. This is essentially so because of the need
to harness the existing huge resources of about 3.0 million carabaos against
the background of the country’s 99% import dependence on milk and dairy
products and about 50% import dependence on carabeef.
For its part, the Philippine Carabao Center (PCC) will continue its strong resolve
of extending necessary services to the farmers, the local government units and
other organizations that play important part in the faster development of the
Philippine carabao industry.
This publication is designed to guide the carabao industry stakeholders and
the public who are interested on the services of PCC. Detailed procedures on
how to avail of each service are provided in the succeeding pages.
It is our hope that the industry stakeholders benefi t from this piece of
publication.
FOREWORD
ARNEL N. DEL BARRIO
Executive Director III
publication.	publication.

QUALITY POLICY
The Philippine Carabao Center aims to be a premiere research
and development institution for the sustainable growth of the
livestock industry.
In order to achieve this, we, at PCC, are dedicated to provide
quality products and services that address customers’ needs
consistent with statutory, regulatory and other requirements,
and the International Standards; and committed to
continuously improve the effectiveness of our integrated
management systems, products and services, processes,
people, and workplace by ensuring safety of our workers; and
protection of the environment.

SUMMARY
The Philippine Carabao Center, an attached agency of the Department of
Agriculture created by virtue of Republic Act 7307, is mandated to conserve,
propagate and promote the carabao as a source of milk, meat, draft power and
hide to help achieve better nutrition, higher levels of income and improved
general well-being of the rural farming families.
The PCC mandate is pursued through the implementation of the following
major services:
• 	Artifi cial Insemination
• 	Bull Loan Program
• 	Frozen Buffalo Semen Distribution
• 	Provision of Superior Breeding Animals
• 	Training of Technicians and Farmers
• 	Technical Assistance and Extension
a) Animal Reproduction
b) Animal Nutrition
c) Animal Health
d) Forage Production and Improved Feeding System
e) Cooperative Development
f) Dairy Production and Processing
• 	Analysis of milk samples
• 	Nutrition Laboratory Services
• 	Biosafety and Environment Laboratory Services
• 	Information and Library
• 	Visitors’ Assistance
• 	Marketing Assistance

8 	Service Guide
ARTIFICIAL
INSEMINATION
Brief Description
Artifi cial insemination (AI) is one of the agency’s banner services rendered
nationwide in villages by trained private village-based AI technicians (VBAITs) as
well as technicians of local government units (LGUs), DA-Regional Field Offices
(DA-RFO) and PCC regional centers.
AI is a reproductive tool used to produce animals with better productivity for
milk and meat, without disregard for draft power through harnessing superior
genetic materials of dairy buffalo breed. 	The strategy is to cross the native
swamp buffaloes with the dairy breed following a sustained backcrossing to
at least four generations to produce animals with milk and meat producing
potentials equivalent to the purebred dairy parents.
Service Standard
The PCC trains VBAITs to provide AI services in the community with a fee, which
is based on the existing price acceptable in the locality (ranges from Php300-
Php1,000). In places, where there is no trained VBAIT or LGU AI technician, the
conduct of AI in the villages is usually based on the schedules agreed upon
during the annual planning activities of PCC and the LGUs. However, there are
cases when requests outside of the annual plan come in. For those coming
from the LGUs, processing of request is completed within 3-7 days. For “on-call
A.I.” (usually in areas that are at close proximity to the centers) that is based on
natural estrus, processing of request usually takes only 30 minutes to one hour.
The actual conduct of A.I. takes around 1 to 2 hours, including travel time (for
natural estrus), and 3 to 4 days (for synchronized estrus). Take note that estrus
synchronization/artificial insemination (ES/AI) scheme is conducted only on a
case-to-case basis and not a regular activity of the center.

10 	Service Guide
BULL LOAN PROGRAM
Brief Description
Purebred dairy-type bulls are loaned out to qualified farmers for natural mating
with purebred dairy-type buffaloes, crossbreds and native carabaos in areas
where AI services are limited and not readily available. This service is an integral
part of the genetic improvement program aimed at producing animals with
improved productivity for milk and meat, without disregard to draft power.
Service Standard
If the bull is available and all evaluation criteria or requirements are met,
coordination and evaluation activities, including the processing of related
documents (from the day of receipt of the request to the release of the bull), are
completed within 11.5 working days.
Bulls for loan are availed of for the following purposes: (1) to service purebred
dairy-type buffaloes and crossbreds in a dairy module under the cooperative/
association/dairy-buffalo multiplier farm schemes; and (2) to service native or
crossbred carabaos for crossbreeding (upgrading) program in the villages.
Repayment Scheme
Loan Scheme 1: Bulls servicing purebred and crossbred dairy-type buffaloes
under the cooperative/association/dairy buffalo multiplier farm
Bulls loaned under this scheme will be PCC-owned and continuously replaced
every three to four years to avoid inbreeding.
Loan Scheme 2. Bulls to be used in the carabao crossbreeding (upgrading) in
the villages
A junior bull (2.5 years old and below) and socialized, is considered paid in full
when it has produced 25 calves. This is subject to proper proof and certification
from the Municipal Agriculturist, Veterinarian or Livestock Inspector.
After submitting a copy of proof and certifi cation to PCC, ownership of the bull
shall be awarded to the bull handler.

Brief Description
The PCC maintains a Semen Processing Laboratory in Carranglan, Nueva Ecija
(managed by PCC at CLSU), in Los Baños, Laguna (managed by PCC at UPLB), and
in Maramag, Bukidnon (managed by PCC at CMU). These laboratories produce
and process frozen semen from genetically superior sires or bulls to be used for

Service Guide 	29
BIOSAFETY
AND ENVIRONMENT
LABORATORY
Brief Description
To maintain a disease-free environment and control possible disease outbreaks,
the PCC established its own Biosafety and Environment Laboratory. This facility
caters to the National Impact Zone ( Nueva Ecija ) clientele, National Gene Pool,
Livestock Biotechnology Research and Animal Facility and PCC Regional Centers
nationwide. It will also provide assistance to researchers and academicians
involved in animal health and biological sciences, and conduct collaborative
researches.
At present, the laboratory performs fecalysis, blood parasite examination,
serological testing (Brucella Test, ELISA for Neospora and CAE), molecular
testing for detection of microbial pathogens (PCR, nPCR among others), and
conventional microbiological testing (bacterial isolation and identifi cation,
antibiotic sensitivity testing, coliform count and total plate count).
Service Standard

the results can be released within 2 to 6 working days except for the mouse
inoculation test (MIT) which needs 21-day observation. Release of the results also
depends on the number of samples submitted and tests conducted. The clients
are then informed with the unoffi cial laboratory results in advance.

QUESTION 1

What does the limit of a function describe?
A. The slope of the graph
B. The exact value at a point
C. The behavior of the function as it approaches a point
D. The area under the curve
Answer: C – A limit describes the behavior of a function as it approaches a certain value.
QUESTION 1

LIMITS
What Is a Limit?
The limit of a function describes the behavior of the
function as the input (usually 𝑥) approaches a specific
value. It answers the question:
“What value does the function approach as 𝑥 gets close to
a number?”
Example:
If 𝑓(𝑥) = 2𝑥, then as 𝑥 → 3, 𝑓(𝑥) → 6. So we write:
𝑙𝑖𝑚
𝑥→32𝑥 = 6

LIMITS
Types of Limits
A. Finite Limits at Finite Points
Function approaches a real number as 𝑥 → 𝑎.
B. Infinite Limits
Function grows without bound:\
lim
𝑥→𝑎𝑓(𝑥) = ∞(or − ∞)
C. Limits at Infinity
Describes end behavior:\
lim
𝑥→∞𝑓(𝑥)

What is the primary concept behind evaluating a limit
numerically?
A. Plugging the value directly into the function
B. Analyzing the function's behavior as inputs get
infinitely close to the point
C. Finding the derivative at that point
D. Graphing the function and finding the y-intercept
QUESTION 2

What is the primary concept behind evaluating a limit
numerically?
A. Plugging the value directly into the function
B. Analyzing the function's behavior as inputs get
infinitely close to the point
C. Finding the derivative at that point
D. Graphing the function and finding the y-intercept
Answer: B – Numerical evaluation of a limit involves examining function values for inputs progressively closer to
the point of interest, from both sides, to see if they approach a specific value.
QUESTION 2

LIMITS
One-Sided Limits
Left-hand limit: lim𝑥→𝑎− 𝑓(𝑥) – values of 𝑥 approaching 𝑎
from the left.
Right-hand limit: lim𝑥→𝑎+ 𝑓(𝑥) – values approaching from
the right.
The two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits
exist and are equal.

When does a limit not exist due to unbounded behavior?
A. When the function has a jump discontinuity
B. When the left-hand limit equals the right-hand limit\
C. When the function approaches positive or negative
infinity
D. When the function is continuous
QUESTION 3

When does a limit not exist due to unbounded behavior?
A. When the function has a jump discontinuity
B. When the left-hand limit equals the right-hand limit\
C. When the function approaches positive or negative
infinity
D. When the function is continuous
Answer: C – An infinite limit means the function's values grow without bound (approaching ∞ or −∞), implying the
limit does not exist as a finite number.
QUESTION 3

LIMITS
When Does a Limit Exist?
A limit exists at 𝑥 = 𝑎 if and only if:
lim𝑥→𝑎− 𝑓(𝑥) = lim𝑥→𝑎+ 𝑓(𝑥)
The value approached from both sides is the same.
It does not require that the function is defined at 𝑎.

Which type of discontinuity is characterized by a "gap" in
the graph where the function value is either missing or
misplaced?
A. Jump discontinuity
B. Infinite discontinuity
C. Removable discontinuity
D. Oscillating discontinuity
QUESTION 4

Which type of discontinuity is characterized by a "gap" in
the graph where the function value is either missing or
misplaced?
A. Jump discontinuity
B. Infinite discontinuity
C. Removable discontinuity
D. Oscillating discontinuity
Answer: C – A removable discontinuity is a "hole" in the graph, where the limit exists but either the function is
undefined at that point or its value doesn't match the limit.
QUESTION 4

LIMITS
Types of Discontinuities Related to Limits
• Removable discontinuity: Hole in the graph; limit exists,
but function is undefined or has a different value at that
point.
• Jump discontinuity: Left and right limits exist but are
not equal.
• Infinite discontinuity: The function approaches infinity
near the point.
• Oscillating discontinuity: Function wildly fluctuates
near the point, like sin(1/𝑥) as 𝑥 → 0.

Answer: B – A limit as x→∞ or x→−∞ describes the function's end behavior and often corresponds to a horizontal
asymptote.

asymptote at x=a

Differential calculus is the branch of mathematics
concerned with:
Rates of change
Slopes of curves
Instantaneous velocity
Optimization
Its central concept is the derivative, which tells you how a
function is changing at a specific point.

DIFFERENTIAL CALCULUS
Derivative as a Limit
The derivative of a function 𝑓(𝑥) at a point 𝑥 = 𝑎 is defined
as:
𝑓′(𝑎) = lim
ℎ→0

This is the limit of the average rate of change over a small
interval as the interval shrinks to zero. It gives the
instantaneous rate of change at 𝑥 = 𝑎.

DIFFERENTIAL CALCULUS
Geometric Interpretation
The derivative at a point gives the slope of the tangent
line to the graph of the function at that point.
The tangent line "touches" the curve at just one point and
has the same slope as the curve there.
Steeper curves = larger derivative; flat parts = zero
derivative.

1. Which condition is necessary for a function to have a limit at x = a?
A. The function is increasing
B. The function is differentiable
C. Left-hand and right-hand limits exist and are equal
D. The function is periodic
Answer: C – A limit exists if both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
2. What kind of discontinuity occurs when the left-hand and right-hand limits are not
equal?
A. Removable
B. Jump
C. Infinite
D. Oscillating
Answer: B – A jump discontinuity occurs when the left and right limits differ.
3. For a function to be continuous at a point x=a, which of the following conditions
must be met?
A. limx→af(x) exists.
B. f(a) is defined.
C. limx→af(x)=f(a).
D. All of the above.
Answer: D – Continuity at a point requires three conditions: the limit must exist, the
function must be defined at that point, and the limit must equal the function's value.
4. Consider a function f(x) that approaches 5 as x approaches 2 from the left, and
approaches 3 as x approaches 2 from the right. What can be concluded about limx→2
f(x)?
A. The limit is 5.
B. The limit is 3.
C. The limit is 4.
D. The limit does not exist.

Answer: C. Interval
Explanation:
A: Labels only, no order (e.g., gender)

QUESTION 2

A. Types of Data
Qualitative (Categorical): Data that describes qualities or
characteristics.
Examples: Gender (male/female), Eye Color (blue,
brown).
Quantitative (Numerical): Data that can be measured.
Discrete: Countable whole numbers.
Examples: Number of students in a class, number of
defective items.
Continuous: Measurable and can take any value within
a range.
Examples: Height, weight, temperature.

B. Levels of Measurement
Nominal: Categories with no order. Example: Types of soil.
Ordinal: Categories that can be ranked, but differences
are not meaningful. Example: Customer satisfaction (Poor,
Fair, Good).
Interval: Ordered categories with equal intervals, but no
true zero. Example: Temperature in Celsius.
Ratio: Ordered categories with a meaningful zero point.
Example: Height, weight, age.

C. Data Presentation
Frequency Distribution Tables: Tabular presentation
showing values and their frequencies.
Graphs:
Histograms: Bar graph for continuous data with
adjacent bars.
Bar Graphs: Separate bars for categorical/discrete data.
Pie Charts: Circle divided into slices representing
proportions.
Stem-and-Leaf Plots and Boxplots: Visualizations for
distribution and spread.

QUESTION 25

I. Probability Sampling Techniques
In these methods, every member of the population has a known, non-zero
chance of being selected.
1. Simple Random Sampling (SRS)
Definition: Every member of the population has an equal chance of being
selected.
Example: Drawing names from a hat.
Tools: Random number generators, lottery methods.
2. Stratified Random Sampling
Definition: Population is divided into strata (groups) based on shared
characteristics, and a random sample is taken from each stratum.
Purpose: To ensure representation from each subgroup.
Example: Dividing students by year level and randomly sampling from each
year.

3. Systematic Sampling
Definition: Selecting every k-th item from a list after a random starting point.
Formula: Sampling interval = Population size / Sample size
Example: Surveying every 10th person on a list.
4. Cluster Sampling
Definition: The population is divided into clusters (often geographically), then
entire clusters are randomly selected.
Useful when: Populations are large and spread out.
Example: Choosing 3 barangays randomly and surveying everyone in each.
5. Multi-Stage Sampling
Definition: A complex form combining two or more probability sampling
methods in stages.
Example: Randomly select provinces → randomly select schools → randomly
select students.

II. Non-Probability Sampling Techniques
In these methods, the chance of any particular member being
chosen is unknown. These are easier and cheaper but risk bias.
1. Convenience Sampling
Definition: Sampling individuals who are easiest to access.
Example: Surveying people in a nearby café or classroom.
2. Judgmental or Purposive Sampling
Definition: Researcher selects subjects based on their judgment
about which are most useful or representative.
Example: Selecting key informants with expert knowledge.

3. Snowball Sampling
Definition: Existing study subjects recruit future subjects from
among their acquaintances.
Used for: Hard-to-reach or hidden populations (e.g.,
undocumented workers).
Example: Asking a participant to refer others in the same group.
4. Quota Sampling
Definition: Researcher ensures specific quotas (subgroups) are
met, but selection within the subgroup is non-random.
Example: Choosing 50 male and 50 female respondents without
randomization.

Layout: Units are grouped into blocks (replicates), each

Latin Square Design (LSD)
Use Case: Controls for two sources of variability (e.g., row and
column effects like soil depth and slope).
Layout: Treatments arranged in a square so that each treatment
appears once per row and column.
Example: Comparing 4 irrigation methods across different field
locations and equipment operators.
Analysis: ANOVA with Row, Column, and Treatment effects.
Advantages: Efficient for small experiments with two confounding
factors.
Disadvantages: Number of treatments must equal number of rows

effects.
Advantages: Efficient, reveals interaction between factors.
Disadvantages: Complexity increases with more factors.

Use Case: When some treatments are difficult or costly to randomize
(e.g., irrigation).
Layout:
Whole plots receive one level of the main factor (e.g., irrigation
method).
Sub-plots within the whole plots receive levels of a sub-factor (e.g.,
fertilizer type).
Example: Irrigation as whole-plot factor; fertilizer type as sub-plot
factor.
Analysis: Mixed-model ANOVA; two error terms (main and subplot).
Advantages: Practical for large-scale field experiments.
Disadvantages: Requires more complex statistical analysis.

Split-Plot Design

standard deviation of the mean?

• ~99.7% within ±3 SD

In the equation y = a + bx:

T-tests are used when sample size is small (n < 30) and population variance is
unknown.

D. Mode

D. 5/36

A. It increases error variance
B. It improves precision and allows for estimation of error
C. It reduces the number of treatments
D. It blocks out variability
Answer: B. It improves precision and allows for estimation of error
Replication improves the reliability of results and allows for estimation of variability.
45. Which type of design would you use if you wanted to study the effect of two

A. CRD
B. Latin Square
C. Factorial Design
D. Randomized Block
Answer: C. Factorial Design
Factorial design is ideal for studying interactions between two or more factors.
46. What is the main advantage of blocking in an experiment?
A. Introduces variability
B. Simplifies analysis
C. Reduces variability due to nuisance factors
D. Increases treatment levels
Answer: C. Reduces variability due to nuisance factors.
Blocking groups similar experimental units to control for variability.
47. In a split-plot design, which is typically true?
A. All treatments are randomized equally
B. Subplots receive primary treatments
C. Whole plots receive primary treatments
D. There is no need for replication
Answer: C. Whole plots receive primary treatments
Whole plots get main treatments, and subplots get secondary ones; useful when

Answer: C. Systematic error
Randomization helps reduce bias and systematic errors.

GREEN-GEARS REVIEW CENTER
ABE LAWS
Prepared by: Engr. Michael John Labiano
1. Republic Act No. 10915, also known as the Philippine Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineering Act, mandates the transformation of the existing
Philippine Agricultural Engineering Standards (PAES) into what new code of
technical standards?
a. Philippine National Standards (PNS)
b. International Standards Organization (ISO) Standards
c. Philippine Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering Standards
(PABES)
d. Agri-fishery Mechanization Standards (AFMS)
2. The Professional Regulatory Board of Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering
is described as the ultimate authority in the practice of the profession. How
many members, including the Chairperson, comprise this Board?
a. One chairperson and one member
b. One chairperson and three members
c. One chairperson and two members
d. Three members without distinct Chairperson position
3. According to the IRR of RA 10915, what do the twelve (12) sides of the
dodecagon in the official seal of the Professional Regulatory Board of
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering represent?
a. The twelve months of annual professional development
b. The twelve major regions where ABEs first practiced
c. The twelve scopes of practice of agricultural and biosystems
engineering
d. The twelve historical milestones of agricultural engineering in the
Philippines
4. An applicant for the ABE Licensure Examination who fails to pass for the third
time faces specific requirements before being allowed another attempt. What
are these requirements?
a. They shall be allowed to take another examination only after the
lapse of one year and after undertaking a refresher program in duly
accredited institutions

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
b. They shall be allowed to take another examination only after the lapse
of one year and after undertaking a refresher program in any institutions
available
c. They shall be allowed to take another examination only after the lapse
of two years and after undertaking a refresher program in duly accredited
institutions
d. They shall be allowed to take another examination only after the lapse
of one year, not needing to take a refresher program anymore.
5. What are the penalties for any person found guilty of violating the provisions of
RA 10915 or its Implementing Rules and Regulations?
a. A fine of more than one hundred pesos (Php 100,000), but not less than
five hundred thousand pesos (Php 500,000), or imprisonment of not less
than six (6) months and not more than five (5) years, or both fine and
imprisonment
b. A fine of not less than one hundred pesos (Php 100,000), but not
more than five hundred thousand pesos (Php 500,000), or
imprisonment of not less than six (6) months and not more than
five (5) years, or both fine and imprisonment
c. A fine of not less than one hundred pesos (Php 100,000), but not more
than five hundred thousand pesos (Php 500,000), or imprisonment of not
less than six (6) months and not more than six (6) years, or both fine and
imprisonment
d. A fine of not less than one hundred pesos (Php 100,000), but not more
than five hundred thousand pesos (Php 500,000), or imprisonment of not
less than six (6) months and not more than five (5) years, either fine or
imprisonment only
6. Which government agency is designated as the focal agency for integrating and
unifying all agricultural and fisheries mechanization, research, development,
and extension programs, and projects?
a. Bureau of Agricultural Research
b. Agricultural Training Institute
c. Philippine Center for Postharvest Development and Mechanization
d. Bureau of Agricultural and Fisheries Engineering
7. Which entity is institutionalized as the premier and reference testing center for
agricultural and fisheries machinery in the country?
a. Philippine Center for Postharvest Development and Mechanization
(PhilMech)
b. Bureau of Agricultural and Fisheries Engineering (BAFE)
c. Agricultural Machinery Testing and Evaluation Center (AMTEC)

d. Department of Science and Technology – Agri-Machinery Information
Network
8. Within how many years from the enactment of the AfMech Law must all agri-
fishery machinery be registered?
a. One year
b. Two years
c. Three years
d. Four years
9. This joint memorandum implements guidelines on the strengthening and
establishment of the Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering groups of the
Local Government Units (LGUs).
a. DA-DBM-CSC-DILG Joint Memorandum No. 02, s. 2020
b. DA-DBM-CSC-DILG Joint Memorandum No. 02, s. 2019
c. DA-DBM-CSC-DILG Joint Memorandum No. 03, s. 2020
d. DA-DBM-CSC-DILG Joint Memorandum No. 03, s. 2021
10. Based on the DA-DBM-CSC-DILG Joint Memorandum No. 02 s. 2020, what is
the minimum required educational attainment for an individual to be qualified
for an Engineer I position in an LGU’s ABE Unit?
a. Completion of at least two years of college education in Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineering and other related fields?
b. Any Bachelor’s degree with a professional license in any related
engineering field
c. A Master’s degree in Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering
d. A Bachelor’s degree in Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering
11. What CSC Memorandum Circular states and mandates that Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineering units in provincial, city, and local government units
(LGUs) are mandatory?
a. CSC Memorandum Circular No. 12, s. 2021
b. CSC Memorandum Circular No. 12, s. 2022
c. CSC Memorandum Circular No. 13, s. 2022
d. CSC Memorandum Circular No. 12, s. 2020
12. Who is primarily responsible for delivering direct agriculture and fisheries
extension services according to the Republic Act No. 8435?
a. Department of Agriculture (DA)
b. Local Government Units (LGUs)

c. State Universities and Colleges (SUCs)
d. Department of Science and Technology (DOST)
13. According to RA 8435, for how long are irrigated lands, irrigable lands with firm
funding commitments, and lands with potential for high-value crops within the
delineated Strategic Agriculture and Fisheries Development Zones (SAFDZ)
generally protected from conversion?
a. One year from the effectivity of the Act, renewable annually
b. Indefinitely, unless a specific permit is granted
c. Five years from the effectivity of the Act, with specific conditions
for limited conversion thereafter
d. Ten years from the effectivity of the Act, but only if no public infrastructure
projects are planned
14. According to the RA 10915, who issues the Certificate of Registration and
Professional Identification Card to an Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer?
a. Professional Regulation Commission
b. Professional Regulatory Board
c. The Board and the Commission
d. Philippine Society of Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers, Inc.
15. Which of the following values is explicitly mentioned in the Code of Ethical and
Professional Standards of ABEs as the foundation for every registered
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer to execute their responsibilities?
a. Innovation, efficiency, and global competitiveness
b. Leadership, obedience, and grit
c. Integrity, nationalism, and spiritual values
d. Collaboration, advancement, and resourcefulness
16. What does MFADDIE stands for?
a. Manufacturer, Fabricator, Assembler, Distribution, Dealer, Importer, and
Exporter
b. Manufacturer, Fabrication, Assembler, Distributor, Dealer, Importer, and
Exporter
c. Manufacturer, Fabricator, Assembler, Distributor, Dealer, Importing, and
Exporter
d. Manufacturer, Fabricator, Assembler, Distributor, Dealer, Importer,
and Exporter
17. What is the year of enactment of the first and second Agricultural Engineering
laws, the RA 3927 and RA 8559?
a. 1965 and 1998

b. 1964 and 2000
c. 1964 and 1998
d. 1966 and 2016
18. GEOAGRI is an in-house web-based system used to consolidate the
information on Farm-to-Market Road projects. What does GEOAGRI stands
for?
a. Geographic Information System for Agricultural and Fisheries
Machinery and Infrastructure
b. Geographic Information System for Agricultural and Fisheries Modelling
and Infrastructure
c. Geographic Information System for Agricultural and Farm Machinery and
Infrastructure
d. Geographic Information System for Agricultural and Fisheries Machinery
and Infrastructure Plan
19. How many consecutive years is the lapse before the license is revoked due to
unjustified non-renew of Professional Identification Card (PIC)?
a. 3 years
b. 4 years
c. 5 years
d. 6 years
20. How is “air pollution” defined under the Republic Act No. 8749 (Clean Air Act)
distinguishing it from other natural atmospheric components?
a. Any visible smoke and particulate matter emitted from stationary sources
exceeding specific opacities
b. The natural concentrations of oxygen, nitrogen, water vapor, and inert
gases in the atmosphere
c. Any alteration of the physical, chemical, and biological properties
of the atmospheric air, or any discharge thereto of substances
detrimental to public health
d. The emission of unwanted sound from known sources into the
atmosphere
21. What is the initially mandated minimum blend by volume for biodiesel into all
diesel engine fuels sold in the country, and within what specific time frame from
the effectivity of the Act?
a. Minimum of five percent, within two years

b. Minimum of one percent, within three months
c. Minimum of two percent, within four years
d. The Act recommends voluntary blending without mandatory limits
22. Under Republic Act No. 11203 or the Rice Tariffication Law, the Rice
Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (RCEF) was initially set to have an annual
appropriation of how much for the first six years?
a. Php 5,000,000,000.00
b. Php 10,000,000,000.00
c. Php 10,000,000.00
d. Php 5,000,000.00
23. Republic Act No. 12078 strengthens the regulatory function of the Department
of Agriculture through which specific bureau of the department?
a. Bureau of Customs
b. Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources
c. Bureau of Plant Industry
d. Bureau of Agriculture and Fisheries Engineering
24. The Republic Act No. 12078 states that the RCEF shall consist of annual
appropriations of thirty billion pesos until what year?
a. 2030
b. 2031
c. 2032
d. 2033
25. Under RA 11203, what percentage of the RCEF is allocated for Rice Farm
Machineries and Equipment, to be released and implemented by PhilMech?
a. Thirty percent (30%)
b. Forty percent (40%)
c. Fifty percent (50%)
d. Sixty percent (60%)
26. Within the Php 9 billion allocation for farm machineries and equipment, how
much is specifically allotted for the promotion, establishment, support, and
development of Fabrication, Repair, and Maintenance Centers (FARM-Cs)?
a. Php 420 million
b. Php 425 million
c. Php 450 million

sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
d. Php 465 million
27. Beyond providing farm equipment, RA 12078 expands PhilMech's role under
the RCEF to also include grants for which of the following?
a. Irrigation and drainage facilities for farmers
b. Postharvest and processing facilities
c. New crop seed variety development
d. International training program for farmers
28. Among the priority programs under the P15 billion allocation, financial
assistance is specified for rice farmers tilling up to what maximum area of rice
land?
a. One hectare
b. Two hectares
c. Three hectares
d. Four hectares
29. How often must the Professional Identification Card be renewed and how many
CPD points are needed for renewal for 2027 onwards?
a. Every three years; 30 CPD points
b. Every three years; 45 CPD points
c. Every three years; 25 CPD points
d. Every four years; 40 CPD points
30. Which of the following best describes the nature of a contract?
a. It is always a formal, written document expressing a legal agreement
b. It is an agreement between two or more parties for certain acts,
enforceable by law
c. It is any promise between individuals, regardless of legal enforceability
d. It is primarily a social agreement, becoming legal if disputes arise
31. Republic Act No. 10915, also known as the Philippine Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineering Act of 2016, expressly repealed which previous
Republic Act?
a. RA 7722
b. RA 8981
c. RA 3927
d. RA 8559

32. To successfully pass the Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering Licensure
Examination, what is the minimum required weighted average, and what is the
lowest permissible grade in any single subject?
a. A 70% weighted average grade, with no grade lower than 60% in every
subject
b. A 70% weighted average grade, with no grade lower than 65% in every
subject
c. A 70% weighted average grade, with no grade lower than 50% in every
subject
d. A 70% weighted average grade, with no grade lower than 55% in
every subject
33. What are the specific design requirements for the seal of a registered
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer, as adopted by the Board?
a. A circular seal with a 42 mm diameter, drawn with a dodecagon 5
mm inward from the circumference, and a 5 mm width rectangular
band horizontally across the middle for the registration number
b. A circular seal with a 45 mm diameter, drawn with a dodecagon 5 mm
inward from the circumference, and a 5 mm width rectangular band
horizontally across the middle for the registration number
c. A circular seal with a 42 mm diameter, drawn with a dodecagon 5 in
inward from the circumference, and a 5 mm width rectangular band
horizontally across the middle for the registration number
d. A circular seal with a 42 mm diameter, drawn with a dodecagon 5 mm
outward from the circumference, and a 5 mm width rectangular band
vertically across the middle for the registration number
34. According to the IRR of RA 10601, what minimum total area defines “contiguous
farming” for synchronized production?
a. Twenty-five hectares for specialized crops
b. Fifty hectares for the synchronized production of a crop
c. One hundred hectares for mixed-crop systems
d. Any size of adjoining lands, provided it involves advanced machinery
35. Which of the following services are NOT provided by Agri-fisheries Machinery
and Equipment Service Centers (AfMESCs) as outlined in the law?
a. After-sales service and warranty for clients
b. Provisions of direct financial loans for machinery purchase to
farmers

c. Custom plowing, harrowing, harvesting, drying, milling, and other farm
mechanization services
d. Training in maintenance and proper use of agricultural machinery and
equipment
36. In Local Government Units (LGUs), what income classes are required to hire at
least one (1) agricultural engineer at the provincial, city, and municipal levels,
for agricultural and fisheries engineering projects?
a. All LGUs regardless of income class
b. Only highly urbanized cities and independent component cities
c. LGUs belonging to first up to the third income classes
d. LGUs belonging to the fourth up to the sixth income classes
37. Within the structure of the Agri-fisheries Mechanization Research Development
and Extension Network (AFMechRDEN), what agency is mandated to organize
and chair this network, which also serves as the Secretariat?
a. Bureau of Agricultural and Fisheries Engineering
b. Department of Agriculture
c. Philippine Center for Postharvest Development and Mechanization
d. Philippine Society of Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers
38. Which government agency is responsible for the planning, design, and
management of Communal Irrigation Systems (CIS) after the years-devolution
period from the effectivity of RA 8435?
a. National Irrigation Administration exclusively
b. Department of Agriculture directly
c. Private Irrigator’s Associations
d. Local Government Units, with NIA providing technical assistance
39. The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards states that if deviations from
an Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer’s works or opinions are overruled by
a non-technical authority, what must the engineer do?
a. Disclose clearly the consequences that might arise
b. Immediately resign from the project
c. Document the objection without further actions
d. Seek a second opinion from an allied professional

40. What is the disciplinary action that the Board may mete out for a violation of
any provisions of the Code of Ethical and Professional Standards of ABEs,
without prejudice to other liabilities?
a. Revocation of his/her Certificate of Registration (COR)
b. Suspension from the practice of his/her profession
c. Either revocation of Certificate of Registration and suspension
from the practice of profession
d. Both revocation of Certificate of Registration and suspension from the
practice of profession
41. What specific government body is designated and authorized to grant official
accreditation to an Organic Certifying Body (OCB) or entity, according to RA
10068?
a. National Organic Agriculture Board
b. Department of Agriculture
c. Bureau of Agriculture and Fisheries Standards
d. Technical Education and Skills Development Authority
42. Which of the following waste disposal practices is explicitly prohibited by the
Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999?
a. The operation of traditional small-scale community sanitation methods
like siga
b. Incineration, the burning of municipal, biomedical, and hazardous
wastes
c. The burning of agricultural waste for land preparation, as part of the
traditional farming practices
d. All of the above
43. What is the maximum validity period for a Wastewater Discharge Permit issued
by the Department, and what are the implications for renewal, according to the
Clean Water Act?
a. Three years, renewable indefinitely upon application
b. One year, with automatic renewal if no violations occur
c. Five years, and the Department may renew the discharge permit if
waste minimization and waste treatment technologies are adopted
d. Indefinite, provided the discharger submits quarterly self-monitoring
reports

44. Who holds the position as Chairperson of the Climate Change Commission, in
accordance to RA 9729 or the Climate Change Act?
a. Secretary of the Department of Environmental and Natural Resources
(DENR)
b. The President of the Republic of the Philippines
c. Secretary of the Department of Science and Technology (DOST)
d. Director-General of the National Economic and Development Authority
(NEDA)
45. The Professional Regulatory Board, upon petition, reinstate or reissue a
revoked Certificate of Registration (COR) after how many years from the
effectivity of the revocation?
a. One year
b. Two years
c. Three years
d. Four years
46. A Filipino citizen who graduated from a foreign educational institution desiring
to take the Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering Licensure Examination
shall be required to present what before being allowed to take the examination?
a. Letter of recommendation from the foreign institution
b. Proof of residency in the Philippines for five years
c. Endorsement from the AIPO
d. Endorsement from the CHED
47. Professional ethics derives its force primarily through which mechanism?
a. Statutory rules enacted by government bodies
b. The individual’s professional submission to the discipline of their
profession
c. Personal religious beliefs and moral convictions
d. Direct enforcement by clients and employers
48. Under the Republic Act No. 9700 or the law extending the Comprehensive
Agrarian Reform Program (CARP), what is the maximum total area of
landholdings that shall not be covered for acquisition and distribution to
qualified beneficiaries?
a. 3 hectares

b. 4 hectares
c. 5 hectares
d. 6 hectares
49. Under what specific condition may an Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer
sign his/her name, affix his/her seal, or use any other method of signature on
documents made by or under another Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer's
supervision?
a. If the original engineer is unavailable for sealing
b. If the same is made in such manner as to clearly indicate the part
of such work actually performed by him or her
c. If the documents are for public record, and that it is for public use
d. All of the above
50. According to the Implementing Rules and Regulations of the Republic Act No.
10915, the Board shall not register any successful applicant for registration with
or without licensure examination who has been ______?
a. Unjustified refusal to join or to remain a member in good standing of the
AIPO
b. Aiding or abetting the illegal practice of a non-registered and unlicensed
ABE
c. Adjudged guilty for violation of the General Instructions to
Examinees by the Board
d. Gross incompetence, negligence, or ignorance in the conduct of the
profession

1. A 7.5 meter wheel axle hp tractor is running at a speed of 6 kph during harrowing in
a clay soil. The tractor weighs 400 kg. The wheel diameter of the tractor is 1 m and is
able to rotate at 17 revolutions in 75 m distance. The rolling resistance is 0.25 rolling
coefficient. Find the slippage.
a. 13.68%
b. 21.07%
c. 32.98%
d. 40.43%
2. It is the angle the disc makes with the direction of travel to make the disc cut the
proper width and allow the disc to rotate.
a. Tilt
b. Disc
c. Side
d. Tilt
3. In SWEff/10, S is expressed in?
a. kph
b. mph
c. m/s
d. kps
4. Deep tillage is primary tillage operation which manipulates soil to a greater depth
than ______________.
a. 1 m
b. 0.5 m
c. 0.3 m
d. 0.2 m
5. Tillage which forms a ridge and furrow soil configuration.
a. Bedding
b. Ridging
c. Listing
d. All of the above
6. The latest farm mechanization level in the Philippines is at _________.
a. 2.310 hp/ha
b. 2.596 hp/ha
c. 2.679 hp/ha
d. 2.702 hp/ha

as a seed drill?

a. hour meter

25. In mounting a three-point linkage implement (e.g., rotavator) to a four-wheel
tractor, which of the following shows the correct sequence of procedures?
I. Position the tractor and the implement, stop the engine, and engage the hand

II. Align the left draft link with the hitch point of the implement and lock using a

fluorescent triangle from all distances between 306 to 20 m.

b. yellow-red
c. red-orange
d. yellow - orange
28. It is the process of preparing the soil to provide favorable soil environment for plant
germination and growth.
a. Conventional land preparation
b. Land preparation

QUESTION 2

Branches of Fluid Mechanics

Definitions
1. Fluid mechanics: a branch of physics that studies the behavior of fluids
(liquids, gases, and plasmas) and the forces acting upon them.
2. Fluid Statics: Concerned with fluids at rest (pressure, buoyancy, hydrostatic
forces).
3. Fluid Kinematics: Analyzes the motion of the fluid without considering the
forces that caused the motion (flow type, flow velocity and acceleration,
trajectory).
4. Fluid Dynamics: Fluid dynamics is the branch of fluid mechanics that
studies the motion of fluids and the forces and energy that cause or affect
that motion (energy equation, momentum equation, continuity equation).

Definitions
• Hydraulics: branch of mechanics concerned with the laws
controlling the behavior of water and other liquids at rest and
in motion.
• Hydrostatics: study of liquids at rest.
• Hydrokinetics: deals with geometry of motion of liquids
without considering the forces causing that motion.
• Hydrodynamics: deals with forces exerted by or upon liquids in
motion including relations between velocities and
accelerations involved in such fluid motion

What is a Fluid
A fluid is a substance that can flow and continuously deform under any applied
shear stress, no matter how small. It includes both liquids and gases.
Characteristics of a Fluid
• It has low resistance to shear stress (it flows under shear).
• It has no fixed shape.
• It changes volume depending on the pressure applied (not
infinitely).
• It exerts pressure equally in all direction

Fluids where shear stress is

Viscosity (𝜇) is the resistance to

Examples: Water, air, alcohol,

Types of Fluid
Non-Newtonian Fluids:
Fluids where viscosity changes
with shear rate or time, or where
the stress–strain relationship is
nonlinear.

Types of Fluid
Time-independent:
Psuedoplastic (shear-thinning)
Viscosity decreases with increasing
shear rate.
Examples: ketchup and paint.

Types of Fluid
Time-independent:
Dilatant (shear-thicking)
Viscosity increases with increasing
shear rate.
Examples: cornstarch and water
mixture.

Types of Fluid
Time-independent:
Bingham Plastic
Requires a yield stress before flowing,
then behaves like Newtonian
Examples: toothpaste

Types of Fluid
Time-dependent:
Thixotropic
Viscosity decreases with time under
constant shear
Examples: honey and paint

Types of Fluid
Time-dependent:
Rheopectic
Viscosity increases with time under
constant shear
Examples: gypsum paste (plaster) and
printer ink.

The hydrostatic force (F) represents the resultant force acting on the surface of
a body submerged on a fluid as a result of the pressure of that fluid.
Much like most stress distribution, the hydrostatic force is given by the general
formula:
F = PA;
Where P is the pressure and A is the area upon which the pressure is acting.
Hydrostatic Forces on Submerged Plane Surfaces

However, in the case of surfaces submerged in fluids, the magnitude of
pressure acting on the surface varies with depth (h).
Thus, the hydrostatic force (F) is given by the equation:
F = PcgA;
Where Pcg is the pressure at the centroid of the surface (this represents the
average pressure acting on the surface).
Further:
Pcg = γhcg;
Where hcg is the depth of the centroid from the surface.
Hydrostatic Forces on Submerged Plane Surfaces

1. Which of the following best defines a fluid?
A. A substance with fixed shape and volume
B. A substance that can resist shear stress
C. A substance that flows and deforms continuously under shear stress
D. A solid with elastic properties
Explanation: A fluid deforms continuously under applied shear stress, no matter how
small.
2. Which of the following is a non-Newtonian fluid?
A. Air
B. Water
C. Honey
D. Kerosene
Explanation: Honey is a non-Newtonian fluid; its viscosity changes with shear rate.
3. If a fluid has a specific gravity of 0.85, what does it mean?
A. It is heavier than water
B. It is the same weight as water
C. It is 85% the density of water
D. It is 15% denser than water
Explanation: Specific gravity is the ratio of the fluid’s density to that of water.
4. What is the correct formula for specific weight (γ)?
A. γ = ρg
B. γ = mg
C. γ = ρV
D. γ = P/A
Explanation: Specific weight is the weight per unit volume: γ = density × gravity.
5. Capillary rise is due to:
A. High viscosity
B. High pressure
C. Surface tension
D. Gravity alone
Explanation: Surface tension causes capillary rise, especially in narrow tubes and
porous media.
6. Which of the following best describes Pascal’s Law?
A. Pressure decreases with depth
B. Pressure acts only downward

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
C. Fluids always flow from low to high pressure
D. Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions
Explanation: Pascal's Law, states that pressure changes in a confined incompressible
fluid are transmitted equally to every point within the fluid and to the walls of the
container.
7. Which pressure does a piezometer measure?
A. Positive Gauge Pressure
B. Positive and Negative Gauge Pressure
C. Absolute pressure
D. Atmospheric pressure
Explanation: Explanation: A piezometer measures gauge pressure by the height of a
liquid column which means it can only measure positive gauge pressure.
8. Hydrostatic force on a vertical submerged surface acts:
A. At the top of the surface
B. At the bottom of the surface
C. At the centroid
D. Below the centroid
Explanation: The center of pressure is below the centroid due to increasing pressure
with depth.
Pressure is smallest at the top; the resultant can’t act there.
At the bottom – Not all the force is concentrated at the deepest point; it’s a distributed
load.
At the centroid – True only for horizontal submerged surfaces; for vertical ones, the
center of pressure is lower than the centroid.
9. A tank contains water with a depth of 3 meters. What is the pressure at the bottom
of the tank?
A. 9810 Pa B. 29430 Pa C. 19620 Pa D. 10000 Pa
Explanation: P=ρgh=1000 kg/m3 × 9.81 m/s2 × 3m = 29430Pa

Explanation: γf = SGf x γwater ; P = γf (Δh)
γf = 13.6 x 9.81 kN/m3 = 133.416 kN/m3
P = 133.416 kN/m3 x 0.15 m = 20.0124 kPa

A. Pump efficiency
B. Velocity in a channel
C. Head loss due to friction

equation in fluid dynamics?

losses.
