GREEN-GEARS REVIEW CENTER
ENGINEERING MECHANICS
Prepared by: Fernando A. Paralejas Jr.
Definition of Terms
Basic Concepts and Principles
• Mechanics – Branch of physics that studies the behavior of bodies under
the action of forces.
• Statics – Mechanics of bodies at rest or moving at constant velocity
(equilibrium).
Equilibrium Equations
Σ𝐹𝑥 = 0, Σ𝐹𝑦 = 0, Σ𝑀 = 0
These are the conditions of equilibrium.
For a body in rest (static equilibrium), the sum of horizontal forces, vertical
forces, and moments must all equal zero.
Used to solve reactions at supports, unknown forces, and internal forces.
• Dynamics – Mechanics of bodies in motion (non-equilibrium). Subdivided
into:
o Kinematics – Study of motion without regard to forces.
o Kinetics – Study of motion considering forces.
• Rigid Body – An idealized body that does not deform under load.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
• Particle – A body with mass but negligible size and shape.
• Force – A push or pull acting on a body that tends to change its motion.
Characterized by magnitude, direction, and point of application.
• Resultant Force – A single force that can replace two or more forces acting
on a body.
Resultant Force
𝑅 = √(Σ𝐹𝑥)2 + (Σ𝐹𝑦)2
The resultant of concurrent forces is the vector sum.
Used in problems where several forces act at a point.
tan𝜃 = Σ𝐹𝑦
Σ𝐹𝑥
Gives the direction of the resultant.
• Equilibrant Force – A force equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to
the resultant, bringing the body to equilibrium.
• Moment of a Force – The tendency of a force to cause rotation about a
point or axis (M = F·d).
Moment of a Force
𝑀 = 𝐹 ⋅ 𝑑
Where 𝐹 = force, 𝑑 = perpendicular distance from point to line of action of
force.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
Explains tendency to rotate.
Vector form:
𝑀	⃗⃗ = 𝑟 × 𝐹
Varignon’s Theorem
𝑀𝑂 = Σ(𝐹𝑖 ⋅ 𝑑𝑖)
Moment of a resultant force about a point = sum of moments of
components.
Useful for simplifying calculations.
• Couple – Two equal, opposite, parallel forces separated by a distance,
producing pure rotation without translation.
Force Systems and Equilibrium
• Concurrent Force System – Forces that meet at a single point.
• Coplanar Force System – Forces that lie in the same plane.
• Non-Coplanar Force System – Forces that do not lie in the same plane.
• Equilibrium – Condition when the resultant force and resultant moment
acting on a body are both zero.
• Free-Body Diagram (FBD) – A graphical representation showing all
external forces acting on a body.
• Support Reactions – Forces developed at supports or connections to resist
applied loads. Examples: pin support, roller support, fixed support.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
•
Center of Gravity and Centroid
• Centroid – Geometric center of an area or volume.
• Center of Gravity (CG) – The point at which the entire weight of a body
may be considered to act.
Centroid / Center of Gravity
𝑥‾ = Σ(𝐴𝑖𝑥𝑖)
Σ𝐴𝑖
, 𝑦‾ = Σ(𝐴𝑖𝑦𝑖)
Σ𝐴𝑖
Finds location of centroid for composite areas.
Important for distributed loads and beam analysis.
• Composite Area – Area made up of simpler shapes used to find centroids.
• Moment of Area – Product of area and the distance of its centroid from a
reference axis.
Moments of Inertia

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
• Moment of Inertia (Area) – A measure of a shape’s resistance to bending
or buckling (I = ∫y²dA).
• Polar Moment of Inertia (J) – Resistance of a section to torsion (J = ∫r²dA).
• Radius of Gyration (k) – Distance from axis at which area can be assumed
concentrated (k = √(I/A)).
• Product of Inertia (Ixy) – Describes distribution of area with respect to two
axes.
• Parallel Axis Theorem – Used to transfer moment of inertia from centroidal
axis to any parallel axis.
Kinematics of Particles
• Displacement (s) – Change in position of a particle.
• Velocity (v) – Rate of change of displacement (v = ds/dt).
• Acceleration (a) – Rate of change of velocity (a = dv/dt).
Kinematics of Rectilinear Motion
𝑣 = 𝑢 + 𝑎𝑡, 𝑠 = 𝑢𝑡 + 1 2	⁄ 𝑎𝑡2, 𝑣2 = 𝑢2 + 2𝑎𝑠
𝑢 = initial velocity, 𝑣 = final velocity, 𝑎 = acceleration, 𝑠 = displacement, 𝑡 =
time.
Used in motion without rotation.
• Projectile Motion – Motion of a particle under gravity, following a parabolic
trajectory.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
• Relative Motion – Motion of a body described with respect to another
moving body.
Kinetics of Particles
• Newton’s Laws of Motion – Fundamental laws governing force and motion.
• Newton’s First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia) – A body remains at rest, or
continues to move in a straight line with constant velocity, unless acted
upon by an external unbalanced force.
• Newton’s Second Law of Motion (Law of Acceleration) – The acceleration
of a body is directly proportional to the net force applied and inversely
proportional to its mass, expressed as 𝐹 = 𝑚𝑎.
• Newton’s Third Law of Motion (Law of Action and Reaction) – For every
action, there is an equal and opposite reaction; forces always occur in
pairs acting on different bodies.
• Work (W) – Product of force and displacement in the direction of the force
(W = F·d).
• Kinetic Energy (KE) – Energy possessed by a body in motion (KE = ½mv²).
• Potential Energy (PE) – Energy stored due to position (PE = mgh).
• Work-Energy Principle – Work done = Change in kinetic energy.
Work-Energy Principle
𝑊 = Δ𝐾𝐸
1
2 𝑚𝑣2 − 1
2 𝑚𝑢2 = Σ𝐹 ⋅ 𝑑
Work done by forces = change in kinetic energy.
Useful when force and displacement are known.
• Impulse (J) – Product of force and time (J = F·Δt).
• Momentum (p) – Product of mass and velocity (p = mv).
• Impulse-Momentum Principle – Impulse = Change in momentum.
Impulse-Momentum Principle

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
𝐹Δ𝑡 = 𝑚𝑣 − 𝑚𝑢
Force acting over time changes momentum.
Useful in collision or impact problems.
• Power (P) – Rate of doing work (P = W/t = F·v).
• Elastic Collision – Collision where kinetic energy is conserved.
• Inelastic Collision – Collision where kinetic energy is not conserved.
Kinematics and Kinetics of Rigid Bodies
• Translation – Motion where all points of the body move in parallel paths.
• Rotation – Motion where a body turns about a fixed axis.
• General Plane Motion – Combination of translation and rotation.
• Angular Displacement (θ) – Rotation about an axis, measured in radians.
• Angular Velocity (ω) – Rate of change of angular displacement (ω =
dθ/dt).
• Angular Acceleration (α) – Rate of change of angular velocity (α = dω/dt).
Kinematics of Rotation
𝜔 = 𝜔0 + 𝛼𝑡, 𝜃 = 𝜔0𝑡 + 1 2	⁄ 𝛼𝑡2, 𝜔2 = 𝜔0
2 + 2𝛼𝜃

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
Angular analog of rectilinear equations.
𝜔 = angular velocity, 𝛼 = angular acceleration.
• Moment of Inertia (Mass) – Resistance of a body to angular acceleration (I
= ∑mr²).
For basic shapes:
o Rectangle: 𝐼 = 𝑏ℎ3
12
o Circle: 𝐼 = 𝜋𝑑4
64
• Torque (T) – Rotational effect of a force (T = Iα)
•
Friction
• Friction – Resistance to motion between two contacting surfaces.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
•
Friction
𝐹 = 𝜇𝑁
𝐹 = max frictional force, 𝜇 = coefficient of friction, 𝑁 = normal force.
At impending motion, friction is maximum.
tan𝜙 = 𝜇
𝜙 = angle of repose
• Coefficient of Friction (μ) – Ratio of frictional force to normal force.
• Static Friction – Friction that resists the start of motion.
• Kinetic (Sliding) Friction – Friction that opposes motion once it has started.
• Angle of Repose – Angle at which a body just begins to slide down an
inclined plane.
Trusses, Frames, and Machines
• Truss – Structure made of straight members connected at joints, carrying
loads at joints only.
• Method of Joints – Analyzing forces in truss members using equilibrium at
joints.
• Method of Sections – Cutting through a truss to solve for member forces.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
• Zero-Force Member – A truss member that carries no force under certain
loading conditions.
• Frame – A structure with members designed to carry loads applied at
intermediate points.
• Machine – A device with moving parts designed to transmit or modify
forces.
• Static Determinacy – Structure that can be solved using equilibrium
equations alone.
• Redundant Structure – A structure with more unknown forces than
equilibrium equations.
Questions and Answers
1. Which of the following best describes mechanics?
A) Science of motion without regard to its causes
B) Study of forces and their effects on matter
C) Study of fluids at rest and in motion
D) Branch of thermodynamics related to work
Answer: B
Explanation: Mechanics is the branch of physical science that studies forces,
motion, and equilibrium. A is kinematics; C is fluid mechanics; D is
thermodynamics.
2. The branch of mechanics that deals with bodies at rest under action of forces
is:
A) Dynamics
B) Statics
C) Kinematics
D) Thermodynamics
Answer: B

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
Explanation: Statics deals with equilibrium of bodies; dynamics with moving
bodies; kinematics studies motion only.
3. The assumption that a body does not deform under load defines:
A) Particle idealization
B) Rigid body idealization
C) Point mass approximation
D) Fluid assumption
Answer: B
Explanation: In rigid body mechanics, deformations are neglected. Particle model
(A, C) neglects size/rotation.
4. Mechanics is broadly divided into:
A) Classical and Quantum Mechanics
B) Statics, Dynamics, Fluid Mechanics
C) Engineering Mechanics and Theoretical Mechanics
D) Statics, Dynamics, Kinematics
Answer: A
Explanation: In physics: classical and quantum. In engineering, engineering
mechanics branches into statics and dynamics. Strictly, correct classification is A;
others mix branches.
5. Which law of Newton forms the foundation of statics?
A) First Law
B) Second Law
C) Third Law
D) Law of Gravitation

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
Answer: A
Explanation: Newton’s First Law: a body remains at rest unless acted on—basis of
equilibrium analysis.
6. When the net force on a particle is zero, the particle is:
A) At rest only
B) In uniform motion or at rest
C) Accelerating
D) Rotating
Answer: B
Explanation: From Newton’s First Law: zero net force → either rest or constant
velocity.
8. If mass 𝑚 = 2 kg, force 𝐹 = 10 N acts, what is acceleration?
A) 2 m/s²
B) 5 m/s²
C) 10 m/s²
D) 20 m/s²
Answer: B
Explanation: Newton’s 2nd Law 𝐹 = 𝑚𝑎; 𝑎 = 𝐹/𝑚 = 10/2 = 5 m/s2.
8. Mechanics of deformable bodies includes:
A) Strength of Materials
B) Kinematics
C) Statics
D) Dynamics
Answer: A

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
Explanation: Strength of Materials/Mechanics of Materials considers
deformations, unlike rigid-body mechanics.
9. Which principle states that a force system’s effect on a body is unchanged if a
force is replaced by a set of forces with the same resultant?
A) Principle of transmissibility
B) Superposition principle
C) Varignon’s theorem
D) D’Alembert’s principle
Answer: A
Explanation: Transmissibility: Same effect if force is shifted along its line of action.
Superposition: Total response = sum of individual responses. Varignon’s Theorem:
Moment of a force = sum of moments of its components. D’Alembert’s Principle:
Dynamics treated as statics with an added inertia force.
10. Which is a scalar quantity?
A) Velocity
B) Displacement
C) Work
D) Force
Answer: C
Explanation: Scalars: magnitude only (e.g., work, mass, time). Vectors: magnitude
+ direction (force, velocity, displacement).
11. If a body has a mass of 80 kg on Earth, what is its weight? (Take 𝑔 = 9.81 m/s²)
A) 80 N
B) 784 N
C) 9.81 N

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
D) 8.16 kN
Answer: B
Explanation: Weight 𝑊 = 𝑚𝑔. 𝑊 = 80 ⋅ 9.81 = 784.8 N.
12. A particle in mechanics is defined as:
A) An atom
B) A rigid body
C) A body whose size and shape can be neglected
D) A body with internal stresses
Answer: C
Explanation: A particle is treated as a point mass with no rotational effects.
13. Which of the following is TRUE?
A) Weight is a scalar, mass is a vector
B) Mass depends on gravity, weight is constant
C) Weight is force due to gravity, mass is amount of matter
D) Mass changes with altitude, weight remains same
Answer: C
Explanation: Mass is constant, weight varies with gravity.
14. Which of the following sets are vector quantities?
A) Force, displacement, momentum
B) Mass, work, time
C) Speed, distance, energy
D) Power, pressure, volume
Answer: A

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
Explanation: Only option A includes vectors. Others are scalars.
15. If a mass of 50 kg is on the moon (gravity = 1.62 m/s²), its weight is:
A) 50 N
B) 81 N
C) 490 N
D) 800 N
Answer: B
Explanation: 𝑊 = 𝑚𝑔 = 50(1.62) = 81 N.
16. Rigid body assumption means:
A) Body cannot move
B) Body undergoes no deformation under load
C) Body is infinitely heavy
D) Body is indestructible
Answer: B
Explanation: Rigid body approximation simplifies mechanics by neglecting
deformation.
17. Which of the following is dimensionally consistent with force?
A) 𝑀𝐿/𝑇2
B) 𝑀/𝐿2𝑇
C) 𝑀𝐿2/𝑇
D) 𝑀/𝑇
Answer: A
Explanation: Force = mass × acceleration. Dimensions = 𝑀(𝐿/𝑇2) = 𝑀𝐿/𝑇2.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
18. What is the magnitude of the resultant of two forces 30 N and 40 N at right
angles?
A) 50 N
B) 70 N
C) 35 N
D) 10 N
Answer: A
Explanation: Pythagoras: 𝑅 = √302 + 402 = 50.
19. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a vector?
A) Magnitude
B) Direction
C) Point of application
D) Temperature
Answer: D
Explanation: Temperature is scalar, not a property of vectors.
20. Which of the following is a derived unit in the SI system?
A. Kilogram
B. Meter
C. Newton
D. Second
Answer: C. Newton
Explanation: Kilogram, meter, and second are base SI units. Newton is derived
from the combination of kg·m/s². 1 𝑁 = 1 𝑘𝑔 ⋅ 𝑚/𝑠2.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
21. What is the dimensional formula of pressure?
A. 𝑀𝐿𝑇−2
B. 𝑀𝐿−1𝑇−2
C. 𝑀0𝐿𝑇−2
D. 𝑀𝐿𝑇−1
Answer: B. 𝑀𝐿−1𝑇−2
Explanation: Pressure = Force/Area.
Force = 𝑀𝐿𝑇−2, Area = 𝐿2. So Pressure = (𝑀𝐿𝑇−2)/𝐿2 = 𝑀𝐿−1𝑇−2.
22. Which of the following pairs is dimensionally consistent?
A. Work and Energy
B. Stress and Strain
C. Force and Momentum
D. Velocity and Acceleration
Answer: A. Work and Energy
Explanation: Work and Energy both have 𝑀𝐿2𝑇−2. Stress and strain differ, Force
and momentum differ, Velocity and acceleration differ.
23. The dimensional formula of angular velocity is:
A. 𝑇−1
B. 𝐿0𝑇−1
C. 𝑀0𝐿0𝑇−1
D. All of the above (equivalent)
Answer: D. All of the above
Explanation: Angular velocity = θ/time. Angle is dimensionless. So 𝑇−1. Other
representations are equivalent.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
24. Which is a non-SI unit still commonly used in mechanics?
A. Pound-force (lbf)
B. Newton (N)
C. Pascal (Pa)

25. Which of the following is NOT dimensionless?

C. Specific gravity
D. Stress
Answer: D. Stress

B. Joule
C. Newton
D. Pascal
Answer: B. Joule
Explanation: Joule = Work = Force × Distance = N·m. Watt is power, Newton is

B. Force = mass × acceleration.

Answer: C. For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
28. If a force of 50 N acts on a 25-kg body, the acceleration is:
A. 0.5 m/s²
B. 1 m/s²
C. 2 m/s²
D. 25 m/s²
Answer: B. 2 m/s²
Computation: 𝑎 = 𝐹/𝑚 = 50/25 = 2 𝑚/𝑠2.
29. Which of the following demonstrates Newton’s 1st law?
A. A rocket lifting off the ground.
B. A car stopping when brakes are applied.
C. A book on a table remains at rest until pushed.
D. A ball thrown upwards falls down due to gravity.
Answer: C. A book on a table remains at rest until pushed.

Answer: D. Both A and B

41. A 200 N force acts at the end of a 0.5 m lever arm at 60° to the arm. The
moment about the pivot is:
A. 50 N·m
B. 100 N·m
C. 86.6 N·m
D. 200 N·m
Answer: C
Explanation: M = F × d × sinθ = 200 × 0.5 × sin60° = 86.6 N·m.

A. Increased
B. Decreased

D. Zero

to the right of 𝐴:

• At (0.8, 0.3) m: 500 N downward
• At (−0.5, 0.6) m: 400 N to the right
• At (0.2, −0.4) m: 350 N at 45∘ (so 𝐹𝑥 = 𝐹𝑦 = 350/√2 = 247.49)
Find the net moment about 𝑂 (CCW +).
A. −491.51 N·m (CW)
B. −451.51 N·m (CW)
C. −400.00 N·m (CW)
D. +148.49 N·m (CCW)
Answer: A
Computation:
𝑀1 = 𝑥𝐹𝑦 − 𝑦𝐹𝑥 = 0.8(−500) − 0.3(0) = −400.00
𝑀2 = (−0.5)(0) − 0.6(400) = −240.00
𝑀3 = 0.2(247.49) − (−0.4)(247.49) = 49.50 + 99.00 = 148.49
𝑀res = −400.00 − 240.00 + 148.49 = −491.51 N·m (CW)
47. A couple consists of:
A. Two equal and collinear forces
B. Two equal and opposite parallel forces
C. Two unequal forces acting at a point
D. A single force and a moment
Answer: B
Explanation: A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces not collinear.

𝑇 = 500

51. In the method of joints, the assumption is that truss members are:
A. Rigid and carry moments
B. Two-force members only
C. Three-force members
D. Subjected to torsion
Answer: B. Two-force members only
Explanation: Each member of a truss ideally carries only axial force (tension or

52. A pin-jointed plane truss has 20 members and 11 joints. Is it statically
determinate, indeterminate, or unstable?
A. Determinate
B. Indeterminate
C. Unstable
D. Cannot be determined
Answer: B. Indeterminate
Explanation: 𝑚 = 20, 𝑗 = 11. Determinacy: 𝑚 = 2𝑗 − 3 = 2(11) − 3 = 22 − 3 = 19. Since

A. Members can carry bending moments
B. Members are only axial-force carriers

54. A machine structure differs from a truss because:

Answer: B. Machines transmit and modify forces
Explanation: Machines are structures with moving parts used to transmit forces.

Answer: A
Explanation: Angle of friction = angle between resultant reaction 𝑅 and normal 𝑁.

GREEN-GEARS REVIEW CENTER
STRENGTH OF MATERIALS
Prepared by: Fernando A. Paralejas Jr.
Definition of Terms
1. Fundamentals and Basic Concepts
1. Strength of Materials – Branch of mechanics that studies the behavior of solid
objects subject to stresses and strains, focusing on their strength, stiffness, and
stability.
2. Stress (σ) – Internal resistance of a material to deformation per unit area,
expressed in Pascals (Pa) or N/m².
3. Normal Stress – Stress perpendicular to the surface, caused by axial forces
(tension or compression).
4. Shear Stress (τ) – Stress parallel to the surface, caused by forces acting
tangentially.
5. Bearing Stress – Contact stress between two bodies, often at a joint.
6. Factor of Safety (FoS) – Ratio of the material’s strength to the actual working
stress, used to ensure safety in design.
2. Deformation and Strain
7. Strain (ε) – Measure of deformation representing the elongation or shortening of
a material per unit length (dimensionless).
8. Normal Strain – Change in length per original length due to axial stress.
9. Shear Strain (γ) – Angular deformation caused by shear stress.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
10. Poisson’s Ratio (ν) – Ratio of lateral strain to axial strain in a material subjected
to uniaxial stress.
11. Modulus of Elasticity (E) – Ratio of normal stress to normal strain in the elastic
region, also known as Young’s Modulus.
12. Modulus of Rigidity (G) – Ratio of shear stress to shear strain in the elastic
region.
13. Bulk Modulus (K) – Ratio of volumetric stress to volumetric strain.
3. Stress–Strain Relationship
14. Hooke’s Law – States that stress is directly proportional to strain within the
elastic limit.
15. Elastic Limit – Maximum stress a material can withstand without permanent
deformation.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
16. Proportional Limit – Stress up to which stress is directly proportional to strain.
17. Yield Strength – Stress at which a material begins to deform plastically.
18. Ultimate Strength – Maximum stress that a material can withstand before
failure.
19. Fracture Point – Stress and strain value where material breaks completely.
20. Modulus of Resilience – Energy per unit volume that a material can absorb
without permanent deformation.
21. Modulus of Toughness – Energy per unit volume that a material can absorb
before fracturing.
4. Physical Properties of Materials (Related to Stress–Strain)
22. Elasticity – Ability of a material to return to its original shape after removal of
load. How well a material springs back to its original shape after the load is
removed. (like a rubber band)
23. Plasticity – Ability of a material to undergo permanent deformation without
breaking. How well a material stays deformed (permanently changes shape)
without breaking. (like modeling clay)
24. Ductility – Ability of a material to undergo significant plastic deformation before
fracture, usually measured by percentage elongation. How well a material can be
stretched into a wire before breaking. (like copper)

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
25. Malleability – Ability of a material to be deformed under compressive stress
without cracking (important for shaping metals). How well a material can be
hammered or rolled into thin sheets without cracking. (like gold foil)
26. Brittleness – Tendency of a material to fracture with little or no plastic
deformation. How easily a material breaks without much bending or stretching.
(like glass)
27. Toughness – Ability of a material to absorb energy and plastically deform before
fracturing (area under the stress–strain curve). How much energy a material can
take before it breaks (resists both force and fracture). (like leather or steel)
28. Resilience – Ability of a material to absorb energy within the elastic limit and
release it upon unloading. How much energy a material can store and release
within the elastic limit (springiness). (like a trampoline spring)
29. Hardness – Resistance of a material to localized plastic deformation
(scratching, indentation, or wear). How well a material resists scratching or
denting. (like diamond)
30. Strength – Ability of a material to resist applied forces without failure. How much
load a material can handle without failing. (like concrete under compression)
31. Stiffness – Resistance of a material to deformation under load, related to the
modulus of elasticity. How resistant a material is to bending or stretching under
a load. (like a steel rod vs. a rubber rod)
5. Stress–Strain Diagram (Tensile Test Curve)
32. Stress–Strain Diagram – Graph showing the relationship between stress
(vertical axis) and strain (horizontal axis) for a material under tensile load.
33. Proportional Limit Point – First point where stress and strain are directly
proportional.
34. Elastic Limit Point – Highest stress where material returns to original shape
after unloading.
35. Yield Point – Point where plastic deformation begins; in some materials there is
an upper yield point and a lower yield point.
36. Yield Plateau – Region of nearly constant stress during yielding in some
materials.
37. Strain Hardening Region – Portion of the curve where material becomes
stronger with increasing strain after yielding.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
38. Ultimate Stress Point – Highest stress reached before necking begins.
39. Necking – Localized reduction in cross-sectional area before fracture.
40. Fracture Point – End of the curve where the material fails completely.
6. Axial Loading
41. Axial Load – Load applied along the longitudinal axis of a member.
42. Elongation (ΔL) – Change in length due to axial load.
43. Thermal Stress – Stress induced in a material due to temperature changes when
expansion or contraction is restrained.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
7. Torsion
44. Torsion – Twisting of a structural member due to an applied torque.
45. Torque (T) – Rotational force causing angular deformation.
46. Polar Moment of Inertia (J) – Measure of an object’s resistance to torsion.
47. Angle of Twist (θ) – Angular displacement per unit length in a shaft subjected to
torque.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
8. Shear and Bending
48. Shear Force (V) – Force acting perpendicular to the axis of a beam that causes
shear deformation.
49. Bending Moment (M) – Moment that causes a beam to bend.
50. Flexure Formula – Relationship between bending stress, bending moment,
moment of inertia, and distance from the neutral axis.
51. Moment of Inertia (I) – Geometric property indicating the distribution of cross-
sectional area about a given axis, affecting bending resistance.
52. Parallel Axis Theorem – the moment of inertia of an area (or body) about any
axis parallel to its centroidal axis is equal to the moment of inertia about the
centroidal axis plus the product of the area (or mass) and the square of the
distance between the two axes.
53. Section Modulus (S) – Ratio of the moment of inertia to the distance from the
neutral axis to the outermost fiber.
54. Neutral Axis – Axis in a beam cross-section where the bending stress is zero.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
9. Combined Stresses
54. Principal Stresses – Maximum and minimum normal stresses occurring at a
point.
55. Mohr’s Circle – Graphical method to determine principal stresses, principal
planes, and maximum shear stresses.
56. Combined Loading – Occurrence of more than one type of stress at a point (e.g.,
bending + axial + torsion).
10. Deflection of Beams
57. Deflection (δ) – Displacement of a structural element under load.
58. Slope – Angular change of the beam axis due to bending.
59. Elastic Curve – Shape of the deflected axis of a beam.

© 2025 Green Gears Review and Mentorship Program
All rights reserved. This material is protected under a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). Redistribution, reproduction, or
sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
11. Columns and Buckling
60. Column – Structural member primarily subjected to axial compression.
61. Buckling – Sudden lateral deflection of a slender member under axial load.
62. Slenderness Ratio (L/r) – Ratio of the column’s effective length to its radius of
gyration, indicating susceptibility to buckling.
63. Euler’s Formula – Equation for critical buckling load of long, slender columns.
12. Energy Methods
64. Strain Energy – Energy stored in a material due to deformation.
65. Castigliano’s Theorem – Method of determining deflections in elastic structures
based on strain energy.

sharing of any part of this content without prior written consent is strictly prohibited.
Most Common Conversion Factor for Stress
Understanding the units
• Pa (Pascal) = 1 N/m2
• MPa (Megapascal) = 1,000,000 Pa = 106 Pa
• GPa (Gigapascal) = 1,000,000,000 Pa = 109 Pa
Quick rule of thumb

Bearing stress occurs at the surface of contact between two materials where one
pushes against another (e.g., a bolt pressing against a hole wall).
It is different from normal stress (which acts over a whole cross-section) because
here, the stress is localized in the contact area.
High bearing stresses can cause surface crushing or permanent deformation of the
hole.

original length. It’s unitless.

1. Which of the following best describes the Second Law of Thermodynamics?
a. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
b. Heat flows naturally from a hotter to a colder body
c. The internal energy of a system remains constant
d. Work is a form of heat
Explanation: The second law states that it is impossible to construct a device that
operates in a cycle and produces no effect other than the transfer of heat from a lower-
temperature body to a higher-temperature body.
2. Which of the following statement is true about heat pumps?
a. It cools by evaporating a fluid
b. It transfers heat from hot to cold
c. It can heat a space using refrigeration principles
d. It only works in cold weather
Explanation: Heat pumps are devices that use work to heat a space.
3. It is the measure of how well a refrigeration system removes heat from a cold space
compared to the energy it consumes?
a. Efficiency b. Refrigerating
Power
c. Coefficient of
Performance
d. None of the
Above
Explanation: Coefficient of Performance (COP) is a measure of how efficiently a
refrigeration system uses work to remove heat from the refrigerated space.
4. Which statement is true for Reverse Carnot Cycle?
a. It performs the reversed effect of a heat engine.
b. It transfers energy from a low level of temperature to a high level of temperature.
c. It is the most efficient refrigeration cycle.
d. All of the above
Explanation: The Reverse Carnot Cycle is the most efficient refrigeration cycle, which
performs the reversed effect of a Carnot heat engine.
5. In a reverse Carnot refrigerator, the low temperature reservoir is at 273 K and the high
temperature reservoir is at 303 K. What is the theoretical COP?
a. 7.0 b. 9.1 c. 10.1 d. 8.5

8. What property makes a good refrigerant desirable for environmental safety?
a. Low boiling point at low pressure
b) Low ozone depletion potential
c) Classified as Pure Fluid Refrigerant
d) High compressibility
Explanation: Ozone depletion potential (ODP) refers to the relative harmfulness of a
substance to the ozone layer.
9. Which of the following is a natural refrigerant?
a. R-22 b.R-134a c. R-717 d. R-410a
Explanation: R-717 is also known as Ammonia, an organic/natural refrigerant.
10. What happens to heat load if doors are opened frequently?
a. It decreases
b. It remains the same
c. It increases
d. It’s not affected
Explanation: Infiltration load is caused by warm air entering through doors or leaks. If
doors are opened frequently, infiltration load increases.
11. Lighting, people, and forklifts contribute to what kind of heat load
a. Sensible load
b. Internal load
c. External load
d. Product load
Explanation: Heat generated inside by people, lighting, motors, etc. is called internal
load.
12. Which of the following contribute the most heat load in a typical cold storage
design?
a. Product Load
b. Transmission Load
c. Infiltration Load
d. Internal Load

Explanation: In typical cold storages, product load is often the biggest contributor to
heat load since it includes sensible and latent heat removal of large quantities of
products stored.
13. Which statement correctly reflects the Kelvin–Planck statement of the Second Law?
a. Heat cannot spontaneously flow from hot to cold
b. No engine can convert all absorbed heat into work
c. Entropy of isolated systems always decreases
d. All reversible processes are isentropic
Explanation: The Kelvin-Planck Statement states that it is impossible for any device
that operates on a cycle to receive heat from a single reservoir and produce only a net
amount of work.
14. It states that it is impossible for heat to spontaneously transfer from a lower-
temperature body to a higher-temperature body.
a. Boyle Statement
b. Gay-Lussac Statement
c. Kelvin-Planck Statement
d. Clausius Statement
Explanation: The Clausius Statement says that it is impossible to construct a device
that operates on a cycle and produces no effect other than the transfer of heat from a
lower-temperature body to a higher-temperature body.

d. 5

COPHP = 3 +1
COPHP = 4

temperature of the refrigerant in the system is 120°F and the lower is 10°F. The capacity

20. A heat pump working on a reversed Carnot cycle has a COP of 5. It works as a
refrigerator taking 1kW of work input. What is the refrigerating effect?
a. 5 kW b. 4 kW c. 3 kW d. 2 kW
Explanation: COPR = COPHP -1

21. Which of the following processes occurs in the expansion valve?
a. Isobaric cooling
b. Isothermal expansion
c. Isenthalpic expansion
d. Adiabatic compression
Explanation: Expansion valves perform isenthalpic throttling — pressure drops, but
enthalpy remains the same.
22. What is the ideal process assumed during compression in a Vapor Compression
Cycle?
a. Isothermal
b. Isentropic
c. Isobaric
d. Isenthalpic
Explanation: In theory, compression is isentropic (adiabatic and reversible) to minimize
entropy generation.

a. High specific heat
b. Low initial temperature
c. Low moisture content
d. Small latent heat
Explanation: Higher specific heat means the product holds more heat per °C,
increasing the load.

29. A refrigerant with a very high critical temperature is generally preferred for:
a. Low-pressure applications
b. High COP systems
c. High superheat cycles
d. Subzero temperature freezers
Explanation: Higher critical temperature allows the refrigerant to condense at lower
pressures, improving COP.
30. Why is latent heat load often overlooked in non-freezing storage?
a. It’s negligible at above freezing
b. It is calculated separately
c. Moisture content is constant
d. Cooling capacity compensates
Explanation: Above freezing, products don’t undergo phase change, so latent heat is
typically negligible.
31. When the air is fully saturated, the relative humidity is _______.
a. 0%
b. 50%
c. 100%
d. Depends on air pressure
Explanation: 100% relative humidity means the air cannot take on any more water and
is therefore saturated.

a. The one with higher dry bulb temperature
b. The one with higher pressure
c. The one with higher moisture content
d. The one with higher dew point temperature
Explanation: Humidity measures how much moisture is in the air.
33. A thermometer with a gauze-covered bulb that permit to determine the relative
humidity of the air.
a. Dry bulb thermometer
b. Wet bulb thermometer
c. Dewpoint thermometer
d. All of the Above
Explanation: A wet bulb thermometer looks like a regular glass thermometer but has its
bulb wrapped in a wet cloth to allow cooling by evaporation.
34. Which of the following best describes absolute humidity?
a. Percentage of moisture in air
b. Temperature of moist air
c. Mass of water vapor per unit volume of air
d. Ratio of water vapor to dry air
Explanation: Absolute humidity is measured in grams of water vapor per cubic meter of
air.
35. Moist air with high absolute humidity has:
a. High dry-bulb temperature
b. High water vapor content
c. Low enthalpy
d. Low dew point
Explanation: Absolute humidity measures how much water vapor is in a unit volume of
air.
36. Which of the following decreases when moist air is heated at constant moisture
content?
a. Specific humidity
b. Relative humidity
c. Dew point
d. Dry-bulb temperature
Explanation: Heating air increases dry-bulb temperature but reduces RH if no moisture
is added.

a. Barometer
b. Anemometer
c. Hygrometer
d. Psychrometer

a. Cooling and humidifying

d. Cooling with constant enthalpy
Explanation: Sensible heating increases dry-bulb temperature at constant humidity

c. Sensible heating

a. Enthalpy
b. Humidity ratio
c. Dew point temperature
d. Relative humidity
Explanation: No moisture is added or removed — only the temperature changes.

b. Cooling and humidification
c. Sensible heating
d. Heating and humidification
Explanation: This combination increases relative humidity and humidity ratio while

Ideal Vapor Compression Refrigeration Cycle
The ideal vapor compression cycle is a theoretical model used to
represent the basic operation of most refrigeration and air conditioning
systems. It consists of four main processes: isentropic compression,
constant-pressure heat rejection (condensation), isenthalpic expansion,
and constant-pressure heat absorption (evaporation).

Ideal Vapor Compression Refrigeration Cycle
• 1-2 Isentropic Compression
• 2-3 Isobaric Heat Rejection
• 3-4 Isenthalpic Expansion
(Throttling)
• 4-1 Isobaric Heat Absorption

Ideal Vapor Compression Refrigeration Cycle
Enthalpy is a thermodynamic property that is equal to the internal
energy of the system plus the flow work exerted by the system.
In short, Enthalpy is equivalent to the total heat content of the system.
H = U + PV

Ideal Vapor Compression Refrigeration Cycle
Work:
W = m(h2 – h1)
Heat Absorbed
QA = m (h1 – h4)
Heat Rejected
QR = m(h3 – h1)
h3 = h4

Key Info:

Components of VC Refrigeration System
Compressor
• A mechanical device that increases the pressure and temperature of the
refrigerant vapor.
• Draws in low-pressure vapor from the evaporator and compresses it to a
high-pressure, high-temperature vapor before sending it to the
condenser.
• It is sometimes referred to as the “heart” of the refrigeration system.

Components of VC Refrigeration System
Evaporator
• A heat exchanger where the refrigerant absorbs heat and evaporates.
• Removes heat from the refrigerated space or product by allowing low-
pressure refrigerant to absorb it and change from liquid to vapor.
• This is where the refrigeration effect happens and is often found in the
freezer compartment of a typical household VC refrigeration.

Components of VC Refrigeration System
Condenser
• A heat exchanger where the refrigerant releases heat and condenses.
• Rejects heat from the high-pressure vapor refrigerant to the
surroundings, causing it to condense back into a liquid.
• This is where the rejection of heat happens.

Components of VC Refrigeration System
Expansion Valve
• A flow-restricting device that drops the pressure of the refrigerant.
• Reduces the high-pressure liquid refrigerant from the condenser to a
low-pressure mixture before it enters the evaporator, enabling
evaporation and heat absorption.
• It is the component responsible for lowering the temperature of the
refrigerant to provide the cooling effect in the refrigerated area.

Global Warming Potential (GWP)
GWP is a measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere
compared to carbon dioxide (CO₂) over a specific time period (usually 100 years).
• CO₂ has a GWP of 1, and other gases are rated relative to it.
• Higher GWP means greater contribution to global warming.

Ozone Depletion Potential (ODP) is a measure of how much a substance can damage
the Earth's ozone layer compared to a reference substance.
• CFC-11 (Trichlorofluoromethane) has an ODP of 1.
• ODP values range from 0 (no harm) to 1 or higher (high ozone-depleting potential).

Cold Storage Heat Loads
1. Transmission Load
•Heat transfer through walls, floors, ceilings, and doors due to temperature
difference between inside and outside.
•Depends on insulation quality, surface area, and ambient conditions.
2. Product Load
•Heat brought in by the product when it enters the cold room.
•Includes:
-Sensible heat: Cooling the product to storage temperature.
-Latent heat: If product moisture freezes (for freezing storage).
-Respiration heat: For living products like fruits and vegetables.
3. Infiltration Load
•Heat and moisture carried in by warm air leakage through door openings or
gaps.
•Increases with frequency and duration of door openings.

Cold Storage Heat Loads
4. Internal Load
•Heat generated inside the cold room from:
•Lights
•Personnel
•Forklifts or other equipment
•Electric motors and fans
5. Equipment Load
•Heat generated by refrigeration equipment components within the cold
space, such as:
•Evaporator fans
•Defrost heaters
6. Service Load (Miscellaneous)
•Includes additional loads such as cleaning with warm water or heat from
special processes inside the cold room.

QUESTION 1

This 	branch 	of 	physics 	that 	deals 	with 	the 	relationships
between 	heat, 	work, 	and 	energy. 	This 	studies 	how
energy 	is 	transferred 	and 	transformed 	in 	physical
systems.
A. 	Mass 	and 	Heat 	Transfer
B. 	Heat 	Transfer
C. 	Thermodynamics
D. 	Refrigeration 	Engineering
QUESTION 1

Thermodynamics
Thermodynamics 	is 	the 	study 	of 	energy, 	heat, 	work, 	and 	their 	transformations.
In 	ABE, 	it 	is 	crucial 	for 	designing 	systems 	like 	dryers, 	refrigeration 	units,
bioenergy systems, and environmental control structures.

Defined 	as 	a 	definite 	space 	or 	area 	on 	which 	the 	study 	of
energy 	transfer 	and 	energy 	conversion 	is 	made.
A. 	System
B. 	Boundary
C. 	Surrounding
D. 	Space
QUESTION 2

Defined 	as 	a 	definite 	space 	or 	area 	on 	which 	the 	study 	of
energy 	transfer 	and 	energy 	conversion 	is 	made.
A. 	System
B. 	Boundary
C. 	Surrounding
D. 	Space
QUESTION 2

Thermodynamic Systems and Control Volumes
System 	is 	a 	definite 	space 	or 	area 	on 	which 	the 	study 	of 	energy 	transfer 	and
energy 	conversion 	is 	made.
Boundary 	is 	what 	separates 	the 	system 	and 	the 	surrounding. 	It 	may 	be 	fixed,
movable, 	or 	imaginary. 	It 	will 	not 	occupy 	any 	volume 	or 	mass 	in 	space.
Surrounding 	is 	anything 	outside 	the 	system 	which 	affects 	its 	behavior.

Thermodynamic Systems and Control Volumes
Control 	Volume 	– 	a 	specified 	large 	number 	thermal 	device 	has 	mass 	flow 	in
and 	put 	of 	the 	system.
Control 	Surface 	– 	both 	mass 	and 	energy 	can 	cross 	the 	boundary 	of 	a 	control
volume.

Which 	of 	the 	following 	best 	defines 	a 	closed 	system 	in
thermodynamics?
A. 	No 	mass 	or 	energy 	crosses 	the 	boundary
B. 	Only 	mass 	can 	cross 	the 	boundary
C. 	Energy 	can 	cross 	the 	boundary, 	but 	not 	mass
D. 	Both 	mass 	and 	energy 	can 	cross 	the 	boundary
QUESTION 3

Which 	of 	the 	following 	best 	defines 	a 	closed 	system 	in
thermodynamics?
A. 	No 	mass 	or 	energy 	crosses 	the 	boundary
B. 	Only 	mass 	can 	cross 	the 	boundary
C. 	Energy 	can 	cross 	the 	boundary, 	but 	not 	mass
D. 	Both 	mass 	and 	energy 	can 	cross 	the 	boundary
QUESTION 3

Thermodynamic Systems and Control Volumes
Open 	System 	– 	the 	mass 	as 	well 	as 	the 	energy 	may 	take 	place 	between
system 	and 	its 	surrounding.
Example: 	internal 	combustion 	engines, 	air 	compressor, 	water 	pump, 	steam
engine, 	boiler, 	turbine
Closed 	System 	– 	the 	mass 	within 	the 	boundary 	of 	the 	system 	remains
constant 	and 	only 	the 	energy 	transfer 	may 	take 	place 	between 	the 	system
and 	its 	surrounding.
Example: 	Pressure 	cooker, 	gas 	confined 	between 	a 	piston 	and 	cylinder

A. 	Positive
B. 	Negative

D. 	Cannot 	be 	determined

Which 	property 	of 	thermodynamic 	is 	extensive?

QUESTION 5

Thermodynamic Properties
Thermodynamic 	Property 	– 	any 	measurable 	or 	observable 	characteristics 	of
the 	substance 	when 	the 	system 	remains 	in 	equilibrium 	state 	(i.e., 	pressure,
temperature, 	density, 	volume, 	energy, 	specific 	volume).
Intensive 	Property 	– 	one 	whose 	value 	does 	not 	depend 	on 	the 	mass 	of 	the
system 	(i.e., 	temperature, 	pressure, 	density, 	specific 	volume, 	etc.).
Extensive 	Property 	– 	one 	whose 	values 	depend 	on 	mass 	of 	the 	system 	(i.e.,
volume, 	total 	energy)

This 	describes 	the 	condition 	when 	a 	system 	is 	isolated
from 	its 	surroundings 	or 	is 	free 	from 	any 	unbalanced
potentials, 	such 	as 	forced 	flows 	of 	mass 	or 	energy.
A. 	Quasi-equilibrium
B. 	Equilibrium
C. 	Static 	process
D. 	State
QUESTION 6

This 	describes 	the 	condition 	when 	a 	system 	is 	isolated
from 	its 	surroundings 	or 	is 	free 	from 	any 	unbalanced
potentials, 	such 	as 	forced 	flows 	of 	mass 	or 	energy.
A. 	Quasi-equilibrium
B. 	Equilibrium
C. 	Static 	process
D. 	State
QUESTION 6

Thermodynamic State, Process, and Cycle
Types of equilibrium:
1. 	Thermal 	equilibrium: 	a 	system 	that 	features 	spatially-uniform
temperature.
2. 	Chemical equilibrium: a 	system 	free 	from 	chemical 	reactions.
3. 	Mechanical 	equilibrium: 	a 	system 	has 	no 	tendency 	for 	a 	change 	of
pressure 	over 	time.
4. 	Phase 	equilibrium: 	a 	system 	consisting 	of 	a 	mixture 	of 	multiple 	phases,
such 	as 	liquid 	water 	and 	water 	vapor, 	if 	the 	composition 	of 	the 	mixture
remains 	constant 	over 	time.

This 	refers 	to 	the 	condition 	of 	a 	system, 	which 	may 	be
described 	by 	a 	unique 	set 	of 	properties, 	such 	as
pressure, 	temperature, 	and 	specific 	volume.
A. 	Quasi-equilibrium
B. 	Condition
C. 	Static 	process
D. 	State
QUESTION 7

This 	refers 	to 	the 	condition 	of 	a 	system, 	which 	may 	be
described 	by 	a 	unique 	set 	of 	properties, 	such 	as
pressure, 	temperature, 	and 	specific 	volume.
A. 	Quasi-equilibrium
B. 	Condition
C. 	Static 	process
D. 	State
QUESTION 7

Thermodynamic State, Process, and Cycle
The 	state 	of 	a 	system 	in 	equilibrium 	is 	called 	equilibrium state.
A 	system 	may 	change 	from 	one 	state 	to 	another 	state 	through 	a 	process.
If 	all 	states 	in 	a 	process 	are 	equilibrium 	states, 	the 	process 	is 	called 	quasi-
equilibrium process.
If 	a 	system 	undergoes 	a 	series 	of 	processes 	and 	finally 	returns 	to 	its 	initial
state, 	we 	say 	that 	the 	system 	completes 	a 	cycle.

In 	a 	grain 	drying 	system, 	which 	process 	assumes 	no
heat 	exchange 	with 	the 	surroundings?
A. 	Isothermal
B. 	Isobaric
C. 	Adiabatic
D. 	Isochoric
QUESTION 8

In 	a 	grain 	drying 	system, 	which 	process 	assumes 	no
heat 	exchange 	with 	the 	surroundings?
A. 	Isothermal
B. 	Isobaric
C. 	Adiabatic
D. 	Isochoric
QUESTION 8

Thermodynamic State, Process, and Cycle
An 	adiabatic 	process 	involves 	no 	heat 	transfer 	into 	or 	out 	of 	the 	system.
In 	agriculture, 	this 	is 	important 	in 	rapid 	drying 	or 	insulated 	reactor 	designs
where 	heat 	retention 	is 	critical 	for 	energy 	efficiency.
Related terms:
Adiabatic: no 	heat 	exchange 	(e.g., 	sudden 	expansion 	in 	dryers)
Isothermal: constant 	temperature
Isobaric: constant 	pressure 	(e.g., 	atmospheric 	drying)
Isochoric: constant 	volume 	(e.g., 	rigid 	containers 	in 	storage)
Isentropic: the 	entropy 	remains 	constant 	in 	the 	process.

This 	law 	states 	that 	the 	entropy 	of 	an 	isolated 	system
always 	increases.
A. 	Zeroth 	Law
B. 	First 	Law
C. 	Second 	Law
D. 	Third 	Law
QUESTION 9

This 	law 	states 	that 	the 	entropy 	of 	an 	isolated 	system
always 	increases.
A. 	Zeroth 	Law
B. 	First 	Law
C. 	Second 	Law
D. 	Third 	Law
QUESTION 9

Second Law of Thermodynamics
The 	Second 	Law 	of 	Thermodynamics 	introduces 	the 	concept 	of 	entropy, 	which
measures 	the 	disorder 	in 	a 	system.
It 	implies 	that 	energy 	conversions 	are 	never 	100% 	efficient, 	such 	as 	in
combustion 	engines 	or 	drying 	systems 	where 	some 	energy 	is 	lost 	as 	heat.

Law 	that 	states 	that 	two 	systems 	in 	equilibrium 	with 	the
third 	system 	are 	in 	thermal 	equilibrium 	with 	each 	other.
A. 	Zeroth 	Law
B. 	First 	Law
C. 	Second 	Law
D. 	Third 	Law
QUESTION 10

Law 	that 	states 	that 	two 	systems 	in 	equilibrium 	with 	the
third 	system 	are 	in 	thermal 	equilibrium 	with 	each 	other.
A. 	Zeroth 	Law
B. 	First 	Law
C. 	Second 	Law
D. 	Third 	Law
QUESTION 10

Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
The 	Zeroth 	Law 	states 	that 	if 	two 	systems 	are 	each 	in 	thermal 	equilibrium 	with
a 	third 	system, 	they 	are 	also 	in 	thermal 	equilibrium 	with 	each 	other.
This 	allows 	for 	the 	use 	of 	thermometers 	to 	compare 	temperatures 	and 	is
foundational 	in 	climate 	control 	in 	greenhouses 	or 	cold 	storage.

This 	law 	states 	that 	the 	entropy 	of 	a 	system 	approaches
a 	constant 	as 	temperature 	approaches 	zero.
A. 	Zeroth 	Law
B. 	First 	Law
C. 	Second 	Law
D. 	Third 	Law
QUESTION 11

This 	law 	states 	that 	the 	entropy 	of 	a 	system 	approaches
a 	constant 	as 	temperature 	approaches 	zero.
A. 	Zeroth 	Law
B. 	First 	Law
C. 	Second 	Law
D. 	Third 	Law
QUESTION 11

Third Law of Thermodynamics
The 	Third 	Law 	explains 	that 	at 	absolute 	zero 	(0K), 	a 	perfect 	crystalline
substance 	has 	minimal 	entropy.
While 	this 	is 	a 	theoretical 	concept, 	it 	sets 	a 	baseline 	for 	entropy 	calculations 	in
chemical 	and 	biological 	processes 	in 	biosystems.

Energy 	cannot 	be 	created 	nor 	destroyed; 	it 	can 	only 	be
changed 	from 	one 	form 	to 	another.

Energy 	cannot 	be 	created 	nor 	destroyed; 	it 	can 	only 	be

First Law of Thermodynamics
The 	First 	Law 	of 	Thermodynamics, 	also 	known 	as 	the 	law 	of 	energy
conservation, 	explains 	that 	the 	total 	energy 	of 	an 	isolated 	system 	is 	constant.
In 	agricultural 	systems, 	this 	principle 	is 	applied 	in 	machines 	and 	dryers 	where
mechanical 	or 	electrical 	energy 	is 	transformed 	into 	heat 	energy.

commonly 	used 	terminology 	— 	the 	more 	accurate 	and 	accepted 	term

Irreversibility
Mixing 	increases 	entropy 	and 	cannot 	be 	reversed 	without 	external 	work.
The 	system 	and 	its 	environment 	cannot 	be 	restored 	to 	their 	original 	states 	at
the 	same 	time. 	The 	sign 	of 	an 	irreversible 	process 	comes 	from 	the 	finite
gradient 	between 	the 	states 	occurring 	in 	the 	actual 	process.
For 	example, 	when 	heat 	flows 	from 	one 	object 	to 	another, 	there 	is 	a
finite 	temperature 	difference 	(gradient) 	between 	the 	two 	objects. 	More
importantly, 	at 	any 	given 	moment 	of 	the 	process, 	the 	system 	most 	likely 	is 	not
at 	equilibrium 	or 	in 	a 	well-defined 	state. 	This 	phenomenon 	is
called 	irreversibility.

Reversibility
A 	reversible 	process 	is 	a 	process 	in 	which 	the 	system 	and 	environment 	can 	be
restored 	to 	exactly 	the 	same 	initial 	states 	that 	they 	were 	in 	before 	the 	process
occurred, 	if 	we 	go 	backward 	along 	the 	path 	of 	the 	process.
The 	necessary 	condition 	for 	a 	reversible 	process 	is 	therefore 	the 	quasi-static
requirement. 	Note 	that 	it 	is 	quite 	easy 	to 	restore 	a 	system 	to 	its 	original 	state;
the 	hard 	part 	is 	to 	have 	its 	environment 	restored 	to 	its 	original 	state 	at 	the
same 	time.
For 	example, 	in 	the 	example 	of 	an 	ideal 	gas 	expanding 	into 	vacuum 	to 	twice
its 	original 	volume, 	we 	can 	easily 	push 	it 	back 	with 	a 	piston 	and 	restore
its 	temperature 	and 	pressure 	by 	removing 	some 	heat 	from 	the 	gas. 	The
problem 	is 	that 	we 	cannot 	do 	it 	without 	changing 	something 	in
its 	surroundings 	such 	as 	dumping 	some 	heat 	there.

The 	fundamental 	thermodynamic 	cycle 	used 	in 	all 	steam 	power 	plants 	is 	the
Rankine 	cycle. 	Other 	applications, 	such 	as 	solar 	thermal 	power 	plants 	and
geothermal 	power 	plants, 	also 	make 	use 	of 	it.
The 	Rankine 	cycle 	is 	a 	thermodynamically 	reversible 	cycle, 	which 	means 	that
all 	of 	the 	heat 	input 	may 	be 	converted 	back 	into 	labor. 	Friction, 	heat
transmission, 	and 	other 	variables 	cause 	losses 	in 	practice 	nevertheless. 	As 	a
result, 	the 	Rankine 	cycle's 	efficiency 	is 	normally 	between 	30 	and 	40%.
The 	Rankine 	cycle 	is 	available 	in 	a 	variety 	of 	forms, 	including 	the 	supercritical,
reheat, 	and 	regenerative 	cycles. 	Through 	a 	reduction 	in 	the 	quantity 	of 	heat
rejected 	by 	the 	environment, 	these 	modifications 	aim 	to 	increase 	the 	cycle's
efficiency.

Diesel Cycle
Diesel 	cycle 	is 	more 	effective 	than 	Otto 	cycle. 	This 	is 	so 	that 	the 	gasoline 	may
ignite 	more 	readily 	and 	completely. 	A 	diesel 	engine's 	increased 	compression
ratio 	raises 	the 	temperature 	at 	the 	end 	of 	the 	compression 	stroke. 	Diesel
engines 	are 	therefore 	more 	efficient 	than 	petrol 	engines.
Additionally, 	the 	Diesel 	cycle 	is 	stronger 	than 	the 	Otto 	cycle. 	This 	is 	due 	to 	the
fact 	that 	a 	spark 	plug 	is 	not 	used 	to 	ignite 	the 	fuel 	in 	a 	diesel 	engine, 	thus
there 	is 	no 	chance 	of 	a 	misfire 	if 	the 	spark 	plug 	breaks. 	As 	a 	result, 	diesel
engines 	are 	frequently 	utilized 	in 	settings 	where 	dependability 	is 	crucial, 	such
as 	heavy-duty 	vehicles 	and 	buses.

a. Malfunctioning coolant temperature sensor
b. Low oil pressure due to worn bearings or defective oil pump

Low oil pressure prevents sufficient oil from being delivered to critical engine components, leading to increased wear and potential
engine damage. Even with an adequate oil level, issues such as worn bearings, a faulty oil pump, clogged oil filter, or oil of the

a. Clogging oil filter

c. Insufficient water in the radiator
d. Alternator is not working
Black smoke coming out of the exhaust pipe of an engine is primarily caused by incomplete combustion of fuel, which leads to
excess unburnt fuel particles being expelled. This typically occurs when the air-to-fuel ratio is too rich (more fuel than air), resulting
in poor fuel burning efficiency.
Common causes of black exhaust smoke include:
- Dirty or clogged air filters preventing adequate air supply for combustion.
- Leaking or faulty fuel injectors delivering too much fuel into the combustion chamber.
- Damaged piston rings allowing engine oil to enter the combustion chamber and burn with fuel.
- Engine deposits and carbon buildup affecting combustion quality.

1. Water Conveyance Efficiency - the ratio between the water

expressed in percent.
2. Water Application Efficiency - the ratio between water stored in
the soil root zone during irrigation and the water delivered to the
farm expressed in percent.
3. Water-use Efficiency - the ratio of water beneficially used on the
project, farm or field to the amount of water delivered to the farm
expressed in percent.

zone during the irrigation to the water needed in the root zone prior
to irrigation, expressed in percent.

use of water to the net amount of water depleted from the root zone
soil.

solutions. Magreview ng palawak, huwag palalim. Quality over Quantity always.

Nothing is impossible. Believe that you can and you will achieve it. If it scares

importantly PRAY. PRAY. PRAY. Ask GOD and He will always provide. NEVER
doubt the power of prayers.

We are all rooting for you, Bayaw!
Good luck and God Bless!
- Engr. Heaven Scent (double meaning)

R = 0.287 kJ/kg-K

Thank You!
