☐ Careful appraisal and good planning must be undertaken before
making an investment in an agricultural machines.
☐ Economic analysis determines which of the different alternatives
of agricultural machines is most viable to purchase and operate.
INTRODUCTION

☐ Timeliness - Ability to perform an activity at such a time that crop
return is optimized considering quantity and quality of the product.
☐ Timeliness coefficient - A factor used to estimate the reduction
in crop return (quantity and quality) due to lack of timeliness in
performing an activity.
☐ Economic life of machine - The useful service life of a machine
before it becomes unprofitable for its original purpose due to
obsolescence of wear.
☐ Custom cost, machine - The amount paid for hiring equipment
and operator services to perform a certain task. Custom cost
normally includes a charge or fee for the operation of the basic
machine, and may or may not include supplemental labor and
equipment for such tasks as handling into storage or transport of
a harvested crop, transportation of seed or fertilizer to the field,
etc. Charges may be determined on the basis of area, time,
transport distance or quantity of crop processed.
INTRODUCTION

☐ Operating costs, machine - Costs associated with the amount of
materials used in operating the machine. Examples are labor,
fuel, lubrication, and repair and maintenance costs.
☐ Ownership costs, machine - Costs which do not depend on the
amount of operating the machine. Examples are depreciation,
interest on investment, taxes, insurance, and storage.
☐ Total cost, machine - The sum of ownership and operating
costs.
☐ Actual depreciation - Change in value of a machine.
☐ Estimated depreciation - The change in value as determined by
the difference between purchase price and estimated future
value.
☐ Straight line, declining balance, sum of years' digits
depreciation - Methods to spread the change in machine value
over its economic life. This method may disagree with estimated
depreciation.

☐ Lease - A lease in a contract for the use of a machinery for an
agreed period of time in return for periodic payments. Ownership
remains with the lessor. The lessee acquires the right of
temporary possession and use.
☐ Obsolescence - The process of becoming obsolete.
☐ Obsolete - The condition of a machine when it is either out of
production and parts to repair and update it are not available from
normal suppliers, or it can be replaced by other machine or
method that will produce greater profit.
☐ Price - Market value per unit. Examples are the price of grains,
usually peso per unit measure; of labor, peso per hour; or
machines, peso per machine.
☐ Rent - A rental agreement is a short-term contract that permits the
use of machinery in exchange for a fee.

☐ Gross - The return for sale of a service or product and the value
received for a service or product before expenses are deducted.
☐ Net - The return for sale of a service or product and the value
received for a service or product, less all expenses except income
taxes.
☐ Continuous duty - A service requirement that demands
operation for an indefinitely long period of time.
☐ Failure - The inability of a machine to perform its function under
specified field and crop conditions.
☐ Fuel consumption, specific - The fuel consumed by an engine
to deliver a given amount of energy (kilograms of fuel per kilowatt-
hour).

☐ Maintenance and service - Periodic activities to prevent
premature failure and to maintain good functional performance.
Examples are refueling, changing oil and filters, cleaning,
lubricating, and adjusting components.
☐ Major overhaul - Extensive rebuilding which extends the useful
life of a machine, increases its value or adapts the machine for
different uses.
☐ Repair - Restoring a machine to operative condition after
breakdown, excessive wear, or accidental damage. Repairs are
less extensive than major overhauls and normally do not alter the
value of the machine.

n Discounted Method
• 	It involves discounting and allows payment and receipts
occurring at different times in the future to be converted to a
common standard in terms of their present value.
n Undiscounted Method
• 	It does not consider timing of cost and benefit flows and the
changing value of money over time.
Methods of Appraising Investment

n Cost Factors – total cost of using the machine which includes
charges for ownership and operation.
Fixed Cost – It is the ownership cost which is independent of
use.
Variable Cost – It is the cost associated with the operation of the
machine, which varies directly with the amount of
use.
n Depreciation – This reflects the reduction in value of an asset with
the use and time. The actual total depreciation can never be
known until the equipment has been sold. It can be estimated by
using different computational methods, depending on the
objective.
Terms

n Interest – It is the interest charged for the use of the money
invested in a machine. Simple interest on the average
investment over the life of the machine can be added to the
annual depreciation to estimate the yearly capital cost of
ownership.
n Repair and Maintenance Cost – It is the cost associated with
maintaining the machine, including its repair.
n Fuel Cost – It is the cost incurred for the fuel consumed in
operating the machine.
n Labor Cost – It is the cost incurred in operating the machine
based on the 8-hour rate. For owner operator, labor cost is
determined from alternative opportunities for the use of time.
This cost varies depending on the prevailing labor cost in a
certain area.
n Machine Custom Cost – It is the amount paid for hiring the
equipment and operator services to perform a certain task.

n Operating cost – It is the cost which depend directly on the
amount spent in operating the machine. This includes labor,
fuel, lubrication, as well as repair and maintenance.
n Ownership Cost – It is the cost which does not depend on
the amount spent in operating the machine. It includes
depreciation, interest on investment, taxes, insurance, and
storage.
n Lease – It is the contract for the use of a machine for an
agreed period of time in return for periodic payment. The
ownership remains with the lessor and the lessee acquire the
right of temporary possession and of operating the machine.
n Obsolete – It is the condition of a machine when it is out of
production and parts to repair and update it are not available
from local suppliers, or it can be replaced by other machine
or method that will produce a greater profit.
n Price – It is the market value per unit of a machine.

n Rent – It is a short-term contract for the use of machinery in
exchange for a fee.
n Gross – The return for sale or product and the value received
for a service or product before expenses are deducted.
n Net – It is the return for sale of a service or product and the
value received for a service or product less all expenses
except income taxes.
n Maintenance and Service – It is the periodic activities carried
out to prevent premature failure and to maintain good
functional machine performance.
n Specific Fuel Consumption – The fuel consumed by an engine
in delivering a given amount of energy.
n Repair – It is the restoration of a machine to operative
condition after breakdown, excessive wear, or accidental
damage.

• 	Prepare a list of all the materials needed to build the machine.
Lists must be classified into fabrication materials like metal plates
and bars; standard materials like bearings, bolts and nuts; and
consumables like paints, brush, cutting discs, etc.
• 	Determine the price of each material needed by canvassing from
suppliers. Price per unit of each materials must be reflected so
that it would be easy to tabulate and compute for the total cost at
the end.
• 	Determine the sub total cost for the fabricated, standard and
consumables needed.
• 	Compute for the labor cost to build the machine. Usually it is 60%
of the total material cost. The percentage cost can be adjusted
depending on how difficult the fabrication is to be done.
PRODUCTION COST ANALYSIS

• 	Determine the direct cost in producing the machine by adding the
materials and labor costs.
• 	Determine the indirect cost associated with the fabrication of the
machine by adding the cost of electricity needed or consumed and
the administrative cost. Usually, 15% of the direct cost is allocated
for the cost of electricity and 10% of the direct cost is allocated for
administrative cost.
• 	Compute for the fabrication cost by adding the direct and indirect
costs needed or spent in building the machine.
• 	Add a contingency of 10% to the fabrication cost to get the total
production cost.
• 	Determine the selling price by add mark up, which is 25% of
production cost, and taxes, which includes 3% percentage sales
tax and 12% income tax.

n Determine the annual fixed cost, which includes depreciation,
interest on average capital investment, repair and maintenance,
and tax and insurance. Usually depreciation is determined using
the straight line method with the formula
D 	= (P-S) / L
where:
D 	- depreciation, P/year
P 	- principal, P
S 	- salvage value, P
L 	- life span
Operating Cost Analysis

The salvage value is usually 10% of the purchase price of
the machine. The life span depends on the machine and is
usually 5 to 7 years for field equipment; while, 10 to 15 years
for farmstead equipment. The interest on investment
depends on the prevailing interest rate charged by banks on
loans and is usually 24%. Repair and maintenance is
usually 10%; while, insurance is 3%. Tax includes 3%
percentage sales tax and 12% income tax.

n Determine the variable cost which includes fuel, oil, and wage
of the operator. It depends on how long the machine is
operated. Fuel consumption and oil requirement of the
machine can be determined from the manufacturer’s brochure
or catalogue. The cost of labor depends on the prevailing
wage for laborer in the area, depending on the skills of the
operator.
n Determine the total operating cost of the machine by adding
the total fixed costs and the total variable cost.
n Determine the operating cost per unit by dividing the total cost
by its field or functional capacity. This is expressed in P/hr,
P/hectare, or P/kg.

n Calculate the BEP by dividing the purchase price by the
difference between the commercial rate of the machine and
the computed operating cost.
n Calculate the payback period (PBP) which is the length of
time from the start of purchasing the machine until its net
benefit equal cost.

n Break-Even Point – It is the level of operation at which total cost
equal to total benefits or gross income. It is useful in determining
the level at which the machine should be operated in one year to
cover the annual cost.
n Payback Period – It is the time it takes to recover the cost
invested on the machine. It is useful in choosing among the
investment alternatives when there is a high degree of risk
involved and/or financial resources are limited to decide for a
short period.
Undiscounted Measures

n Internal Rate of Return – It is the discount rate that equates the
present value of the expected cash outflows with the present value
of the expected inflows.
n Net Present Value – It is a discounted cash flow approach to
capital budgeting. With the present-value method, all cash flows
are discounted to present value using the required rate of return.
Discounted Measures
n Benefit-Cost Ratio – It is the ratio of the total benefits derived
from operating the machine to the total cost needed for operation.

AGRICULTURAL IMPLEMENTS AND
EQUIPMENT
Agricultural Field Implement - These are the machines used
to perform specific task during crop production and post
production operations. This includes tillage, seeding and
planting, crop, cultivating, spraying and dusting, harvesting and
threshing/shelling operations.
Power Source for Field Implement
1. 	Human
2. 	Draft Animal
3. 	Engine and Tractor
3
☐ Tractor – a machine used primarily
for traction or pulling purposes. It can
also deliver both power for stationary
and mobile tasks. It can pull or tow
implement through traction from drive
wheel and or pull implement through
the draft developed from the drawbar
hitch of the tractor.
☐ Internal Combustion Engine (ICE)
is a device that produces power by
burning normally liquid fuel inside the
combustion chamber of an engine.
Available as spark-ignition or diesel
ignition engines with single or multiple
cylinders depending on the power
needed.
4

7/22/25
3
(1) Pull-Type or Trailing
Implement
It is pulled and guided from a
single hitch point and is not
completely supported b the
tractor. The implement is
provided with a ground wheel
which can be used during
transport and trailing operation.
Depth of tillage implement is
completely controlled by the
hydraulic drive of the tractor by
changing the position of the
ground wheel.
TRACTOR-DRAWN IMPLEMENT
TYPES
5
(2) Mounted Implement
It is hitch completely to the
three-point hitch system of a
tractor. The implement is
usually carried by the tractor
during travel to the field.
Depth of implement cut is
controlled by the three-point
hitch system of the tractor
operated by its hydraulic
system. Commonly used for
small to medium size
tractors or ease of transport
and maneuverability during
operation.
6

7/22/25
4
Advantages
(1) Mounted equipment are less expensive that equivalent
pull-type equipment;
(2) Support wheels and accompanying structure required
on pull-type equipment is eliminated;
(3) Single-depth or height control system forming a part of
the tractor.
● Maneuverability better
● Visibility is better
● Transport is easier
● Draft-sensing is advantage
● Vertical load transfer to aid in traction is possible
● Attaching and detaching is easier
● Standardization of three-point hitch and quick attaching
couplers are available.
Limitations
(1) Carrying capacity of tractor chassis
(2) Transport stability is a limitation
7
(3) Semi-Mounted Implement
It is attached to the tractor
through a horizontal or nearly
horizontal hinge axis and
partially supported by the
tractor at least during transport,
but it is never completely
supported by the tractor.
Support wheel at the rear or in
the middle together with remote
hydraulic are utilized for raising
and lowering the complete
implement machine or it
individual units.
8

7/22/25
5
Advantages
(1) Greater flexibility
(2) Better Maneuverability
(3) Better visibility
(4) Better control by operator
(5) Improved mobility
(6) Reduce losses when cutting mechanism is in front of the unit
Disadvantages
(1) High initial investment hence it should have higher annual
use to be economically competitive with pull=type machine.
SELF-PROPELLED MACHINE
☐ Self-Propelled
An implement with propelling unit as
integral part of the machine. Example of
this is rice transplanter, combine harvester,
etc.

☐ Self-Driven or Autonomous
An implement that is equipped
with integrated systems,
computers, and processors.
Electrical impulses is transferred
into the controller or CPU to
enable the equipment to perform.
Example, drone sprayer, field
mower, etc.
The machine is automated to
perform farming tasks, reduce
labor cost, and improve the
efficiency, yield, and crop quality.
SELF-DRIVEN OR AUTONOMOUS
MACHINE
The main disadvantages are:
high initial cost, limited
capability, dependence n
technology, lack of flexibility,
impact on employment.

(1) Individual operation - Operating one or

(3) Series operation - Causing two or more

(3) Field Patterns

(1) Amount of field travel should be minimum;
(2) Number of non-working turn should be minimum;
(3) Number of non-working travel in interior of field should be
minimum;
(4) Field pattern should produce level surface to eliminate
water ponding; and
(5) Repeated machine travel over a particular area of field will
cause compaction of soil.

An irregular field has less field efficiency than rectangular field.

(5) Field Size
Field efficiency of large field is more than smaller field due to less
time consume in turning the field.
(6) Field Condition
This includes slopy field, type of soil to be processed (example
plowing, harrowing, etc), moisture content of the soil like dry land
farming or wet field and many others.
Therefore it is important to properly select the power source for the
machine and equipment needed in order to properly mechanize the farm.

☐ Crop production and processing play important roles in
producing food for consumption of million Filipinos and of
people around the world.
☐ Agricultural machines for field operation as well as postharvest
processing equipment necessitated information on the required
energy to provide power in performing the tasks to produce the
expected output for which they are designed and used.
☐ Efficient method of energy conversion to power and their
transmission play a vital role in achieving a shorter process
time and cheaper products.
INTRODUCTION
3
☐ Reports revealed that more energy is used during the field
operation than during the processing of the product. In US, 90%
of the total energy demanded is used during the field production
and the remaining 10% is used during product processing.
☐ Knowing carefully the importance of efficiently using energy for a
particular application or task would be significantly helpful in
maximizing the use of the available energy; thus, would result in
a more reduced cost in operating the machines and would
achieve cheaper product.
☐ Below describes some important considerations in achieving a
more desirable efficient operation of agricultural machines. Data
on the various efficiencies of agricultural machines during

OPTIMIZING TRACTOR EFFICIENCY
1. Select AMTEC Test Data as

and other relevant information.

the different makes and models of

2. Properly maintain tractor condition
always. Timely replacement of air
and fuel filters and lubricants can
reduce fuel use while increasing
horsepower. Repair of leaking valve
and piston rings will improve engine
performance and therefore increase
energy efficiency.
3. Reclaim old fuels and oil in one
way to minimize energy use by
using fewer fossil fuels.

generally uses less fuel than full tillage system because the
soil is tilled less intensively and not frequently. These tillage
practices may also allow seedbed preparation, fertilizer
application, and seeding in fewer passes. Such practices are
also eligible for carbon credits.
5. Gear up and throttle back to save on fuel. Make sure not
to overload the engine; excessive black smoke indicates
overloading.

the large tractor. Using tractor to perform operations that
require more horsepower can overload a smaller tractor;

PREDOMINANT MEASURES IN
ACHIEVING ENERGY
EFFICIENCY
☐ Use Diesel Fuel and Engines
They are more advantageous for agricultural
applications because they are capable of
accomplishing a given amount of work with
approximately only 10% or less fuel than
gasoline engines. Diesel contains more
energy per liter and usually less expensive
than gasoline. Diesel engines require less
maintenance. Typically, however, diesel
engine requires more capital investment
than gasoline engine.
13
☐ Match the Equipment with the Operation
Use appropriate machinery for a given task. Tractors are more
efficient when used near capacity. It is desirable to use smaller
tractor for operation requiring lighter load and larger tractors for
operation requiring heavier load.
14

7/22/25
8
☐ Follow Good Maintenance Practices
A little preventive maintenance goes a long way towards improving
efficiency. Tune up engine regularly, clean air filters, clean electrical
equipment, and provide proper lubrication. Insure tractor tires are
inflated to the correct pressure to optimize traction. Keep
implements in good repair. Make sure that the blades are sharp in
order to reduce resistance during field operation.
15
☐ Operate Equipment Properly
Careful operation of the tractor and implements optimizes fuel
efficiency. Make sure that the machinery and controls are adjusted
correctly for the particular operation. Reduce unnecessary idling. It
is more efficient to turn the equipment off during extended breaks
than to run it. Tractor will also work efficiently if the correct tire
tread is chosen for the soil condition.

☐ Use Ballast of the Tractor Correctly
Provide proper ballast for the tractor for a given field condition. If
the tractor is heavier than necessary for an operation, the additional
weight can result in soil compaction as well as decrease fuel
economy. If there is no enough ballast on the tractor, on the other
hand, the wheels are more prone to slip and wear on the tires is
increased. For tractor with insufficient ballast for a particular
operation, adding wheel weights can increase the ballast.
17
☐ Optimize Traffic Patterns on the Field
It is best to reduce the frequency of turns during the field
operation. One way to accomplish this is by traveling lengthwise
along a rectangular field. This will reduce the number of turns
when compared with traveling parallel to the width of short sides.
Also, it is important to eliminate unnecessary overlap while
traversing the field. Reducing turns and minimizing overlap save
both fuel and time.

☐ Balance Yield with Energy Use
The yield is increased by using equipment capable of operating at
higher speeds and with wider implements. Heavy duty equipment is
more expensive and use more fuel than slower, lighter equipment.
The benefits of increased yield need to be balanced with the higher
capital and energy cost associated with heavier tractors and wider
implements.

☐ Combined Operations to Reduce Trips
Over the Field
To reduce fuel use is to combine multiple implements and operation
in one past. In some cases, it is possible to form seedbed, fertilize,
and sow the seeds in a single pass rather than in three passes.

☐ Select Efficient Equipment
The energy efficiency of the equipment being used is an obvious
determinant of fuel consumption per unit output. It is best to
purchase efficient equipment at the outset even though it might
require a higher initial investment than standard equipment.
However, it is important to conduct an economic analysis to insure
that the calculated payback periods are acceptable. Tractors are
often operable for several decades so inefficient equipment can
result in high operating cost that can continue for many years. It is
less cost-effective to replace existing equipment with high-
efficiency equipment before the original equipment has reached
the end of its useful life.

OPERATION
☐ Intake Stroke – Fuel and air or air
alone is sucked into the combustion
chamber as the piston moves in a
downward direction.
☐ Compression Stroke – Fuel and air or
air alone is compressed by the piston as it
moves in upward direction.
☐ Power Stroke – Fuel and air is ignited
to produce power at the downward
movement of the piston and the power is
transmitted to the crankshaft of the engine.
☐ Exhaust Stroke – Fuel is burned and
gas is discharged from the combustion
chamber.
3
Internal combustion engines
(ICEs) convert the chemical
energy of fuel into mechanical
work through a controlled
combustion process inside
the engine. Repair and
maintenance of ICEs involve
a range of procedures,
including routine checks,
replacing worn parts, and
more extensive repairs like
engine rebuilding or cylinder

Operation:
☐ Combustion Cycle:
•ICEs typically operate on a four-stroke cycle: intake (drawing fuel and air
into the cylinder), compression (compressing the mixture), power
(combustion and expansion), and exhaust (removing burnt gases).
☐ Key Components:
•Cylinders, pistons, crankshafts, camshafts, valves, and fuel and ignition
systems work together to create the combustion and convert it into
rotational motion.
☐ Types of Engines:
•Common types include spark-ignition (SI) engines (using gasoline) and
compression-ignition (CI) engines (using diesel fuel).
☐ Power Output:
•The energy from combustion is converted into rotational torque, which is
then transferred to the vehicle's wheels through the drivetrain.
5
Engine Maintenance:
☐ Oil Changes:
•Regular oil changes are crucial for lubricating engine parts, cooling the
engine, and preventing wear and tear.
Frequency of changing oil of farm engines ranged from 50 to 300 hours of
operation
☐ Filter Replacements:
•Replacing air, oil, and fuel filters helps ensure clean air and fuel for the
engine.
☐ Cooling System Checks:
•Maintaining the cooling system (radiator, hoses, etc.) is essential for
preventing overheating.
☐ Spark Plug Replacement:
•Replacing spark plugs helps ensure proper ignition and combustion.
☐ Belt Inspection:
•Regularly inspecting and replacing belts (serpentine, timing) is vital for
engine performance and longevity.

•A comprehensive process of disassembling, inspecting, repairing, and
reassembling the engine to restore its performance.

Regular oil changes, filter replacements (air, fuel, oil), spark plug
replacement, and checking fluid levels are essential.

Damaged gaskets, seals, timing belts, and other components need to be
replaced to maintain engine performance and longevity.
3. Engine Rebuilding:
In cases of severe damage, an engine rebuild involves disassembling,
inspecting, and replacing worn parts to restore functionality.
4. Cylinder Head Repair:
This involves addressing issues with valves, valve seats, and camshafts,
ensuring proper air and fuel flow.
5. Engine Block Repair:
Addressing cracks, scoring, or other damage to the engine block itself.

1. Regular Inspections:

Adhere to recommended maintenance schedules for oil changes, filter
replacements, and other services.
3. Proper Fuel:
Use the correct type of fuel and ensure it's clean and free of
contaminants.
4. Preventative Measures:
Addressing minor issues early can prevent more serious and costly
repairs down the road.

manufacturer.

TROUBLE SHOOTING
Engine troubleshooting involves a systematic process of identifying the root cause
of engine problems, ranging from a check engine light to issues with starting, idling,
or performance. Common problems include those related to fuel, ignition, cooling,
and lubrication.
Troubleshooting Steps:
1.Observe Symptoms: Note any unusual noises, lights, or performance issues.
2.Check Basic Systems:
2. Battery: Ensure it's connected and functioning.
3.Spark Plugs: Inspect for wear or fouling.
4.Fuel System: Check for fuel leaks, blockages, or a weak fuel pump.
5.Ignition System: Inspect ignition coils, wires, and distributors for issues.
Diagnostic Tools: Use a scan tool to read and clear diagnostic trouble codes
(DTCs).
Systematic Checks: Examine each system (fuel, ignition, cooling, lubrication) for
potential problems.
Component Testing: Test individual components (e.g., sensors, relays) using
appropriate tools.
Professional Help: If the problem is complex or you're not comfortable with repairs,
seek professional assistance.
22

7/22/25
12
Common Engine Problems and Solutions:
Difficulty Starting:
May be due to fuel delivery problems (clogged filters, weak pump), ignition issues
(faulty spark plugs or coils), or a starter motor problem.
Rough Idle:
Could be caused by a bad vacuum leak, misfires, or a dirty or clogged fuel filter.
Misfires:
Can be due to a variety of ignition problems (faulty spark plugs, coils, or wiring), fuel
system issues, or problems with the engine's internal components.
Overheating:
May result from a faulty thermostat, radiator, water pump, or a coolant leak.
Oil Leaks:
Can be caused by worn gaskets, seals, or a cracked engine block.
Lack of Power:
May indicate a problem with the fuel system, ignition, or engine's internal components.
Decreasing Fuel Economy:
Could be due to fuel system problems, or issues with the engine's air/fuel mixture.
23
Troubleshooting Tools:
☐ Scan Tool: Reads and clears DTCs.
☐ Multimeter: Tests electrical circuits and components.
☐ Fuel Pressure Gauge: Measures fuel pressure.
☐ Compression Tester: Checks engine cylinder compression.
☐ Vacuum Gauge: Detects vacuum leaks.
☐ Oil Pressure Gauge: Measures oil pressure.
Preventive Maintenance:
☐ Regularly check and replace fluids (oil, coolant).
☐ Maintain proper tire pressure.
☐ Replace worn or damaged parts.
☐ Regularly inspect and maintain the fuel, ignition, and cooling systems.
☐ By following a systematic approach and using appropriate tools, you
can effectively troubleshoot and diagnose common engine problems.
Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs), or engine fault codes, are five-digit codes that
identify specific issues in a vehicle's system. These codes, displayed by OBD-II scanners,
help pinpoint problems within the engine, transmission, and other systems.

GASOLINE ENGINE

engine and it has the tendency to die over a period of
usage. It supplies the spark for the fuel and air mixture to
ignite. Dead spark plug appears corroded with carbon
deposits on its tip.
3. 	Dirty/Clogged Air Filter – If the air filter is too clogged with
dirt and dust, air will not be sufficient in reaching the

exhaust manifold. Check oil level to ensure it is within the

engine to make banging noise.

3. 	Oil supply problem
4. 	Using a wrong fuel
☐ Engine Overheating - It is caused when engine is pushed
too hard and can give rise to a whole host of negative side
effects such as damage to the bearings and crankshaft,
piston expanding and scraping against cylinder walls,
cylinder head swelling, distorting and breaking.
DIESEL ENGINE

left unattended, oil leaks can cause serious diesel problems as
they pose both environmental threats and serious fire risks that

☐ Oil Supply Problem – This stems out from either incorrect oil
use or lack of oil. Using the wrong-type of oil negatively affects
engine parts; whereas, not priming the engine causes it to run
on air rather than on oil, breaking the engine in the process.
☐ Using the Wrong Fuel – Diesel engines are high susceptible to
damage caused by misfueling, which commonly results in either
the need for new diesel engine parts or a completely new
engine altogether. To avoid this common problem with diesel

INTRODUCTION
☐ Internal combustion engine (ICE) is a device that produces
power by burning normally liquid fuel inside the combustion
chamber of an engine.
☐ It is conventionally used as power source for agricultural machines
to perform various tasks in crop production, in poultry and livestock
farms, as well as in fishery mechanization.
☐ In agriculture and fishery mechanization, small single-cylinder
engines are commonly used by farmers, ranging from 3hp to 16hp
gasoline and up to slightly higher hp diesel engines.
☐ Multiple-cylinder diesel engines are commonly adopted for large
applications like tractors, self-propelled combine harvester, and
many others.
☐ Knowledge on ICE would be helpful for ABE especially when
dealing agricultural and fishery mechanization. It serves as
backbone in ensuring proper and efficient operation of the different
agri-fishery machines.
3
TERMINOLOGIES
☐ Internal combustion engine (ICE) - is an engine that burns fuel
and air inside a combustion chamber. It can either be piston or
reciprocating engine, rotary engine, gas turbine, jet engine, or rocket
engine.
• It is a machine used to power tractors, combine harvesters,
and other self-propelled field equipment.
• In farmstead equipment, it is used to drive generator set to
provide electricity for lighting, driving motors, and providing
power for heating and cooling in various processes.
4

7/21/25
3
☐ Bore – refers to the size of the opening of the cylinder which is
almost equal to the diameter of the piston plus the rings.
☐ Stroke – refers to the distance traveled by the piston from the
TDC to the BDC.
☐ Top Dead Center (TDC) – is the uppermost position of the piston
during the compression and exhaust stroke.
☐ Bottom Dead Center (BDC) – is the lowest most position of the
piston during the intake and power stroke.
☐ Engine/Piston Displacement (PD) – is the volume displaced by
the piston in one stroke.
☐ Clearance Volume (CV) – is the volume in the combustion
cylinder when the piston is at the TDC position.
☐ Compression Ratio (CR) – is the ratio of the total volume to the
clearance volume.
5
☐ Mean Effective Pressure (MEP) – is the amount of pressure
generated during the power stroke of engine.
☐ Revolution – is equivalent to one complete rotation of the
crankshaft.
☐ Cycle – refers to the series of events occurring one after the other
in a definite order and repeating the event after the last one has
occurred.
☐ Indicated Horsepower – is the power generated at the
combustion chamber.
☐ Brake Horsepower – is the power available at the drive shaft or at
the crankshaft of an engine.
☐ Friction Horsepower – is the power loss due to friction of piston
and other components of the engine.
☐ Rated Horsepower – is the power of the engine as specified by
the manufacturer.

☐ Specific Fuel Consumption – is the rate of fuel consumed of
an engine per unit brake horsepower.
☐ Idle Speed – is the minimum speed of the engine at no load.
Usually, it runs at around 900 rpm.
☐ Optimum Throttle Opening - is the opening adjustment of the
engine throttle at the best operating condition, which is usually
75% of the total opening.

• Uses spark to ignite the fuel.
• Uses gasoline as fuel.
• Has a carburetor to mix fuel and air.
☐ Compression-Ignition Engine
• Uses high compression to raise the
temperature of the air in a chamber and
ignites the injected fuel without a spark.
• Uses diesel as fuel.
• Uses an atomizer to spray the fuel inside
the combustion chamber of the engine.

• Fuel and oil is mixed in the combustion

• Usually high in speed and light in weight.
☐ Four-Stroke-Cycle Engine
• Produces power in two revolutions of the
crankshaft.
• Fuel is burned inside the combustion
chamber.
• Relatively low in speed and heavy in
weight.

☐ Cylinder Head – houses the valves and the
spark plug or fuel injector, and serves as cover for
the cylinder block.
☐ Cylinder Block – encloses the piston and
confines the expanding gases.
☐ Valves – allow the flow of fuel, of air, or of
exhaust gases.
☐ Piston - is a hollow cylinder with closed top
upon which the expanding gases act and transmit
force to the crankshaft.
☐ Camshaft – actuates the valves through a
rocker arm to open and close during engine
operation.

☐ Piston Rings (compression and oil

wall contact thereby reduce friction losses
and wear.
☐ Piston pin – joins the connecting rod and

☐ Connecting Rod – connects the piston
and the crankshaft. Transmits power from

☐ Piston Pin – Fixes the piston to the
connecting rod. It is removable to facilitate
replacement of piston.

speed at some fixed value while power output
changes to meet demand.

☐ Starting System – responsible for starting-on the engine.
☐ Cooling System – responsible for keeping the temperature of the
engine low.
☐ Exhaust System – responsible for discharging combustible gases
from the combustion chamber.
☐ Transmission System – responsible for transferring the power
generated from the combustion chamber to the drive shaft.
☐ Lubrication System – ensure that lubricants are properly provide to

friction.

☐ Intake Stroke – Fuel and air or air
alone is sucked into the combustion
chamber as the piston moves in a

☐ Compression Stroke – Fuel and air or

moves in upward direction.
☐ Power Stroke – Fuel and air is ignited
to produce power at the downward
movement of the piston and the power is
transmitted to the crankshaft of the engine.
☐ Exhaust Stroke – Fuel is burned and
gas is discharged from the combustion
chamber.

Running Mates
Vertical Engine 	V-Engine	Horizontal Engine
☐ Running mates are pistons that go up and down together in exactly
the same position but of different function. One of them is
performing compression or power stroke, and the other is on the
intake or exhaust stroke.
☐ To find the running mate, simply take the firing order and split it in
half. If firing order is 153624, for example, split it into half (153-624)
then put the second number under the first to get the running mates.
Hence, 1/6, 5/2, and 3/4.

FUEL INJECTION
☐ It is a fuel feeding method for most diesel engines and newer models
of gasoline engines where high-pressure electric pump mixes precisely
measured amount of filtered fuel and air. The mixture of fuel and air is
then sprayed into the cylinders by fuel injectors.

Turbo Chargers
☐ A turbo charger is designed to improve the power output of
an engine beyond its normal operating capacity. A normally aspirated
engine uses a mixture of air and of fuel that is pulled into it from
the vacuum created by the cylinders.
☐ It increases the amount of air injected into the engine, which also
allows more fuel to be injected and increases the power output by 30%.
29
☐ Its function is the same as that of turbo charger, except that it is
engine driven rather than exhaust-gas driven.
☐ Super charger is used in spark ignition (gasoline engines) since the
power from exhaust gases is low as a result of low compression ratio.

☐ When the inlet gases get compressed by the engine compressor,
the temperature of the gases increases which results in its expansion
at the inlet manifold of the engine and reduces the volumetric
efficiency of the engine.
☐ To avoid this, an inter cooler is used to cool the gases coming out of
the compressor which then reduces the volume of the inlet gases and
increases the volumetric efficiency of the engine.

INTRODUCTION
☐ Agricultural tractors have been used to supply power in Philippine
agriculture specifically for field operation like tillage cultivation and
many others.
☐ In early 80s large tractors have been used for rice cultivation.
Because of their weight that cause the development of hard pan,
however, these large tractors became unattractive to rice farmers.
Instead, they sort to till their land using small hand tractors or power
tillers.
☐ The use of large tractors remains for large farm on dry land where
operation becomes more efficient without the problem of bug down.
☐ With the advent of rice combine harvester, power tillers are
rendered unable to till the land; thus, small 4-wheel farm
tractors become attractive and are presently utilized in rice farms.
3
TRACTOR DEFINITION
☐ Tractor is an engineering vehicle specifically designed to deliver a
high tractive effort (or torque) at slow speeds for the purpose of
hauling a trailer or a machinery used in agriculture.
☐ A machine used primarily for traction or for pulling an implement.
☐ A versatile machine and a mobile power source for wide variety of
agricultural tasks.
☐ A machine that can perform both stationary and mobile jobs.
☐ A machine that can pull or tow implement through traction from the
drive wheel and/or pull implement through the draft developed from
its drawbar hitch, or power implement through its PTO drive.
4

FUNCTIONS OF TRACTORS
☐ Pulling machine behind it;
☐ Pushing machine in front of it;
☐ Operating machine mounted on it;
☐ Transmitting power to other machines through the PTO drive;
☐ Raising, lowering, and controlling machines and attachment by
its hydraulic power;
☐ Driving machines through belt power;
☐ Transmitting power through flexible shaft; and
☐ Furnishing power for fast highway transportation and handling.
5
Advantages and Disadvantages
☐ Can work continuously even with heavy load.
☐ Not affected by bad weather.
☐ Can be adapted for draft, belt, or PTO work.
☐ Has considerable range of working speed.
☐ Requires little attendance when not in use.
☐ Readily available when urgently needed.
☐ Requires small storage space.
Advantages
☐ Limited overload capacity.
☐ Requires cash outlay for fuel and lubricants.
☐ Requires the operator to have some mechanical skill for
successful operation.
☐ Under some condition, inflexibility of size of power unit for
economical power production.
Disadvantages

TRACTOR TERMINOLOGIES
☐ 3-Point Hitch: The 3-point hitch is used to attach rear-mounted
attachments like mowers, blades, scrapers, posthole diggers, tillers
and backhoes. It consists of two lift arms and one top link where pins
anchor the implement.
☐ Ballast: An added weight that serves as a counter balance for a
heavy load, such as the one carried in FEL. It is usually found in the
rear of the tractor.
☐ Chassis: The framework that supports the tractor frame and guts
including the engine, transmission, suspension, etc.
☐ Drawbar: A bar on the rear of the tractor used for towing.
☐ Fast Hitch or Quick Hitch: The quick hitch is attached to the
tractor 3-point hitch allowing the operator to easily hook onto
implement, without leaving the tractor seat.
53
☐ FEL (Front-end Loader): A large bucket-like implement attached
to the front of the tractor to lift materials such as rocks, dirt, etc.
☐ Horsepower (HP): The amount of energy the engine takes to lift
550 pounds one foot in one second.
☐ Hydrostatic Transmission: A hydraulically-driven transmission
that offers variable speeds with the use of a foot pedal.
☐ Implement: Rugged, high performance work tools that can be
added to the tractor to increase its job functions.
☐ Powertrain: Transfers the power from the engine to the drive
wheels and to the power take off (PTO). Main functions include
selecting the speed ratios, balancing the power to drive wheels for
turning, and allowing the tractor to reverse.
54

7/21/25
28
☐ PTO (Power Take Off): Used to provide power to an attachment
allowing the attachment to draw energy from the tractor’s engine.
☐ ROPS (Roll-over protective structure): A frame on open station
(non-cab) tractors that provides a safe environment for the operator in
the event of a rollover.
☐ Synchronized Transmission: Allows the shifting of gears on the
move without the gears clashing.
☐ Transmission: A system of gears that determines the speed and
the direction of a tractor.
☐ Zero Turning Radius: The ability of a tractor to turn on a dime;
adding more maneuverability to the tractor.
55
TRACTOR SELECTION
1. Land Holding – Under single cropping pattern, it is recommended
1hp tractor for every 1 hectare land. Example one tractor having
20 to 25hp is suitable for a 20-hectare farm.
2. Cropping Pattern – Generally, less than 1.0 ha/hp where
adequate irrigation facilities are available and more than one crop
is taken. A 30 to 35hp tractor is suitable for a 25-hectare farm.
3. Soil Condition – A tractor with less wheel base, higher ground
clearance and low overall weight may work successfully in lighter
soil but it will not be able to give sufficient depth in hard soil.
56

7/21/25
29
4. 	Climatic Condition – Air-cooled engines are preferred than
water-cooled in very hot areas as well as in high altitude areas.
5. 	Repairing Facilities – Should be ensured that the tractor has a
dealer in the nearby area so repair and maintenance of the
machine will not be a problem.
6. 	Running Cost - Tractor with low fuel specific consumption
should be preferred.
7. 	Initial Cost and Resale Value – Initial cost should not be very
high and the resale value, if later will be sold, should be high.
8. 	Test Report – Result of test report from accredited Test Centers,
like AMTEC, need to be consulted for guidance.

Operation

the product to a level that it can be stored with minimum loss from
spoilage.

from deterioration or spoilage for prolonged storage period.

POWER TILLERS

☐ Machine used to open a furrow, place the

REAPER

STRIPPER HARVESTER

Table of Contents

1. Application, use and management
of various agricultural machines, tools
and equipment used for production
and post-production operations.
a. Agricultural Mechanization
b. Agricultural Machinery
c. Agricultural and Fishery Machinery
d. Agricultural and Food Machinery
e. None of the above

production, harvesting, processing,
storage, manufacture, transportation
and distribution of agricultural and
fishery products.
a. Agricultural and Fisheries
Machinery
b. Agricultural and Aquacultural
Machinery
c. Agricultural and food machinery
d. Agricultural Machinery
e. None of the above

implement for draft animals, and
mechanically-powered machines for
agricultural land development,
production, harvesting and on-farm
processing.
a. Agricultural development
b. Agricultural machinery and
equipment
c. Agricultural mechanization
d. All of the above
4. Equipment designed primarily for
agricultural field operation.
a. Farmstead Equipment
b. Agricultural Implement
c. Agricultural Field Equipment
General Information
d. Self-Propelled Machine
e. None of the above
5. Traction machine designed
primarily to supply power to
agricultural implement and
farmstead equipment.
a. Agricultural Tractor
b. Agricultural Implement
c. Agricultural Field Equipment
d. Self-Propelled Machine
e. None of the above

agricultural operations and is further
classified as towed, mounted and
semi-mounted implement.
a. Agricultural Tractor
b. Agricultural Implement
c. 	Agricultural Field Equipment
d. Self-Propelled Machine
e. None of the above

unit designed to provide both
mobility and power for performing
agricultural operations.
a. Mounted implement
b. Self-propelled machine
c. Trailed-mounted implement
d. None of the above

and Fisheries Mechanization
Development in the Philippines.
a. Republic Act 10600
b. Republic Act 10601
c. Republic Act 10602

and the fishery groups of DA, the ___
was created to prepare, evaluate and
recommend engineering plans for
farm and fisheries machinery.

Mechanization Committee
b. National Agro-fishery
Mechanization Program
c. Bureau of Agricultural and
Fisheries Engineering
d. None of the above

AFMech Law aimed to provide
farmers after-sales service and
warranty, to provide custom farm
mechanization services, and services
on repair and trouble shooting, as
well as to provide training on
maintenance and on proper use of
agricultural machinery and
equipment.
a. Agri-fisheries Machinery and
Equipment Service Centers
b. Farmer’s Machines Service
Centers
c. Farm Machines Service Center
d. None of the above

farm equipment between the
Department of Agriculture (DA) and
qualified farmers’ organization.
a. 50 : 50
b. 85 : 15
c. 15 : 85
d. None of the above

warranty provided by the
assemblers, manufacturers,
importers, suppliers, distributors,
and dealers of agri-fishery
machines under AFMech Law.
a. LGU and BAFE
b. AMTEC and BAFE
c. PSAE and MATEC
d. None of the above
13. The Bureau Director and the
Assistant Director of BAFE were
appointed by the ___.
a. DA Secretary
b. President of the Philippines
c. Board of Directors of BAFE
d. None of the above
14. AFTA means ___.
a. Alternative Fuel Treaty
Association.
b. ASEAN Free Trade Agreement
c. ASEAN Fuel Trade Association
d. None of the above
15. Level of mechanization of rice
and corn farms.
a. 0.92 horsepower per hectare
b. 1.23 horsepower per hectare
c. 2.31 horsepower per hectare
d. None of the above
16. Present farm mechanization
level based on latest survey of
PHILMECH for rice farms (As of
2024).
a. 2.31 horsepower per hectare
b. 2.68 horsepower per hectare
c. 2.77 horsepower per hectare
d. None of the above

17. Which of the following is a
declaration of the policy of AFMech
Law?
a. Promote the development and
adoption of modern, appropriate and
cost-effective and environmentally-safe
agricultural and fisheries machinery
and equipment to enhance farm
productivity and efficiency in order to
achieve food security and safety and
increase farmer’s income.
b. Provide a conducive environment
for local assembling and manufacturing
of engines, machinery and equipment
for agricultural and fisheries
production, processing and marketing.
c. Ensure the quality and safety of the
locally manufactured or imported
machinery and equipment by
strengthening regulation through the
development and enforcement of
machinery and machine performance
standards, regular testing and
evaluation, registration, and the
accreditation and classification of
suppliers, assemblers and
manufacturers to ensure compliance to
prescribe quality standards.
d. Strengthen support services such
as credit facilities, research, training
and extension programs, rural
infrastructure, and marketing services.
e. Unify, rationalize and strengthen the
implementation, coordination of
activities and mechanism on
agricultural and fisheries
mechanization programs and projects.
f. Deliver integrated support services
to farmers and other stakeholders, and
assist them to be able to viably operate
and manage their agricultural and
fishery mechanization projects.
g. All of the above

level.
a. 	Nueva Ecija
b. 	Pangasinan
c. 	Iloilo
d. 	None of the above

a. 	Kalinga
b. 	Nueva Viscaya
c. 	Zambales
d. 	None of the above

a. not capable of being tilled and
planted
b. capable of being plowed and used
to grow crops.
c. a dry land that needs irrigation.
d. None of the above
21. Arid land is a land with ___.
a. scarce of water resources where
crop is difficult to grow.
b. sufficient supply of water for crop
growth.
c. water-logged condition where
crops is difficult to grow.
d. None of the above
22. Factors affecting the level of
agricultural mechanization in the
ASEAN countries.
a. Size of land
b. Labor availability
c. Economic development
d. All of the above
e. None of the above

progress in mechanization, it still
faces challenges in fully mechanizing
agriculture due to ___.
a. Small landholdings
b. Cost of machinery
c. Availability of labor
d. All of the above
e. Some of the above
24. Which of the following is true?
a. Large farms are more likely to
adopt mechanization, as it can be
cost-effective for larger operations.
b. Abundant labor can make manual
work more attractive, potentially
hindering mechanization adoption.
c. More developed countries tend to
have higher levels of mechanization,
as they can afford to invest in
machinery and technology.
d. All of the above
e. Some of the above
25. Agricultural mechanization is
measured in terms of ___.
a. horsepower rating of agricultural
machines being used
b. horsepower per hectare (hp/ha)
applied in farming operation
c. the number of equipment used in
farming operation.
d. All of the above
e. None of the above
26. Which of the following is a key
aspect of farm mechanization?
a. Automation - Replacing human
labor with machines.
b. Increased Efficiency - Reducing
the time and effort required for
agricultural operations, allowing for
faster and more efficient production.
c. Improved Productivity -
Enhancing yields and output through
the use of machinery and
technology.
d. Reduced Labor Costs - Lowering
the need for human labor and
associated costs, especially during
the peak season.
e. Use of various equipment -
Involves a wide range of equipment
from simple hand tools to
sophisticated machinery.
f. All of the above
g. Three of the above
27. Which of the following are the
benefits of mechanization?
a. Increased Food Production -
Enabling to produce more crops in
less time,
b. Reduced Labor Intensity - Less
physically-demanding and relieving
labor shortages.
c. Timely Operations - Allowing to
complete crucial tasks.
d. Improved Crop Quality - Optimize
input use and enhance crop quality.
e. Economic Growth – Increases
productivity and efficiency
f. Sustainable Farming Practices -
Can contribute to more sustainable
farming practices, such as reducing
water consumption and minimizing
soil erosion.
g. All of the above
h. Three of the above
28. Which of the category among
the levels of technology adopted
mechanization?
a. Hand-tool technology
b. Draft-animal technology
c. Mechanical-power technology
d. All of the above

stamp his duly registered seal on
the designs and plans of
agricultural machines ___.
a. after passing the board exam
b. even with expired license
c. only during the validity of his
professional license
d. None of the above
2. Credential issued to applicants
after passing the licensure
examination upon payment of
registration fees.
a. Certificate of registration
b. Professional license
c. Seal
d. All of the above

registrant indicating the registration
number, date of issuance, and
expiry date upon payment of
professional fee.
a. Certificate of registration
b. Professional license
c. Seal
d. All of the above

required to indicate his ___ on the
documents he signs in connection
with the practice of his profession.
a. professional license number

c. professional tax receipt number
d. All of the above

other documents to be used for the
design, construction, test, and
evaluation related to agricultural
engineering ___.
ABE Role in Farm Mechanization
a. will only require the signature of
a licensed Agricultural Engineer
b. will only require the seal of a
licensed Agricultural Engineer

seal of a licensed Agricultural
Engineer

specifications are duly signed and
stamped by an Agricultural
Engineer, ___.

not

d. None of the above
7. Which of the following is not the
role of ABE in farm mechanization?
a. Applying engineering principles
to optimize agricultural processes.
b. Developing and implementing
innovative technologies addressing
challenges like climate change.
c. Promoting sustainable practices
for increase efficiency and food
security.
d. All of the above
e. None of the above
8. ASABE stands for ___.
a. American Society of Automotive
and Biosystems Engineers
b. American Society of Agricultural
and Biological Engineers
c. American Society of Agricultural
and Biosystems Engineers
d. All of the above

9. Which of the following is the
detailed role of ABE in farm
mechanization?
a. Technology innovation by
developing and adapting new
technologies to improve farm
mechanization.
b. Efficiency and productivity by
helping farmers select the
appropriate machinery and
equipment they need.
c. Addressing challenges related to
food security, climate change
affecting agricultural production.
d. Collaborate with farmers,
researches and other stake holders
to develop and implement solution
for farm mechanization.
e. All of the above
f. None of the above
10. Which of the following is not
ABE role in farm mechanization?
a. Develop solutions to water
management, soil conservation, and
pest control, contributing to
sustainable agriculture.
b. Play a role in policy development
and advocacies promoting the
importance of farm mechanization
for agricultural development.
c. Explore renewable energy
sources and sustainable practices to
minimize environmental impact and
reduce cost.
d. All of the above
e. None of the above
11. Who has the ability to apply
engineering design to produce
solutions that meet specified needs
with consideration of public health,
safety, and welfare, as well as
global, cultural, social,
environmental, and economic factors
in agriculture?
a. Agricultural and Biosystems
Engineer
b. Food Engineer
c. Environmental Engineer
d. Aquacultural and Fishery
Engineer
e. None of the above
12. Field of study and application of
engineering science and design
principles for agriculture purposes,
combining the various disciplines of
mechanical, civil, electrical, food
science, environmental, software,
and chemical.

c. Civil Engineering

f. None of the above

g. All of the above

approaches applies to achieving
reduction of drudgery, or tedious
and repetitive manual labor in
agriculture?

machinery that automate or
streamline tasks

methods
c. Improve access to resources
and information
d. All of the above

for tasks like weeding, planting, and
harvesting.

a. Hand-Tool Technology
b. Draught-Animal-Power Technology
c. Motorized Technology

a. 	Hand-Tool Technology

d. 	All of the above

power agricultural machinery.

d. 	None of the above

b. Renewable energy
c. Geothermal energy
d. All of the above

b. 	Productivity
c. 	Efficacy
d. 	None of the above

A tractor, shown below, has the following engine specifications: number of cylinders, 6;
cylinder bore, 0.15 m; piston stroke, 0.20 m; engine speed, 2200 rpm; mean effective

Piston stroke 	- 0.20 m

Transmission efficiency 	- 90% pto, 92% wheel axle, and 81% db

horsepower of the tractor; and (3) tractive efficiency of the tractor wheel.

= 44.7 hp

DHP 	= 100 hp – (58.09)

= [41.9 hp x 100] / 100 hp
= 41.9%

Problem 1
Two hundred (200) liters of water is to be heated from 30° to 80°C in 1 hour. What

= 12 kW

= 16.8 m2

= 14.15 m2

Ten tons of paddy is to be sundried from 20% to 14% wet basis. What is the amount

floor needed if the collection efficiency of the drying system is 60%? Assume a 0.89

Drying Floor Area
Paddy Thickness on the drying
floor

= 10 (0.80) / (0.86)
= 9.3 tons

= 0.7 ton

Thickness of Bed = (10 tons x 1000 kg/ton)/ (580 kg/m3 x 314.6 m2)
= 0.0548 m

The Author:
Alexis T. Belonio is a Professional Agricultural Engineer and a registered ASEAN Engineer. He
finished his Bachelor of Science in Agricultural Engineering and Master of Science degrees from
CLSU. He is a Senior Research Fellow at the Philippine Rice Research Institute, Science City of
Munoz, Nueva Ecija. He served as Affiliate Professor at the College of Engineering, Central
Luzon State University (CLSU), Science City of Munoz, Nueva Ecija and as Adjunct Assistant
Professor at the Departments of Agricultural and Chemical Engineering at the College of
Engineering and Agro-Industrial Technology, University of the Philippines at Los Banos. He was
former an Associate Professor at the Department of Agricultural Engineering and
Environmental Management, College of Agriculture, Central Philippine University, Iloilo City.
Since 1983, he has been deeply involved in teaching, research, technology development, and
entrepreneurial activities related to the field of agricultural engineering. He served as a
Reviewer for the Agricultural Engineering Board Examination at TGIM, CLSU, BUCAF, CBSUA,
SPAMAST, MSU-Gen San, BPSU, and MRI Review Centers in the fields of Agricultural Power,
Machinery and Allied Subjects as well as Agricultural Processing, Structures and Allied Subjects.
He was awarded by the Philippine Society of Agricultural Engineers (PSAE) as the “Most
Outstanding Agricultural Engineer in the field of Farm Power and Machinery”, in 1993. In that
same year, he was named by the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) as the “Outstanding
Professional in the field of Agricultural Engineering”. And in 1997, he was awarded by the TOYM
Foundation and the Jerry Roxas Foundation as the “Outstanding Young Filipino (TOYF) in the field
of Agricultural Engineering”. In 2008, he was awarded as “Associate Laureate of the Rolex Awards
for Enterprise ” (Geneva, Switzerland) and in 2010 as a “Laureate in Economic Business
Development Category of The Tech Awards” (San Jose, California). He was adjudged as one of the
“Inspiring Modern-Day Filipino Heroes” by Yahoo Southeast Asia in 2011 and one of the “25
Heroes-for-Better” by the Western Union in 2015. Recently, he has received the “2016 ASEAN
Outstanding Engineering Achievement Awards” given by the ASEAN Federation of Engineering
Organizations (AFEO).
As a dedicated professional, he is technically assisting various agricultural companies in the country
and abroad. He has written and published several research and technical papers, technical
handbooks, including instructional and review materials.

At all times from start to full speed, the torque supplied by
the motor > than that required by the load.
If the load torque becomes higher than the motor torque,
the motor will stall.

Service factor indicates the maximum load that can be successfully

BIOGAS PLANT AND ITS
COMPONENTS
1.Input of Feedstock: Collects organic waste (dung, food scraps,
crop residues) and mixes with water.
2.Mixing Tank: Chops and mixes feedstock into slurry; removes
non-biodegradables.
3.Inlet Tank: Creates oxygen-free zone for microbes to digest
organics and produce biogas (CH₄, CO₂).
4.Gas Storage: Stores, compresses, and purifies biogas in
pressurized tanks.
5.Outlet Tank: Collects leftover slurry for use as organic fertilizer.
6.Control & Monitoring: Tracks temperature, pH, gas quality, and
feed to keep the plant efficient and reliable.

text:
Feasibility Study
Design
Prepared by:
Keno Jay M. Balogbog, PhD
Full Professor VI
Director, Extension Services Office

What is the difference between
conducting feasibility study and
writing a business plan?

Feasibility Study
➢ is an exploratory and evaluation tool used
to determine whether an intended venture
/business idea is viable/profitable or not
➢ it is a tool that systematically explores
whether a given idea will work and whether
it should be pursued further for
implementation.

Feasibility Study
➢ systematic exploration is done based on
information acquired regarding the various
resources that go into the undertaking
associated with a certain idea.
➢ the evaluation is done based on past and
existing information that are projected into
the future. The resulting evaluation will
serve as a basis of deciding whether the
proposed idea is to be pursued or not.

Feasibility Study
➢ as an evaluation and exploratory tool, the
feasibility study finds wide uses for a
variety proposed ideas; from the
introduction of a new business, the adoption
of new methods, a change in organizational
structure, the adoption of new technology,
or to simply choose from various
alternatives.

Feasibility Study
➢ if you are having an idea for business
venture, then the feasibility study will be
your first recourse.
➢ by conducting feasibility study, you will be
on your first step towards putting your
business ideas towards reality.
➢ through a feasibility study, your idea starts
to become real. Things that are real are
easier to deal with, than when they are
unreal.

Source: DA Memo Order No. 29 Series of 2019

Advantages in Preparing
Feasibility Study
1. It offers means of determining whether
valuable resources may be committed in an
undertaking
2. It reduces the potential risk of failure for
an undertaking
3. It allows for the identification of critical
issues and critical resources in an
undertaking

Disadvantages in Preparing
Feasibility Study
1. It requires technical knowledge
2. It requires initial expenses
3. It requires time and effort

Uses/Purpose of Feasibility
Study
a. to evaluate the profitability of a new
businesses
b. to evaluate the benefits gained in the
expansion of a business
c. to evaluate the financial impact for
changes in business location

Uses/Purpose of Feasibility
Study
d. to evaluate the benefits from the new
methods of production, technology, or
machinery
e. to evaluate changes in an organization
f. to evaluate benefits from business mergers
or business acquisition

Preparation
➢ Inasmuch as the feasibility study will serve
as a basis for making a decision about the
viability/profitability of a given business
undertaking, then the information contained
in it must have the following characteristics;
a. accuracy
b. reliability
c. timeliness

Sources of Data
1. Primary
2. Secondary

Sampling Techniques
1. Scientific sampling (probability sampling)
- a sampling technique where each element of the
population has a fixed probabilistic chance of being
selected for the sample.
2. Nonscientific sampling (non-probability sampling)
- a sampling technique where the samples are
gathered in a process that does not give all the
individuals in the population equal chances of being
selected.

Probability Sampling Techniques
1. Simple random sampling
2. Systematic sampling
3. Stratified sampling
4. Cluster sampling
a. area sampling
b. multistage

Non-probability Sampling
Techniques
1. Convenience sampling
2. Judgmental sampling
3. Quota sampling
4. Snowball sampling
5. Purposive sampling

The Research Instrument
➢ is a tool for consistently executing a
scientific procedure for obtaining data
from respondents.
➢ it includes questions that address specific
study objectives and may also be used to
collect demographic information for
calculating survey weights.

Validation of the Instrument
✓ validating the survey instruments requires
atleast ten (10) representatives of the
samples.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
✓ it should be the first thing in the feasibility
study, after the Table of Contents.
✓ it consist of;
1. Business structure and ownership
2. Products or services being sold
3. How and who to market?
4. Positive viewpoint

If the FS will be used to apply for loan,
the following must be included:
1. How much money to request?
2. How much money does the owner of the startup
business already have invested or will invest on his
own?
3. How it will the money be used?
4. How money will help start or grow the business?
5. How long before the proposed feasibility study be
able to pay back the money?

Business Description
✓ allows getting ideas, plans and visions
down on paper before going any further
with the startup business.
✓ mainly to provide an outline of what will
be further explored in the feasibility study.

Mission statement
✓ Express what the startup business will do.
✓ Explain how the startup business will do it
✓ Add the reason why
✓Implement mission statement

Vision Statement
✓ it describes the startup business views in the
future. It is inspirational in nature
✓ Study the mission statement
✓ Challenge the business dream
✓ Shape the vision statement; apply the formula
✓ Commit to the vision statement
✓ Keep your vision statement alive

Product/Service Description
3 Types of Product Uniqueness
1. Simple – based on variety of
characteristics
2. Horizontal – based on a single
characteristic but consumers are not clear
on quality
3. Vertical – based on a single characteristics
and consumers are clear on its quality

Methods in Making a Detailed
Product Description
1. The N – S – P - P – USP Model
N – Need
S – Situation
P – Person
P - Product Description
USP – Unique Selling Proposition

Methods in Making a Detailed
Product Description
2. BAFF Matrix
B – Benefits
A – Advantages
F – Features
F - Functions

Product Upgrading/Product Line
Expansion
1. Life Cycle
2. Market Opportunities
3. Customer Needs
4. Customer Loyalty

Target Market
B2B vs B2C

Common Measures for Target Markets
(B2B)
1. Geographic target market segmentation
2. Firmographic target market segmention
3. Psychographic target market segmentation
4. Need-driven target market segmentation

Common Measures for Target Markets
(B2C)
1. Demographic factors
2. Psychographic factors
3. Behavioral factors (frequency of purchase,
shopping behavior, etc)
4. Consumer lifestyles (consumer trends)

6 Basic Parts of a Feasibility
Study
1. Project Summary
2. Market Feasibility
3. Technical Feasibility
4. Financial Feasibility
5. Socio-Economic Feasibility
6. Management Feasibility

Introduction
• Introduce what your proposed project is all about and
where to be established
• The name of the project
• The potential of the project (could also include
potential of the industry)
• Importance and objectives of establishing the proposed
project
• Project Timetable
timetable of activities from project conceptualization to
start of project implementation

I. Project Summary
Market Feasibility
– Summary of your market study
– establish the trend/behavior of demand and supply
– establish the demand and supply situation to show whether the
project is assured of its market (unsatisfied demand figures)
– establish price trend
- who will be the target market of your product
Technical Feasibility
– Summary of your technical study
– availability of raw materials
– accessibility of the area to the source of raw materials and
market

Financial Feasibility
– initial capital investment
– results of the financial analysis to show whether proposed project is
financially feasible and profitable (ROI, BCR, NPV, IRR, Payback Period)
Organization and Management Feasibility
– form of business enterprise to be organized
– manpower requirement
– qualifications and responsibilities of the people who will be involved
in the project
Socio-Economic Feasibility
– the benefits the project can give to the owner(s), workers and the
community as a whole
– a need in the community that the project can address (if there are any)
– the benefit(s) it can give to the government

II. Market Study
Product
✓what is the final product of the proposed project
(popular
& scientific)
✓what are the market characteristics of the product
✓why would consumers prefer to use/consume the
product
✓uses of the product
✓who will be the users of the product

II. Market Study
Demand
✓historical and projected demand data
✓establish trend of the demand
✓discuss its implications
Supply
✓historical and projected supply data
✓establish trend of the supply
✓discuss its implications

Demand Analysis
✓ is making a numerical evaluation of the
market and the segments of the market that
you have defined in the ff. areas;
1. Potential demand
2. Actual demand
3. Future demand
4. Evolution of demand

Demand and Supply Analysis
– historical and projected unsatisfied
demand (demand gap)
– establish trend of the unsatisfied
demand
– discuss its implications
Price Study
– historical and projected prices
– establish trend of the price
– discuss its implications

Competition and Industry Analysis
Factors to consider in analyzing competition:
1. Financial resources
2. Staff
3. Products
4. Service
5. Market share
6. Pricing
7. Customers
8. Financial data
9. Brand recognition

Industry Analysis
➢ is the collection of competitors that
produces similar or substitute products or
services to a defined market.
➢ an assessment of the profitability of an
industry
➢ describe the driving forces of competition
within an industry.
➢ SWOT Analysis

Marketing and Sales Strategy
Product Strategy:
1. Who is the product aimed at?
2. What benefit will customers expect from
it?
3. What will be its advantage over competitor
products? Or its unique selling point?
4. How does the firm plan to position the
product within the market?

Place Strategy
1. Convenient for the customer and the
business
2. Accessible for the customer if it is the
place where the product is sold
3. Low cost or free for the customer if it is
the place where the product is sold
4. Reasonable cost to the business

Pricing Strategy
1. Fixed and variable costs
2. Competition
3. Company objectives
4. Proposed positioning strategies
5. Target group and willingness to pay

Promotion Strategy
1. Advertising
2. Public Relations
3. Sales Promotion
4. Personal Selling
5. Direct Mail
6. Internet marketing
7. Sponsorship

Additional 3 elements
✓ People strategy
✓ Process strategy
✓Physical evidence

Factors Affecting the Market
– discuss specific factors affecting the market of the
product
– discuss its implications
Marketing Program
– who will be the market of the product
– manner of disposal
– frequency of disposal
– volume of disposal
– manner of payment
– marketing strategies to be employed to assure
market of the product
– channel of distribution (diagram)

III. Technical Study
Project Location
– where will you establish the proposed project
– accessibility of the area to the source of raw
materials and market
– location map
Project Lay-out
– lay-out of the proposed project

The Product
– describe the product to be
produced/manufactured or service to be
offered
Source (s) of Raw Materials
– Indicate sources where you can avail/buy
your raw materials for the project
Project Size and Yield
– Production capacity (production schedule)

Production/Manufacturing/Service Process
– Detailed discussion of the cultural
management practices/production process,
manufacturing or service process of the
proposed project
Fixed Asset Requirements
– List of fixed assets the project will need
(land, buildings, farm facilities/machineries,
etc)

IV. Financial Study
Major Assumptions
– All financial assumptions which serve as your basis in
computing the incomes and expenses of the proposed
project
Total Project Cost
– The initial investment the project will need to start
until its first harvest/production
Details of Costs
– All schedules of costs associated with the proposed
project

Financial Statements
Projected Cashflow Statement
– Projected cash inflows and cash outflows
Projected Income Statement
– Projected incomes and expenses
Projected Balance Sheet
– Projected assets, liabilities and owner`s equity
Financial Analysis
ROI
BCR
NPV
IRR
Payback Period

Financial Ratios and Analysis
Liquidity Ratios
- Measure the short term solvency of
financial position of a firm
a. Current ratio
- Is the ratio of current assets of a business to
its current liabilities
Current ratio = Current assets / Current
Liabilities

b. Acid test ratio
- Is the ratio of liquid assets to current
liabilities
Acid test ratio = Liquid assets / current
liabilities
c. Working capital
- Is a measure of liquidity of a business.
Working capital = Current assets – Current
liabilities


Stability/Solvency
➢ is the long term counterpart of
liquidity.
➢ investigates how much debt can
be supported by the company and
whether debt and equity are
balanced.

a. Debt-to-asset ratio
- Is a measure of the relationship between the
capital contributed by creditors and the
capital contributed by shareholders.
Debt to equity ratio = Total debt / Total equity
b. Debt-to—equity ratio
- Indicates the relationship between the
external equities or outsiders funds and the
internal equities or shareholders’ funds.
Debt Equity Ratio = Total longterm debts/
Total longterm funds

V. Organization and Management Study
– Form of business organization the business will
take
– qualifications and functions of all the people who
will be involved in the business
– management capability of the owner-
manager/owner of the proposed project
– skills of the laborers/workers
– Labor Requirements (number of workers the
project will need; number of mad/md required for
the production operations
– Organizational structure

Types of Business Ownership
1. Sole Proprietorship
2. Partnership (General)
3. Corporation
4. Cooperative

VI. Socio-Economic Study
– what the project can contribute to its owner(s), workers
and the community as a whole
– a need in the community that the project can address
(if there are any)
– The benefit it can give to the government
VII. Conclusion and Recommendation
– Based on the five major aspects of your study, discuss
the feasibility of the proposed project in terms of
market, technical, financial, organization and
management, and socio-economic.
– Recommendations to efficiently and effectively
implement the project

5 FEASIBILITY INDICATORS for both financial and
economic analyses in Feasibility Studies, ranked by
importance:
1. Net Present Value (NPV)
2. Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
3. Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR)
4. Return on Investment (ROI)
5. Payback Period

Measurement of economic
desirability, sensitivity analysis
and selection of projects based on
economic feasibility indicators

Economic Internal Rate of
Return (EIRR)
➢ defined as the discount rate which
equates the net present social value
(NPSV) of the benefits and costs of
the project such that the NPSV is
zero and the benefit cost ratio
(BCR) is one.

Net Present Social Value (NPSV)
➢ is the discounted net economic
benefit accruing to the project. The
decision rule is to accept projects
where the NPV is greater than
zero.

Benefit Cost Ratio (BCR) &
Return on Investment (ROI)
➢ According to Brinkerhoff (1991), ROI
(Return on Investment) is the ratio
between the cost of a program and the
value (monetary) of its outcomes.
BCR = Program Benefits ⁄ Program Costs
ROI = Net Benefits ⁄ Program Costs X 100


Example:
BCR = Program Benefits ⁄ Program Costs
= 82,050 ⁄ 59,717 = 1.37
➢As this calculation shows, for every 1peso
invested returns 1.37 in benefits.
Thus, the ROI would be:
ROI = Net Benefits ⁄ Program Costs X 100%
Where, Net Benefits = Program Benefits – Program Costs
= 82,050 – 59,717 ⁄ 59,717 X 100 = 37.4%
➢This means that, for each 1 peso invested in the
program, the ROI is 1.374.

Payback Period – a period of
time or number of years wherein
you can recover your initial
investment.
P = Initial Investment/Expected Return
- it can be used only when
your expected return is the
same through out the years.

Example:
Investment – 100,000
Return:
1 – 25,000 P = 100,000
2 – 25,000 25,000
3 – 25,000 = 4 years
4 – 25,000
5 – 25,000

2. Return on Investment
(ROI) = Net income x 100
Total Expenses
ROI = 100%

3. Benefit Cost Ratio = Total Income
Total Expenses
BCR = 2

4. Net Present Value
- present value of a future income
- assumes the rate of return is the discount rate
Example: 100,000 – Initial Investment
NPV = P1 + P2 + ………….+ Pn - Investment
( 1 + i) (1 + i )2 (1 + i)n


Another Example of NPV
1. On an investment of 7,407, cash returns have
been estimated as follows:
Year 1 ………………. 3,000
Year 2 ……………… 2,000
Year 3 ………………. 5,000
Present value of cash returns discounted at 12%


Net Present Value – Uneven Cash
Returns
Net Present Value:
Present value of cash returns discounted
at 12%
Year 1: 3,000 x .893 = 2,679
Year 2: 2,000 x .797 = 1,594
Year 3: 5,000 x .712 = 3,560
7, 833
Less – Investment 7, 407
Net Present Value 426

5. Internal Rate of Return
(IRR)
- it is the actual rate of return.
- your marginal efficiency of capital.
- it is a trial and error method in solving
the IRR.

Example:
Investment = 50,000
