Socio-Economic Appraisal
(DEPDEV)
The economic appraisal of projects shall be made to ascertain
the project’s desirability in terms of its net contribution to the
economic and social welfare of the country as a whole. It
shall consider the following;
1. Economic Costs
➢ The basic guidelines in identifying the costs of a
project stems from the definition of cost itself, or
activities that involve use of real resources. Cost
items are usually classified into capital costs and
operating and maintenance costs .

Capital Costs
➢ include land; detailed engineering design;
preparatory installation work; cost of
equipment; raw materials and supplies for
construction; cost of buildings and auxiliary
installations; engineering and administrative
cost during construction, organization cost;
Operating and Maintenance Costs
➢include raw materials and other supplies;
energy and fuels; labor; rent and insurance;
depletion of natural resources.

Sunk costs
➢ are defined as all those costs incurred on
the project prior to the preparation of the
feasibility study. Since these expenses have
already been incurred, they shall no longer
be subject to investment decision-making.
As such, this component of project cost
should not be included in the analysis.

2. Benefits
➢ A benefit constitutes an increase in output
or savings in resource use. To the extent
possible, the effects of all benefits on
national income should be quantified (e.g.,
value of each human life saved in terms of
the capacity to earn during productive life);

3. Externalities
➢ In several instances, project effects may be
positive or negative and extend beyond the
contours of the project, but not reflected in
the financial analysis of the project. If these
effects, known as “externalities,” involve a
significant economic cost or confer a
significant economic benefit, these should
be taken into account in evaluating the
overall economic impact of the project;

4. Secondary benefits
➢ refer to the beneficial effects on
activities that are technologically
linked to the project’s direct users.
These benefits should, whenever
possible, be incorporated into the
analysis and the appraisal process.

The following parameters provided by DEPDEV
shall be used for estimating the economic stream
of costs and benefits:
1. Shadow Exchange Rate
➢ the shadow exchange rate (SER) is applied to
correct the distortion in the prevailing exchange
rate due to balance of payments disequilibrium
and the projection structure. The SER currently
adopted is 1.20 of the prevailing exchange rate,
and shall be applied to all direct and indirect
foreign exchange costs of a project and those
benefits which may be expressed in foreign
exchange;

2. Shadow Wage Rate
➢ the shadow wage rate (SWR) is
used to reflect the true economic
value of labor employed in a project.
The SWR is applicable only to the
unskilled labor component of wages
paid and is currently estimated at
60% of legislated wage rates

3. Social Discount Rate
➢ shall be used to discount the stream of
economic costs and benefits to their present
values. It is the rate at which the social value
of project costs and benefits decline over time.
The SDR, currently set at fifteen (15%)
percent or as may be changed, amended or
updated, shall likewise be used as the hurdle
rate for a project’s EIRR

RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering
refers to the application of engineering science and designs to the
processes and systems involved in the sustainable production,
post production and processing of safe food, feed, fiber, timber
and other agricultural and biological materials
and the efficient utilization, conservation, and management of
natural and renewable resources in order to enhance human
health in harmony with the environment.
Agricultural and biosystems consist of crops, forestry and other
plants, poultry, livestock, fisheries and aquaculture resources and
other animals, wildlife and other living things;

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer
refers to a person who is registered and licensed to practice
agricultural and biosystems engineering in the country and
who holds a valid certificate of registration and professional
identification card from the Board of Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineering and the PRC;

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Agricultural and Biosystems Power and Machinery
refers to farm power and machinery for the production,
harvesting, processing, storage, manufacture, preserving,
transporting and distribution of agricultural and biological
products/materials and includes, but is not limited to, tractors
and their attachments, power tillers, seeders, transplanters,
windmills, harvesting machines, crop protection and
maintenance equipment, irrigation equipment and accessories,
greenhouses and other thermal conditioning equipment,
livestock, poultry, fishery and forest equipment, slaughtering
equipment, meat/fishery and crop processing equipment, post
harvest machines such as milling machines, dryers, threshers,
grain and other strippers, agricultural transport machinery and
storage;
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Agricultural and Biosystems Buildings and Structures
Agricultural and Biosystems Buildings and Structures refer to
buildings and structures for the production, harvesting,
processing, storage, manufacture, preserving, transporting and
distribution of agricultural and biological products/materials and
includes, but is not limited to, silos and its components,
agricultural and biosystems machinery and equipment sheds,
farm houses, green/screen houses, poultry houses, piggery
houses, slaughterhouses, farm-to-market roads, farm bridges,
agricultural and biological products storage/warehouse,
buildings and structures for poultry, livestock, fishery, and
forestry production and processing, kiln drying and lumber
treatment structure, farm equipment, farm supplies, and other
structures such as self-feeders, and soil and water conservation
structures;
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Agricultural and Bioprocessing
refers to local activity or series of activities to maintain or raise
the quality or change the form or characteristics of agricultural,
fishery, forestry and biological products/materials and includes,
but is not limited to, cleaning, sorting, grading, treating, drying,
dehydrating, grinding, mixing, milling, canning, dressing,
slaughtering, freezing, pasteurizing, conditioning, packaging,
repacking, transporting of agricultural, fishery, forestry and other
biological products/materials;
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Agricultural and Biological Waste Utilization and Management
refers to the development of systems, processes, and
equipment for agricultural waste disposal and utilization and
environment-friendly technologies such as, but is not limited to,
compost plants, biogas plants, biomass utilization technologies,
systems and processes;
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Agricultural and Bio-Information System
refers to utilization of information systems, database, and other
information management tools for agricultural use, biological
systems modeling to understand the mutual response between
life and the environment; and application of Geographic
Information System (GIS) technology for inventory, analysis, and
management of agricultural and biological resources, and
remote sensing technology for observation and examination of
the landscape and its local forms and agricultural activities;
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Agricultural and Biosystems Automation and Instrumentation
refers to the use and application of agricultural and biosystems
sensors such as, but is not limited to, computer models for
control and automation in the agricultural and fishery production
industry and the biological systems and likewise, robotics for
farm operation when use of machines are difficult or impossible,
agricultural and biosystems machine design and automated
controls, precision farming systems, agricultural safety and
controlled-environment agriculture; and the development and
application of metrology equipment such as moisture meters,
weighing scale and other metrology equipment;
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Agricultural and Biosystems Resource Conservation and
Management
refers to measures of conservation and proper management of
agricultural and biological resources such as, but is not limited
to, area development for agriculture, settlement and recreation;
parks and plant nurseries; beneficial ecosystem of life and
environment; study and analysis of agricultural system as an
integrated component of landscape; monitoring and
conservation of natural resources; rehabilitation of forest, lakes,
rivers and idle lands; and the sustainable development,
management, and exploitation of the agricultural ecosystem;
RA 10915 – Sec. 4. Definition of Terms

RA 10915 – Sec 27. Seal and Use of Seal
The seal shall be circular in shape with 42mm diameter, drawn with dodecagon 5
mm inward measured from circumference to one of its sides. Top and bottom sides
of the dodecagon shall rest horizontally straight.
A 5 mm width rectangular band shall
be drawn horizontally across the
middle part of the seal with end
points resting on the dodecagon.
The name of the Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineer shall be written, all in
capital letters, at the upper part of the seal,
middle center in between the circle and the
dodecagon. Two dots shall be placed
before and after the last name.

BIOSYSTEMS ENGINEER” shall be
written at the lower part of the seal

RA 10915 – Sec 35. National Career Progression and
Specialization Program
There shall be an institutionalized national agricultural and biosystems
engineering career progression and specialization program to be formulated by
the Board in consultation with the AIPO, Civil Service Commission and
concerned government agencies:
Provided, That any agricultural and biosystems engineer before being allowed
to work in specialty areas to perform beyond generalist function or have specific
specialties, must finish the formal education or training towards specialization,
possess recognized practice competencies and must be certified by the Board
and must be a member of a relevant and accredited agricultural and biosystems
specialty organization; Provided, further, That agricultural and biosystems
engineering specialty organizations shall be recognized and certified by the
Board.

(j) Forest Engineering;

RA 10915 – Sec 40.
Continuing Professional Development (CPD)
The Board and the Commission, in consultation with the academe, AIPO,
concerned government agencies and stakeholders, shall prescribe guidelines in
the implementation of the CPD programs for agricultural and biosystems
engineers. The CPD for every agricultural and biosystems engineer registered
under the PRC is hereby made mandatory for the practice of the profession.
The CPD credit units earned by the professional shall be required in the
renewal of professional license and accreditation systems for advance level of
practice and for ASEAN Chartered Professional Engineers, Asia-Pacific
Economic Cooperation (APEC) Engineers and other international
accreditations.
The CPD credit units earned by an agricultural and biosystems engineer shall
likewise be applied as the training requirement for promotion for positions in
government agencies and private firms and for teaching positions in academic
institutions, and shall be accumulated subject to credit transfer under the
Pathways and Equivalencies of the Philippine Qualification Framework.

Sec. 2 Duties and Responsibilities
1. Act with fidelity, fairness, and impartiality to their
clients/employers;
2. Uphold the honor and dignity of the Agricultural and Biosystems
Engineering profession and avoid connection with any enterprise
or individual with questionable character;
3. Be ready to apply their technical knowledge for the benefit of
mankind and the agri-fisheries modernization and agro-industrial
development of the country;
4. Be fair, professional, and prudent in his dealings with fellow
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers.
The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards for AB Engineers

Sec. 3 Professional Life of Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineers
All AB Engineers shall endeavor to make the ABE profession
effective, relevant, competitive and dignified through the sharing
of information and experiences with other ABEs and ABE
students,
as well as through their active participation, support and
contribution to the programs, projects, and activities of ABE
societies/associations, schools, and other related organizations.
The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards for AB Engineers

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Sec. 3 Professional Life of Agricultural and
Biosystems Engineers
In the pursuit of this endeavor, they shall:
a) Not advertise their work or represent themselves as well as their
qualifications/credentials in a self-laudatory manner;
b) Avoid engaging in any activity or practice that would taint or be
detrimental to the interest, dignity and honor of the profession;
c) Strive to continuously update and enhance their professional
knowledge, skills and competitiveness through their active and
meaningful participation in the Continuing Professional
Development (CRD) programs required by the CRD Council for
Registered Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers and the
Board.
The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards for AB Engineers

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Sec. 4 Relations with the Public
All Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers shall endeavor to establish
and maintain good public relations and, accordingly, shall:
a) Endeavor to disseminate public knowledge on Agricultural and Biosystems
Engineering, and to discourage, if not curb, the spread of untrue, unfair and
exaggerated statements regarding Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering;
b) Have direct responsibility for safeguarding the life and health of the public and
employees who may be affected by their work for which they are responsible;
c) Express only such opinions, that are founded on adequate knowledge and honest
conviction when serving as a witness before a court, commission, or other tribunal;
d) Not make statements, criticisms or opinions affecting the public or the profession,
which are motivated by personal or private interest, unless they indicate on whose
behalf they are making such statements; and
e) Refrain from publicly expressing opinion on any Agricultural and Biosystems
Engineering-related issue unless they are well-informed of the facts relating thereto.
The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards for AB Engineers

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Sec. 5 RELATIONS WITH CLIENTS AND EMPLOYERS
All Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers shall establish and maintain good
relations with their clients and employers and, accordingly, shall:
a) Act as faithful agents and trustees;
b) Observe proper attire in meetings and in attending to their other related functions;
c) Exercise fairness and justice in the execution of contracts;
d) Make their position clear before undertaking an engagement, particularly when it
requires the use of inventions, agricultural and biosystems engineering apparatus
and equipment, among others;
e) Guard against conditions that are dangerous or threatening to life, limb, or property
in relation to any work for which they are responsible;
f) Disclose clearly the consequences that might arise if deviations from their
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering works or opinion would be overruled by
nontechnical authority;
g) Assist or advise their clients and/or employers on matters pertaining to Agricultural
and Biosystems Engineering and cooperate with other experts and specialists
whenever their client’s and/or employer’s interest will best be served by such
service; and
h) Not disclose any information concerning the business affairs or technical processes
The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards for AB Engineers

Prepared by: B.U.Sioquim	ABE Related Laws, Specs, Contracts & Ethics
Sec. 6 RELATIONS WITH FELLOW AGRICULTURAL AND
BIOSYSTEMS ENGINEERS AND ALLIED PROFESSIONALS
All Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers shall establish and maintain good
relations with fellow Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers and other allied
professionals and, accordingly, shall:
a) Endeavor, either individually or collectively, to protect and uphold the dignity, honor
and prestige of the Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering profession;
b) Ensure that credit for engineering work is given to those to whom credit is properly
due;
c) Maintain the standards of the profession and observe the principles of reasonable
or adequate compensation for those engaged in Agricultural and Biosystems
Engineering work/s, including those employed in subordinate capacity;
d) Endeavor to create opportunities for the professional development and
advancement of the Agricultural and Biosystems Engineers in his/her employ;
The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards for AB Engineers

Sec. 8 Administrative Penalties
The Code of Ethical and Professional Standards for AB Engineers
Any registered and licensed Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer who violates
any provision of this Code shall be administratively liable under R.A. No. 10915.

either the revocation of his/her COR or the suspension from the practice of
his/her profession, but without prejudice to his/her other liabilities under
applicable laws as may be warranted.

METROLOGY
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
Means science of measurements. In practical applications, it is the
enforcement, verification, and validation of predefined standards.
Deals with establishing the units of measurements and their
reproduction in the form of standards
The word metrology is derived from the Greek word ‘metrologia’,
which means measure.

TERMINOLOGIES
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
Inspection is defined as a procedure in which a part or product
characteristic, such as a dimension, is examined to determine
whether it conforms to the design specification.
Accuracy is the degree of agreement of the measured dimension
with its true magnitude.
Precision is the degree of repetitiveness of the measuring process.

Accuracy and Precision
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y

TERMINOLOGIES
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
Repeatability is the ability of the measuring instrument to repeat
the same results during the act of measurements for the same
quantity.
Error can also be defined as the difference between the indicated
value and the true value of the quantity measured.
The ratio of the change of instrument indication to the change of
quantity being measured is termed as sensitivity.

TERMINOLOGIES
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
When successive readings of the measured quantity obtained from
the measuring instrument are same all the time, the equipment is
said to be consistent.
Range is defined as the difference between the lower and higher
values that an instrument is able to measure.

Objectives of Metrology
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
1. To ascertain that the newly developed components are
comprehensively evaluated and designed within the process,
and that facilities possessing measuring capabilities are
available in the plant
2. To ensure uniformity of measurements
3. To carry out process capability studies to achieve better
component tolerances
4. To assess the adequacy of measuring instrument capabilities to
carry out their respective measurements

Objectives of Metrology
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
5. To ensure cost-effective inspection and optimal use of available
facilities
6. To adopt quality control techniques to minimize scrap rate and
rework
7. To establish inspection procedures from the design stage itself,
so that the measuring methods are standardized
8. To calibrate measuring instruments regularly in order to maintain
accuracy in measurement

General Measurement Concepts
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
1. Measurand, a physical quantity such as length, weight,
and angle to be measured
2. Comparator, to compare the measurand (physical
quantity) with a known standard (reference) for
evaluation
3. Reference, the physical quantity or property to which
quantitative comparisons are to be made, which is
internationally accepted

Errors in Measurements
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
A. Systematic Errors
- a type of error that deviates by a fixed amount from the true
value of measurement. These types of errors are controllable in
both their magnitude and their direction. Minimization of
systematic errors increases the accuracy of measurement.
- errors can be due to: Calibration errors, Ambient Condition,
Deformation of workpiece, and Avoidable Errors

Errors in Measurements
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
Avoidable Errors
1. Datum errors - difference between the true value of the
quantity being measured and the indicated value, with due
regard to the sign of each.
2. Reading errors
3. Parallax errors - occur when the sight is not perpendicular
to the instrument scale or the observer reads the
instrument from an angle.

Errors in Measurements
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
Avoidable Errors
4. Misalignment errors - occur due to the inherent
inaccuracies present in the measuring instruments. These
errors may also be due to improper use, handling, or selection
of the instrument.
5. Zero errors - defined as that value when the initial value of a
physical quantity indicated by the measuring instrument is a
non-zero value when it should have actually been zero.

Errors in Measurements
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
B. Random Errors
provide a measure of random deviations when measurements of a physical
quantity are carried out repeatedly.

METHODS OF MEASUREMENT

quantities used to define the quantity

METHODS OF MEASUREMENT
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
1. Direct Method - the quantity to be measured is directly compared with the
primary or secondary standard. Scales, vernier callipers, micrometers, bevel
protractors, etc., are used in the direct method.
2. Indirect method - the value of a quantity is obtained by measuring other
quantities that are functionally related to the required value. Some examples of
indirect measurement are angle measurement using sine bar, measurement of
strain induced in a bar due to the applied force, determination of effective diameter
of a screw thread.
3. Fundamental or absolute method - the measurement is based on the
measurements of base quantities used to define the quantity.

METHODS OF MEASUREMENT
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
4. Comparative method - the quantity to be measured is compared with the known
value of the same quantity or any other quantity practically related to it.
5. Transposition method - involves making the measurement by direct
comparison, wherein the quantity to be measured (V) is initially balanced by a
known value (X) of the same quantity
6. Coincidence method - a differential method of measurement wherein a very
minute difference between the quantity to be measured and the reference is
determined by careful observation of the coincidence of certain lines and signals

METHODS OF MEASUREMENT
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
7. Deflection method - this method involves the indication of the value of
the quantity to be measured directly by deflection of a pointer on a
calibrated scale.
8. Complementary method - the value of the quantity to be measured is
combined with a known value of the same quantity.
9. Null measurement method - the difference between the value of the
quantity to be measured and the known value of the same quantity with
which comparison is to be made is brought to zero.

METHODS OF MEASUREMENT
B A S I C P R I N C I P L E S O F E N G I N E E R I N G M E T R O L O G Y
10. Substitution method - involves the replacement of the value of the quantity to
be measured with a known value of the same quantity, so selected that the effects
produced in the indicating device by these two values are the same.
11. Contact method - the surface to be measured is touched by the sensor or
measuring tip of the instrument.
12. Contactless method - there is no direct contact with the surface to be
measured. Examples of this method include the use of optical instruments, tool
maker’s microscope, and profile projector.
13. Composite method - the actual contour of a component to be checked is
compared with its maximum and minimum tolerance limits.

S T A N D A R D S O F M E A S U R E M E N T S
Classification of Standards
1. Primary Standards- International yard and international metre are examples of
standard units of length.
2. Secondary Standards - standards usually used for calibration purposes
3. Tertiary Standards - reference standards employed by NPL and are used as the
first standards for reference in laboratories and workshops.
4. Working Standards - standards widely used by operators

S T A N D A R D S O F M E A S U R E M E N T S
Line and End Measurements

S T A N D A R D S O F M E A S U R E M E N T S
Line and End Measurements
The end and line standards are initially calibrated at 20 ± ½ ºC. Temperature
changes influence the accuracy of these standards.

S T A N D A R D S O F M E A S U R E M E N T S
Calibration of End Bars
A calibrated metre end bar, which has an actual length of 1000.0005 mm, is to
be used in the calibration of two bars X and Y, each having a basic length of
500 mm. When compared with the metre bar, the sum of LX and LY is found to
be shorter by 0.0003 mm. When X and Y are compared, it is observed that X is
0.0004 mm longer than Y. Determine the actual length of X and Y.
Given: L = 1000.0005 𝑚𝑚
𝑒1 = 0.0003 𝑚𝑚
𝑒2= 0.0004 𝑚𝑚
Lx = 500 mm
Ly = 500 mm

S T A N D A R D S O F M E A S U R E M E N T S
Calibration of End Bars
A calibrated metre end bar, which has an actual length of 1000.0005 mm, is to
be used in the calibration of two bars X and Y, each having a basic length of
500 mm. When compared with the metre bar, the sum of LX and LY is found to
be shorter by 0.0003 mm. When X and Y are compared, it is observed that X is
0.0004 mm longer than Y. Determine the actual length of X and Y.

S T A N D A R D S O F M E A S U R E M E N T S
Calibration of End Bars
A calibrated metre end bar, which has an actual length of 1000.0005 mm, is to
be used in the calibration of two bars X and Y, each having a basic length of
500 mm. When compared with the metre bar, the sum of LX and LY is found to
be shorter by 0.0003 mm. When X and Y are compared, it is observed that X is
0.0004 mm longer than Y. Determine the actual length of X and Y.
𝑳𝒀 = 𝟒𝟗𝟗. 𝟗𝟗𝟗𝟗 𝒎𝒎 𝐿𝑋 = 499.9999 mm + 0.0004 mm
𝑳𝑿 = 500.0003 mm
Therefore, the actual length of X and Y is 500.0003 mm and
499.9999 mm respectively.

Tolerances
L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
the total permissible variation in the size of a dimension, that is, the difference
between the maximum and minimum limits of size.
Limits of size - the maximum and minimum permissible sizes acceptable for a
specific dimension.
Classifications:
1. Unilateral tolerance - when the tolerance distribution is only on one side of the
basic size

Tolerances
L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
2. Bilateral tolerance - when the tolerance distribution lies on either side of the
basic size
3. Bilateral tolerance - when tolerance is determined by established tolerances on
more than one dimension
4. Geometric tolerance
a. Form tolerance - limit the amount of error in the shape of a feature
b. Orientation tolerance - limit the direction or orientation of a feature in
relation to other features
c. Positional tolerance - controls the extent of deviation of the location of a
feature from its true position.

Tolerances
L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
Maximum Metal Limit (MML) corresponds to the lower limit of a hole and higher
limit of the shaft.
Least Metal Limit (LML) corresponds to the higher limit of a hole and lower limit of
the shaft

Fits
L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
the relationship that exists between two mating parts, a hole and a shaft, with
respect to their dimensional difference before assembly.
Classifications:
1. Clearance Fit- the largest permissible diameter of the shaft is smaller than the
diameter of the smallest hole.
2. Interference Fit - the minimum permissible diameter of the shaft exceeds the
maximum allowable diameter of the hole.
3. Transition Fit - the diameter of the largest permissible hole is greater than the
diameter of the smallest shaft and the diameter of the smallest hole is smaller than
the diameter of the largest shaft

Allowance
L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
difference between the maximum material limits, that is, LLH and HLS (minimum
clearance or maximum interference) of the two mating parts.
In a hole basis system, the fundamental deviation or lower deviation of the hole is
zero, that is, the lower limit of the hole is the same as the basic size.
In a shaft basis system, the fundamental deviation or the upper deviation of the
shaft is zero, that is, the HLH equals the basic size.
Hole and Shaft Basis Systems

L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
Tolerances for a hole and shaft assembly having a nominal size of 50 mm are
as follows:
Higher limit of the hole: 50.02 mm
Lower limit of the hole: 50 mm
Higher limit of the shaft: 49.05 mm
Lower limit of the shaft: 49.02 mm
Determine the maximum and minimum clearances, tolerances on hole and
shaft, allowance, and type of fit.
Maximum clearance = HLH − LLS
= 50.02 − (50 − 0.08) = 0.10 mm
Minimum clearance = LLH − HLS
= 50.00 − (50 − 0.005) = 0.05 mm
Tolerance on hole = HLH − LLH
= 50.02 − 50.00 = 0.02 mm
Tolerance on shaft = HLS − LLS
= [(50 − 0.05) − (50 − 0.08)] = 0.03 mm

L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
Tolerances for a hole and shaft assembly having a nominal size of 50 mm are
as follows:
Higher limit of the hole: 50.02 mm
Lower limit of the hole: 50 mm
Higher limit of the shaft: 49.05 mm
Lower limit of the shaft: 49.02 mm
Determine the maximum and minimum clearances, tolerances on hole and
shaft, allowance, and type of fit.
Allowance = Maximum metal condition of hole − Maximum metal condition of shaft
= LLH − HLS
= 50.00 − (50 − 0.05) = 0.05 mm

L I M I T S , F I T S , A N D T O L E R A N C E S
Tolerances for a hole and shaft assembly having a nominal size of 50 mm are
as follows:
Higher limit of the hole: 50.02 mm
Lower limit of the hole: 50 mm
Higher limit of the shaft: 49.05 mm
Lower limit of the shaft: 49.02 mm
Determine the maximum and minimum clearances, tolerances on hole and
shaft, allowance, and type of fit.
Since both maximum and minimum clearances are positive, it can be
concluded that the given pair has a clearance fit.
If both the differences are positive, the fit obtained is a clearance fit, and if
negative, it is an interference fit. If one difference is positive and the other is
negative, then it is a transition fit.

Linear Measurement Instruments
L I N E A R A N D A N G U L A R M E A S U R E M E N T I N S T R U M E N T S
1. Surface Plates - a hard, solid, and horizontal
flat plate, which is used as the reference plane
for precision inspection, marking out, and
precision tooling set-up . (Cast iron, graphite
and glass)
2. V-blocks- are extensively used for inspection
of jobs with a circular cross section which hold
cylindrical workpieces to enable measurement.

Linear Measurement Instruments
L I N E A R A N D A N G U L A R M E A S U R E M E N T I N S T R U M E N T S
3. Depth Gauge- preferred instrument for measuring holes,
grooves, and recesses. It basically consists of a graduated rod or
rule, which can slide in a T-head (simply called the head) or
stock.
4. Combination Set - has three devices
built into it: a combination square
comprising a square head and a steel
rule, a protractor head, and a centre
head.

Linear Measurement Instruments
L I N E A R A N D A N G U L A R M E A S U R E M E N T I N S T R U M E N T S
5. Calliper - duplicates the separation between
the reference point and measured point of any
dimension within their range
6. Vernier instruments - a precision instrument
that can be used to measure internal and
external distances extremely accurately.
7. Micrometer- a C-shaped frame instrument used for making precise linear
measurements of dimensions such as diameter, thickness, and lengths of solid
bodies.
8. Slip Gauge - also known as a gauge block or gage block, is a precision measuring
tool used to calibrate or verify the accuracy of various measurement equipment,

Angular Measurement Instruments
L I N E A R A N D A N G U L A R M E A S U R E M E N T I N S T R U M E N T S
1. Protractor- a basic device used for
measuring angles
2. Sine bars- used to measure angles based on
the sine principle.
- provide the most reliable measurements for
angles less than 15°

Angular Measurement Instruments
L I N E A R A N D A N G U L A R M E A S U R E M E N T I N S T R U M E N T S
3. Spirit Level - a basic ‘bubble instrument’ in which the bubble always moves to the
highest point of a glass vial.
4. Clinometer - instrument, consisting of a level
mounted on a frame that can be turned to any
desired angle relative to a horizontal reference,
- used to measure larger angles than a spirit
level as well as to determine the straightness
and flatness of surfaces

Angular Measurement Instruments
L I N E A R A N D A N G U L A R M E A S U R E M E N T I N S T R U M E N T S
5. Autocollimator - a special form of telescope that is used to measure small angles
with a high degree of resolution.
6. Angle Dekkor - a small variation of
the autocollimator. This instrument is
essentially used as a comparator and
measures the change in angular position
of the reflector in two planes.

SOLID FUELS
S O U R C E S O F F U E L S
ADVANTAGES
- They are easy to transport.
- The production cost is low.
- They are convenient to store
without any risk of spontaneous
explosion.
- They possess moderate ignition
temperature.
DISADVANTAGES
- The ash contents are high.
- They burn with clinker
formation.
- Large proportion of heat is
wasted.
- Their combustion operation
cannot be controlled easily.
- Handling cost is high.

LIQUID FUELS
S O U R C E S O F F U E L S
ADVANTAGES
- Possess higher calorific value per unit mass
- They burn without dust, ash, clinkers.
- Easy to fire and fire can be extinguished easily by stopping
liquid fuel supply.
- Easy to transport through pipes.
- Can be stored indefinitely without any loss.
- They are clean in use and economic to handle.
- Heat loss in chimney is very low due to greater cleanliness.
- They require less furnace space and excess air for complete
combustion

LIQUID FUELS
S O U R C E S O F F U E L S
DISADVANTAGES
- The cost of liquid fuel is relatively much higher as compared
to solid fuel.
- There is a greater risk of five hazards, in case of highly
inflammable and volatile liquid fuels.
- They give bad odor.
- Special storage tanks are required for storing liquid fuels.
- Specially constructed burners and spraying apparatus are
required for efficient burning of liquid fuels.

GASEOUS FUELS
S O U R C E S O F F U E L S
ADVANTAGES
- Clean in use.
- Can be lighted at ease.
- Do not require any special burner.
- Have high heat contents therefore
provides higher temperatures.
- Burn without any shoot, smoke and
ashes.
- Free from impurities found in solid
and liquid fuels.
- Can be conveyed easily through
pipelines to the actual place of
need
DISADVANTAGES
- Very large storage tanks are
needed.
- They are highly flammable; the
fire hazards are possible.

Classification of Combustion
C O M B U S T I O N P R O C E S S
In Premixed Combustion, fuel and oxidizer are mixed at the molecular level
prior to ignition. Examples of premixed combustion include aspirated internal
combustion engines, lean premixed gas turbine combustors, and gas-leak
explosions.

Classification of Combustion
C O M B U S T I O N P R O C E S S
Partially premixed combustion systems are premixed flames with
non-uniform fuel oxidizing mixtures (equivalence ratios). Flames include
premixed jets discharged into a quiet atmosphere, lean premixed
burners with diffusion pilot flames and/or cooling air jets, and
imperfectly mixed inlets.

Classification of Combustion
C O M B U S T I O N P R O C E S S
In Diffusion Combustion, fuel and air enter process separately and are
mixed at the flame front itself either through random molecular motion
or turbulent eddies.

Abnormal Combustion in Engines
C O M B U S T I O N P R O C E S S
Incomplete combustion occurs when too little air is supplied into the
fuel resulting in the production of unburned carbon, which forms CO
instead of CO2.
Vapor Lock/gas lock/ air lock is the partial or complete interruption of
the fuel flow in the fuel feed system as a result of vaporization of the fuel
and the formation of vapor or gas bubbles at some point.
Spontaneous combustion is a type of combustion which occurs by self-
heating (increase in temperature due to exothermic internal reactions),
followed by thermal runaway (self heating which rapidly accelerates to
high temperatures) and finally, ignition.

Abnormal Combustion in Engines
C O M B U S T I O N P R O C E S S
Pre-ignition occurs when the fuel charge is fired too far ahead of
the compression Top Dead Center (TDC) of the piston.
Detonation occurs in the process of combustion of the mixture
within the cylinder after ignition takes place in high compression
engine.
Wild Ping is a variation of knocking surface ignition which
produces sharp cracking sounds in bursts.

Abnormal Combustion in Engines
C O M B U S T I O N P R O C E S S
Run-on occurs when the fuel-air mixture within the cylinder
continues to ignite after the ignition system has been switched off
and usually emits knock-like noises.
Rumble is a relatively stable low-frequency noise (600 to 1200 Hz)
phenomenon associated with deposit caused by surface ignition in
high-compression-ratio engines.

Methods to control Detonation
C O M B U S T I O N P R O C E S S
A. Using cylinder head and piston materials such as aluminum alloys
that provide more heat dissipation
B. Using properly designed spark plugs and locating it on the “hot
region” preferably near the exhaust valve.
C. Using especially treated or so called “doped” or antiknock fuels
D. Reducing or eliminating carbon deposits.
E. Providing more effective water circulation and cooling
F. Using designed cylinder heads and pistons to so shape the
combustion space that the last to burn portion of the charge will be
spread out into a thin sheet and its temperature held down more
effectively.
G. Maintaining the correct mixture of fuel and air and the proper spark
setting and valve adjustment

E U R O E M I S S I O N S T A N D A R D S
The Euro emissions standards are a set of environmental regulations
established by the European Union (EU) to reduce harmful emissions produced
by new vehicles with internal combustion engines.
EURO 1 - mandated the manufacturers to equip new vehicles with catalytic
converters and transition to using unleaded petrol. It established specific limits
for CO emissions at 2.72 g/km, HC+NOx at 0.97 g/km for both petrol and diesel
vehicles, and a PM limit of 0.14 g/km for diesel vehicles.
EURO 2 - For petrol vehicles, the regulation set new thresholds for CO at 2.2
g/km and for a combination of HC+NOx at 0.5 g/km.
For diesel vehicles, the limits were set at 1.0 g/km for CO, 0.7 g/km for
HC+NOx, and 0.08 g/km for PM.

E U R O E M I S S I O N S T A N D A R D S
The Euro emissions standards are a set of environmental regulations
established by the European Union (EU) to reduce harmful emissions produced
by new vehicles with internal combustion engines.
EURO 3 - introduced a separate NOx limit for diesel engines, as well as
individual limits for HC and NOx emissions in petrol engines and revised the
testing process by eliminating the engine warm-up phase to make sure
emissions were measured under more realistic conditions.
For petrol vehicles, the Euro 3 limits were set at 2.3 g/km for CO, 0.20 g/km for
HC, and 0.15 g/km for NOx. Diesel vehicles faced limits of 0.64 g/km for CO,
0.56 g/km for a combination of HC+NOx, 0.50 g/km for NOx alone, and 0.05
g/km for PM.

established by the European Union (EU) to reduce harmful emissions produced
by new vehicles with internal combustion engines.
EURO 4 - introduced particulate emission limits for diesel vehicles, leading to
the adoption of particulate filters for diesel cars.
For petrol vehicles, the emission limits were set at 1.0 g/km for CO, 0.10 g/km

restrictions of 0.50 g/km for CO, 0.30 g/km for a combination of HC and NOx,

Lubricants in engines are substances used to reduce friction and
wear between moving parts, ensuring smooth operation and
longevity of the engine.
Classifications:
Liquid lubricants - most diverse and widely utilized category of
lubrication materials in industrial applications. This group
encompasses mineral lubricating oils, synthetic lubricating oils,
bio-based oils (animal and vegetable), and water-based fluids.
Synthetic lubricant- is a non-naturally occurring product made by
chemical reaction of two or more simpler chemical compounds
which display lubricating properties.

L U B R I C A T I O N S Y S T E M S
Semi-solid lubricants - commonly referred to as grease, exhibit a
unique consistency between solid and liquid states at standard
temperature and pressure.
Solid lubricants - reduce friction and wear through three main
mechanisms, especially in conditions where liquid lubricants fail. First,
compounds like MoS₂ and WS₂ form strong, low-shear films on
surfaces. Second, soft metals such as lead, indium, and silver deform
easily under load, creating protective layers. Third, lamellar solids
like graphite and hexagonal boron nitride use weak interlayer bonds to
form transfer films on mating surfaces that enable smooth motion.

L U B R I C A T I O N S Y S T E M S
Functions of Lubrications
1. To eliminate friction and wear of moving
parts and loss of power.
2. To absorb and dissipate heat.
3. To serve as piston seal.
4. To act as cushion to deaden the noise of
moving parts and absorb shock.
5. To keep the engine working parts clean
and free of dirt, gum, corrosive acids,
and other contaminants.

SAE Viscosity Classification
L U B R I C A T I O N S Y S T E M S
Oil grading system based upon viscosity grade of engine oil taken at 0
and 210oF which indicates how the oil flows at cold and hot
temperatures.
Monograde Oils: Used mainly in stable climate regions (e.g.,
SAE 30 – summer grade; SAE10W – winter grade ).
Multigrade Oils: Suitable for varying temperatures, indicated
as XW-XX (e.g., SAE 15W-40)

What does 15W-40 mean in engine oil?
L U B R I C A T I O N S Y S T E M S
15W-40 is a multigrade oil.
15W: The oil’s viscosity rating at cold temperatures. The lower the
number, the easier it flows in winter.
40: The oil’s viscosity rating at high operating temperatures. A higher
number means it’s thicker at higher temperatures, providing more
protection.
This oil is commonly used in diesel engines and heavy-duty
vehicles.

API Engine-Oil Service Classification
L U B R I C A T I O N S Y S T E M S
Oil classification system which identifies engine oil quality and
performance standards.
API Gasoline Classifications (Current):
SN: High-performance engines (since 2010)
SP: Latest for modern engines, turbocharged support, LSPI
protection
API Diesel Classifications (Current):
CJ-4: Diesel engines with EGR, particulate filters
CK-4: Replaces CJ-4, enhanced oxidation stability

L U B R I C A T I O N S Y S T E M S
Engine Oil Additives
1. Oxidation inhibitor – slows down oil oxidation and protects
bearings.
2. Corrosion and rust inhibitor – eliminates corrosion by forming
unbroken protective film on engine parts or by completely
encircling individual water and acid molecules.
3. Detergents – cleans the engine of carbon and gums
4. Dispersants – cause carbon and gum to remain in suspension in
the oil.
5. Extreme –pressure agents – enable the lubricant to withstand
the unusual high pressure and temperature conditions
developed by hypoid gears. Prevent metal to metal contact.

L U B R I C A T I O N S Y S T E M S
Engine Oil Additives
6. Foam inhibitors – accelerates the breakdown of foam.
7. Pour-point depressants- lower the temperature at which oil will
pour or flow.
8. Viscosity-index improvers- retards the tendency of oil to thicken
as temperature drops.
9. Antiscuff/Antiwear agent – used to form lubricating films strong
enough to carry the load imposed to the engine.

What is Torque?
Torque is the rotational force applied to the crankshaft.
It reflects how much twisting force the engine can produce.
Unit: Newton-meter (Nm) or foot-pound (ft-lbf)
What is RPM?
Revolutions Per Minute: the number of times the crankshaft
completes a full rotation each minute.
RPM tells us how fast the engine is running.

TORQUE, RPM, AND HORSEPOWER
This graph showcases the dynamic interplay between torque and
horsepower as engine speed increases:
Torque (N·m) rises quickly and peaks at a relatively low RPM (~1000–1500
RPM), indicating the engine’s maximum twisting force is available early
in the power band. This is ideal for tractors and heavy-duty applications
that require strong pulling power at lower speeds.
Horsepower (hp), calculated from torque and RPM, continues to climb
beyond the torque peak because it integrates both force and speed. It
reaches its highest point at higher RPMs (~2000–2500 RPM), where
engine speed amplifies power output.
The crossover point, where the horsepower curve overtakes
torque, is a critical marker. It often reflects the optimal
operating range for balancing load efficiency and fuel
economy in field operations.
🚜 Agricultural Implication: Engines tuned for higher torque at lower RPMs
offer:
Superior pulling performance for soil cultivation
Enhanced stability for PTO-driven tasks
Better fuel efficiency under continuous load

ENGINE EFFICIENCY
Engine efficiency measures how effectively an engine converts the
chemical energy of fuel into mechanical energy or useful work. It
reflects energy losses due to heat, friction, incomplete combustion,
and auxiliary systems.
1. Thermal Efficiency
Ratio of useful work output to heat energy input from fuel
Influenced by compression ratio, combustion process, and
engine design
2. Mechanical Efficiency
Ratio of brake power (measured output) to indicated power
(total power generated inside the cylinder)
Indicates frictional losses and mechanical wear

Fuel quality and combustion: Efficient atomization leads to
better combustion.
Lubrication and cooling systems: Minimize friction and
thermal losses.
Load and RPM management: Operating near optimal load and
RPM enhances efficiency.
Maintenance: Clean injectors, valves, and proper tuning sustain
peak performance.

to 	80% 	is 	used 	for 	Continuous 	rating 	and 	90% 	for

Purpose of Ignition System in ICEs
To initiate combustion by igniting the air-
fuel mixture inside the cylinder at the
precise moment, ensuring efficient
engine performance, reduced emissions,
and optimal power output.

Senyor

System
Types of Ignition System in ICEs
1. Conventional (Breaker Point) Ignition
Uses mechanical contact points to trigger a spark
Includes distributor, coil, and capacitor
Now mostly obsolete, seen in older small farm engines
2. Electronic Ignition System (EI)
Replaces mechanical points with electronic sensors
Components: crankshaft position sensor, ignition control module, coil
Delivers precise timing → better fuel efficiency and smoother power
3. Distributor-less Ignition System (DIS)
Uses multiple coils, each serving one or two cylinders
Eliminates distributor → reduces maintenance
Ideal for high-RPM and modern compact engines
4. Capacitor Discharge Ignition (CDI)
Charges capacitor quickly and releases high voltage to coil
Common in small gasoline engines, motorcycles, garden equipment

text:
BASIC SURVEYING
CONCEPTS AND
METRICATION
Prepared by: Engr. Xymel Pearl S. Almocera

SURVEYING
• is the process of measuring the
relative positions of objects
near the earth’s surface.
• It involves making distance
and angular measurements.
• Surveyors use these
measurements to calculate
the position of objects in three-
dimensional space relative to
a known point.
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
Surveying is an essential process for identifying
and mapping the position of terrain.

The main principle of surveying is:
A. Measuring the area directly
B. Working from part to whole
C. Working from whole to part
D. Setting out curves

SURVEYING
Principles of Surveying
• Work from whole to part
• Establish control points
• Measure from known
positions
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
Surveying is an essential process for identifying
and mapping the position of terrain.

It is a type of surveying that treats the surface of the earth
as flat surface. The spheroidal shape is neglected, with
regard to horizontal distances and directions.
A. Hydrographic Surveying
B. Plane Surveying
C. Geodetic Surveying
D. Construction Surveying

TYPES OF SURVEYING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
The type of surveying that takes
into account the true shape of
the earth.
Spheroidal shape is neglected, with
regard to horizontal distances and
directions.

2. This surveying made to determine the length and
direction of land lines and to establish the position of these
lines on the ground.
A. Control Surveying
B. Route Surveying
C. Boundary Surveying
D. Mining Surveying

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON METHOD/NATURE OF SURVEY
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON METHOD/NATURE OF SURVEY
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Control Survey: Made to establish
the horizontal and vertical positions
of arbitrary points.
• Boundary Survey: Made to
determine the length and direction
of land lines and to establish the
position of these lines on the ground.
• Topographic Survey: Made to
gather data to produce a
topographic map showing the
configuration of the terrain and the
location of natural and man-made
objects.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON METHOD/NATURE OF SURVEY
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Hydrographic Survey: The survey of
bodies of water made for the
purpose of navigation, water
supply, or subaqueous
construction.
• Mining Survey: Made to control,
locate and map underground and
surface works related to mining
operations.
• Construction Survey: Made to lay
out, locate and monitor public
and private engineering works.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON METHOD/NATURE OF SURVEY
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Route Survey: Refers to those
control, topographic, and
construction surveys necessary for
the location and construction of
highways, railroads, canals,
transmission lines, and pipelines.
• Photogrammetric Survey: Made to
utilize the principles of aerial
photogrammetry, in which
measurements made on
photographs are used to determine
the positions of photographed
objects.

Chain surveying is best suited for:
A. Hilly areas
B. Forested areas
C. Small open areas with simple details
D. Large areas with undulations

A chain is made of:
A. Steel links
B. Wooden strips
C. Plastic tape
D. Linen threads

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Chain: A chain is one of the
oldest and simplest methods of
making measurements.
• Distances can be measured
using the chain’s length.
Angles can either be
measured directly or
calculated by moving one
end of the chain by a known
distance.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Chain:
• Typically, the area to be
surveyed is divided into
triangles for effective
surveying.
• Used for small areas
• Linear measurements only

The length of a Gunter’s chain is:
A. 20 m
B. 30 m
C. 66 ft
D. 100 ft

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Chain:
Gunter’s chain (also called a
surveyors' chain or Gunter’s
measuring chain) is a measuring
device that was traditionally
used for land measurement. It
was invented by Edmund Gunter
in 1620 to help simplify the
measurement of land and
facilitate calculations of area,
especially in acres.

A prismatic compass reads:
A. Quadrantal bearing
B. Whole circle bearing
C. Reduced bearing
D. Magnetic declination

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Compass- this survey uses
the principle of traversing.
This method does not
requires the need to
create triangles.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Compass- this survey uses
the principle of traversing.
This method does not
requires the need to create
triangles.
• It uses a prismatic compass
for measuring magnetic
bearing of line and the
distance is measured by
chain.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• What does a prismatic compass
read?
• Magnetic bearing: The angle
measured clockwise from the
magnetic north to the survey line
(or the line of sight to the object).
• Whole Circle Bearing (WCB): It
usually reads bearings in the
whole circle system, i.e., 0° to 360°,
measured clockwise from
magnetic north.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Compass
• Measures angles with
magnetic compass
• Useful in rough terrain

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Plain table- The
principle of plane table
survey is parallelism.
They are plotted
directly on paper with
their relative position.
The rays are drawn from
station to object on
ground. The table is
placed at each of the
successive station
parallel to the position
of the last station.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Plain table-
• Direct plotting on field
• Quick, good for
preliminary farm
layout

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Theodolite: A theodolite is a
precise angle measuring
tool. The device is zeroed
using a reference point
then horizontal and vertical
angles can be easily
calculated by pointing the
targeting lens at the
desired object. It is used
with a chain to measure
distances.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Theodolite:
• Accurate angle
measurement
• Used for large-scale farm
layouts

The least count of a vernier theodolite is
usually:
A. 10'
B. 20''
C. 1'
D. 1''

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Vernier Theodolite:
• a type of optical surveying
instrument used to measure
horizontal and vertical
angles with high precision.
• It is called vernier
theodolite because it uses
vernier scales on both the
horizontal and vertical
circles to achieve fine
angular measurements.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Vernier Theodolite:
The least count is the smallest angle that
can be measured accurately by the
instrument.
For a standard vernier theodolite:
The main scale is divided into degrees
(°) and minutes (′).
The vernier allows readings up to 20
seconds (20″) of arc.

This is a special form of theodolite that has a stadia
diaphragm and an anallatic lens. This eliminates the need
for a chain because the distance can be calculated using
the diaphragm.
A. Tachometer
B. Total Station
C. Plane table
D. NOTA

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Tacheometer: This is a
special form of theodolite
that has a stadia diaphragm
and an anallatic lens.
• This eliminates the need for
a chain because the
distance can be calculated
using the diaphragm. This
method has been almost
completely replaced by
using a total station.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Total Station: This is a
theodolite with an
electronic distance
measuring system. With the
EDM, the distances can be
measured without a chain.
This can allow a single
surveyor to capture much
more information in a faster
timeframe.

CLASSIFICATION BASED ON SURVEY INSTRUMENTS
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Total Station:
• High precision
• Fast data collection

LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Levelling (or leveling) in surveying is the process of determining and
measuring the elevation (height) of points on the earth’s surface relative
to a common datum (usually mean sea level), and establishing points at
a given elevation.

LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Level surface: A level surface
is defined as a curved
surface which at each point
is perpendicular to the
direction of gravity at the
point.
• The surface of a still water is a
truly level surface.
• Any surface parallel to the
mean spheroidal surface of
the earth is, therefore, a level
surface.

LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Level line: A level line is
a line lying in a level
surface. It is, therefore,
normal to the plumb
line at all points.

LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Horizontal line: It is a
straight line
tangential to the
level line at a point. It
is also perpendicular
to the plumb line.

LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Vertical line: It is a
line normal to the
level line at a point. It
is commonly
considered to be the
line defined by a
plumb line.

The R.L. of a point stands for:
A. Reduced Level
B. Right Level
C. Relative Location
D. Reference Latitude

COMMON TERMS IN LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Benchmark (BM): A point of
known elevation used as
reference.
• Reduced level (RL): The elevation
of a point relative to the chosen
datum.
• Back sight (BS): Reading taken on
a point of known elevation.
• Fore sight (FS): Reading taken on
a point whose elevation is to be
determined.
• Intermediate sight (IS): Reading
on points between BS and FS
along the survey line.

TYPES OF LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Barometric levelling
• The measurement of elevation
is based on atmospheric
pressure by using a barometer.
• The main principle of
Barometric leveling is the
difference between the
elevation of two points.
• This difference is proportional
to the difference between the
atmospheric pressure of the
points.

The other term of indirect levelling is:
A. Differential Levelling
B. Trigonometric Levelling
C. Spirit Levelling
D. Stadia Levelling

The other term of direct levelling is:
A. Differential Levelling
B. Trigonometric Levelling
C. Spirit Levelling
D. Stadia Levelling

TYPES OF LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Trigonometric levelling
• process of levelling in which
the elevations of points are
computed from the vertical
angles and horizontal
distances measured in the
field, just as the length of any
side in any triangle can be
computed from proper
trigonometric relations.

TYPES OF LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Stadia levelling
• Stadia levelling is similar to
trigonometric levelling.
• To determine the elevation of
points, we use a tacheometer.
• Hence, It is an optical distance
measurement method. This type
of levelling is suitable in hilly
regions.

TYPES OF LEVELLING
Source: https://www.engineersupply.com/The-basics-of-surveying.aspx#:~:text=Defining%20Surveying,relative%20to%20a%20known%20point.
• Spirit levelling
• Direct levelling is also known as
spirit levelling. It is the most precise
and commonly used levelling
method.
• In this method, the vertical
distance is taken with respect to
the horizontal line.
• This determines the relative position
between the points.
Direct levelling is further
divided into:
• Simple levelling
• Differential levelling
• Profile levelling

Fluid Mechanics
&
Hydraulics

Properties of Fluids
Feature Ideal Fluid Real Fluid
Existence Imaginary/Theoretical
(does not exist) Exists in nature
Viscosity Zero (non-
viscous/inviscid)
Possesses viscosity
(internal friction)
Compressibility Incompressible
(density is constant)
Compressible (density
can change with
pressure)
Rotation
Irrotational (no
particle rotation,
smooth flow)
Can be rotational
(leads to turbulence)
Flow Always steady Can be steady or
unsteady
Surface Tension None Present
Energy Loss No energy loss due to
friction
Energy loss due to
friction (viscous
effect)

Properties of Fluids
• Mass Density (ρ)
• Specific Volume (ν)
• Unit Weight or Specific Weight (γ)
• Specific Gravity (S.G.)
• Viscosity (Dynamic Viscosity, μ)
• Kinematic Viscosity (ν)
• Surface Tension (σ)
• Capillarity
• Compressibility and Bulk Modulus (K)

Gas LawsGas Law Relationship Formula Description
Boyle's Law
Pressure is inversely
proportional to volume
(at constant
temperature and number
of moles).
P1V1=P2V2 or PV=k
If you increase the
pressure on a gas, its
volume will decrease,
and vice versa, as
long as the
temperature and amount
of gas remain
constant. Imagine
squeezing a balloon.
Charles's Law
Volume is directly
proportional to
absolute temperature
(at constant pressure
and number of moles).
V1/T1=V2/T2
V/T=k
If you heat a gas, its
volume will expand,
and if you cool it,
its volume will
contract, assuming the
pressure and amount of
gas are constant.
Think of a hot air
balloon.
Gay-Lussac's Law
Pressure is directly
proportional to
absolute temperature
(at constant volume
and number of moles).
P1/T1=P2/T2
0r P/T=k
If you heat a gas in a
rigid container, its
pressure will
increase, and if you
cool it, its pressure
will decrease, as long
as the volume and
amount of gas are
constant. Think of a
pressure cooker.

Gas Laws
Gas Law Relationship Formula Description
Combined Gas Law
Combines Boyle's,
Charles's, and Gay-
Lussac's Laws. It
relates pressure,
volume, and temperature
for a fixed amount of
gas.
P1V1/T1=P2V2/T2
This law is useful when the
amount of gas is constant,
but pressure, volume, and
temperature might all be
changing.
Ideal Gas Law
Relates pressure,
volume, temperature,
and the number of moles
of an ideal gas.
PV=nRT
This is the most
comprehensive gas law and is
derived from the combination
of the simpler gas laws. It
holds true for ideal gases,
which are theoretical gases
that obey certain
assumptions (e.g.,
negligible molecular volume,
no intermolecular forces). R
is the ideal gas constant.
Key:
P = Pressure
V = Volume
T = Absolute Temperature (always in Kelvin, K)
n = Number of moles
k = Constant
R = Ideal Gas Constant (a universal constant R=8.31446261815324 J/mol⋅K )
Subscript 1 refers to initial conditions, and subscript 2
refers to final conditions.

Principles of Hydrostatics
Unit Pressure
- is a foundational concept
representing the intensity of force
distributed over an area (N/m2).

Pascal's Law
First Law: At any point in a fluid
at rest, the pressure of the fluid is
equal in all directions.
Second Law: Pascal’s law states that
when a confined fluid is placed under
pressure, the pressure is transmitted
equally in all directions and on all
faces of the container.

Pascal's
Law

Absolute and Gage Pressure
Feature Absolute Pressure
(Pabs) Gauge Pressure (Pg)
Reference Point
Perfect vacuum
(absolute zero
pressure). This is a
theoretical state where
there are no gas
molecules present,
resulting in zero
pressure.
Local atmospheric
(ambient) pressure.
This is the pressure of
the air surrounding the
measurement device,
which varies with
altitude, weather, and
temperature.
Formula Pabs=Pg+Patm Pg=Pabs−Patm
Value at Vacuum 0 (at a perfect vacuum)
Negative, indicating
pressure below
atmospheric (e.g., -
14.7 psi or -101.3 kPa
at a perfect vacuum at
sea level).
Value at Atmospheric
Pressure
Equal to the local
atmospheric pressure
(e.g., ~14.7 psi or
~101.3 kPa at sea
level).
0 (the gauge reads zero
when exposed to the
atmosphere).

Absolute and Gage Pressure
Feature Absolute Pressure (Pabs) Gauge Pressure (Pg)
Range Always positive or zero.
Cannot be negative.
Can be positive (above
atmospheric), negative
(below atmospheric, also
called vacuum pressure), or
zero.
Units
Often denoted with an 'A'
or 'abs' suffix (e.g.,
psia, kPaa, bara).
Often denoted with a 'G' or
'g' suffix (e.g., psig,
kPa(g), barg). Sometimes no
suffix is used, which can
cause confusion.
Impact of Atmospheric
Changes
Unaffected by changes in
atmospheric pressure.
Provides a consistent, true
pressure reading regardless
of altitude or weather.
Affected by changes in
atmospheric pressure. A
gauge reading will change
if the ambient atmospheric
pressure changes, even if
the absolute pressure of
the system remains
constant.
Common Applications
Scientific experiments, gas
law calculations, vacuum
systems, aerospace,
measuring barometric
pressure, systems where the
true pressure relative to
absolute zero is critical.
Tire pressure, utility
lines, air compressors,
hydraulic systems,
measuring pressure in open
tanks, systems where the
pressure relative to the
surroundings is important.

Variations in Pressure
- It dictates how pressure changes
with depth (hydrostatic pressure), how
atmospheric pressure changes with
altitude, and how pressure changes in
flowing fluids (Bernoulli's principle).
This understanding is crucial for
designing fluid systems, predicting
forces, and ensuring the stability of
structures interacting with fluids.

Pressure Below Layers of
Different Liquids
- Many engineering applications
involve systems with multiple
immiscible fluid layers, such as oil
and water in storage tanks, stratified
reservoirs, or various chemical
processes. Accurately calculating
pressure at different depths within
these layered systems is essential for
structural design, level sensing, and
ensuring operational safety, as it
involves summing the contributions from
each distinct layer.

Manometers
- Instruments used to measure
pressure by balancing a column of fluid
against the pressure to be measured.
They are broadly categorized into
Simple Manometers (which measure
pressure at a single point relative to
the atmosphere) and Differential
Manometers (which measure the
difference in pressure between two
points). More modern Digital Manometers
have also become very common.

Manometers
Manometer
Type Description Applications &
Characteristics
Piezometer
Tube
The simplest form of manometer. It
consists of a vertical glass tube
open at the top and connected to the
point where pressure is to be
measured.
Measures gauge pressure of liquids
(not gases, as gases would escape).
Only suitable for positive pressures
and relatively low pressures. Common
in laboratories for static fluid
pressure.
U-Tube
Manometer
Consists of a U-shaped glass tube
containing a manometric fluid (e.g.,
mercury, water, oil). One end is
connected to the pressure source,
and the other can be open to the
atmosphere (for gauge pressure) or
connected to another pressure source
(for differential pressure).
Measures positive, negative
(vacuum), or differential pressures
for both liquids and gases. Widely
used in laboratories, HVAC systems,
and industrial processes.
Inverted U-
Tube
Manometer
A U-tube manometer that is inverted
(upside down) and typically filled
with a light manometric fluid (e.g.,
oil) on top of the two liquids whose
pressure difference is to be
measured. Used for measuring the
difference in low pressures of
liquids.
Measures small pressure differences
between two liquid points,
especially when the pressure
difference is low and the fluids are
less dense than the manometer fluid.
Common in hydraulic systems.
Digital
Manometer
Utilizes an electronic pressure
transducer (e.g., piezoresistive,
capacitive) to convert pressure into
an electrical signal, which is then
processed and displayed digitally.
Wide range of applications in HVAC,
medical, industrial, and laboratory
settings for measuring gauge,
absolute, or differential pressure.

Dams
- Dams are critical infrastructure
for managing water resources, serving
purposes such as hydroelectric power
generation, irrigation, flood control,
and water supply. Engineers must
understand their fundamental purpose,
the forces they withstand, and their
essential components (like spillways)
to design, construct, and operate them
safely and efficiently, ensuring long-
term sustainability and public safety.

Dams
Classificati
on Category Dam Type Description Common Materials Used
By Structure Gravity Dam Relies on its massive weight to resist
the horizontal force of water. It is
typically a large, solid structure,
often triangular in cross-section.
Concrete, Masonry (stone,
brick, or concrete blocks
with mortar)
Arch Dam Curved upstream to transfer the water
pressure to the canyon walls or
abutments. This design is highly
efficient for narrow, steep valleys,
requiring less material than a gravity
dam. Can be single-arch, double-
curvature, or multiple-arch.
Concrete, Masonry
Buttress Dam Consists of a sloping watertight
upstream face supported at intervals
by a series of triangular-shaped walls
(buttresses) on the downstream side.
This design uses less material than a
solid gravity dam.
Reinforced Concrete,
Masonry
Embankment
Dam
Constructed from compacted natural
materials like earth, rock, or a
combination (earthfill or rockfill).
They are broad at the base and taper
towards the crest. Often have an
impervious core (clay, concrete,
asphalt) to prevent seepage.
Earth (clay, sand,
gravel), Rock, Industrial
Waste (e.g., tailings),
Asphaltic Concrete

Dams
By Material
Concrete Dam Dams primarily constructed using
plain or reinforced concrete.
This category often encompasses
gravity, arch, and buttress dams.
Concrete, Reinforced
Concrete
Masonry Dam Built using stone, brick, or
concrete blocks joined with
mortar. Often used for smaller
dams or older constructions,
though some large masonry dams
exist.
Stone, Brick, Concrete
blocks, Mortar
Earthfill Dam A type of embankment dam where
the primary construction material
is compacted earth, often with
different zones for
imperviousness and stability.
Compacted Earth
(various soil types)
Rockfill Dam A type of embankment dam where
the main material is dumped or
compacted rock, often with an
impervious face (e.g., concrete
slab, asphalt) or an internal
impervious core.
Dumped or Compacted
Rock, Asphaltic
Concrete, Reinforced
Concrete (for facing)
Steel Dam Less common, these dams are
constructed primarily from a
steel framework with a thick
steel plate. Often used for
temporary structures or low-
capacity reservoirs.
Steel
Timber Dam Built using wood, typically for
smaller or temporary dams.
Requires the wood to be kept wet
to prevent rot. Less common in
Wood

Dams
By Function/Purpose Storage Dam Designed to impound water in a reservoir
for various uses such as irrigation,
drinking water supply, industrial
processes, and hydroelectric power
generation. They ensure water
availability during periods of scarcity.
Any structural type (Gravity,
Arch, Embankment, etc.)
Diversion Dam Built to raise the water level of a
river or stream to divert flow into a
canal, channel, or pipe for irrigation,
municipal water supply, or hydropower.
They typically create minimal storage.
Often weir-type structures (low
height), Barrages, or small-
scale versions of other types
Detention Dam Primarily constructed for flood control.
They temporarily store floodwaters
during heavy rainfall or snowmelt and
release them gradually downstream,
reducing flood risk. Often dry except
during flood events.
Embankment, occasionally other
types
Cofferdam A temporary structure built to enclose a
construction area and keep it dry,
typically during the construction of a
main dam or other in-water structures.
Earth, Rockfill, Steel,
Inflatable structures
Debris Dam Constructed to retain debris, sediment,
sand, gravel, and driftwood from a river
or stream.
Often similar to embankment or
small gravity dams
Hydroelectric
Dam
Specifically designed to generate
electricity by harnessing the energy of
falling water. This involves a dam that
creates a head of water, and associated
powerhouses with turbines and
generators.
Often large Storage Dams (e.g.,
Gravity, Arch)
Multipurpose
Dam Designed to serve several functions
simultaneously, such as flood control,
irrigation, water supply, and
hydroelectric power generation. Many
major dams today are multipurpose.
Any structural type (Gravity,
Arch, Embankment, etc.)

Analysis of Gravity Dam
- The stability analysis of gravity
dams is a cornerstone of hydraulic
engineering design. It involves
calculating and balancing various
forces (hydrostatic pressure, uplift,
seismic, self-weight) to ensure the dam
is safe against overturning, sliding,
and excessive stresses. This detailed
analysis ensures the long-term
integrity and safety of these critical
water infrastructure projects.

Buoyancy
Buoyancy is a fundamental principle
governing the behavior of objects
immersed in fluids, explaining why some
float and others sink. This concept is
critical for engineers designing ships,
submarines, offshore platforms, and
other floating structures, as well as
for understanding fluid flow and
sediment transport. It directly relates
to the concept of the buoyant force,
which is the upward force exerted by a
fluid that opposes the weight of an
immersed object.

Open Channel Flow & Froude
Number
- Open channel flow, which involves
a free surface exposed to atmospheric
pressure, is prevalent in natural
rivers, canals, and drainage systems.
The Froude number is a dimensionless
parameter crucial for characterizing
the flow regime in open channels

• branch of agriculture that deals with field

• the science and practice of managing land
and crops to produce food, feed, fiber, and

sustainability in agriculture.
KEY AREAS OF STUDYING AGRONOMY
Soil Management:
Understanding soil properties, fertility, and how to
manage it to support plant growth.
Crop Production:
Studying plant growth, development, and how to
maximize yields while minimizing environmental impact.
Crop Protection:
Managing pests, diseases, and weeds that can affect
crop health and yield
Sustainable Agriculture:
Applying ecological principles to minimize negative
impacts of agriculture on the environment
