Mechanical/Engineering Measures
• Terracing – involves the construction of
broad channels or benches across the
slope to break the flow of rundoff water.
Not practical for shallow soils.
• Grassed Waterways – refers to canals
or channels planted with grasses to
provide outlets for disposal of
unavoidable runoff water.
• Pond – a depression of considerable size
located below the check dam to collect
runoff
• Check Dam – a structure above the pond
which retards runoff velocity.

Biological/Vegetative Measure
Strip Cropping (Pilas-tanim)
• Refers to the growing of erosion-permitting
crop and soil conserving crop in alternate strips
aligned on the contour
Crop Rotation (Ikot-tanim)
• The systematic planting of different crops in
succession on the piece of land.
• Allows the soil to renew the supply of nutrients
which are preferentially depleted by specific
crops.

Biological/Vegetative Measure
Alley Cropping (Interhedgerow cropping)
• Systems where arable crops are grown in the alleys
between rows of shrub/tree legumes which are pruned
periodically to prevent shading and to provide green
manure to the companion crops.
High Density planting
• Practice of increasing the population of the crop per unit of
land area with due regard to the effect of crop competition.
Agroforestry
• Refers to the system of land management where woody
perennials and agricultural crops are raised at the same
time or sequentially.

Biological/Vegetative Measure
Relay Cropping (Usod-tanim)
• Involves the planting of two or more annual crops
with the second crop planted after the first crop
has flowered or nearing its harvest.
• To allow the second crop to make use of the
residual moisture and to provide continuous
ground cover to protect the soil from erosive rains
throughout the year.
Mutiple Cropping
• Refers to the practice which increase crop
productivity while providing better protection of
the soil from erosion.
• Can be sequential cropping or intercropping
and/or mixed cropping.

June 25, 2023
MSU-GSC, College of Agriculture
Review Center for ABE Licensure Examination
FUNDAMENTALS OF
AQUACULTURE AND
AQUACULTURE
ENGINEERING
Frederick John C. Bernardo

FUNDAMENTALS OF
AQUACULTURE

✓ Fisheries refers to all activities relating to
the act or business of:
➢ fishing,
➢ culturing,
➢ preserving,
➢ processing,
➢ marketing,
➢ developing,
➢ conserving and managing
aquatic resources and the fishery areas,
including the privilege to fish or take
aquatic resource thereof (RA 10654).
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ The farming of aquatic organisms in
inland and coastal areas, involving
intervention in the rearing process to
enhance production and the individual
or corporate ownership of the stock
being cultivated (FAO)
✓ Fishery operations involving all forms
of raising and culturing fish and other
fishery species in fresh, brackish, and
marine water areas (RA 8550; RA 10654)
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ In 2018, the Philippines ranked 8th among the top fish producing
countries in the world with its total production of 4.35 million metric tons
(MT) of fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and aquatic plants (including seaweed).
✓ In terms of aquaculture production, the country ranked 11th in the world with
826.01 thousand MT or 1.01% share of the total global aquaculture production
of 82.10 million MT.
➢ The total value of the country’s aquaculture production including fish,
crustaceans, and mollusks is USD 1.89 billion (FAO, 2020).
✓ The Philippines is also the world’s 4th largest producer of aquatic plants
(including seaweed) having a total of 1.48 million MT or 4.56% of the total
world production of 32.39 million MT (FAO, 2020).
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Aquatic Environment
✓ Freshwater Aquaculture - This involves the culture of
organisms that live mainly in inland waters with 0.1 parts per
thousand (ppt) or less salt content.
✓ Brackishwater Aquaculture - This involves the culture of
organisms that live in water with a salt content between 0.1ppt
and full strength seawater.
✓ Mariculture - This involves the culture of organisms that live in
coastal lagoons or in the open sea.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

End-product
✓ Seed Production - The main objective of this type of culture is to
produce small fishes or other organisms, usually called “seed,” which
are stocked into ponds or other culture devices to be grown into adult
organisms for market.
✓ Grow-out Production - The main objective of this type of culture is
to grow seed stock until the commercial size or weight is achieved.
✓ Broodstock Production - The main objective of this type of culture is
to grow, breed and improve cultured species genetically, so as to
improve aquaculture productivity.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Seed Production Grow-out Production Broodstock Production

Level of intensity
✓ Extensive Aquaculture
✓ Semi-Intensive Aquaculture
✓ Intensive Aquaculture
depending on the following:
➢ Stocking and fertilization rates
➢ Supplementary feed quality and rates
➢ Level of technology employed
➢ Level of investment and resultant yields
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Stocking rate is defined as the number of fish seed stocked per
unit water surface, with due consideration to the size and/or age
group of the stocking material (e.g. 10 pcs per m2).
✓ Stocking density is the total number of animals (or
liveweight) on a part of the area for a certain portion of time
(100,000 pcs in a particular area).
✓ Fish seed refers to the fry, post-larvae and fingerlings of the
species to be cultured, and they are usually obtained from natural
waters and hatcheries.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Extensive Culture
✓ This is the simplest method of culture, and is characterized by
a low stocking rate, use of fertilizer, little or no use of
supplementary feed and consequently, a relatively low level of
technology.
✓ As a result, the level of investment is low, and consequently,
yields are low.
✓ Stocking rate is 1 to 4 fish per square meter.
✓ Availability of food is enhanced by the application of fertilizer.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Semi-intensive Culture
✓ This method of culture is more complicated than the
extensive method of culture.
✓ The stocking rate used is higher, both feed and fertilizer may be
used, and consequently, the level of technology is higher,
compared to extensive culture.
✓ The level of investment required is higher than the extensive
method, and as a result, yields are higher.
✓ Stocking rate of 5 to 9 fish per square meter.
✓ Combination of fertilizer application and supplemental
feeding.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Intensive Culture
✓ This method of culture is the most complicated way of growing
fish.
✓ The stocking rate is usually very high (10 fish per square meter and
above).
✓ Combination of fertilizer application and giving large amounts of
supplemental feeds.
✓ Water exchange must be done regularly and mechanical aerators
may be needed to increase the dissolved oxygen level.
✓ This requires a high level of investment, but yields are much higher
than the semi-intensive culture method.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Systems/Structures Utilized
✓ Ponds
✓ Cages
✓ Pens
✓ Tanks
✓ Raceways
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Fish Ponds Fish Pens

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Marine Cages Cages in Lakes

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Fish Tanks Raceways	Fish Tanks Raceways

Pond Culture:
✓ A pond is an earthen, or sometimes concrete, impoundment
that holds water.
✓ Pond culture is perhaps the simplest way of practicing
aquaculture.
✓ Most of the aquaculture production in the world is carried out
in ponds.
✓ Earthen ponds are the most widely used structures, mainly due
to their relatively low cost.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Cage Culture:
✓ Cage culture is the practice of rearing fish in cages.
✓ It can be applied in existing bodies of water that cannot be
drained or seined and would otherwise not be suitable for
aquaculture.
✓ These include lakes, large reservoirs, farm ponds, rivers, cooling
water discharge canals, estuaries and coastal embankments.
✓ Cages have a rigid framework, and a bag suspended below
the water surface, in which the culture species are retained.
✓ The upper surface is provided with flotation devices, which can
be manipulated to raise or lower the cage in the water.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Pen Culture:
✓ Pens are similar to cages, except that the species is allowed to
access the bottom of the water body.
✓ Pens are generally built in large open waters such as lakes,
reservoirs and rivers.
✓ However, waters used for pen culture are relatively shallow
when compared with cage culture, and usually possess a
medium to high level of dissolved nutrients.
✓ Fish therefore have access to natural food.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Raceway Culture:
✓ A raceway is a long, narrow rectangular trench in which water is
flushed through continuously.
✓ If the land is sloping, a series of raceways can be constructed,
linked to each other end to end, one unit flowing into the other,
and separated by filters.
✓ Oxygen is added to the water by the splashing action as water
exits one cell and drops into the other.
✓ This high rate of water movement gives raceway systems
distinct advantages over the other culture systems.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ The objective of pond preparation is to provide the aquaculture
species to be stocked with a grow-out environment having
optimal environmental conditions, free of diseases and their
vectors, without predators and competitors, as stress-free as
possible, and with ample supply of adequate food organisms.
✓ Pond preparation provides the farmer with a mechanism to
control the pond bottom environment and minimize animal
stress, and promote desirable natural primary productivity.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Routine pond preparation involves several steps:
1. Draining
2. Drying
3. pH Mapping
4. Tilling
5. Disinfection
6. Liming
7. Fertilization
8. Water filling
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Open all water inlet/outlet gates, quickly drain the pond as
completely as possible and flush vigorously the internal drain
canals to resuspend and flush out as much as accumulated
sludge as you can.
✓ This should be done before the sludge dries out and solidifies.
➢ Sludge is a waste by-product of fish farming consisting of
feces and excess feed.
✓ Heavy chains and rakes are dragged along, or people can walk
along the internal canals to resuspend sludge material.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Sludge removal is critical, because if left undisturbed, it will
become anaerobic, reduced sediment which will generate toxic
metabolites such as methane, hydrogen sulfide, ammonia,
nitrite, ferrous iron and others, negatively affecting water
quality and production during the next production cycle.
✓ Low areas with standing water should be drained by pumping, or
digging drainage ditches, if possible.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ The next step is to allow the pond to partially dry for varying
periods of time (~1-3 weeks, max. 1 month).
✓ Exposing the pond bottom soil to the sun and air includes the
following advantages:
➢ enhance organic matter decomposition by bacteria,
➢ eradicate viruses, bacteria, and fungi,
➢ eradicate eggs, larvae and adults of predators and competitors,
and
➢ dry out undesirable filamentous algae.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ The rate of decomposition is greatest at a soil pH of 7.5-8.5, so in
acidic pond soils many farmers add lime products to enhance soil pH
and hence increase organic matter decomposition.
✓ Pond drying out and disinfecting may be, to date, the most effective
method in controlling viral epidemics in shrimp production ponds.
✓ If disease epidemics have occurred on site within the last production
cycle a pro-longed dry out of two to three months is
recommended.
✓ The pond’s surface should be cracked to a minimum of two inches
(5 cm) during this process, to oxidize the soil eliminating anaerobic
conditions.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ In acidic soils with low pH (under 7), mapping of pond bottom
pH should be done promptly by sampling soil pH at various
stations within the pond, and while the soil has a humidity of
around 30%, in order to calculate lime requirements.
✓ Once the pond surface is hard enough to walk on, soil pH
measurements using standardized procedures are taken to
determine lime requirements.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Tilling aids in aerating soils that may have anaerobic areas
where organic matter and hydrogen sulfide (toxic to shrimp)
accumulate.
✓ Tilling or plowing the bottom soil to a depth of 10-20 cm is
optional, depending on condition of bottoms.
✓ This particularly important in areas of heavy sludge
accumulation, such as internal canals or areas adjacent to
drainage gates, but it is usually difficult to get heavy equipment
into/out of these areas, so specialized equipment has been
develop for these areas.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ It is also common to incorporate a nitrogen source such as
urea into the soil before tilling, with the objective of increasing
the rate of organic matter decomposition.
✓ Some farmers apply about 50% of the calculated lime
requirements during tilling.
✓ Tilling the surface soil of pond bottoms ensures complete
oxidation of lower layers of anaerobic mud.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Why is it needed to scrape the pond bottom?
✓ It is necessary to remove, or dry out excess black (sulfuric)
mud, debris, and organic compounds that accumulate in the
surface of the soil since it negatively affects with the water.
✓ Also, certain viruses and pathogenic bacteria can be harbored
in the mud.
✓ This practice is very important in shrimp farms since shrimp
forage and spend most of their time on the bottom.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ The purpose of disinfection is to eradicate all stages (eggs,
larvae, juveniles and adults) of species of fish, crustaceans,
insects and other predatory and competitor species.
✓ Many products are commonly used to disinfect ponds before
stocking shrimp.
✓ In general, the use of pesticides is not recommended, because
of their slow biodegradation, and potential to accumulate in
sediments and bioaccumulate in the food web.
✓ Chlorination is the disinfection method of choice for many
farmers.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Ponds may be limed to obtain one or more of the following
benefits:
1. Total hardness and total alkalinity are increased, and the pH
buffer system is enhanced.
2. Liming neutralizes acid soil conditions, thus increasing the
pH and availability of phosphorus.
3. Liming adds calcium, a plant nutrient. If dolomitic
limestone is used, magnesium, also a plant nutrient is
added.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Ponds may be limed to obtain one or more of the following
benefits:
4. Addition of calcium is directly beneficial to crustaceans

✓ Stocking rate is defined as the number of fish seed stocked per
unit water surface, with due consideration to the size and/or age
group of the stocking material (e.g. 10 pcs per m2).
✓ Stocking density is the total number of animals (or liveweight)
on a part of the area for a certain portion of time (100,000 pcs in a
particular area).
✓ Fish seed refers to the fry, post-larvae and fingerlings of the
species to be cultured, and they are usually obtained from natural
waters and hatcheries.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ A fishpond can only support a certain quantity of fish because of
its limited space and the amount of natural food available.
✓ The natural food is affected mainly by the soil conditions and
water quality of the pond.
✓ This limit is usually called the carrying capacity (or maximum
standing crop) of the pond.
✓ It is defined as the maximum weight of fish stock that can be
sustained by a pond (by either the food produced within the pond
or made available to the fish) without gaining or losing weight.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ The carrying capacity of a pond can be increased by fertilization and/or
supplemental feeding.
✓ Fertilization increases the production of plankton or benthic algae
as fish food.
✓ Supplemental feeding compensates for nutrients which are in short
supply in the pond.
✓ Aeration and running-water systems increase the amount of
dissolved oxygen thereby increasing the carrying capacity of a pond.
➢ Take note that an increased carrying capacity of a pond (semi-
intensive or intensive systems) allows higher stocking rates thus
higher yield/harvest.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Monoculture
✓ Monoculture is the stocking of a single species in a pond.
✓ Within the monoculture system, there are several stocking
practices that affect pond production like mono-size stocking,
multi-stage stocking and multi-size stocking.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Monoculture: mono-size stocking
✓ Mono-size stocking is the stocking of one species of the same size
in a pond and to harvest all the fish at marketable size.
✓ This practice has some disadvantages.
➢ If stocking density is too high, the fish would be overcrowded
when they reach adult size. Thus, growth and survival rates
would be reduced.
➢ On the other hand, if stocking density is low, the water space
and the natural food in the pond will not be efficiently utilized
during the earlier part of the rearing period.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Monoculture: multi-stage stocking
✓ Multi-stage stocking or modular method involves the stocking of
fish of uniform size in progressively larger ponds as more space
is needed.
✓ This method takes advantage of the growth potential of the fish
and their density can be adjusted as they are transferred to larger
ponds.
✓ This practice enables the fish farmers to undertake a continuous
cycle of stocking and harvesting.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Monoculture: multi-size stocking
✓ Multi-size stocking involves the stocking of different size
groups of fish in the same pond.
✓ Ponds produce a variety of natural food and the feeding habits
of the young and adult fish are often quite different.
✓ The stocking rate and the total yield of a pond can be increased
by stocking different age groups to more efficiently utilize the
forage.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Polyculture
✓ Polyculture is based on the principle that fertile bodies of water
produce a variety of food organisms and stocking of a variety
of species is effective in utilizing all these food organisms.
✓ By stocking different species having complementary feeding
habits or that feed in different zones, this will efficiently utilize
space and available food in the pond and increase total fish
production.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ There are two major types of factors associated with water, biotic

larvae, snails etc.
➢ Abiotic factors are the nonliving factors such as light,

✓ The water in which the aquaculture species is farmed has a

✓ Water in the pond is kept at certain levels for optimal fish
growth.

✓ In general, a pond water depth of 1-1.5 meters is considered best
for culture of most finfishes.
✓ Pond water is not just maintained at a certain depth; its quality
must also be kept high to ensure optimal growth of the culture
organism.
✓ This is particularly important in semi-intensive and intensive culture
systems where large amounts of metabolites are continuously
excreted into the pond and where excess, unconsumed feeds add to
the bottom load and serve to pollute the water.

✓ To prevent the deterioration of the pond environment, pond water
is continuously freshened by the entry of new water from the
river or water source (through the supply canal) while old water is
drained through the outlet/drainage gate and through the drainage
canal into the sea or river.

change necessary for medium-high density aquaculture, semi-
intensive culture systems usually change water at the rate of
10% daily for an equivalent total replacement of water every ten
days or three times per month.

✓ In ponds used for aquaculture, the major
source of oxygen is photosynthesis by
phytoplankton.

✓ Since sunlight is essential for photosynthesis, this activity is carried out

✓ In the night, the phytoplankton carry out only respiration, a process in
which they use up oxygen and produce carbon dioxide.
✓ This means that the dissolved oxygen levels are lower in the night,
and higher during the day.
✓ The lowest levels of oxygen are encountered very early in the
morning, just before the sun rises.

✓ Maintenance of adequate level of dissolved
oxygen in pond water is very important to
fish growth and survival.
✓ Prolonged exposure to the stress of low
oxygen concentration lowers their
resistance to disease and inhibits their
growth.
✓ In most cases, oxygen depletion often
results in mass mortality (anoxia) of shrimp
stock.

Factors leading to oxygen depletion:
Increased water temperatures
✓ As temperature levels increase, the
amount of dissolved oxygen in
water decreases due to the inverse
relationship between dissolved
oxygen and temperature.
✓ The solubility of oxygen decreases
as water temperature increases.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Factors leading to oxygen depletion: Increased water salinity
✓ As salinity increases, dissolved oxygen decreases, which is why
saltwater holds 20% less dissolved oxygen than freshwater.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Factors leading to oxygen depletion:
Discharge increasing nutrients
✓ A sudden increase in bio-available
nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus)
can stimulate algal blooms which
eventually decay and are consumed by
bacteria, resulting in a depletion of
oxygen in the subsurface water.
✓ A prime example of this is the Gulf of
Mexico “dead zone”.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Factors leading to oxygen depletion:
Discharge increasing nutrients

Overstocking
✓ The greater the number of fish in a
pond, the greater is the consumption of
oxygen as well as the amount of waste
products produced.
✓ The waste products in turn use up
oxygen when they decay.
✓ For these reasons, farmers are urged to
follow the recommended stocking rates
for the particular species of fish or
shrimp.

oxygen in the culture water
✓ Aerators use an energy input to improve the liquid surface area

concentration is brought in contact with the atmosphere.

Aeration System
✓ The transfer of oxygen from the atmosphere to the water is a
three step process:
1. Transfer from the air to the gas-liquid interface
2. Transfer across the gas-liquid interface
3. Transfer from the gas-liquid interface to the water

✓ Several types of aerators are used for fish/shrimp farming.
✓ The objective of aeration is to force diffusion of oxygen from the
air into the water.
✓ Paddlewheel aerators accomplish this by breaking water into
small droplets and increasing exposure to air using paddles.
✓ Aspirator aerators force air into the water via a venturi and a
propeller.
✓ Another important goal of aeration is to circulate aerated water
throughout the pond.

Total Ammonia Nitrogen (TAN)
✓ Ammonia is present in two forms, ionized (NH4+) which is
nontoxic, and the toxic form, un-ionized (NH3).
✓ The concentration of these depends on water temperature and
pH.
✓ The higher the water temperature and pH, the greater the
concentration of the toxic form.
✓ The summation of both the ionized and un-ionized forms is
termed total ammonia nitrogen or TAN.

pH is important to understand
because chemical test kits
measure TAN.
✓ The concentration of toxic

Ammonia test kits

Toxic Ammonia (NH3)
✓ Ammonia in ponds comes from feed and nutrients entering with
the water.
✓ If feed is uneaten, then more ammonia is present than if it is
consumed by fish/shrimp.
✓ For every kilogram of feed fed, about 30 grams of ammonia
will be excreted by fish/shrimp into the pond.
✓ Un-ionized ammonia is very toxic to fish/shrimp and causes gill
damage and reduced growth at low concentrations.
✓ Ammonia can be a problem anytime during the culture cycle and
must be monitored once or twice per week.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S)
✓ Hydrogen sulfide is a by-product of the breakdown of organic
matter, usually under anaerobic conditions.
✓ Soils with moderate to high organic concentrations that have
anaerobic conditions can be a significant source of hydrogen sulfide,
which is toxic to shrimp even at low concentrations.
✓ If an eggy odor is noticed when sediment is disturbed, it is an
indication of anaerobic conditions and the presence of hydrogen
sulfide.
✓ Drying and tilling pond bottoms, as well as maintaining thorough
aeration of ponds are effective tools in reducing hydrogen sulfide
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Harvesting of fish means the complete removal of fish from the pond
at the end of production.
✓ A single stocking and a single harvesting are the common practice in
existence.
✓ However, the technique of partial harvesting and restocking is now
being practiced and has been found to yield better results in terms of
fish production per unit area.
✓ Bigger size fishes should be harvested and sold in batches and the pond
should immediately be restocked with the same number of fishes of
such species.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Marketable-size fish/shrimps are harvested at the end of the culture
period by draining the pond and using harvesting nets to catch the fish or
shrimps.
✓ There are generally two types of harvest:
➢ Partial harvest or thinning - Partial harvesting is normally practiced
in culture operations with higher stocking density (i.e. in semi-
intensive or intensive culture). The stock, upon reaching the
marketable size can be harvested by the use of selective harvesting
net.
➢ Full harvest or draining – Fish/shrimps are harvested with a bag-net
attached to the sluice gate as water is drained out of the pond.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Upon harvesting, fish/shrimps should be washed and placed
immediately in chilled water (10– 15°C) for about 15 minutes.
✓ They are then packed in styrofoam box with alternate layers of
crushed ice at a ratio of 1:1.
✓ Smaller styrofoam boxes are preferred to facilitate transportation.
✓ If bigger styrofoam boxes are used, it is better to fill up the box
with chilled water, shrimps and ice to avoid physical damage on
the shrimps at the bottom.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

AQUACULTURE ENGINEERING
(Fishpond design and
construction)

✓ Aquaculture engineering, or fishpond engineering, is defined as
the science of planning, designing and constructing ponds,
including water control structures.
✓ The primary aim of aquaculture engineering is to utilize technical
engineering knowledge and principles in aquaculture and
biological production systems.
✓ Some developments within the field of aquaculture engineering:
➢ improvements in technology allowing reduced consumption
of water through development of re-use systems
➢ development of offshore cages
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

The evaluation of an existing area takes into account the
following criteria:
➢ Water supply
➢ Tidal characteristics and ground elevation
➢ Soil properties
➢ Studies of watershed and flood hazard
➢ Climatic conditions
➢ Type and density of vegetation
➢ Ecological factors
➢ Other factors
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

available year round in the site.
✓ Good quality water suitable for fish culture is rich in oxygen,
nutrients and free from pollutants.

source can be evaluated using the formula:

plants, oil rigs and densely populated areas should be
avoided.

✓ Tides are defined as the alternate rising and falling of the sea, usually twice in
each lunar day at a particular place, due to the attraction of the moon and
sun.
✓ Spring Tides
➢ the sun, the moon & the earth are in a straight line, producing the highest
tides
➢ This happens every two weeks during a new moon or full moon.
✓ Neap Tides
➢ The sun and the moon are in extreme position with the earth at the apex of
right triangle, producing smaller tides.
➢ This causes the sun and moon to pull the water in two different directions.
➢ Seven days after a spring tide—refers to a period of moderate tides when
the sun and moon are at right angles to each other.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

✓ Because the Earth rotates through two tidal “bulges” every lunar
day, coastal areas experience two high and two low tides
every 24 hours and 50 minutes.
✓ High tides occur 12 hours and 25 minutes apart. It takes six
hours and 12.5 minutes for the water at the shore to go from high
to low, or from low to high.
✓ The type of gravitational force that causes tides is known as
"Tractive" force.
✓ The variation in height that is often observed between adjacent
high waters and low waters is called diurnal inequality.
Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓Whenever possible, the available tidal range must be able to fill
the ponds by gravity to the specified depths.
✓The elevation of pond bottom is considered ideal if it enables
draining of the pond almost any day of the year and flood it
with seawater to the desired depth within five days or less
during the critical spring tides.
✓The critical spring tides usually occur in the Philippines during the
months of February, March and April.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ High Elevation
➢ Areas reached only by the high spring tides should not be
selected as it is expensive to move large quantities of soil during
excavation.
✓ Low Elevation
➢ Low areas on the other hand will require much higher and wider
dikes, thus soil is moved at far distances further increasing
construction cost.
➢ While constructing higher and wider dikes may solve the problem,
this would result to occupying more space in the pond
compartment and hence, less area intended for fish production.

✓ Both physical and chemical properties of the soil must be
investigated and considered in making the final decision
on the suitability of a site for fishpond development.

Soil Investigation procedures and equipment
✓ Measurements to be done from the soil
➢ for physical properties — textural class, load bearing
capacity, and permeability;
➢ for chemical properties — soil pH and presence of
acid-forming substance such as pyrites and sulfides

✓ As standard practice, several samples

✓ For relatively shallow boring, soil

✓ The texture is the most important physical property of
the soil in fishpond engineering.
✓ Knowing the texture, much can already be said on the
characteristics of the soil.
✓ Soil texture gives information on its ability to resist the
flow of water through it (seepage), attainable compaction,
and load bearing capacity.

Soil Investigation procedures and equipment
✓ Load bearing capacity refers to the capability of the soil
to carry, heavy loads.
✓ This information guides designers in determining the type
of foundation for structures (gates and dikes) and the
amount of pilings needed up to a certain point.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Soil Investigation procedures and equipment
✓ Soil pH provides an initial and immediate measure of the
chemical nature of the site.
✓ The soil reaction whether basic or acidic has direct
relationship to fish production.
✓ The pH scale varies from 1 to 14 units and the desirable
range of soil as well as water pH for aquaculture is 6.5 to
8.5.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Acid sulfate soils
✓ A large hectarage of coastal areas tend to have acidic pH.
✓ Acid sulfate soils are associated with the accumulation
of sulfides and pyrites after undergoing biological and
chemical processes.
✓ Sulfides are compounds that produce acidity upon
oxidation.
✓ The resulting acidic soil condition in turn facilitate the
release of aluminum and iron to levels that may be toxic
to pond biota including the cultured species.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Acid sulfate soils
✓ Pyrite is formed by bacteria that
remove oxygen from sulfate in the
water, producing sulfide that
reacts with iron to form pyrite.
✓ High acidity conditions cause
slow fish growth and mortalities,
poor fertilizer response, low natural
food production, and erosion of
dike soils because of poor grass
cover.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Acid sulfate soils

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Acid sulfate soils
✓ The potential adverse effect of acid sulfate soils can be
prevented with proper engineering and construction work and
good management practices.
➢ Reducing the volume of exposed dike soil in relation to
pond area
➢ Liming
➢ Drying and flushing acid sulfate soils with seawater
➢ Covering acid sulfate soil with suitable soil
➢ Appropriate water management
➢ Control of dike soil erosion (acid-resistant African star grass)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ Topography refers to the “lay of the land” or the changes
in the surface elevations of the ground whether flat,
rolling or sloping, undulating, and hilly.
✓ Fishpond design, layout and specifications are made
largely in accordance with the land topography.
✓ A suitable site for fishpond has a topography that can be
converted into a pond economically (least cut and fill).

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Four zones in the coastal edge as probable sites for fishpond
✓ Zone A. Marginal lands along edges usually planted to lowland
rice but generally unproductive due to salt water seepage can
be converted into fishpond by lowering the elevation through
excavation.
✓ These are usually productive as fishponds because of good
soil quality.
✓ The cost of excavation can make these areas relatively more
expensive to develop due to their high elevation.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Four zones in the coastal edge as probable sites for fishpond
✓ Zone B. The elevation is generally high with occasional earth
mounds along the edges but can be reached by tides.
✓ High dikes not necessary but development cost may be
expensive if a big portion of the area needs excavation.
✓ Zone C. This area is within the ideal range of pond bottom
elevation, thus excavation cost is less.
✓ However, extreme acidity may occur because of the presence
of vegetation that contributes to acidity.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Four zones in the coastal edge as probable sites for fishpond
✓ Zone D. The elevation is low or just a little higher than the 00
datum (MLLW).
✓ It is very exposed to wave action which may require expensive
big dikes and wave protection structures.
✓ No acidity problem, hence, may be ideal for shrimp culture.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Four zones in the coastal edge as probable sites for fishpond

fishpond site selection. Knowledge of their composition and

evaluation of the physical and chemical properties of soil.
➢ Mangroves with
Avicennia usually
indicate productive soil.
➢ Mangroves with

✓ There is a direct relationship between vegetation and the

✓ Areas where mangrove trees with dense rooting systems like

✓ At the same time, densely vegetated areas takes longer time to

✓ As a result, cost of fishpond construction is higher.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ The climatic factors largely affecting site selection and fishpond
design are wind and rainfall.
✓ The direction of prevailing wind is reckoned with in designing
the layout of fishponds as it generates erosive wave action
against the dikes.
✓ The wind energy also causes natural water circulation and
aeration in the pond.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ For rainfall information,
➢ maximum intensity,
➢ duration,
➢ frequency and
➢ annual distribution within the watershed

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ A watershed is a land area that channels rainfall (as runoff
water) to creeks, streams, and rivers, and eventually to
outflow points such as reservoirs, bays, and the ocean.
✓ The volume of flood water or runoff are affected by the
rainfall and soil characteristics, type of vegetative cover,
topography, and area of the watershed.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ Much higher rate of runoff can be expected in a watershed
that has
➢ high rainfall intensity and duration,
➢ clay or heavy-textured soil covered with less vegetation or
grassland,
➢ high slopes and covering large area
✓ than a watershed characterized with
➢ low rainfall intensity and short duration,
➢ loamy or coarse-textured soil that is forested
➢ with flat or gently rolling slope and small area.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ The pattern and recurrence of maximum height of flood
waters in the site must be determined.
✓ These information can be obtained from the rainfall or
flood records of appropriate agency for each country.
✓ The design of fish farm should be based on a flood height
with recurrence interval of 10–15 years.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ Fish farm layouts that are properly engineered should
strike a balance considering economy, functionality and
aesthetics.
✓ The basic principle is to minimize the number of gates,
and the size and length of the main secondary and tertiary
dikes and canals.
✓ But this should not sacrifice the biological requirements
for suitable environment of the cultured species.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ Fishponds should be planned in such a way that the length
of the pond is positioned parallel to the prevailing wind
direction.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ As such, the length of dike
exposed to wave action is
lessened, thus, the cost of
repairs also less.
✓ The position also takes
advantage of the wind energy
in effecting good water
aeration through mixing
and circulation.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Location of aquaculture farms
✓ Fish farms should be located at convenient distance from
the sea or river.
✓ In the Philippines, a sanctioned buffer zone (salvage zone)
at least 100m from the sea to the main perimeter dike
and 20m along river banks should be established for
ecological consideration as well as physical protection
against flooding and wave action

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Components of an aquaculture farm: Pond system
✓ various compartments with specific uses
➢ nursery or fry pond, transition or holding stunting pond,
production or rearing ponds and other features (catching,
desilting food-growing ponds)
✓ Water control structure or gates, pipes or culverts and water
supply or drainage canals.
✓ Each of these units should be properly located and fitted in the
system in order to have ease in water management and
manipulation of cultured stock.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Components of an aquaculture farm: Support facilities
✓ Farm buildings
✓ Road dikes
✓ Fish tanks
✓ Storage shed (for feed and equipment)
✓ Other ancillary structures
➢ Laboratory
➢ Living quarters
➢ Kiosks
➢ Kitchen
✓Farm roads
✓Bridges
✓Chilling tanks
➢ Feed mill
➢ Warehouse
➢ Offices

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Fry acclimatization pond
✓ Sometimes called fry box this is the smallest unit in a
pond system usually 4 to 8 m2 in size.
✓ Fry are first stocked in this pond for 1 to 4 days and then
allowed passage to the nursery pond proper by just
cutting open the small dike partition

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Nursery pond
✓ small in size (about 1 to 4% of total production area)
and usually square or rectangular in shape
✓ It may be a single pond unit or made up of two, four, six,
etc. sub-compartments which form the whole nursery unit
✓ It is used for rearing the fry for at least 30 days (in the case
of milkfish) before transferring into another larger pond

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Nursery pond
✓ Avoid locating nursery ponds directly adjacent to
perimeter dikes.
✓ Crab holes and leaks that might occur during the rearing
period will serve as exits of fry from the nursery pond to
the river.
✓ These can also serve as entrance for predators and
unwanted species into the nursery pond, causing further
loss of stock.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Transition pond
✓ Holding or stunting pond
✓ Located adjacent to the NP in order to have efficient and
quick transfer of fingerlings
✓ Depending on the management scheme, close to 10% of
the TPA is usually allocated for this purpose.
✓ The fingerlings or post-fingerlings are reared here for
varying periods before finally stocking them in the
production or rearing ponds.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Production or rearing pond
✓ also called grow-out pond
✓ the largest compartment in the pond system occupying
about 80% of total production area
✓ The bottom elevation of the rearing pond should be
about 0.2 m lower than that of the transition pond but
slightly higher than the MLLW or zero tidal datum.
✓ The pond bottom slopes toward the catching pond or
water supply canal to facilitate harvesting of marketable-
sized fish.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Catching pond
✓ serves as a concentration area or basin for the fish
during harvest
✓ constructed adjacent to the gate inside a bigger pond
compartment
✓ catching pond for the nursery and transition ponds is
usually about 2% of the respective compartments'
water surface area

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Food growing pond (kitchen pond)
✓ These pond is is optional and may be built, if deemed
necessary.
✓ compartment set aside for growing live food organisms at
high density

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Conventional Pond System (CPS)
✓ Nursery pond (NP) or
similyahan
➢ comprises 1% of TPA
➢ 1,000-5,000 m2 area is
preferred
✓ Transition pond (TP) or
bansutan
➢ comprises 9% of TPA
➢ 5,000-15,000 m2 is preferred
✓ Rearing pond (RP)
➢ comprises 80% of TPA
➢ 1-5 ha per compartment
is preferred
✓ Catching pond (CP)
➢ comprises 2% of TPA
✓ Dikes and canals
➢ comprises 8% of TPA

➢ 1,000-5,000 m2 area is
preferred
➢ 4% of TPA

➢ Divided into PPS1, PPS,
PPS3

from the smaller
module to the larger
module

1:3:9

Multiple Stock/Harvest System
(MSHS)
✓ Nursery pond (NP)
➢ 1,000-5,000 m2 area is
preferred
➢ atleast 2 NPs
➢ 6% of TPA
✓ Fish Holding Canal (FHC)
➢ hold fingerlings while RPs

✓ Rearing Pond (RP)
➢ 1-5 h per compartment
is preferred
➢ 94% of TPA

with different size-
groups of fingerlings
(continuous)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Multiple Stock/Harvest System (MSHS)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Gates and water supply/drainage canals
✓ Each pond compartment should have
individual water supply and drainage
outlets to make them independent from
each other.
✓ Main gates and secondary gates are
positioned where entrance and circulation
of water could be most efficient.
✓ Canals should be located where it could
connect or serve the most number of
pond compartments.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Gates and water supply/drainage canals

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Gates - either sluice, culvert, or pipe
✓ Floor
✓ serves as foundation of the structure
✓ elevation must be lower than the pond bottom elevation
✓ must not be exposed even during extreme low tide
✓ Apron
✓ rests on the foundation piles (made of bamboo driven at 0.3m
intervals with butt up)
✓ Serves as protection to scouring and future seepage at the
gate’s sides
✓ Cut-off walls
✓ prevent seepage and undercutting on gates foundation
✓ integral part of gate’s foundation

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Floor

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Foundation and elevation plan of concrete main gate (single opening)
Foundation support and piling scheme (Portion of flooring only)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Gates - either sluice, culvert, or pipe
✓ Side or breast walls
✓ grooves or double cleats for flashboards and screens are
built on these walls
✓ Buttress
✓ built against the side walls to support or reinforce it
✓ helps in reducing seepage flow along the side walls
✓ Wing walls
✓ provides transition from the sluice way into the main
canal in addition to retaining the earth at both sides of the
gate

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Gates - either sluice, culvert, or pipe
✓ Bridge or catwalk
✓ A reinforced concrete slab or thick wooden planks that span the side
walls
✓ At least two catwalks are provided, located at regular intervals near
the flashboard grooves
✓ Flashboards
✓ slabs or flashboards are generally wooden pieces, 1”–1½” X 10”
inserted into grooves or double cleats
✓ used to control the amount of water flowing through the gate
✓ Screens
✓ Attached to a wooden rectangular frame that fit into the grooves
✓ Used to prevent the exit of the cultured fish and the entry of
predators into ponds

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Gates - either sluice, culvert, or pipe
✓ Pillars
✓ In wooden gates, these are vertical supports where wooden
walls are nailed
✓ placed at regular intervals so that they form a framework for the
gate itself
✓ Braces
✓ In wooden gates, these frames hold or fasten two or more pillars
together or in place
✓ control the steady opening of a gate (keeps the opening of gate
rigid)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Main Gate
✓ links the pond system to the source of water
✓ regulate the exchange of water between the pond system
and the tidal stream or sea
✓ should be made of concrete for effective control to last
longer
✓ usually located centrally to proposed pond facing the
source of water

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Main Gate: Floor Elevation
✓ should be lower than the lowest pond bottom elevation
inside the pond system
✓ should be lower than the extreme low tides
✓ preferred elevation is -0.30m or 0.3m lower than zero
datum

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Main Gate: Height
✓ depends upon the highest tide and flood
✓ should be the same as the elevation of the main dike
✓ also dependent upon the tidal fluctuations, floods and
other factors in the area

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Main Gate: Opening
✓ Main gates may have single, double, or triple or even
quadruple or more openings
✓ It should not have too wide opening so that they would
be difficult to manage
➢ 1-1.2 m wide per opening has been found
appropriate for easy handling of wooden slabs and
screens
➢ 1m opening will flood 10-15 ha in 2-3 successive HT

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Main Gate: Other Specifications
✓ Separate grooves for slabs and screens
✓ Necessary to have 4 pairs for grooves: 2 for slabs and 2
for screens
✓ Wings should be properly designed to provide easy
current flow
✓ The best angle of inclination should be 45o towards the
outside

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Secondary and tertiary gates
✓ Provide the control of water to and from the main canal and into
the different pond
✓ Considerations in the planning and designing of secondary and
tertiary gates are the same as those of the main gate except
that their respective elevations are dependent upon the
elevation of the canal bed where they are being constructed.
✓ The usual elevation of the flooring of these gates above the
canal is 0.15 m.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Culvert or Pipe
✓ These structures convey water across dikes, roads, and
similar embankments.
✓ Recent innovation for a smaller or less expensive gate:
made of concrete hollow blocks or asbestos cement or
wooden boards (low-cost)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Culvert or Pipe

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ system of partitioning of fishpond area for water control and
stock manipulation
✓ made of soil (in the area)
✓ trapezoidal in shape; width, side slope, and height depends on
the properties of the soil material
✓ must be of adequate size and shape to hold the water to
prevent seepage

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Design and Specifications
✓ retains water for use in the fish farming operation
✓ protects the ponds, fish crops and other farm facilities from
destruction by floods and tidal inundation.
✓ design types:
✓ for exposed areas
✓ for protected areas

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Design and Specifications
Sample designs of perimeter dike within the reach of coastal waves

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Location
✓ usually built along the river banks, on the seaward side or in
certain spots that are vulnerable to flooding
✓ In the Philippines, it requires a belt of mangroves of 20 m from
a river bank, and 100 m wide from seashore to be left
✓ protect the dikes against waves and currents, and absorption of
wave energy, and for flood control and conservation of the
environment

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Cross-section

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination of Height
✓ Top of the dike should extend above the waterline to
provide safe margin against overtopping at high tide &
flood
✓ Perimeter dike normally has a freeboard, after shrinkage
and settlement, of 0.6 -1.0m above the max flood water
level observed in the locality for at least 10-15 years
✓ Freeboard is the added dam height provided as a safety
factor to prevent overtopping of the dam.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination of Height
✓ Allowance for shrinkage and settlement depends on the
characteristics:
➢ soil fill
➢ soil foundation
➢ method of construction
✓ It is expressed as a %age of dike height
✓ usually at 25%
✓ if organic matter is high, 40% or more
✓ if compacted by construction equipment, 5-10%

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination of Height
✓ Determine the height of the main dike if the highest astronomical
tide is 2.04m and the elevation of the land is 0.91m. The flood
allowance is 30 cm, allowance of shrinkage is 15% and freeboard is 30
cm.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination of side slopes, crown and
base
✓ The dike should also be of adequate width so that it could
hold water inside and prevent flooding from outside
✓ side slope 1:1 (horizontal to vertical) for clay soil, height
up to 3m
✓ side slope of 2:1 (horizontal to vertical) is used for height
>4m
➢ even flatter if located along seashore and being
subject against wave action

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination of side slopes, crown and
base
✓ If available soil permits, provision for a berm (single or both
sides) is desirable for additional stability.
✓ A Berm should slope towards the dike wall to trap eroded
soil particles during rains and lessen the impact of water
on pond dike
✓ It serves also as small ditch that conveys runoffs towards
the outlet gate especially when acidity of exposed dike is a
management problem

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination of side slopes, crown and
base

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination of side slopes, crown and
base
✓ Booms and ripraps are also often used in perimeter dikes to
protect the ponds.
✓ Booms consist of one or more rows of logs chained
together and anchored securely in front of a dam about
2 m in front.
✓ Rip-rap is composed of stone, concrete blocks or concrete
slab construction placed on the dam face .

base
✓ The top width or crown of the dike should be designed so

✓ For dikes used as roadways, top width of 3.5 m to 4.0 m

✓ 0.6m wide allowance on each side of a roadway dike to
prevent ravelling (disintegration)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Perimeter Dike: Determination
of side slopes, crown and base
✓ In the Philippines, the
desirable minimum crown is
at least 2m for main dike
✓ Dikes subjected to wave action
should have a minimum
crown of approximately
equal to the height of the
maximum wave.

of side slopes, crown and base
✓ Determine the width of base if
the dike should have a top
width of crown of 2.5 m, height
of 1.3 m and a side slope of
1.5:1 (or z = 1.5).
b = T + 2(zd)
b = 2.5m + 2(1.5) (1.3m)
b = 6.4 m

✓ Determine the cross-sectional area of the dike if the width of
the base is 6.4m, width of the crown is 2.5m, and height of the
dike is 1.3m. If the length of the dike is 1,250m, determine its

b= 6.4
T= 2.5
h= 1.3
L= 1,250

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Secondary and Tertiary Dike
✓ These dikes are both smaller than the main (perimeter)
dikes
✓ Secondary dikes are usually provided on both sides of
the canals and should be able to contain the mean high
water springs.
✓ Tertiary dikes are partition dikes that separate the ponds
and should be able to contain the desired water levels in
the ponds.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Secondary and Tertiary Dike: Determination of Height
✓ If the mean high spring tide above the zero datum is 1.55 m (Hst), the
ground elevation at the side of dike is 1.00 m (Gs), and maximum
24hour rainfall in the locality for 15year interval is 12 cm (Mr).
Determine the height of secondary dike needed. Provide 25%
allowance for shrinkage and 30 cm freeboard (F).
Gs= ground elevation
F= freeboard

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Secondary and Tertiary Dike: Determination of Height
✓ Determine the height of a tertiary dike if the desired water level in the
pond is 1.35 m (Dwl) from the zero datum and the ground elevation is
1.00 m (Gs). The maximum 24hour rainfall is 12 cm (Mr), allowance of
shrinkage is 20% and freeboard is 30 cm (F).
Gs= ground elevation
F= freeboard

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Secondary and Tertiary Dike: Determination of side slope,
crown and base
✓ Top width of secondary and tertiary dikes are narrower
than the perimeter or main dike (1 to 2 m for secondary
dike, <1m for tertiary dike)
✓ Side slope is usually 1:1
✓ Side berms in secondary dike may be provided if there is

✓ The computation of the width of base is done in the same
way as in the perimeter or main dike.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Design of water canals or channels
✓ Canals comprise about 1-2% of the total farm area.
✓ The whole bottom should slope towards the drainage gate
to facilitate removal of water.
✓ modified: bottom ditch within the pond running along and
close to base of dike
➢ collects and leads the water to the catching pond where
the drainage gate is also located
✓ Peripheral canals are provided to:
➢ serve as shelter for the shrimp
➢ increase the pond bottom surface area
➢ have better water circulation

Design of water canals or channels
Peripheral Canals Middle ditch

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Main Water Supply Canal (MWSC)
✓ starts at the main gate usually
traverse the central portion of the
fish farm
✓ sloping towards the floor of the
main gate
✓ has a main gate opening of 1m and
have a canal bed of at least 3.0m
wide, that can supply a 10-15ha with
dike slope of 1:1

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Secondary Water Supply Canal

✓ starts from the main canal to
inner portion
✓ smaller than main canal
✓ canal bed of width of 2.0m

Tertiary Water Supply Canal

✓ supply water to nursery pond
and transition pond
✓ usually considered part of NP or
TP system
✓ modified as catching pond
✓ canal bed width of 1.0 -1.5m

Diversion Canal
✓ Protect the farm from being flooded with run-off water
from watershed
Drainage Canal
✓ improve water management
✓ usually located at the other side of the pond parallel to the
supply canal
✓ recommended in intensive culture

✓ Determine the bottom width and capacity of an earthen canal
with water depth of 0.75 m (d) and side slope of 1.5:1 (z=1.5).
The canal has a bed slope of 0.0010 or 1/1 000.
d = 0.75m
z = 1.5 b = 2(0.75m)( 1 + 1.52 − 1.5)
b = (1.5m) (0.30)

Determination of canal bed width and capacity
d = 0.75m
z = 1.5
b = 0.45

Determination of canal bed width and capacity
d = 0.75m
z = 1.5
b = 0.453m
Canal bed
slope is
1/1000
velocity of flow at bed slope of 1/1000 is 0.44 m/sec

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Determination of canal bed width and capacity
✓ The design discharge or capacity of a canal for steady and
uniform flow is calculated by using the continuity equation:
Q = AV
➢ A= area of trapezoidal earth canal (m2)
➢ V = velocity of flow (m/s)
➢ Q = discharge or rate of flow in m3/s
✓ Hence, the capacity of the canal:
1.184 m2 × 0.44 m/s = 0.521 m3/s

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Underbrushing
✓ vegetation including nipa trees and shrubs, of less than 10 cm
in diameter are cut with the use of bolo
✓ done before the perimeter dike and the main gate are
completed
Withering (optional)
✓ to kill the trees by filling up the pond with water
✓ Rhizophora usually die out when their trunks are constantly
soaked with water at a depth of more than 0.5 m for a period
of 4 to 6 months

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Falling
✓ cutting down big trees left after underbrushing
✓ Either manual or mechanical method (chain saw)
Uprooting of stumps
✓ complete removal of tree stumps and root system by
manual labour or by the use of small machines(winch and
pulley block or a mechanical tree puller)

AQUACULTURE ENGINEERING
(Fish cage design and
construction)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ A cage is defined as “an enclosure with bottom and sides of
netting or bamboo etc., whether floating at the surface or totally
submerged.”
✓ Cages have enclosed bottom and sides made of net screens,
wood or wire mesh
✓ Size range: 1- 1,000m3
✓ The two most important things to remember are:
➢ Cages should be made of sturdy materials.
➢ The cage materials should be strong, durable, and non-
toxic.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ The cage (mesh size) must be
able to retain the fish, yet allow
maximum circulation of water
through the cage.
✓ It is best to select the largest
mesh possible that will retain
your fish.
✓ Adequate water circulation
brings oxygen into the cage
while washing wastes away.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Size and Shape
✓ Cages in a variety of shapes such as rectangular, square shape,
cylindrical or polygonal
✓ It can be easily constructed by the fish farmer using materials such as
bamboo or wooden slats and wire, nylon and other synthetic
meshes or can be purchased already made from several sources.
✓ Cages can be made almost any size but most round cages are 4 feet
deep and a little less than 4 feet in diameter
✓ rolls of plastic mesh or plastic coated welded wire are sold in 4 foot
widths
✓ Rectangular cages are usually
8 ft. x 4 ft. x 4 ft.
8 ft. x 8 ft. x 4 ft
12 ft. x 6 ft. x 4 ft.
(length x width x depth)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Materials
✓ Cage components consist of frame,
nets, floats, weights and ropes.
Frame
✓ The frame of the cage can be made
from wood, plastic, fiberglass, PVC
or metal.
✓ Frames made from metals and
wood should be coated with a
water resistant paint.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Net Materials
✓ Plastic coated, welded wire, solid plastic mesh or nylon
netting.
✓ Mesh size of the net depends on the culture species,
initial size of the seed, and the culture method.
✓ If we use 6-8 inch fingerlings as seed to culture most
suitable mesh size is ½ inch and nets with 1/8, ¼ or 3/8
inch (0.5 – 1.0 mm) mesh sizes can be used for fry to
fingerling rearing cages (nursery).

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Floats
✓ flotation can be provided by
waterproof foam rubber,
Styrofoam, sealed PVC pipes,
plastic bottles or barrels, sealed
metallic barrels or any other
suitable floating material
➢ Small cages: Styrofoam or
foam rubber floats
➢ Large cages: Plastic or metal
barrels

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Anchors
✓ anchored using stones or
cement or metallic anchors
✓ For fixed cages the cage
should be fixed to the
bottom using bamboo, PVC
pipes or metallic pipes and
nylon ropes to avoid drift.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Floating Cages
✓ Floating net fish cages are made of
nylon net material, all sides and
corners supported with polyethylene
rope fixed by a nylon twine.
✓ Cage is suspending within a
rectangular area.
✓ Whilst the top is clamped to bamboo
structure which are suspended by
floaters (generally barrels), the bottom
is provided with lead, stone or cement
sinkers.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Fixed Cages
✓ Fixed cages can be designed with a
frame which is used to hold the net
material or without the frame.
✓ Using poles, this type of cage
can be fixed to the pond bottom.
✓ For the cages without frame, these
fixing poles also can be used to
tide up the net and keep the shape
of the cage.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ Water body must have at least 1/2 ha or more in surface area.
✓ Cage should be placed in an area where there is at least two
feet of water between the bottom of the cage and the pond or
lake bottom.
✓ The cage should also be placed where the maximum natural
water circulation present which can move water freely through
and around the cage.
✓ It is better if the longest side of the cage is oriented
perpendicular to the direction of the wind.

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ Shelter, protected from strong winds and waves
✓ Currents, stagnant waters with currents
✓ Water quality, less turbidity
✓ Water depth, should be 2-3m
✓ Services & security, land area availability

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
✓ Should satisfy the ff:
➢ hold the fish securely
➢ Remove potentially harmful metabolites
➢ Cage volume must remain relatively resistant to deformation
by external forces
✓ Circular in shape
➢ make efficient use of materials
➢ Have higher construction cost than square
➢ Stable even during rough weather

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Cage Bags
✓ Netting materials can be flexible or rigid
➢ Flexible: natural or synthetic fibers
nylon nets: knotless, knotted
➢ Rigid: plastics and metals mesh
square or diamond mesh

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Cage Collars
✓ Three different methods may be used to construct the
framework/collar for a sea cage:
➢ Stiff framework: The framework does not follow the wave
movements (steel cages)
➢ Framework with movable joints: follow the wave movements to
some extent (traditional steel cage system, where joints are used to
connect the single elements in the framework)
➢ Flexible framework: The framework is quite flexible and will
follow the wave movements well (frames made of plastic
polyethylene, PE which are flexible to some degree; and those
made of rubber)

Fundamentals of Fisheries and Aquaculture Engineering
Cage Collars

Mooring Systems
✓ Consists of lines and anchors
✓ Chain, nylon ropes or
combination
✓ Length should not be less
than 3x the water depth of the
site
✓ Anchors: fabricated or bought
➢ concrete blocks with steel
rods and eyebolt

Mooring Systems
✓ Different types of anchors

✓ Consists of lines and anchors
✓ Chain, nylon ropes or

✓ Length should not be less
than 3x the water depth of the
site

1. Which is not a problem caused by acid rain?
a. Soil acidity
b. Structure corrosion
c. Soil erosion
d. Structure erosion
e. Water acidity
Answer: a. Soil erosion

Acid rain is rain that has been made acidic by
certain pollutants in the air.
"Acid rain" is a broad term referring to a mixture of
wet and dry deposition from the atmosphere
containing higher than normal amounts of acids.
Acid rain occurs when these gases react in the
atmosphere with water, oxygen, and other
chemicals to form various acidic compounds.
What is acid rain?

• Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water and then,
like carbon dioxide, hydrolyses in a series of
equilibrium reactions:
SO2 (g)+ H2O ⇌ H+ + HSO3-
HSO3- ⇌ H+ + SO32-

• Nitrogen dioxide, nitrogen monoxide and
carbon dioxide:
2 NO2 (g)+ H2O ⇌ HNO2 + HNO3
2 NO (g)+ H2O ⇌ 2 HNO3
CO2 (g)+ H2O ⇌ H2CO3


Wet deposition
Wet deposition of acids occurs when any
form of precipitation (rain, snow, and so on.)
removes acids from the atmosphere and
delivers it to the earth's surface
Dry deposition
Acid deposition also occurs via dry deposition in the
absence of precipitation. This can be responsible for as
much as 20 to 60% of total acid deposition. This occurs
when particles and gases stick to the ground, plants or
other surfaces.

What causes acid rain?
Acid rain is caused by the burning of fossil fuels.
Burning oil, gas and coal in power stations releases
Sulphur Dioxide (SO2) into the atmosphere.
Burning oil and petrol in motor vehicles puts nitrogen
oxides (NOX) into the atmosphere.

Natural Causes
The principal natural phenomena that contribute
acid-producing gases to the atmosphere are
a. Emissions from volcanoes
b. Emissions from biological processes that occur
on the land, in wetlands, and in the oceans.
* The major biological source of sulfur containing
compounds is dimethyl sulfide.


What problems are caused by acid
rain?
Acid rain increases the
acidity levels of soils.

Acid rain increases the acidity levels of
rivers, lakes and seas, destroying its
chemical balance.

Acid rain can erode buildings
and monuments (particularly
if they are made from
limestone).

2. Refers to an increase in the primary productivity
of any ecosystem caused by the increase of
chemical nutrients, typically compounds of N & P
a. Ecological succession
b. Eutrophication
c. Environmental degradation
d. Both a & b
e. All of the above
Answer: d. Both a & b


• Eutrophication generally promotes excessive
plant growth and decay, favors certain weedy
species over others, and is likely to cause
severe reductions in water quality .
• In aquatic environments, enhanced growth of
choking aquatic vegetation (algal bloom)
disrupts normal functioning of the ecosystem,
causing a variety of problems

Atmospheric Optics
All atmospheric optical phenomena are produced when the
path of sunlight is obstructed.
The path of light can be obstructed in several ways:
a. Light is scattered in all directions when it passes microscopic
particles such as aerosol particles or even air molecules
b. It is reflected from the surface of larger particles such as
raindrops and ice crystals.
c. It is refracted (bent) gradually as it travels through the
atmosphere, or abruptly as it passes between water and air.
d. It is also diffracted into a field of patterned waves as it skirts
around tiny cloud droplets.
e. Finally, it can be absorbed by matter and extinguished.

29. This type of precipitation results from the
differential heating of air masses near the
ground surface resulting in the upward
movement of warmer air masses.
a. Convective precipitation
b. Orographic precipitation
c. Cyclonic precipitation
d. Frontal Precipitation
e. Both c and d
Answer: a. Convective precipitation

TYPES OF PRECIPITATION
1. Convective precipitation
2. Orographic precipitation
3. Cyclonic precipitation

1. Convective Precipitation
This type of precipitation results from the differential heating of air
masses near the ground surface resulting in the upward movement
of warmer air masses.
A heated air mass moving
upward is cooled down by the
surrounding air and by the
expansion process. Cooling
brings about condensation
which may develop into
precipitation.

➢ Convective precipitation are usually highly localized
and of short duration.
➢ Typical of the tropics
➢ May be in the form of light showers to cloudburst or
thunderstorm depending on the temperature and
moisture conditions

2. Orographic precipitation
Precipitation influenced by topography
Moist air masses moving
over mountain barriers are
cooled, resulting in
condensation and
precipitation. Such air
masses get dry and warm
as they move downslope
on the leeward side of the
mountain barriers.

The influence of this type of
precipitation on the climate of
many areas in the Philippines
is very significant considering
that the Philippines is
mountainous and made up of
a chain of many islands
Orographic types of rainfall are usually of very
low intensity.

3. Cyclonic precipitation
Are associated with the movement of air masses due
to differences in barometric pressure
This type of precipitation is
triggered by the presence of a
low pressure into which air flow
converges resulting in the lifting
and subsequent cooling of air
masses.
In most parts of the Philippines, more than 80% of the total rainfall
are attributable to cyclonic precipitation.

54. The passage of water into the soil surface
a. Infiltration
b. Seepage
c. Percolation
d. Leaching
e. All of the above
Answer: a. Infiltration

Infiltration is the passage of water into the
soil surface.
In general, infiltration has a high initial rate that diminishes with time.

It is a key to successful irrigation and water conservation in rainfed agriculture.
It is also an important hydrologic process that must be considered in drainage and
flood control work.

FACTORS AFFECTING INFILTRATION
Infiltration may be considered as a three-stage sequence.
(1) surface entry
(2) filling up of soil profile storage potential, and
(3) movement or transmission of water within the soil profile
* The three phases are interactive in nature.

(1) The fluid or water
Specific fluid properties influencing infiltration
✓ Viscosity
✓ Turbidity
✓ Depth of water over the soil surface

(2) The porous medium or soil
Soil properties affecting infiltration
◆ Porosity
◆ Structure
◆ surface stability
◆ moisture holding capacity
◆ antecedent soil moisture
◆ mineralogy

Lateritic soils are non-swelling and are usually
characterized by high infiltration rates.
Montmorillonitic clay soils crack upon drying and have high
initial infiltration rates. They however, swell upon wetting and,
hence, have very low permeabilities.

(3) Vegetation and soil cultural practices
- are the most significant factors affecting infiltration
Vegetal cover protects the soil against raindrops energy and improves soil
structure through organic matter production and root penetration.
Tillage practices loosen up the upper soil layer thereby tremendously
increasing the rate of surface entry of water and the porosity of the plowed
layer.

MEASUREMENT OF INFILTRATION

2. Basin Method
3. Watershed Hydrograph Method

3. Watershed Hydrograph Method
- characterizing infiltration from watersheds

INFILTRATION EQUATION
An infiltration equation may be expressed as:
a. Instantaneous infiltration rate (f)
b. Cumulative infiltration rate (i)

1. Gardner and Windsoe Equation
i = C1t + C2 (1-eβt)
Where: i = cumulative infiltration at time t
C1, C2 and β = constants or parameters

2. Lewis-Kostiakov
i = ctα
Where: c and α are constants with the value
of α in between zero and unity
f = αctα-1

log i = log c + α log t
Hence, it will be very easy to test for the fit of infiltration test
data into this equation.
Lewis-Kostiakov equation implies that at t → ∞, f = 0. This
is only possible if the soil is underlain by an impermeable
layer. As such, the equation will only apply for soil
underlain with impervious layers or for small t values in
soils with pervious layers.

3. Horton Equation
f = fc + (fo - fc)e-kt
Horton realized that infiltration rate is a decay type function
whereby continuous infiltration and wetting of the soil will
decrease infiltration due to decrease in soil profile storage
potential, inwashing of fine soil particles into soil voids and
swelling of soil colloids and closing of soil cracks.
All these processes have the nature of an exhaustion
phenomenon.

chance and time -dependent. What type of process is
this?
a. Deterministic process
b. Stochastic Process
c. Probabilistic process
d. Hydrolistic Process
e. Partial Duration Process
Answer: b. Stochastic Process

Hydrologic process
-is any hydrologic phenomenon which undergoes
continuous changes with time
It is either deterministic, probabilistic, or
stochastic in nature.

A deterministic process is one in which a definite law of
certainty exists. It is one where the chance element is ignored as
in the case of flood routing.
A probabilistic or stochastic process is one governed by chance
phenomena, that is, there are so many causes at work that the
influence of one cannot be readily identified.
A stochastic process is time dependent.
This means that the sequence of occurrence of events
or the time series is considered in its analysis.
A probabilistic process, on the other hand, is time series independent.

All hydrologic processes are more or less stochastic.
They are assumed to be either deterministic or
probabilistic to simplify their analysis.
Probabilistic analysis of hydrologic processes deals with the
estimation of the chance or likelihood of occurrence of a given
event by determining the frequency curves of best fit to samples
of hydrologic data.

How to Convert Degrees Minutes Seconds To Decimal
Degrees
Decimal degrees = Degrees + (Minutes/60) +
(Seconds/3600)
For Example, to convert 39° 25' 30" to decimal degrees
First, convert minutes and seconds to their degree
equivalents and add the results
25'/60 = 0.4167°
30"/3600 = .0083°
and 0.4167° + 0.0083° = 0.425°
Then, add this number to the number of degrees.
39° + 0.425° = 39.425°
So, the final result is:
39° 25' 30" = 39.425°

How to Convert Decimal Degrees to DMS
There are 60 minutes per degree, and 60 seconds per
minute. So the conversion factor for each decimal is to
multiply by 60.
For Example, to convert decimal degrees 156.742 to
degrees minutes seconds
1. The whole number is degrees. So 156.742 gives you 156
degrees.
2. Multiply the remaining decimal by 60.
0.742*60 = 44.52, so the whole number 44 equals minutes.
3. Multiply the remaining decimal by 60.
0.52*60 = 31.2, so the whole number 31 equals seconds.
Decimal degrees 156.742 converts to 156 degrees, 44
minutes and 31 seconds, or 156° 44' 31".

28. What is the UTM coordinate of a location which is
located in 3,550,000 meters south of the equator and
85,000 meters West from the central meridian.

UNIVERSAL TRANSVERSE MERCATOR (UTM) CRS
- The zones are called
UTM 33S, UTM 34S,
UTM 35S and UTM
36S.
- The S after the zone
means that the UTM
zones are located
south of the equator.
- For Philippines, we
are WGS 84 / UTM
zone 51N You can see, that the area is located within the UTM zone 35S. This
means, to minimize distortion and to get accurate analysis results, we
should use UTM zone 35S as the coordinate reference system.

UNIVERSAL TRANSVERSE MERCATOR (UTM) CRS
- In UTM coordinate
reference system,
we have to add a
so called false
northing value of
10,000,000 m to the
northing (Y) value
and a false easting
value of 500,000 m
to the easting (X)
value. You can see, that the area is located within the UTM zone 35S. This
means, to minimize distortion and to get accurate analysis results, we
should use UTM zone 35S as the coordinate reference system.

UNIVERSAL TRANSVERSE MERCATOR (UTM) CRS
The northing (Y) value
- The place we are looking for is
3,550,000 meters south of the
equator, so the northing (Y)
value gets a negative sign
and is -3,550,000 m.
- According to the UTM
definitions we have to add a
false northing value of
10,000,000 m.
- This means the northing (Y)
value of our coordinate is
6,450,000 m (-3,550,000 m +
10,000,000 m).

UNIVERSAL TRANSVERSE MERCATOR (UTM) CRS
The easting (X) value
- The place we are looking for is
85,000 meters West from the
central meridian.
- Just like the northing value, the
easting (X) value gets a negative
sign, giving a result of -85,000 m.
- According to the UTM definitions
we have to add a false easting
value of 500,000 m.
- This means the easting (X) value
of our coordinate is 415,000 m
(-85,000 m + 500,000 m).

UNIVERSAL TRANSVERSE MERCATOR (UTM) CRS
As a result, the coordinate for our
Point of Interest, projected in UTM
zone 35S would be written as:
415,000 m E / 6,450,000 m N.
In some GIS, when the correct UTM
zone 35S is defined and the units are
set to meters within the system, the
coordinate could also simply
appear as 415,000 6,450,000.
