4
Principle of Storage
☐ Grains are living organisms that require
nourishment, grow, and die. They must
have essentially the same care required by
other living organisms if they are to remain
alive and in good condition. The grains’
embryo is particularly sensitive to
temperature and humidity.
☐ If the temperature and humidity are kept
low at about 15°C and at moisture content
of 14 to 15%, the embryo remains viable
but inactive and the grains can be stored
for long period. However, when the
temperature and humidity increase, the
viable embryo becomes active, draw
nourishment from the concentrated
nutrients, particularly starch and protein
stored in the endosperm.
7
☐ Heat and moisture result from the process and soon the grain
mass begins to warm up. This further stimulates the activity of the
embryo and chain reaction is formed. Molds and microorganisms are
frequently present in the kernels; and if insects are also present, they
are assumed to become active thereby still producing more heat and
moisture. Eventually, part of the grain mass develops a temperature
of 57°C at which time visible deterioration and rotting begins. Good
storage must then provide an environment in which grains will remain
viable but inactive.

CATEGORIES OF STORAGE PRACTICES
☐ Farm Level
The amount stored in this level of operation is small, sufficient for
family consumption in one season. The common methods used are
storing grains in plastic bags, bamboo basket, “tabungos”, or tin
cans of about a cubic meter in size.

☐ Commercial Level

• Warehouse – is a flat and long building with several side doors
and roof ventilators. Materials of construction are usually
concrete flooring, GI roofing, and either GI or concrete hollow
block walling. Grains are sacked and stacked on the floor.
• Flat Store - is similar to a warehouse but the grains are stored in
bulk rather than in sacks.
• Rectangular-Steel/Wooden Bin – is normally used for bulk
storage of grains inside the building.
• Steel/Concrete Silos – are slender and tall structures for bulk
storage of grains with individual roofs.

☐ During storage, the physical factors like temperature, moisture
and pests are the most important ones that influence the keeping
quality of the grains. The grains being hygroscopic in nature, picks
up moisture from the atmosphere and attains its equilibrium.
Moisture and temperature produce favorable condition for the
multiplication of insects and fungi. The important deteriorative
changes that take place in storage are either visible type such as
sprouting, olding, weevilization and discoloration, or invisible
chemical and biochemical changes such as less viability,
development of free fatty acid, loss of nutritive values, cooking
quality, etc.
29
☐ Rodents and birds also cause qualitative and quantitative
losses by direct feeding or contamination by their dead bodies,
urine, fecal matter, etc. In addition, they are responsible for
spreading a number of diseases also.
☐ Hygiene and sanitary conditions in and around the storage
structure is an essential requirement for scientific storage
management as clean surroundings can do away with 70 to 80%
of infestation problem. Pesticides, when used on dusty surface,
do not give desired results.
30

7/26/25
16
MAIN REQUISITES FOR QUALITY
CONTROL IN GRAINS DURING
STORAGE
☐ Selection of suitable and
adequate facilities.
☐ Preparation of warehouse
for receipt of grains to eliminate
all sources of infestation.
☐ Planning for proper storage
by acquiring adequate quantity
of pallets, pesticides and other
pest control equipment in
advance.
31
☐ Inspection of grains at the
time of receipt in warehouse with
a view to have first-hand
information about the quality of
the incoming grains and also to
segregate weevil, dump or
damaged and contaminated
grains.
☐ Care during stacking to build
stable blocks standing on pallets
away from wall with sufficient
alley ways around.
☐ Periodic inspection and
analysis of grains during storage
with view to draw up
disinfestation program ad priority
list for issue of stock.
32

7/26/25
17
☐ Implementation of preventive and curative
disinfestation measure regularly during
storage.
☐ Unkeep of the warehouse throughout the
storage period.
☐ Issue of stock according to drawn out
priority list. Necessary care at the time of
issue needs to be exercised to segregate the
deteriorating grains with a view to avoid any
complaint of substandard.
☐ Timely reconditioning of substandard stock
segregated at the time of receipt/issue and
during storage so as to recover good grains.
☐ Whenever necessary, set rules to avoid
processing and disposal of damaged grains
for human consumption.
☐ Safer handling of pesticides and their
judicious use to avoid contamination of food
grains beyond prescribed tolerance limit.
33
STORAGE REQUIREMENTS
☐ Water tightness to prevent water from reaching the grains.
☐ Air tightness to prevent adsorption of water vapor from high
temperature and high humidity atmospheric air.
☐ Alternative to airtight-storage bins to circulate artificially-cooled
air (15°C) around the grains to prevent moisture accumulation and
quality deterioration.
☐ Drying facilities may be necessary in conjunction with the
storage facilities to assure right moisture content of grains prior to
storage, which is in the range of 12 to 14%.
☐ Rodent proof.
☐ Bird proof.
34

7/26/25
18
☐ Facilities for fumigation to kill insects. An airtight structure
will accomplish this by reducing oxygen to keep the insects
inactive.
☐ Facilities for bulk storage circulation for removal of possible
hot-spot in non-airtight structures.
☐ Material-handling equipment to move bulk grains into and out
of the storage structure mechanically.
☐ Economical with respect to materials and equipment must be
indigenous to the area, if possible.
☐ Storage size must be planned, designed and constructed to
accommodate the need may it be on far, for group of farmers, or
for some central warehouses.
35
36

7/26/25
19
Techniques in Storing Grains
☐ Low-Temperature Storage
☐ Hermitic Storage
☐ Underground Storage
37
LOW-TEMPERATURE STORAGE
☐ In low temperature storage, refrigeration equipment are needed
to maintain the required temperature. Usually, temperature is
maintained not higher than 15°C in a mechanically-cooled
warehouse. In other countries where low-temperature storage in
widely practiced, rice is dried to 15% moisture. Grains are
husked and packed in 60-kg straw bags.
38

7/26/25
20
☐ Respiration of paddy at 15% and 15°C is almost completely
suspended; thus, the loss of viability is prevented.
☐ Germination ratio of more than 80% can be maintained for
two to three years in rice at 15% and 15°C.
☐ Insects and microorganisms’ damage to rice at 15% mc is
prevented as low-temperature storage keep them inactive.
☐ Fumigation of rice is not necessary; thereby, reducing
expenditure and retaining the uncontaminated quality.
☐ Fresh rice taste is maintained for a couple of years.
39
☐ Milling quality is high and energy requirement is low. The milling
yield increases by 1 kg per 60 kg rice.
☐ Warehouse storage capacity can be increased by 20 to 30%
allowing narrower and fewer passage ways in the warehouse.
☐ Storage management is simple since control in temperature and
humidity need to be monitored.
☐ Lower cost of electricity is required for refrigeration than for
fumigation.
☐ Quality of bran does not deteriorate as readily than those stored
at high temperature.
40

7/26/25
21
LIMITATIONS OF LOW-TEMPERATURE
STORAGE
☐ Mechanical refrigeration equipment need to be properly sized
and designed.
☐ The warehouse needs to be insulated to minimize refrigeration
requirements.
☐ Continuous and economical supply of electricity is necessary.
☐ Warehouse should be at least 500sq.m. for 10,000 bags, for
economy.
41
HERMITIC STORAGE
☐ Hermitic storage is a technique of
storage which eliminates exchange of
gases and liquids. Airtight storage
keeps the grains dry even the outside
condition has high temperature and
high humidity. Also, this technique of
storage will prevent rice or other food
grains in storage to respire as soon as
the available supply of oxygen is
exhausted. The resulting storage gas
mixture will be low in oxygen and high
in carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide of 13
to 19% will kill insect eggs, larvae, and
adults.
42

7/26/25
22
Advantages of Hermitic Storage
☐ Disinfects stored food stuff by destroying insects, irrespective of
their stage of development.
☐ Positively prevents the admission of insects, rodents and other
pests.
☐ Inactivates molds and prevents overheating when the product
contains a relatively high moisture level without preventing the
development of acidity caused by anaerobic fermentation when the
humidity is excessive.
☐ All grain products that are dry at the time of storage remain dry.
☐ Saves time and money in inspecting hot spots.
43
Some of the Limiting Factors Pertaining
Gas-Tight Storage
☐ Airtight structure are somewhat expensive and difficult to
manage unless plastic lining materials are used.
☐ Rigid type airtight structures must be provided with a breather
bags as an expansion tank to accommodate the change in air
volume with the change in temperature.
☐ The rate of oxygen reduction through the metabolism process
for dry ice at 12 to 14% must be checked with the initial rate of
activity for weevils, beetles, or other insect contained in the rice
to be sure significant damage does not occur before oxygen
reduction kills them.
☐ It is unlikely that high-moisture rice can be stored in sealed
bins without enough oxidation taking place to alter the taste
undesirably.
44

7/26/25
23
UNDERGROUND STORAGE
☐ This type of storage is readily found in
India. The depth is about 5 meters and
almost the same up to a narrow circular
opening at the top. It may or may not be
lined with bricks or concrete. The grains
are stored in bulk. A layer of straw is
placed on all sided of the grain bulk at the
time of filling. Often, about half-meter
thickness of grain layer at the periphery
adjoining the walls turn black due to rotting
because they are not moisture proof. The
insect infestation is comparatively low
because oxygen is depleted.
45
GRAIN AERATION
☐ Aeration is the process of ventilating
stored grains by moving air through
them to maintain quality. A typical
aeration system moves air down through
the grains as it replenishes stale air
surrounding the grains with fresh air.
This replaces the practice of turning the
grains or moving them to another
storage bin which is much cheaper and
minimizes damage during handling.
46

7/26/25
24
Benefits of Aeration
☐ Removes odors from the grains.
☐ Prevents moisture accumulation.
☐ Controls the condition favorable to mold growth and
insect activity.
47
MAJOR COMPONENTS OF AERATION
☐ Fan – It generates the pressure to force air through the duct
system and the grain mass. Trash and fines create uneven
pressure.
☐ Duct System – Design of air-handling system is crucial to good
fan operation. Poorly designed ducts can create more resistance to
flow.
☐ Drying or Perforated Floor – This factor has prepunched holes
to minimize resistance to airflow and is used for in-bin drying as well
as aeration.
48

7/26/25
25
DESIGNING AERATION SYSTEM
FOR BULK GRAIN STORAGE
☐ Aeration system for bulk storage is designed to remove the heat
generated by the grains in the storage. A device to determine the
volume of air to be delivered per ton-minute is included in the
design of the system, also the fan, duct, motor as well as control
system to deliver the desired amount of air.
49
☐ Basically, air is blown through the
stored grains for the following
reasons:
1. To maintain uniform condition in
the storage;
2. To remove generated water; and
3. To remove generated heat.
☐ In storage, care must be exercised
to prevent rewetting the grains with
aeration, an error that results from
delivery of the air above the
equilibrium relative humidity of the
grains determines the requirements
for aeration.
50

7/26/25
26
STEPS IN DESIGNING AERATION
SYSTEM FOR BULK STORAGE
1. Select the Design Moisture
2. Calculate the Generated Heat
3. Select the Design Day
4. Calculate Equilibrium Humidity
5. Determine Hours of Operation
6. Calculate the Amount of Air Needed
7. Determine the Air Volume and Pressure
8. Determine the Power Requirement
9. Select Fan
10.Design the Air Distribution System
11.Design the Power and Control
51
☐ Select the Design Moisture
The design moisture approximates the equilibrium relative
humidity of a local climate. For rough rice, design moisture
usually ranges between 14.5 to 15.2%. However, for special
storage designed for wet season harvest, design moisture of
up to 17% could be selected. A good indicator in determining
the design moisture is the equilibrium moisture content of the
particular grain on a given condition.
52

7/26/25
27
☐ Calculate the Generated Heat
Generated heat should be estimated as a function of design
moisture. Supposing the grains to be stored is paddy with
16% moisture, the heat and water generated may be
computed using the formula,
log (CO2) = A Mw – B
where:
Mw 	- moisture content, %
A & B 	- constants
53
Rate of Deterioration Constants for
Some Cereal Grains
Grain 	Moisture Ranges
(%)
A 	B
Corn, yellow dent 	10.0 – 13.2 	0.17 	2.00
13.3 – 17.0 	0.27 	3.33
Sorghum 	10.0 – 13.2 	0.12 	1.65
13.3 – 17.0 	0.32 	4.19
Rough Rice 	10.0 – 14.1 	0.21 	3.04
14.2 – 17.0 	0.44 	6.08
Polished Rice 	10.0 – 14.1 	0.16 	2.83
14.2 – 17.0 	0.49 	7.48
Brown Rice 	10.0 – 13.7 	0.17 	2.67
13.8 – 17.0 	0.44 	6.41
Wheat, soft 	14.2 – 17.0 	0.36 	5.14
54

7/26/25
28
☐ Select the Design Day
In selecting the design day, local weather data must be used
and, as much as possible, these data should have information
on local weather at least for the last 10 years. The wettest
month appearing in the data should be selected.
55
☐ Calculate the Equilibrium Humidity
Equilibrium relative humidity or reciprocally, grain moisture in
equilibrium with air may be computed using the formula,
ERH = Exp[ -A / R x (T + C)] x [Exp (-B x Md)]
where:
ERH 	- equilibrium relative humidity, decimal
R 	- universal gas constant, 1.987
T 	- Temperature, °C
Md 	- moisture content, db decimal
A, B, C - equilibrium constants
56

7/26/25
29
☐ Determine Hours of Operation
Hours of operation must be those hours in the design day
that fall below the equilibrium humidity. Example, for Iloilo
the wettest month is August. To determine the hours of
operation, draw the equilibrium relative humidity level to the
design day relative humidity curve. Those hours that fall
below the equilibrium relative humidity will be considered as
design hours of operation.
57
☐ Calculate the Amount of Air Needed
The amount of air needed can be estimated by allowing 3°C
temperature rise in the aeration air. One kJ basically heats on
kg of air 1°C. For a 3°C rise, the air needed per ton-day
therefore is
85.5 / 3 kJ heat generated = 28.5 kg of air/ton-day
58

7/26/25
30
☐ Determine the Air Volume and Pressure
Air volume, pressure and power are critical in the design of
aeration system. It is sometimes economical to aerate a deep
bin because of excessive power requirement. In storage, air is
used through grains as a vehicle to carry away heat and water.
It is used to maintain uniform temperatures, an important
requirement to eliminate moisture migration.
59
☐ Determine the Power Requirement
Power is the expression of the rate of doing work. In air flow,
the term air horsepower refers to the work done by the flow of
air and is expressed as watts or horsepower. To compute for
the air horsepower,
Air Hp = Airflow (CFM) x Static Pressure (in. water) / 6360
The brake horsepower can be determined by dividing the air
horsepower by the efficiency of the air-moving unit.
60

7/26/25
31
☐ Select Fan
Selection of fan must be made in accordance with the
catalogues that give the fan characteristics. The procedure in
Fan Design provides the basics of determining the size of fan
required for the system.
61
DESIGN THE AIR DISTRIBUTION
SYSTEM
☐ Duct design consists of two basic velocity constraints. The velocity
of the air in the main distribution duct is
• For depth of grains less than 5 meters
V = 300 to 600 m/min
• For depths of grains over 5 meters
V = 400 to 900 m/min
62

7/26/25
32
Design of Power and Control
☐ Power and control can present a problem when the power
network is not reliable, although electric power for fans is much
preferred over gasoline.
☐ Humidistic controls require frequent calibration for accuracy.
They can be adjusted according to readings of wet and dry bulb
sling psychrometers that are quite accurate for humidity
measurement. A sling psychrometer and a manual switch can be
used for control of the fans if a responsible individual is present at
the storage. A recording hygrometer that is calibrated weekly can
be used as an indicator of when the fans should be ran.
63
64

7/27/25
1
SUGAR MILLING
AGRICULTURAL AND FOOD PROCESS ENGINEERING
by
Engr. Alexis T. Belonio, MS
Agricultural and Biosystems Engineer
ASEAN Engineer
2025 AGRICULTURAL AND BIOSYSTEMS ENGINEERING
BOARD EXAM REVIEWER
1
Disclaimer
Photos, illustrations and schematic diagrams of equipment or machine parts shown in
the presentation are solely for educational purposes to facilitate comprehension of the
topics by the students. Showing them does not endorse a product nor imply criticism
of similar products not mentioned.
2

7/27/25
2
INTRODUCTION
☐ Sugarcane processing is the process
of producing cane sugar (sucrose) from
sugarcane.
Sugarcane is produced and harvested for
two purposes:
(1) Production of cane sugar
(2) Planting material
Cane sugar is the unrefined sugar or the
raw sugar.
Refined sugar is the raw sugar that
undergoes refining process to remove all
impurities and the surrounding plant
matter in sugar leaving only the pure
sucrose.
3
Sugar Mill
4

7/27/25
3
5
Traditional Sugar Milling
6

7/27/25
4
STAGES IN PRODUCING SUGAR
FROM SUGAR CANE
¾ Sugar Mill is where the raw sugar
is separated from the plant and
shipped to a refinery. First, the
sugarcane stalks are washed and
cut into shreds by rotating knives.
Next, huge rollers press the juice
out of the shredded pulp. This juice
is then clarified, concentrated, and
crystalized to produce raw sugar.
¾ Sugar Refineries is where raw
sugar are further processed into
different grades of sugar, usually
white crystal sugar for industrial
and home use.
7
Brown Sugar
Refined Sugar
8

7/27/25
5
PROCESSING BY-PRODUCTS
1. 	Bagasse - It is the residual woody fiber of the cane commonly
used as fuel for the boilers and lime kilns, production of
numerous paper and paperboard products and reconstituted
panel board, agricultural mulch, and as a raw material for
production of chemicals.
2. 	Dried filter cake – It is used as an animal feed supplement,
fertilizer, and source of sugarcane wax.
3. 	Molasses – Produced in two forms: (a) Inedible molasses
(blackstrap) which is used primarily as an animal feed additive
also used to produce ethanol, compressed yeast, citric acid, and
rum; (b) Edible molasses syrup are often blended with maple
syrup, invert sugars, or corn syrup.
9
Bagasse
10

7/27/25
6
Filter Cake
11
Bagacilio
12

7/27/25
7
Molasses
Edible 	Blackstrap
13
Mudpress
14

7/27/25
8
SUGARCANE HARVESTING
☐ Hand cutting is the most common harvesting method used in
harvesting sugarcane.
☐ Mechanical harvesters
☐ After cutting, the cane is loaded by hand, mechanical grab
loaders, or continuous loaders.
☐ Cane is transported to the mills using trailers, trucks, railcars,
or barges, depending upon the relative location of the cane
fields and the processing plants.
☐ When the cane is cut, rapid deterioration of the cane begins.
It cannot be stored for later processing without excessive
deterioration of the sucrose content.
15
The feeding table where harvested sugar cane stalks are fed for
cleaning and successive pressing to produce juice.
16

7/27/25
9
Another view of the feeding table showing the knives for cutting the
stalks into pieces before entering the roller press.
17
18

7/27/25
10
19
The drive units of the roller press which controlled by inverters to
vary the speed of each roller.
20

7/27/25
11
Close-up view of the roller press showing the v-ribs that presses the
sugar cane stalks
21
☐ Clarified – By adding milk of lime and carbon dioxide. The carbon
dioxide bubbles through the mixture forming calcium carbonate, a
chalk like crystal which attracts the non-sugar plant materials like
wax, fats, and gums from the juice. In a clarifier, the calcium
carbonate and the other materials fall out of the sucrose solution and
settle to the bottom.
☐ Concentrated by removing water from clarified juice in multiple
stages under vacuum. This allows the juice to boil at lower
temperatures to protect the sugar from caramelization. The juice
becomes a clear, rich brown syrup during this step.
☐ Water under very tight controls in a vacuum pan. Seed grain
(pulverized sugar) is fed into the pan as the water evaporates and
crystals begin to form. The mixture leaves the vacuum pan as a
thick crystal mass is sent to a centrifuge, a large perforated basket
spinning very rapidly much like a washing machine in the spin cycle,
where it is spun and dried, yielding golden raw sugar.
22

7/27/25
12
CANE SUGAR PRODUCTION PLANT
1. Cane is received at the mill and prepared for extraction of the
juice. At the mill, the cane is mechanically unloaded, placed in a
large pile, and, prior to milling, is cleaned. Product of cleaning
sugar cane prior to and after extraction or pressing is mudpress.
It is used as material for production of biofertilizer.
2. The milling process occurs in two steps: (a) breaking the hard
structure of the cane and (b) grinding the cane. Breaking the
cane uses revolving knives, shredders, crushers, or a
combination of these processes. For the grinding or milling of the
crushed canes, multiple sets of three-roller mills are most
commonly used although some mills consist of four, five, or six
rollers in multiple sets. Conveyors transport the crushed canes
from one mill to the next. Imbibition is the process in which
water or juice is applied to the crushed canes to enhance the
23
Sugar
Cane
Extraction
Cane
Juice
Roller
Pressing
Machines
Filtration /
Clarification
Filters/Centrifuge
Clarifiers
Mudpress 	Filter
Cake
Bagacillo
Evaporation
Liquid
Separation
Crystalization
Heat and lime
Added
Heat Exchangers/
Evaporation Pan
Syrup with 65%
and water of
35%
Vacuum Pan/
Centrifuge
Sugar Crystal
Centrifuge
Blackstrap Molasses
(feed mill)
Edible Molasses
(maple syrup)
Sugar crystal is formed
Sugarfor consumption
or for further
processing (refining)
Massecuite is
processed for
several times
24

7/27/25
13
extraction of the juice at the next mill.
In imbibition, water or juice from other
processing areas is introduced into
the last mill and transferred from mill
to mill towards the first two mills while
the crushed canes travel from the first
to the last mill. The crushed cane
exiting the last mill is called bagasse.
Mudpress – solid particle before and
after pressing sugar cane. This is larger
in particle sizes.
Filter cake – separation of juice from
mudpress after washing with water.
Bagacillo – very fine particles during
clarification
25
3. The juice from the mills is strained to remove large particles and
then clarified. In raw sugar production, clarification is done
almost exclusively with heat and lime (as milk of lime or lime
saccharate); small quantities of soluble phosphate may also be
added. The lime is added to neutralize the organic acids, and the
temperature of the juice raised to about 95C (200F). A heavy
precipitate forms which is separated from the juice in the clarifier.
The insoluble particulate mass, called “mud,” is separated from
the limed juice by gravity or centrifuge. The mud is filtered and
the filtered cake is washed with water. Clarified juice goes to the
evaporators without additional treatment.
26

7/27/25
14
4. Evaporation is performed in two stages: (a) initially in an evaporator
station to concentrate the juice and (b) then in vacuum pans to
crystallize the sugar. The clarified juice is passed through heat
exchangers to preheat the juice and then to the evaporator stations.
Evaporator stations consist of a series of evaporators, termed
multiple-effect evaporators; typically a series of five evaporators.
Steam from large boilers is used to heat the first evaporator, and the
steam from the water evaporated in the first evaporator is used to
heat the second evaporator. This heat transfer process continues
through the five evaporators and as the temperature decreases (due
to heat loss) from evaporator to evaporator, the pressure inside each
evaporator also decreases which allows the juice to boil at the lower
temperatures in the subsequent evaporator. Some steam is released
from the first three evaporators, and this steam is used in various
process heaters in the plant. The evaporator station in cane sugar
manufacture typically produces a syrup with about 65 percent solids
and 35 percent water. Following evaporation, the syrup is clarified
by adding lime, phosphoric acid, and a polymer flocculent, aerated,
and filtered in the clarifier. From the clarifier, the syrup goes to the
vacuum pans for crystallization.
27
5. Crystallization of sugar starts in the vacuum pans, which function
is to produce sugar crystals from the syrup. In the pan boiling
process, the syrup is evaporated until it reaches supersaturation
stage. At this point, the crystallization process is initiated by
“seeding” or “shocking” the solution. When the volume of the
mixture of liquor and crystals, known as massecuite, reaches the
capacity of the pan, the evaporation is allowed to proceed until the
final massecuite is formed. At this point, the contents of the
vacuum pans (called “strike”) are discharged to the crystallizer,
which function is to maximize the sugar crystal removal from the
massecuite. Some mills seed the vacuum pans with isopropyl
alcohol and ground sugar (or other similar seeding agent) rather
than with crystals from the process. From the crystallizer, the
massecuite (A massecuite) is transferred to high-speed centrifugal
machines (centrifugals), in which the mother liquor (termed
“molasses”) is centrifuged to the outer shell and the crystals
remain in the inner centrifugal basket. The crystals are washed
with water and the wash water centrifuged from the crystals.
28

7/27/25
15
29
6. The liquor (A molasses) from the first centrifugal is returned to a
vacuum pan and reboiled to yield a second massecuite (B
massecuite), that in turn yields a second batch of crystals. The B
massecuite is transferred to the crystallizer and then to the
centrifugal, and the raw sugar is separated from the molasses.
This raw sugar is combined with the first crop of crystals. The
molasses from the second boiling (B molasses) is of much lower
purity than the first molasses. It is reboiled to form a low grade
massecuite (C massecuite), which goes to a crystallizer and then to
a centrifugal.
30

7/27/25
16
7. This low-grade cane sugar is mingled with syrup and is sometimes
used in the vacuum pans as a “seeding” solution. The final
molasses from the third stage (blackstrap molasses) is a heavy,
viscous material used primarily as a supplement in cattle feed. The
cane sugar from the combined A and B massecuites is dried in
fluidized bed or spouted bed driers and cooled. After cooling, the
cane sugar is transferred to packing bins and then sent to bulk
storage. Cane sugar is then generally bulk loaded to trucks,
railcars, or barges.
31
Biomass-Fueled boiler to supply steam to the sugar mill
32

7/27/25
17
Series of roller mills to press sugar
cane stalk to produce juices
Control panel to adjust operation of
various equipment at the sugar mill
33

FEED MILLING

by

Photos, illustrations and schematic diagrams of equipment or machine parts shown in

of similar products not mentioned.
2

7/27/25
2
INTRODUCTION
☐ Feed milling is the process of
converting agricultural materials
into suitable kind of feeds for
animals’ consumption.
☐ Feed milling industry is an integral
part of the agricultural based
economy linking the grain sector
and the livestock and poultry
industries.
3
4

7/27/25
3
5
COMMERCIALLY-AVAILABLE
FEEDSTUFF
• Common Feed Ingredients

8

7/27/25
5
Feed Milling Plant
9
Feed Milling Plant
10

7/27/25
6
Feed Milling Plant
11
FOUR BASIC FUNCTIONS TO BE
PERFORMED IN THE PRODUCTION OF
ANIMAL FEEDS
• Collection of Raw Materials – This includes operations such as
transporting, receiving, cleaning, drying, and storage.
• Modifying of Raw Materials – This is to allow proper mixing and to
improve digestability. This includes operations such as grinding and
flaking in a roller mill.
• Blending and Mixing of Ingredients – This is to obtain the desired
formulation(s). This includes operation such as weighing and
volumetric dosing.
• Delivering the Compound Feed Produced – This includes
operations such as weighing, bagging, storage, and transport.
Modification of mixed product by pelleting, pressing into cake, or molding
into blocks maybe part of the production process.
12

7/27/25
7
Raw Materials for Feed Production
13
Inside the Feed Milling Plant
14

7/27/25
8
15
Collection of Raw
Materials
Modifying of Raw
Materials
Blending and Mixing of Ingredients
Delivering the Feed Produced
Modification of
Mixed Product
16

7/27/25
9
FEED MILLING OPERATIONS
☐ Transport and Reception – They are generally done by truck
and when the raw materials arrived, they are manhandled or
conveyed mechanically into the materials’ warehouse or silos.
☐ Cleaning and Drying – These are adopted in medium to large
feed milling operation to avoid losses due to damp and dirt from
the raw materials.
17
Transport
and
Reception
Cleaning and
Drying
Storage of
Raw Material
Blending
Grinding
Mixing
Pelleting
Storage of
Mixed Feeds
Bagging and
Delivery
Flow Process of Feed Production
18

7/27/25
10
☐ Storage of Raw Materials – It is
adopted to properly store raw materials
and to keep them away from insect
pests and rodents.
☐ Blending – It is the assembling and
measuring of the required qualities of
raw materials into batch of desired
composition.
☐ Grinding – It is done to prepare raw
materials for blending and or mixing and
to make them more digestible by the
animals.
19
☐ Mixing – It is done to obtain a
homogenous mixture of feeds so that
animal can be offered with different
nutrients in the desired proportions.
☐ Pelleting – It is the process of
making the feed into an acceptable
solid particle so that nutrients are
properly distributed in the feeds.
20

7/27/25
11
☐ Storage of Mixed Feeds – This
is usually done in bags for small
feed mills and in bulk or silos in
larger feed mills. Storage period of
2 to 7 days are usually done for
mixed feeds than for raw materials.
☐ Bagging and Bulk Delivery –
Bagging is usually done to distribute
the feeds in smaller scale. Bulk
delivery is appropriate for large
farm operation.
21
TYPES OF RAW MATERIALS
☐ Dry Macro Ingredients – grains, bran, fish meal, oil cakes, etc
☐ Dry Micro Ingredients – premix, minerals, etc
☐ Liquid Ingredients - molasses
22

7/27/25
12
RECEPTION OF MATERIALS
• Weighing
• Preliminary or physical inspection – This is a vital part of raw
material quality control.
• Color, texture, odor
• Uniformity of appearance
• Presence of stones, wood, and dirt
• Presence of pest, insect, and molds
• Moisture
• Sampling
• Unloading
• Conveying
• Storage
☐ The quality of the compound feeds depends on the quality of the
raw materials used in the production.
☐ Quality control of the materials starts at the receiving center.
23
UNLOADING OF RAW MATERIALS
☐ Bag – When the raw materials are brought to the mill in bags and
stored in bags, unloading and conveying is often done by:
• Completely manual
• Wheel cart
• Fork lift/pallet truck (standard pallet sizes are 120cm-x80cm for
25kg bag, and 120cm-x-160cm for 50kg bag.
24

7/27/25
13
☐ Bulk – The raw materials are in large quantities and stored in
bulk. Transport can be done by:
• Tipper truck
• Bulk tank truck
For unloading in bulk, a dump-pit or receiving hopper connected
to a mechanized conveying system to the bulk storage is
required.
25
☐ Liquid – The principal liquid ingredients are molasses which
is pumped directly from the transporting tankers or drum into
the storage tank.
26

7/27/25
14
WEIGHING OF RAW MATERIALS
☐ Bag – this can be done by
– Weighing the transporting truck with the load on a truck
scale and later weighing the unloaded truck
– Weighing the individual bags on a platform scale.
☐ Bulk – this can be done by
– Weighing the truck on a truck scale
– Weighing in a hopper scale built in a conveying system
with a buffer bin before and after the scale
27
SAMPLING OF RAW MATERIALS
☐ Bags – Samples should be taken from the materials in bags
using sampling spear. The size of the sample depends on the
size of the delivery.
☐ Bulk – Samples taken from the bulk delivery should be mixed
and reduced in size using a sample divider to get 1 to 2kg for
laboratory analysis.
☐ Coarse Materials like oil cakes – Sampling is done on a
different procedure in which sample pieces are selected from
the different parts of the quantity. The pieces selected should
be ground, thoroughly mixed and reduced to 1-2kg using
sampling divider.
☐ Liquid – In drums, samples should be taken according to the
plan for bagged delivery. Bulk tanker should be samples from
the top, middle, and bottom of the tank.
28

7/27/25
15
HANDLING AND CONVEYING
OF RAW MATERIALS
☐ Manual
☐ Gravity Flow
• This is the cheapest way of internal transportation by
using spouts, ducts, and pipes wherein the materials are
allowed to flow by gravity.
• Materials used are mainly made of 2-3mm metal sheet,
wood, or plastic maybe made of round or square cross
section.
• The minimum slope depends on the properties of the
materials to be conveyed.
• Dry grains 	- minimum 35°
• Meal and light ingredients 	- minimum 60°
29
☐ Screw Conveyor – This is most suitable for transport to single
outlet at the end of the screw. Not applicable for intermediate
outlet since the remaining materials may contaminate the
following batches.
•Trough-Screw Conveyor
•Auger pipe screw conveyor
The capacity of the screw conveyor depends on the following:
(1) rpm of the screw (60 to 120 rpm)
(2) pitch of the screw
(3) diameter and filling rate for the trough (45% is the
maximum
for trough-type screw
(4) bulk density of the material
30

7/27/25
16
☐ Drag Conveyor/Chain Conveyor – It is used for horizontal
and slightly inclined transport. It is suitable for distributing
materials over silos as they can have many outlets with flat slide
valves. It has relatively high capacity and can span longer
distances depending on the strength of the chain and the power
applied. Typical chain speed is 20 to 30 m/min. The capacity of
the chain conveyor is higher than that of the screw conveyor of
the same size.
Advantages and disadvantages
(1) Dust free
(2) Good cleanout of outlet valves
(3) Noise
(4) High wear
Capacity of the drag conveyor depends on
(1) Speed of the chain
(2) Shape of the flights or ears
31
☐ Bucket Elevator – It consists of endless belts and buckets or
cups and moves vertically between two wheels. It is used for
vertical conveying and is suitable for meal and granular products,
depending on the shape of the buckets and of belt speed.
• The capacity of the bucket elevator depends on
(1) Number of buckets per meter of belt
(2) Volume of buckets
(3) Belt velocity
(4) Filling rate of buckets
32

7/27/25
17
• Belt Conveyors – It comprises of endless belt made from
rubber, canvass or nylon, friction driven at one end and carried
on an idling drum at the other end. It is suitable for horizontal
or inclined transport of both bulk materials or bags. Belt speed
for bag is about 0.3 m/s while for bulk is 1-2 m/s. Plain belts
maybe used for inclines up to 22°; while, belts fitted with non-
slip device can go as high as 45°.
• Capacity of belts depends on
(1) Belt speed
(2) Cross section of layer of material on the belt
(3) Bulk density of the materials
33
• Air-Conveying System (Pneumatic) – It is used for granular
materials that are fine enough to be suspended in the air. It is
suitable for powder and meal. The ducting can go in any
direction. In small feed mills, this system is used to transport
materials from the hammer mill to the mixer or for filling silos.
• Advantages and disadvantages
(1) Flexible, it can go in any direction
(2) Ducts are cleaned out completely after conveying
(3) Conveying is dust tight
(4) Energy cost is relatively high
(5) High wear-and-tear due to the friction of the solids
particularly at the bends.
34

7/27/25
18
STORAGE OF RAW MATERIALS
• Storage should be done in such a way that there will be no
losses in the quantity and quality of materials. Good storage
facilities and maintaining proper storage conditions,
particularly in terms of temperature and humidity, are required
for storage of raw materials.
• Type of Storage
• Bag storage
• Bulk storage in floor compartments
• Bulk storage in silos and bins
35
POINTS TO CONSIDER IN STORAGE
OF RAW MATERIALS
• Dry raw materials well before storage.
• Put clean raw materials into clean storage.
• Keep the stored materials cool and protect from large changes
in outside temperature.
• Water proofing of storage.
• Check material regularly.
36

7/27/25
19
Safe Storage Moisture Content
of Some Products
Product 	Moisture Content (%)
Corn 	13.0
Sorghum 	13.5
Soybean 	11.0
Copra 	5.8
Cassava Chips 	12-13
Palm kernel 	5.7
37
IMPORTANT FACTORS TO CONSIDER
IN THE STORAGE OF
RAW MATERIALS
• Required length of storage period
• Value of product to be stored
• Prevailing climatic conditions
• Most suitable transport to the mill
• Cost and availability of labor
• Cost and availability of sacks
• Cost of building
• Availability of building space
38

7/27/25
20
BLENDING/DOSING
• Blending is the measuring out and assembly of the required
quantities of raw material to obtain the desired composition
of feeds.
• Ways to formulate the composition of feed:
(1)Gravimetric (by weighing) – This is accurate and can be
used for all types of materials. However, weighing
scales are relative expensive.
(2)Volumetric (by volume)
39
¡ Gravimetric Equipment
• Platform scale – It is the most simple method to weigh out
different feed ingredients.
• Hopper weigher – It consists of a hopper which is suspended
on a weighing mechanism and which has a slide valve or
discharge device at the bottom to discharge the materials into
a conveyor after weighing.
• Tripper weigher – It has a hopper suspended on a weighing
beam with counter weight. The material fills the hopper until it
balances the counterweight and a layer system then shuts off
the materials and the hopper tips over to discharge.
• Belt weigher – It consists of a conveying belt on which the
materials to be dosed are discharged from the storage bins
through extracting screw, rotating lock valves, or other devices.
40

7/27/25
21
GRINDING
• This is used to reduce the particle size of raw materials to
make it more suitable for animal consumption.
• Objectives of size reduction of materials for feed are:
(1)Improve the digestability of the ingredients by
increasing the surface area of the particles.
(2)Improve mixing of materials – When particles to be
mixed differ much in size, it is difficult to obtain a
homogenous mixture.
• 	Homogeneity of the feed mix is important because the
animals to be fed should obtain all the ingredients in
proper proportions in each meal offered much in size,
segregation may occur during the transport of the feed from
feed mill to farm.
• 	It facilitates the pelleting of the feed – When particle size
differ much in a mixed feed, it is difficult to obtain a good
pellet quality.
41
Designs of Size-Reduction Equipment
• Impact – The particles to be reduced in size is hit by a fast moving
metal parts and thrown at high speed against the wall (e.g.
hammer mill).
• Attrition – The particles are reduced in size by friction forces
between two surfaces moving at different speeds (e.g. disc mill).
• Compression – The particles are compressed until they break
(roller mill).
The most commonly used in compound feed production is the
hammer mill or impact grinder.
42

7/27/25
22
Grinding Equipment
¡ Hammer Mill – It consists of a steel
chamber wherein the rotor with
hammer rotates at a high velocity.
The material enters the chamber
from the top and is hit by the fast
rotating hammers against the
breakplate. The particles are
broken up by the impact of the
hammer or of the break plate.
Particles that are small enough
pass through the screen openings
to the outlet. The tip of the hammer
have a velocity of 100 m/s.
43
¡ Grinder Bin – It is used in bath
blending to assemble the
ingredients so that the hammer
mill can grind a batch without
interruptions. Sometimes it is
fitted with mixing screw to
partially mix the batch before
grinding.
¡ Feeder – It is required to control
the flow of the materials as to
ensure that the materials enter
the full width of the mill chamber
and to make sure that the mill is
used at optimum capacity without
overloading the motor.
44

7/27/25
23
¡ Mechanical feeding device commonly used in large mills:
(1) Vibratory feeder – is usually controlled by regulating the
thickness of the layer by means of a slide. The flow is
determined by the amplitude of the vibration.
(2) Rotating lock feeder – the flow is regulated by the speed of
rotation of the compartment valve.
(3) Feeder roll – is similar to rotating lock feeder except that a roll
is used over which the layer of material is conveyed.
45
MAGNETS AND STONE REMOVER
¡ These are used to remove stones and metal parts. These are
necessary to avoid damage to the hammers and the screen and
to avoid sparks which may create dust explosions.
46

7/27/25
24
ASPIRATION
This is to partly cool the mill
chamber but mostly to facilitate
passage of fine materials through
the screen; thus, increasing the
capacity of the mill.
The flow of air in the hammer mill
can be generated by:
(1) Blades inside the rotor.
(2) A fan mounted on the same
shaft as the rotor but outside
the mill chamber.
(3) A separate fan with motor.
47
MIXING
Mixing is the combination of different components into a
more or less homogenous mass that cannot easily be
separated again.
• Material mix in compound feed production
(1) 	Dry ingredients only
(2) 	Dry ingredients with a relatively small proportion
of liquid
(3) 	Wet ingredients
(4) 	Liquid with liquids
48

7/27/25
25
• Method of mixing feed ingredients
(1) 	Batch size ( dry solids)
(2) 	Continuous (+ molasses)
• Mixing Performance is affected by:
(1) 	characteristics of the
ingredients to be mixed;
(2) 	characteristics of equipment
used; and
(3) 	time of mixing.
49
CHARACTERISTICS OF INGREDIENTS
THAT INFLUENCE MIXING PROCESS
• Particle Size – The smaller the particles, the higher is the chance
to obtain homogeneity. The more uniform the particle size is, the
easier it is to obtain homogeneity.
• Particle Shape and Surface Structure – Higher variation in
specific density between materials to be mixed is unfavorable in
reaching homogeneity and may lead to easy segregation.
• Moisture Content and Static Charge – Particles that are
hygroscopic easily attract moisture and form lumps in mixing.
Very dry particles, however, may become charged with static
electricity causing the particles to stick together subsequently
hampering achieving homogeneity.
• Uniformity in Nutrient Content of the Raw Materials – When
ingredient particles differ much in nutrient content, obtaining
homogenous nutrient content is relatively difficult.
50

7/27/25
26
FACTORS INFLUENCING THE
QUALITY OF MIXING
• Transport Effect – The more irregular the direction of the movement
in the mixer are, the shorter the time to obtain the desired
homogeneity.
• Speed Movement – A higher speed of the mixing element gives
faster and better mixing, especially of sticky materials.
• Wall Surface Structure – A rough surface leads to more irregular
movement in the mixer; thus, achieving better mixing.
• Conduction of Static Electricity – Earthing of wall reduces the risk of
lumping of statistically-charged particles.
• Level Filling – A horizontal mixer should be filled with a maximum
level of fifty-five percent for better mixing.
51
MIXING TIME
• The time necessary to reach an acceptable homogeneity is
determined by:
(1) 	The type of mixer employed – In vertical mixer, the
approx. time of 15 minutes is required to obtain a good
mix. In horizontal mixer, however, the mixing elements
induce an intensive movement all over the total volume of
the mixer vessel.
(2) 	The degree of pre-mixing already achieved beforehand.
52

7/27/25
27
VERTICAL MIXER
¡ Vertical mixer consists of a cylindrical,
rectangular, or hexagonal bin with a
conical- shaped bottom. Inside the
vessel is a vertical screw conveyor
which moves the materials upward and
subsequently flows downward at the
wall of the vessel. Filling is on top or
through the screw conveyor into a
dump-hopper at the bottom of the mixer.
After mixing, the materials are
discharged through an outlet at the
bottom or at the side of the vessel.
Mixing time varies between 15 minutes
for normal feeds and 30 minutes for
production of premixes.
53
Advantages and Disadvantages
of Vertical Mixer
• Relatively low installed motor power
• Low investment
• Flexible capacity utilization as the filling rate does not influence
mixing quality
• Relatively long mixing time
• Slow discharging which can reduce the capacity of the feed mill
• Relatively high building height is required
54

7/27/25
28
HORIZONTAL MIXER
¡ Horizontal mixer consists of
a horizontal cylindrical or U-
shaped vessel in which a
shaft, with mixing blades or
paddles, rotates (approx. 25
rpm). It is filled from the top
and discharged through the
valves at the bottom.
Compared with the vertical
mixer, the installed power is
relatively higher and mixing
time is much shorter in this
type of mixer.
55
Advantages and Disadvantages
• Short mixing time resulting in high capacity.
• Rapid discharge.
• Mixing of liquids is possible.
• Low building height.
• Incomplete cleanout when outlet valves are small.
• Higher investment because of more complex construction and
higher installed power.
• Filling level influences mixing efficiency.
56

7/27/25
29
PELLETING
¡ Pelleting is the forming of dense particles from a mixed compound
feed.
57
Pelleting Process
Conditioning of the Meal
Molding of Meal into
Pellets
Cooling of Pellets
Water +
Molasses Steaming
58

7/27/25
30
Advantages of Pelleting
• The higher bulk density of pellets compared with meal results in
lower storage space requirement and lower transport cost.
• Segregation of mixed feed can be avoided or minimized.
• Dusty raw materials that are difficult to include in meal maybe
included in higher percentage in pelleted feed.
• Heating before and during pelleting reduces bacterial count and
can improve the nutritional value.
• Handling of feed on the farm is easier and can be mechanized
better while there will be lower wastage in feeding.
• Feed intake is faster and easier.
• There is no risk of selective feed consumption by poultry.
• No demixing.
59
Disadvantages
• The pelleting installation requires considerable additional
investment.
• Operation requires skilled labor.
• Maintenance and replacement of wearing parts (dies and rolls)
entail high cost.
• Energy consumption is high.
• Strong variation in capacity.
The decision whether or not to include pelleting in the feed mill operation will
require a careful analysis of these advantages and disadvantages and the
resulting cost benefits. For small operations below 3 to 5 tons per hour,
pelleting is often not economically attractive.
60

7/27/25
31
DELIVERY OF FINISHED PRODUCTS
¡ Delivery of mixed feeds in
meal or pellet includes
weighing, bag filling, and/or
bulk handling.
¡ Before the actual transport
from the feed mill to the
costumers’ place, taking a
period of storage of the mixed
feeds is usually also
necessary.
61
PLANT LAYOUT AND DESIGN
• Gather information
• Process information
• Develop possible solutions
• Analyze, compare, test, and modify the various solutions
• Decide for the best solution
• Make detailed drawing and specifications
• Taking bids and letting contract
• Supervising construction to check conformity to contract.
62

7/27/25
32
Schematic Diagram of a Micro Feed Milling Plant
Blending
Grinding
Mixing
Bagging

WHAT IS FOOD PROCESSING?
Food processing is a segment of
manufacturing industry that transforms
animal, plant and marine materials into
intermediate or finished value-added

OPERATIONS

Refrigeration Cycle
¡ Refrigeration cycle is the complete series of events occurring in
order as the refrigerant travels the route.
• Expansion – high pressure liquid escapes through the valve
into low pressure pipe and refrigerant expands.
• Evaporation – liquid refrigerant begins to evaporate and
secures necessary heat from the air inside the refrigerated
room.
• Compression – allows the refrigerant to give up the heat
picked up from the refrigerated room by drawing it with the
compressor.
• Condensation – high-pressure high-temperature gaseous
refrigerant is forced out by the compressor to the condenser.

Introduction
Heat transfer is one of the important subjects in agricultural
engineering especially those dealing with agricultural processes,
thermal power conversion using biomass, solar, and other non-
renewable and renewable energies, and agricultural infrastructures
that deals on cooling and storage of agricultural products, animal
ventilation, and many others. Proper design of equipment relevant to
these systems often requires a thorough understanding of heat
transfer.
3
Definition of Heat Transfer
¾ Heat transfer is the rate of flow of heat from one surface to
the other surface.
4

7/27/25
3
Importance of Heat Transfer
¡ In agricultural engineering, this subject is often encountered in
heating systems such as:
• grain drying and fruit dehydrating plants;
• biomass furnaces, kiln, and stove;
• cold storage facilities for meat, fish, fruit and vegetable; and
• farmstead infrastructures for ventilating poultry and livestock.
5
¡ The question on how to transmit

and how to protect a construction
most efficiently against heat loss
or gain is of significant
importance to most engineers.
Proper application of heat

are used for insulation, give a
much lower investment cost and
make business operation more
economical and feasible.

4
¡ Basically, whenever temperature difference exists in a body
whether it is solid, liquid, or gas, it is reduced in magnitude in the
course of time by heat flowing from one region of high
temperature to the region of low temperature.
7
¡ One illustration of this is the grain
drying system where heat
generated from the fuel is

liberated during burning, some of

some in the heat exchanger, and
other in the drying bin before it
finally reaches the product and is
utilized in removing the water from
the grains. In heat transfer, the
nature of the movement and the
causes of heat losses are dealt
closely to be able to design the
system more efficiently and
economical to operate.

Methods of Heat Transfer
Basically, there are three methods of transferring heat. These are the
following: (1) by conduction, (2) by convection, and (3) by radiation.
The only thing that these three methods are in common is that there
should be a temperature difference that must exist and that the heat is
always transferred in the direction from higher to lower temperature.
9
Conduction
Conduction is the transfer of heat from one part of the solid to
the other under the influence of temperature gradient without
appreciable displacement of particles. Heat transfer by
conduction basically involves the transfer of kinetic energy from
one molecule to adjacent molecule. Moreover, it is the transfer of
heat due to the property of matter which allows the passage of
heat energy even if the physical body is impermeable to any kind
of rays and its parts are not in motion, relative to one another.

¡ Heat exchanger is a device used in some radiant heat systems
to separate dissimilar fluids, such as anti-freeze and water.
¡ It directs heat from one fluid to another, without allowing direct
contact between the fluids.
HEAT EXCHANGER
30

7/27/25
16
¡ Heat exchangers are commonly used to transfer heat from
steam, water, or gases to gases or liquids. Some of the criteria for
selecting materials used for heat exchangers are corrosion
resistance, strength, heat conduction, and cost. Corrosion
resistance is frequently a difficult criterion to meet. Damage to heat
exchangers is frequently difficult to avoid.
¡ The tubes in a heat exchanger transfer the heat from the fluid on the
inside of the tube to the fluid on the shell side (or vice versa). Some
heat exchanger designs use fins to provide greater thermal
conductivity. To meet corrosion requirements, tubing must be
resistant to general corrosion, pitting, stress-corrosion cracking
(SCC), selective leaching or dealloying, and oxygen cell attack in
service.
31
Types of Heat Exchanger
1. Shell and Tube Heat Exchanger – consists of a series of finned
tubes, through which one of the fluids runs. The second fluid runs
over the finned tubes to be heated or cooled.
2. Plate Heat Exchanger - directs flow through baffles so that the
fluids are separated by plates with very large surface area. This
plate- type arrangement can be more efficient than the shell and
tube. Advances in gasket technology have made the plate-type
increasingly practical.
3. Regenerative Heat Exchanger - In this, the heat from a process
is used to warm the fluids to be used in the process, and the same
type of fluid is used either side of the heat exchanger.
32

7/27/25
17
33
Air-Cooled Heat Exchanger	Plate Heat Exchanger
34

7/27/25
18
4. Brazed Heat Exchanger - is a collection of plates, vacuum
brazed together with no gaskets, reducing leakage. They are
compact, lightweight and have a high turbulent flow, which also
reduces deposit build-up and maintenance. The brazed heat
exchanger is ideal for hydronic systems like swimming pools,
spas, radiant floor heating, domestic hot water, and snow and ice
melting.
5. Shell-and-Coil Heat Exchangers - is composed of circular
layers of helically corrugated tubes within a light compact shell.
They are high-efficiency machines with a vertical installation,
flexible design and low maintenance.
35
External Heat Exchanger
Most solar hot water systems use a heat exchanger to extract solar
energy from the collector loop and transfer it to the hot water tank.
Historically, these heat exchangers have coils of copper pipe
located at the bottom of the solar tank. New designs in external
heat exchangers such as the one used in the Solar Boiler™ system
have made the internal heat exchangers obsolete. A properly
designed external heat exchanger has three distinct advantages:
(1) it enhances solar system performance;
(2) it is more efficient thermodynamically; and
(3) it helps lower the life-cycle cost of a solar system.
36

7/27/25
19
External heat exchangers can be configured so that the potable
water side circulates by natural convection (i.e., it thermosiphons).
A properly designed thermosiphoning system results in an excellent
temperature stratification in the storage tank (layers of hot water
form at the top of the tank and do not mix with layers of cold water
at the bottom of the tank). This means that usable hot water is
available more rapidly with an external heat exchanger. A layer of
100°F or hotter water is deposited at the top of the tank soon after
the sun starts shining on the collectors. So, even though the tank
may contain mostly cold water, homeowners can utilize solar-
heated water early in the morning without using their backup heater.
A tank with an internal heat exchanger heats the water from the
bottom of the tank requiring several hours of solar collection to
achieve useable temperatures at the top on the tank.
37
ELECTRICAL HEATING ELEMENTS
Heating element - a material or device that directly converts electrical
energy into heat or thermal energy. They are nearly 100% efficient. It
is done by producing heat by conduction of electricity across electric
heating elements.
Alloys are used in electrical heating devices rather than pure metals
because the resistivity of an alloy is more than the resistivity of pure
metal.
The melting point of an alloy is high and it does not melt or oxidize
easily even at a higher temperature.
38

7/27/25
20
There are three basic types of electric
heating elements:
(1) Open wire
(2) Open ribbon
(3) Tubular cased wire.
Widely used heating elements are:
(1) Nickel-chromium alloy
(2) Iron-chromium-aluminum alloy
(3) Molybdenum disilicide
(4) Silicon carbide
The most commonly used heating
element is nichrome (80% nickel and
20% chromium).
39
Types of Electrical heaters
1. Cartridge Heater – a cartridge heater
contains an electric coil surrounded by an
insulating powder (typically magnesium oxide)
and packed within a tapered sheath.
2. Strip Heater - a relatively flat rectangular
heater made from a strip of mica that has been
wrapped with ribbon wire.
3. Band Heater - bent strip heater into the
shape of a ring. They are clamped around
pipes, barrels, and the base of kettles. to heat
fluids and to assist in the melting of solids.
4. Tubular Heater - an electric coil surrounded
by a ceramic insulating powder encased within
a metal sheath. The terminals exit opposite
ends of the heater.
40

Problem 1
A single-pass rice mill was tested for 30 min. and gave the following results: input
paddy, 1000 kg; milled rice produced, 650 kg; broken rice produced, 150 kg; and
weight of head rice, 200 kg. Compute the following: (a) Throughput capacity, (b) %
Milling recovery, (c) % Broken grains, and (d) % Head rice recovery.
Given:
Wp 	- 1000 kg
Wmr 	- 650 kg
Whr 	- 200 kg
Wbr 	- 150 kg
Time 	- 30 min.
Required: 	% Milling recovery
% Head rice recovery
% Broken grains, and
Throughput capacity
Solution:
% Milling recovery = Wmr 100 / Wp
= 650 kg x 100 / 1000 kg
= 65%
% Head rice recovoery = Whr 100/Wmr
= 200 kg x 100 / 650 kg
= 31%
% Broken rice = Wbr 100 / Wmr
= 150 kg x 100 / 650 kg
= 23%
Throughput Capacity = Wp x MR / To
= 1000 kg x 0.65 / 30 min/60 min/hr
= 1300 kg milled rice per hr

Problem 2
Five tons of paddy milled in 6 hours produces 3950
kg of brown rice and 3250 kg of milled rice. What
is the milling recovery?
Given:
Wt of paddy 	- 5 tons
Milling time 	- 6 hors
Wt of brown rice 	- 3950 kg
Wt of milled rice 	- 3250 kg
Required: 	Milling Recovery
Solution:
MR = Wt milled rice x 100 / wt of paddy
= 3250 kg x 100 / 5000 kg
= 0.65 x 100
= 65%
Problem 3
What is the hulling coefficient of the huller in
Problem 2?
Given:
Weight of brown rice 	- 3950 kg
Weight of paddy 	- 5000 kg
Required: 	Hulling Coefficient
Solution:
Coef. of hulling = Wt of brown rice/Wt of paddy
= 3950 kg / 5000 kg
= 0.79

Problem 4
If the head rice recovery of the paddy in Problem 2
is equal to 85%, what is the amount of broken
grains?
Given:
Head rice recovery 	- 85%
Required: 	Weight of milled rice
Solution:
Wt of broken grains = Wt mr (100 – HRR)
= 3250 (100 – 0.85)
= 487.5 kg
Problem 5
Referring to Problem 2, what is the amount of rice
hull produced during milling?
Given:
Wt of paddy 	- 5000 kg
Required: 	Weight of rice hull
Solution:
Wt of RH = Wt of paddy x 20%
= 5000 kg x 0.20
= 1000 kg

Problem 6
A disk huller with 600-mm diameter will be installed as return huller for a rice
milling plant. As an Agricultural Engineer, determine the diameter of the pulley
required for the huller. The motor for the huller will have a pulley diameter of 4
inches and is expected to run at 1740 rpm.
Given:
Diameter of huller 	- 600 mm
Motor pulley 	- 4 in.
Motor speed 	- 1740 rpm
Required: 	Huller pulley diameter
Solution:
Huller rpm = (14 m/s ) (60 s/min) /[ 3.14 (0.6 m)]
= 445.8 rpm
Huller Pulley D = 4 in (1740 rpm) / 445.8 rpm
= 15.6 in. use 16 in.
Problem 7
A rice milling plant is to be designed to run at 5
tons per hour throughput rate. The design
milling recovery is 69% while the hulling
efficiency is 95%. How many compartments
are needed for the paddy separator of the rice
mill? Assume a 50-kg br/hr-comp.
Given:
Throughput capacity 	- 5 tph
Milling recovery 	- 69%
Hulling efficiency 	- 95%
Required: 	No. of compartments
Solution:
C p 	= 5 tph / 0.69
= 7.25 tph of paddy
C br = 7.25 tph x 0.95
= 6.9 tph brown rice
No. of compartments = 6.9 tph x 1000 kg/ton
x 1 comp/50 kg-hr
= 138 compartments

Problem 8
A rubber roll husker was tested to determine
its performance. The husker ran for 2 hours
at a rate of 1000 kg of input paddy. The
weight of brown rice obtained after passing
the husker was 805 kg. The weight of whole
brown rice obtain per kg of sample was 900
grams. What is the hulling coefficient,
wholeness coefficient, and hulling efficiency
of the huller? What is the throughput
capacity of the husker in kilogram per hour
of brown rice?
Given:
Weight of paddy - 1000 kg
Operating time - 2 hours
Weight of brown rice - 805 kg
Weight of whole brown rice - 900 g per
kg of brown rice
Required:
Hulling coefficient, wholeness coefficient,
husking efficiency, and throughput rate
Solution:
Hulling coefficient 	= 805 kg/1000 kg
= 0.805
Wholeness coefficient 	= (900 g brown
rice x 1kg/1000 g) x 805 kg brown
rice / 805 kg brown rice
= 0.9
Hulling efficiency 	= (0.805 x 0.90) x 100
= 72.45%
Throughput capacity = 805 kg / 2 hours
= 402.5 kg/hr

Problem 1
Compute the amount of heat needed to drop the
temperature of 100 cans of milk from 32°C to
25°C. 	Assume a specific weight of milk equal to
0.99 kg/liter. The specific heat of milk is 0.93
BTU/lb-°F.
Given:
No. of cans 	= 100
Volume per can = ¼ liter
Temp initial 	= 30°C
Temp final 	= 25°C
Cp 	= 0.93 BTU/lb-°F
Required:
Amount of heat to be removed
Solution:
Qs 	= (00.99kg/li x ¼ li x 100 cans)
x (0.93 BTU/lb-°F) (86°F – 79°F)
= 455.75 BTU
Problem 2
Compute the cooling load of a 150-kg
carabeef if it is to be cooled from 28°C to
-2.2 °C, after which it is frozen and
cooled to -20°C. The specific heat of
carabeef above and below freezing are
3.5 kJ/kg-°C and 1.75 kJ/kg-°C,
respectively. The freezing point is -2.2°C
and the latent heat of fusion is 250 kJ/kg.
Given:
m 	- 150 kg
Te 	- 28°C
Tf 	- -2.2°C
Ts 	- -20°C
Cb 	- 3.5 kJ/kg-°C
Ca 	- 1.75 kJ/kg-°C
h1 	- 250 kJ/kg
Required: 	Cooling load (Qt)
Solution:
Qt = m Cb (Te – Tf) + mh1 + m Ca (Tf – Ts)
= 150 kg (3.5 kJ/kg-°C) [28 - (-2.2)°C]
+ 150 kg (250 kJ/kg) + 150 kg (1.75
kJ/kg-°C) [-2.2 – (-20)°C]
= 58, 027.5 kJ

Problem 3
One ton of poultry meat is put in a chiller
at 8°C and frozen to -18°C in 10 hours.
Compute the product load if the latent
heat is 235 kJ/kg and the freezing
temperature is -4°C. The specific heat of
poultry meat is 3.5 kJ/kg-°C above freezing
and 1.5 kJ/kg-°C below freezing.
Given:
Cb 	- 3.5 kJ/kg-°C
Ca 	- 1.5 kJ/kg-°C
Te 	- 8°C
Tf 	- -4°C
Ts 	- -18°C
h1 	- 235kJ/kg
m 	- 1 ton (= 1000 kg)
time 	- 10 hrs
Required: 	Product load (Qt)
Solution:
Qt = [m Cb (Te – Tf) + mh1 + m Ca (Tf – Ts)] / T
= 1000 kg (3.5 kJ/kg-°C) [8 - (-4)] + 1000 kg
(235 kJ/kg) + 1000 kg (1.5 kJ/kg-°C) [.-4 –
(-18)] / 10 hrs x 3600 sec/hr
= 278,000 kJ / 10 hrs x 3600 sec/hr
= 7.72 kJ/sec or 7.72 kW
Problem 4
How many units of 1-hp air conditioning
system is required to maintain the
temperature of a farm house at 27° C? The
floor dimension of the house is 10-m wide x
30-m long. The height of ceiling of the room
is 8 ft .
Given: 	Structure 	- Farm house
Dimension 	- 10-m W x 30-m L
Ceiling Height - 8 ft
Temperature 	- 27°C
Required: 	No. of units of 1-hp air conditioner
Solution:
No. of Units = 10 m x 30 m / 20 m2 per 1-hp unit
= 5 units of 1-hp air conditioner

Problem 5
Determine the heat load of a proposed walk-in
cooler having 6-ft x 8-ft floor space and 7 ft
height. It is designed to have a 4-in cork
insulation (6.5 BTU/hr-ft2) on all surfaces and
an inside temperature of 35°F. The products to
be cooled are: cabbage, 100 lb/day (0.9
BTU/lb-°F) and fresh beef, 200 lbs/day (0.5
BTU/lb-°F). Assume the products are to be
cooled from 85° to 35°F in 24 hours.
Given:
Cooler Type 	- Walk-in
Floor Space 	- 6 ft x 8 ft
Height 	- 7 ft
Insulation 	- 4-in. thick cork
Heat insulating cap - 6.5 BTU/hr-ft2
Temp inside 	- 35°F
Product 	- 100-lb/day cabbage, 200-lbs fresh beef
Temp for cooling 	- 85°F to 35°F
Time of cooling 	- 24 hours
Required: 	Heat Load
Solution:
Product load:
0.9 x 100 x (85-35)/24 	= 187 BTU/hr
0.75 x 200 x (85-35)/24 	= 312 BTU/hr
Space Load:
6 x 8 + 6 x 7 x 2 + 8 x 7 x 2 + 6 x 8 = 292 ft2
Using 6.5 BTU/ft2-hr
292 ft2 x 6.5 BTU/ ft2-hr 	= 1,898 BTU/hr
Total Heat Load:
187 + 312 + 1,898 	= 2,397 BTU/hr

Problem 1
The temperature inside a rice hull furnace is maintained at 1500°F by means of
suitable control apparatus. The wall of the furnace is 9 in. in thickness and
constructed from a material having 0.18 Btu/hr-ft-°F thermal conductivity.
Calculate the heat loss for each square foot of wall surface per hour. Assume that
the inside and outside wall temperatures are 1500°F and 400°F, respectively.
Given:

Wall thickness 	- 9 in.

Outside wall temperature - 400°F

= 300 BTU/hr

= 0.052 BTU/hr-ft-°F

Problem 3
The wall of a kiln is made up of 9-in fire bricks
(k=0.72 BTU/hr-ft-°F), 5-in insulating bricks
(k=0.08 BTU/hr-ft-°F), and 7.5-in red bricks (K=0.5
BTU/hr-ft-°F). The inner (t1) and outer surface
temperatures (t4) are 1500°F and 150°F,
respectively. Neglecting the residences of the
mortar joints, compute the temperatures t2 and
t3 at the contact surface.
Given:
Fire brick 	- 9 in. 	K - 0.72 BTU/hr-ft-°F
Insulating Brick - 5 in. 	K - 0.08 BTU/hr-ft-°F
Red brick 	- 7.5 in. 	K - 0.5 BTU/hr-ft-°F
t1 	- 1500°F
t4 	- 150°F
Required:

contact surface area
Solution:
Qk1-4 = 1 ft2 (1500°F-150°F) /
[(9in/12in/ft/0.72 BTU/hr-ft-°F)
+ (5in/12in/ft/0.08BTU/hr-ft-°F)
+ (7.5in/12in/ft/0.5BTU/hr-ft-°F)]
= 180 BTU/hr
180 BTU/hr = 0.72 BTU/hr-ft-°F x 1 ft2 (1500
– t2) / (9 in/12 in/ft)
t2 = 1312°F
180 BTU/hr = 0.08 BTU/hr-ft-°F x 1 ft2
x (1312°F – t3) / (5 in/12in/ft)
t3 = 375°F

1 in./12 in./ft
T2 = 447°F

Problem 7
A thick-walled stainless-steel tube (k = 19 w/m-°C, with 2 cm ID and 4 cm OD) is
covered with a 3-cm layer of asbestos insulation (k = 0.2 w/m-°C). If the inside
wall temperature of the pipe is maintained at 600°C and the outside of the
insulation at 100°C, what is the heat loss per foot length of the tube?
Given:
Pipe inside diameter 	- 2 cm
Pipe outside diameter 	- 4 cm
Thickness of asbestos 	- 3 cm
K pipe 	- 19 W/m-°C
K asbestos 	- 0.2 W/m-°C
Temperature inside the pipe - 600°C
Temperature outside the asbestos - 100°C
Required:
Heat transfer rate per foot length of pipe
Solution:
Qk = 2 π x L x (600°C – 100°C) / [[(ln 2 cm/1 cm)/19 W/m-°C]
+ [(ln 5 cm/2 cm)/0.23 W/m-°C)]]
= 680 W per m or 207 W/ft
Problem 8
What is the heat loss per ft² of the 9-inch-thick wall of a brick kiln made from a

Outside temperature 	- 400°F

(6 in./12 in./ ft)

The Author:
Alexis T. Belonio is a Professional Agricultural Engineer. 	He is an Affiliate Professor at
the College of Engineering, Central Luzon State University, Science City of Munoz,
Nueva Ecija and a former Associate Professor of the Department of Agricultural
Engineering and Environmental Management, College of Agriculture, Central
Philippine University, Iloilo City. He finished his Bachelor of Science in Agricultural
Engineering and Master of Science degrees from Central Luzon State University,
Muñoz, Nueva Ecija. Since 1983, he has been deeply involved in teaching, research,
technology development, and entrepreneurial activities related to the fields of
agricultural engineering.
He was awarded by the Philippine Society of Agricultural Engineers (PSAE) as the Most
Outstanding Agricultural Engineer in the field of Farm Power and Machinery, in 1993.
In that same year, he was named by the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) as
the Outstanding Professional in the field of Agricultural Engineering. And in 1997, he
was awarded by the TOYM Foundation and the Jerry Roxas Foundation as the
Outstanding Young Filipino (TOYF) in the field of Agricultural Engineering. He was also
awarded as Associate Laureate of the Rolex Awards for Enterprise 2008 (Geneva,
Switzerland) and as a Laureate in Economic Business Development Category of The
Tech Awards 2010 (San Jose, California). He was adjudged as one of the Inspiring
Modern-Day Filipino Heroes by Yahoo Southeast Asia in 2011.
As a dedicated professional, he serves as technical consultant to various agricultural
companies and machinery manufacturers in the country and abroad. He also serves as
a Reviewer for the Agricultural Engineering Board Examination in different universities,
particularly in Luzon, in the fields of Agricultural Power, Machinery and Allied Subjects,
and Agricultural Processing, Structures and Allied Subjects. He has written and
published several research and technical papers, including instructional and review
materials.

Controlled Atmosphere Storage
Agricultural and BioProcess Engineering
Prepared by: RCA
MSU-GSC ABE Review 2025
"If you cannot do great things, you can do small things in a great way."
CAS implies continuous monitoring and precise adjustment of these
gases within the storage container to a predetermined level.
To ensure the supply of quality products and extend their useful
life, this complex process should include control of the:
• Ambient temperature
• Relative humidity
• Ethylene
• Carbon Dioxide
• Oxygen

Ambient Temperature
Agricultural and BioProcess Engineering
Prepared by: RCA
MSU-GSC ABE Review 2025
"If you cannot do great things, you can do small things in a great way."
• Respiration and transpiration processes are reduced by temperature lowering in
storage rooms.
• This prevents premature vegetable and fruit spoilage and also ensures their high
quality.
• Additional benefits of low temperatures are:
1. reduced sensitivity to ethylene
2. suppressed ethylene production
3. slow microbial development

Relative Humidity
Agricultural and BioProcess Engineering
Prepared by: RCA
MSU-GSC ABE Review 2025
"If you cannot do great things, you can do small things in a great way."
• High relative humidity is as important as low vegetable and fruit storage
temperature.
• Keeping a high RH level (in the range of 80-100% RH for different vegetables and
fruit types) lowers the transpiration process, preventing water loss and product
wilting, and consequently, reducing shelf life and decreasing market value.
• Although relative humidity increases as the air cools down, it is still
recommended to check if its levels in storage rooms are satisfactory.

Ethylene (C2H4)
Agricultural and BioProcess Engineering
Prepared by: RCA
MSU-GSC ABE Review 2025
"If you cannot do great things, you can do small things in a great way."
• Climacteric fruits and vegetables, which can ripen on their own, continue to emit
gaseous Ethylene
• In the case of long-term storage, this factor is undesirable in contrast to ripening
rooms since just one ppm C2H4 in the air can trigger the ripening process and
shorten produce shelf life.
• Therefore, keep the Ethylene concentrations as low as possible and ventilate a
room, if necessary.
• For controlling and reliably determining C2H4 levels in storage rooms, gas
detector installation is provided.

Carbon Dioxide (CO2)
Agricultural and BioProcess Engineering
Prepared by: RCA
MSU-GSC ABE Review 2025
"If you cannot do great things, you can do small things in a great way."
• In addition to Ethylene, fruits and vegetables release Carbon Dioxide during
respiration, accumulating in the room.
• For long-term storage, it is necessary to maintain CO2 concentration at the
required level for each product.
• Keeping a high Carbon Dioxide level (up to 14%) can stop Ethylene production
slow down the ripening process and prolong shelf life.
• However, too high CO2 concentrations can negatively affect a product’s
appearance, taste, nutritional value, and storage time.

Oxygen (O2)
Agricultural and BioProcess Engineering
Prepared by: RCA
MSU-GSC ABE Review 2025
"If you cannot do great things, you can do small things in a great way."
• A decrease in Oxygen concentrations reduces respiration rate and Ethylene
production, delays ripening and aging, and slows down pathogens’ growth and,
therefore, prolongs produce shelf life.
• In storage rooms, Oxygen level is reduced (down to 4% of O2 and below
depending on vegetables and fruit types) by replacement with Nitrogen or/Carbon
Dioxide.
• Once the desired O2 level is reached, the fruit will continue to lower its
concentration during respiration. Care must be taken that the oxygen level does
not fall too low (below 1%), as this can cause irreversible changes in the fruit and
affect its quality.

GENERAL RULE
Agricultural and BioProcess Engineering
Prepared by: RCA
MSU-GSC ABE Review 2025
"If you cannot do great things, you can do small things in a great way."
The lower the O2 and the higher the CO2 levels, the better will be
the controlled-atmosphere effects.
However, the extent to which the O2 level can be reduced and the
CO2 level can be elevated is limited due to the shift from aerobic
to anaerobic metabolism, which leads to off-flavors.

A. Mechanical Processing
Mechanical processing refers to the physical methods used to
alter the structure of food materials, such as chopping, grinding,
mixing, and emulsifying.
a. Peeling
Peeling is a unit operation used in fruit and vegetable processing
to remove the outer protective layer (peel, skin, or rind). This is
done to improve the product's appearance, texture, and edibility,
as well as to prepare it for subsequent processing steps.

b. Size Reduction
Cutting (Size Reduction) refers to the mechanical reduction of
raw materials into smaller, defined sizes and shapes using various
cutting implements or machinery.
c. Juicing
Juicing is a mechanical process that separates the liquid fraction
(juice) from the solid components (pulp and fiber) of fruits and
vegetables. This is typically achieved through methods such as
pressing, crushing, blending followed by separation, or
centrifugal extraction, yielding a liquid product rich in water-
soluble vitamins, minerals, and sugars.

Thermal food processing is a cost-efficient treatment widely used by
industries to achieve food safety and extended shelf life. The main purpose
of thermal processing is to inactivate pathogenic micro-organisms
a. Blanching
Blanching involves briefly boiling fruits or vegetables,
followed by rapid cooling, to inactivate enzymes that can
cause spoilage, reduce microbial load, and preserve color
and texture.

b. Pasteurization
Pasteurization is a heat treatment process where food is heated
to a specific temperature for a set period to destroy pathogenic
microorganisms and inactivate spoilage enzymes, thereby
extending shelf life.
c. Sterilization
Sterilization is a thermal process that involves heating food to a
temperature that destroys all forms of microorganisms, including
spores, ensuring the product is shelf-stable and safe for long-
term storage. This method is often applied in canning operations.
