compounds
•Hydrogen peroxide
•Alkalis and acids

Oxidizing chemicals – most common disinfectant
Chlorine – most widely used (3 > pH > 11 is relatively
toxic to bacteria)
Physical Agents:
1. Heat : heating at boiling point, destroys bacteria
commonly used in the beverages and dairy industry
but not so feasible in wastewater treatment.
2. Light : sunlight is also good disinfectant
lamps emitting UV rays have been used successfully
to sterilize small quantities of water.

Mechanical Means:
- coarse screens, fine screen, grit chambers, plain
sedimentation may also removed or destroy
bacteria up to 25%
Radiation:
a. Electromagnetic
b. Acoustic
c. Particle – gamma rays

Mechanisms of Disinfection
➢ Damage to cell wall – result to cell lysis and death
➢ Alteration of cell permeability – like phenolic cpds.
and detergents alter plasma for cytoplasmic
membrane
➢ Alteration of the colloidal nature of the
protoplasm
➢ Inhibition of enzyme activity – alteration of
enzymes and deactivate the enzymes (like action
of chlorine)

DISINFETION WITH CHLORINE
Chlorine is the most commonly used throughout
the world, since it posses most of the actual
characteristics of a disinfectant.
✓ common compounds used are:
Cl2, Ca(OCl)2, NaOCl, and ClO2
✓when chlorine is added to water, it brings hydrolysis
and ionization

DECHLORINATION
➢ removal of the total combined chlorine residual that
exists after chlorination to reduce the toxic effects of
chlorinated effluents discharged to receiving waters
or to be used for reuse applications.
➢ many compounds may react to chlorine to form toxic
compounds that can have long-term adverse effect
on the beneficial uses of the water to waters to
which they are discharged.

➢ Use of Sulfur Dioxide
- successively removes free chlorine,
monochloramine, dichloramine, nitrogen,
trichloride, & polynitrogen chlorine cpds.
➢ Activated Carbon
- provides complete removal of both carbon
and free residual chlorine.
Dechlorination Agents:

DISINFECTION WITH CHLORINE DIOXIDE
ClO2 – another bacteriocide, equal to or greater than
chlorine in disinfecting power proven to be more
effective in inactivation of virus than chlorine
DISINFECTION WITH BROMINE CHLORIDE
⚫ Bromine chloride gas hydrolyzes in water to form
hypobromos acid, the most potent germicide of all
the bromine compounds.
⚫ reliable, flexible, and effective as chlorine
⚫ more effective germicide than chloramines and
degrades quicker, absorbs into bacteria cell and
disrupts critical enzymatic activity.

DISINFECTION BY OZONE
➢ control taste, odor, and color-producing agents
➢ it is more economically more competitive for water
disinfection but since it is chemically unstable, as it
decomposes to oxygen very rapidly after generation,
it must be generated on site
➢ it doesn’t leaves residues since it dissipated rapidly
DISINFECTION BY UV LIGHT
➢ at proper dosage of UV light radiation, it is an
effective bacteriocide and virucide while not
forming or contributing to the formation of toxic
compounds

and Disposal

7
AB FOOD
ENGINEERING
AGRICULTURAL 	AND 	BIOSYSTEMS 	ENGINEERING 	REVIEWER
VOLUME
A.T.Belonio
2025

No. of Pages
General Information
Theories and Principles of GMP, SSOP,EMP, and
HACCP
Unit Operation
Engineering Principle
Role of ABE in Cold Storage and Facilities
Food Process Engineering
Food Processing Equipment
Refrigeration and Cold Storage
Heat Transfer and Thermal Insulation
Table of Contents

1. Study that deals with the application
and practices in converting agricultural
products into different kinds and forms of
food.
a. Agricultural processing
b. Food processing
c. 	Feed processing
d. All of the above
2. Processing operation at which physical
properties of the product change, such as
processing banana into catsup.
a. Primary processing
b. Secondary processing
c. 	Tertiary processing
d. None of the above
3. Processing operation which does not
significantly change the physical
characteristics of the product, such as
drying and dehydration of fruits and
vegetables.
a. Primary processing
b. Secondary processing
c. 	Tertiary processing
d. None of the above
4. Crops that have high moisture content
of 30% and more, such as fruits and
vegetables including dairy, meat, poultry,
and fish and easily deteriorate or spoil.
a. Perishable crops
b. Durable crops
c. 	Flexible crops
d. None of the above
5. Segment of manufacturing industry that
transforms animal, plant, and marine
materials into edible intermediate or
finished value-added food products.
a. 	Food processing
b. 	Food production
c. 	Food products
d. 	None of the above
GENERAL INFORMATION
6. Aim of food processing.
a. Extending the period during which the
food remains wholesome.
b. Providing the nutrient required for
health.
c. Providing variety and convenience in
diet.
d. Adding value
e. All of the above
7. An operation that starts from a specific
sequence and ends at specific final task.
a. Work
b. Process
c. Product
d. None of the above
8. Which of the following is not the goal of
processing agricultural and food products?
a. Removal of inedible parts from
agricultural and fishery products.
b. Processing products of primary
operation for various secondary process
operations.
c. Subjecting the processed products to
various preservation methods to lengthen
the life span.
d. None of the above
9. Processing operation which is usually
smaller in size and only operates on
definite duration.
a. Batch processing
b. Continuous processing
c. Mixed Processing
d. None of the above
10. Processing operation where the
condition at the start may vary but on the
later part may remain constant.
a. Batch processing
b. Continuous processing
c. Mixed Processing
d. None of the above

11. Processing operation where more
difficult to control.
a. Batch processing
b. Continuous processing
c. Mixed Processing
d. None of the above
12. Flow chart showing the graphical
representation of various processes and
their sequence from raw materials to
final product and by products.
a. Flow Diagram
b. Block Diagram
c. Pictorial Diagram
d. All of the above
13. More detailed description of the
process that provides the information on
the main equipment selected to perform
the operation using standard symbols.
a. Flow Diagram
b. Block Diagram
c. Pictorial Diagram
d. All of the above
14. Diagram showing the pictorial of the
equipment, including secondary
equipment such as pump, valves, etc.,
are reflected in the diagram.
a. Equipment-Flow Diagram
b. Block Diagram
c. Pictorial Diagram
d. All of the above
15. Processing operation that combines
continuous and batch processes.
a. Semi-continuous processing
b. Semi-batch processing
c. Mixed Processing
d. All of the above
16. Operations or set of actions from a
specific sequence to the specific final
end.
a. Managing
b. Processing
c. Handling
d. None of the above
17. Action that constitutes a process,
such as cleaning, heating, cooling, size
reduction, particle separation, mixing
and blending, and many others, that
produces a product.
a. Undertaking process
b. Unit Operation
c. Operating procedure
d. None of the above
18. Stages of food processing.
a. Primary stage
b. Secondary stage
c. Tertiary stage
d. All of the above
e. Two of the above
19. Processing stage were there is an
alteration in the form of the initial
produce, such as wine making, crushing
tomatoes to make tomato catsup.
a. 	Primary stage
b. 	Secondary stage
c. 	Tertiary stage
d. 	All of the above
e. 	Two of the above
20. Processing stage where commercial
production of ready-to-eat processed
food, such as meal and snacks.
a. 	Primary stage
b. 	Secondary stage
c. 	Tertiary stage
d. 	All of the above
e. 	Two of the above

THEORIES AND PRINCIPLES OF GMP,
SSOP, EMP, HACCP, AMONG OTHERS.
1. Acronym for GMP.
a. Good manufacturing practices
b. Good manufacturing procedure
c. Good Manufacturing principles
d. All of the above
2. Acronym for SSOP.
a. Sanitation Standard Operating
Process
b. Sanitation Standard Operating
Procedures
c. Sanitation Standard Operating
Protocol
d. All of the above
3. Acronym for EMP.
a. Environmental Monitoring Program
b. Environmental Monitoring Procedure
c. Environmental Monitoring Protocol
d. All of the above
4. Acronym for HACCP
a. Hazard Analysis and Critical Control
Points
b. Hazard Analysis and Critical Control
Parameters
c. Hazard Analysis and Critical Control
Procedure
d. All of the above
5. Set of regulations ensuring that food
is manufactured, processed, packaged,
and stored under conditions that meet
the highest standards of hygiene and
quality.
a. GMP
b. SSOP
c. EMP
d. None of the above
6. Specific, written procedures for
cleaning and sanitizing to prevent
contamination that are essential for
implementing GMP effectively and
ensuring sanitary conditions in the
production environment.
a. GMP
b. SSOP
c. EMP
d. None of the above
7. Systematically monitoring the
environment to identify and control
potential hazards, such as biological,
chemical and physical contaminants.
a. GMP
b. SSOP
c. EMP
d. None of the above
8. System that identifies, evaluates, and
controls potential hazards throughout the
production process.
a. GMP
b. SSOP
c. HACCP
d. None of the above
9. Specific steps where control can be
applied to prevent or eliminate food safety
hazards.
a. 	Critical Control Points
b. 	Coordinated Control Points
c. 	Control Points Procedure
d. 	All of the above
10. CCP example in vegetable processing
during the chilling process to prevent the
growth of bacteria.
a. 	Moisture content of samples
b. 	Temperature
c. 	Humidity
d. 	None of the above

UNIT OPERATION
1. Unit operation where there is
separation of raw materials based on
specifications (color, size, quality).
a. 	Sorting
b. 	Grading
c. 	Sizing
d. 	None of the above
2. Unit operation of heating food at a
very high temperature to achieve
commercial sterility.
a. 	Blanching
b. 	Canning
c. 	Sterilizing
d. 	None of the above
3. Unit operation aimed at producing
gluten in dough.
a. 	Kneading
b. 	Sanitizing
c. 	Proofing
d. 	None of the above
4. Unit operation of rising the shaped
dough before baking.
a. 	Proofing
b. 	Curing
c. 	Blanching
d. 	None of the above
5. Unit operation of heating food at a
maximum temperature of 72°C for 15
seconds to reduce pathogen load.
a. 	Sterilization
b. 	Pasteurization
c. 	Scalding
d. 	None of the above
6. Unit operation of lowering the
temperature of food product to 0°-5°C.
a. 	Refrigeration
b. 	Chilling
c. 	Cooling
d. 	None of the above
7. Movement of raw materials and
finished products within the processing
plant which includes conveying,
pumping, and other methods of
transportation.
a. 	Conveying
b. 	Material Handling
c. 	Pumping
d. 	Noe of the above
8. Reducing the water content of food
through evaporation or other methods
that increases concentration and shelf
life.
a. 	Concentration
b. 	Hydrolysis
c. 	Drying
d. 	None of the above
9. Protecting food products from
contamination and physical damage
while enhancing their presentation and
shelf life.
a. 	Packaging
b. 	Drying
c. 	Storage
d. 	None of the above
10. Shaping food products into desired
forms using techniques like extrusion,
molding, or cutting.
a. 	Forming
b. 	Packaging
c. 	Heating
d. 	None of the above
11. Processes, like grinding, chopping,
and slicing, reduce the size of food
particles to facilitate further processing or
improving appeal of food product to
consumers.
a. 	Size reduction
b. 	Cutting
c. 	Shredding
d. 	None of the above

12. Combining different ingredients to
create a homogeneous mixture that is
essential for many food products.
a. 	Mixing
b. 	Concentration
c. 	Heating
d. 	None of the above
13. Removing contaminants, like dirt,
debris, and microorganisms, from raw
materials which is crucial for food safety
and quality.
a. 	Cleaning
b. 	Grading
c. 	Separating
d. 	None of the above
14. Removing moisture from food,
through various drying methods,
extends shelf life and reduces bulk for
storage and transportation.
a. 	Separation
b. 	Drying
c. 	Heating
d. 	None of the above
15. Applying heat to food achieving
several objectives, such as
pasteurization, sterilization or cooking,
impacting texture, flavor, and shelf life.
a. 	Pasteurizing
b. 	Heating
c. 	Sterilizing
d. 	None of the above
16. Rapid reduction of temperature of
cook food after heating to preserve food
quality and prevents microbial growth,
especially in processes like canning.
a. Cooling
b. Refrigerating
c. Chilling
d. None of the above
17. Food preparation process that
involves briefly scalding food, usually
vegetables or fruits, in boiling water or
steam, followed by an immediate plunge
into cold or ice water to halt the cooking
process.
a. 	Blanching
b. 	Canning
c. 	Cooking
d. 	None of the above
18. Technique used to soften food,
preserve color and texture, and stop
enzyme activity that can lead to flavor
loss, discoloration, and nutrient
degradation.
a. 	Blanching
b. 	Steaming
c. 	Heat sterilization
d. 	None of the above
19. Process that eliminates or destroys
all viable microorganisms, including
bacteria, viruses, and spores, from food
products.
a. 	Boiling
b. 	Freezing
c. 	Heat sterilization
d. 	None of the above
20. Sterilization method includes ___.
a. 	canning
b. 	ultra-high temperature
c. 	radiation
d. 	chemical treatment
e. 	All of the above
f. 	None of the above
21. Absence of microorganisms capable
of growing under normal storage and
distribution condition.
a. 	Sterility
b. 	Treated food
c. 	Safe food
d. 	None of the above

22. What is the importance of blanching
in food processing?
a. Helps deactivates enzymes that can
cause vegetables to lose color, flavor,
and nutrients during storage.
b. Softens vegetables making them
easier to peel and prepare for cooking
or freezing.
c. Helps reduce bacteria on food
surface.
d. Crucial step before freezing,
canning, or drying.
a. 	Helps vegetables retain their vibrant
color and fresh taste.
e. All of the above
f. Three of the above
23. Method of food preservation that
removes moisture, inhibiting microbial
growth and extending shelf life.
a. 	Drying
b. 	Dehydration
c. 	Roasting
d. 	All of the above
e. 	Two of the above
24. What benefit has drying have on the
food?
a. Removal of moisture.
b. Slowing down of enzymatic activity
which changes color and texture of the
food.
c. Stopping the growth and
development of bacteria, yeast, and
mold.
d. All of the above
25. Which of the following affects drying
of food?
a. Temperature
b. Humidity
c. Air circulation
d. All of the above
26. Which of the following is the benefit
of drying food?
a. Extends shelf life of food.
b. Reduces food weight making it easier
to store and transport.
c. Results in stronger flavor of food.
d. Retains significant amount of vitamins
and minerals in food.
e. All of the above
27. Method of food preservation that
involves sealing food in airtight
containers and heating them to destroy
microorganisms, thus extending shelf life.
a. 	Aluminum-foil packaging
b. 	Canning
c. 	Bagging in plastic bag
d. 	All of the above
28. Containers used in food canning.
a. 	Metal cans
b. 	Glass jar
c. 	Retort pouches
d. 	All of the above
29. Shelf life of canned foods.
a. Less than 1 year
b. 1 to 5 years
c. More than 5 years
d. All of the above
30. Canning method suitable for high-
acid food, like fruits and pickles.
a. Boiling water-bath canning
b. Pressure canning
c. Vacuum canning
d. None of the above
31. Canning method for low-acid food,
like vegetables and meats, as it reaches
higher temperature to kill harmful
bacteria.
a. 	Boiling water-bath canning
b. 	Pressure canning
c. 	Vacuum canning
d. 	None of the above

32. Cooking method that involves
submerging food in hot oil or fat and
maintained at 175º to 190ºC.
a. 	Boiling
b. 	Steaming
c. 	Frying
d. 	None of the above
33. Dry-heat cooking method where
food is cooked in an oven or over an
open flame with hot air circulating
around it.
a. 	Grilling
b. 	Roasting
c. 	Frying
d. 	None of the above
34. Cooking method that uses dry heat,
typically in an oven, to prepare a wide
variety of foods, including bread, cakes,
pastries, and cookies.
a. 	Dehydrating
b. 	Drying
c. 	Baking
d. 	None of the above
35. Cooking method that utilizes liquid
vapor to cook food, resulting in tender
and moist dishes.
a. 	Steaming
b. 	Roasting
c. 	Grilling
d. 	None of the above
36. Which of the following is the benefit
of steaming?
a. Nutrient retention – more vitamins
and mineral retained.
b. Moist texture – cook food evenly
resulting in tender and moist texture.
c. Low-fat cooking – doesn’t require
added fat.
d. Versatility – variety of food can be
cooked.
e. All of the above
37. Method of food preservation where
food is placed in airtight containers
(typically glass jars) and then heated to
create a vacuum seal, effectively
preventing spoilage.
a. 	Bottling
b. 	Canning
c. 	Pressure cooking
d. 	None of the above
38. Method of cooking food using steam
and high pressure inside a sealed pot in
order to raise the boiling point of water
consequently allowing the food to cook
faster at a higher temperature than
traditional methods.
a. 	Pressure cooking
b. 	Long duration boiling
c. 	Steaming
d. 	None of the above
39. Versatile food processing technique
where ingredients are forced through a
die to create various shapes and
textures.
a. 	Extrusion
b. 	Screw press
c. 	Puffing
d. 	None of the above
40. Which of the following is the benefit
of food extrusion?
a. Produces a wide range of food
shape and texture.
b. Operates on continuous mode.
c. Advantageous for mass production.
d. All of the above

ENGINEERING PRINCIPLES
1. Engineering principles is crucial in
food processing to ensure ___.
a. 	Efficiency
b. 	Safety
c. 	Quality
d. 	All of the above
e. 	None of the above
2. Applying engineering principles such
as ___ can optimize processes, improve
safety, and extend shelf life of food
products.
a. 	Heat transfer
b. 	Fluid dynamics
c. 	Material science
d. 	All of the above
e. 	Two of the above
3. Heat transfer principle applied in
food processing.
a. 	Pasteurization
b. 	Sterilization
c. 	Cooking
d. 	Baking
e. 	Freezing
f. 	Refrigeration
g. 	All of the above
h. 	Four of the above
4. Heat transfer principles that ensure
food is heated at correct temperature
and for the right duration to kill harmful
bacteria and extended shelf life.
a. 	Cooking and baking
b. 	Pasteurization and sterilization
c. 	Freezing and refrigeration
d. 	All of the above
e. 	None of the above
5. Engineering principles needed in
designing efficient liquid moving devices
and mixers for handling food liquid and
slurries as well as to ensure consistent
and efficient flow of food materials through
processing equipment.
a. Heat transfer
b. Fluid Dynamics
c. Material Science
d. All of the above
6. Knowledge on the engineering
principle of material science can help
engineers in ___.
a. choosing the right materials to protect
food from spoilage, contamination, during
storage and transport
b. designing food process operation
c. optimizing food process operation
d. All of the above
e. Two of the above
7. 	What key engineering principle is
needed in food processing?
a. Process control and automation –
design and implement automated system
for monitoring and control in food
processing.
b. Food safety management systems –
ensure that food products are safe for
consumption, preventing cross-
contamination, and controlling foodborne
pathogens.
c. Waste management systems – design
efficient waste management system for
food processing plant, minimizing
environmental impact and maximizing
resource recovery.
d. All of the above
e. Two of the above

8. What benefit is enjoyed when
engineering principles are applied?
a. Improved food safety
b. Extended shelf life
c. Enhanced food quality
d. Increased efficiency
e. Reduced cost
f. 	All of the above
g. None of the above
9. Which food processing requires the
application of engineering principles to
improve efficiency, safety, and quality?
a. 	Production
b. 	Handling
c. 	Storage
d. 	Preservation
e. 	Control
f. 	Packaging
g. 	Distribution
h. 	All of the above
i. 	Four of the above
10. Engineering principle that ensures
food is handled safely and hygienically
to prevent contamination and maintain
quality.
a. Packaging
b. Handling
c. Distribution
d. None of the above
11. Engineering principles that help
optimize resource utilization, improve
process efficiency, and reduce waste.
a. Production
b. Distribution
c. Handling
d. None of the above
12. Engineering principle that extends
shelf life and ensures food safety by
inhibiting microbial growth and chemical
reactions.
a. Preservation
b. Distribution
c. Handling
d. None of the above
13. Engineering principle that ensures
food products are transported efficiently
and safely to consumers, minimizing
spoilage and maintaining quality, such
as the use of refrigerated trucks,
optimizing routing, and implementing
control during transport.
a. Transportation
b. Distribution
c. Delivery
d. All of the above
e. None of the above
14. What is the purpose of applying the
principles of engineering and of science
in food manufacturing and operation?
a. Optimize food processing.
b. Enhance product shelf life.
c. Improve packaging and distribution.
d. Provide nutritious and safe food for
consumers.
e. All of the above
f. Two of the above
15. Engineering principle that is vital for
understanding and controlling
processes like cooking, pasteurization,
sterilization, and drying.
a. Mass transfer
b. Heat transfer
c. Fluid dynamics
d. None of the above

20. Engineering principle that plays a key
role in optimizing the flow of liquids
during processing, ensuring efficient
mixing, pumping, and cleaning.
a. Mass transfer
b. Heat transfer
c. Fluid dynamics
d. None of the above
21. Engineering principle that slows
down or stop microbial growth, extending
food shelf life.
a. Canning
b. Refrigeration and Freezing
c. Dehydration
d. Salting and Pickling
e. All of the above
22. Engineering and science principles
that create a high osmotic pressure
preventing microbial growth.
a. Canning
b. Refrigeration and Freezing
c. Dehydration
d. Salting and Pickling
e. All of the above
23. Scientific principle for food
manufacturing used to identify and
control hazards in food production.
a. HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical
Control Points)
b. GMP
c. EMP
d. None of the above
24. Systematic approach used to ensure
hygienic conditions and processes
throughout the food manufacturing
environment.
a. HACCP
b. GMP (Good manufacturing practices)
c. EMP (Environmental Monitoring
Program)
d. None of the above
16. Engineering principle that helps in
optimizing the movement of nutrients,
water, and other substances during food
processing.
a. Mass transfer
b. Heat transfer
c. Fluid dynamics
d. None of the above
17. Engineering and science principles
that involve sealing food in containers
and heating to kill microbes, extending
its shelf life.
a. Canning
b. Refrigeration and Freezing
c. Dehydration
d. Salting and Pickling
e. All of the above
18. Engineering and science principles
that remove water from food products
and inhibit microbial growth, thus extend
shelf life.
a. Canning
b. Refrigeration and Freezing
c. Dehydration
d. Salting and Pickling
e. All of the above
19. Purpose of engineering principles in
packaging materials.
a. To design effective packaging
materials that protect food from
spoilage and maintain its quality.
b. To minimize wastes and ensure
product integrity.
c. To optimize transportation and
logistics, ensuring timely and safe
delivery of food products.
d. All of the above
e. None of the above

25. Systematic approach used to
monitor the food production
environment for potential contamination,
ensuring the safety and quality of food
products.
a. HACCP
b. GMP (Good manufacturing
practices)
c. EMP (Environmental Monitoring
Program)
d. None of the above
26. A solution or an environment with
high concentration of solutes resulting in
a strong tendency for water to move
into that solution or environment
through a semipermeable membrane,
like salting or pickling process.
a. High-osmotic pressure
a. 	Low-osmotic pressure
b. 	Mass transfer
c. 	All of the above
27. Food preservation method that
creates a high-osmotic pressure
preventing microbial growth.
a. 	Salting and pickling
b. 	Canning
c. 	Dehydration
d. 	All of the above
e. 	None of the above
28. Process used to concentrate juices
and create products, like tomato paste.
a. Evaporation
b. Condensation
c. Heating
d. All of the above

ROLE OF ABE IN COLD STORAGE
SYSTEMS AND FACILITIES
1. System used for maintaining the
quality and shelf life of perishable
goods, like fruits, vegetables, dairy,
meat, fishery, etc.
a. Cold-storage system

diameter of pipe
c. convection coefficient, velocity of
fluid, diameter of pipe
d. 	None of the above
31. The Prantdl number is a function of
___.
a. viscosity, specific heat, and thermal
conductivity
a. specific heat, heat transfer
coefficient, and thermal conductivity
c. viscosity, diameter of pipe, thermal
conductivity
d. 	None of the above
32. Overall heat transfer coefficient
includes ___.
a. thermal conductivity and heat
transfer coefficient of the materials
b. heat transfer coefficient and
emissivity of the materials
c. thermal conductivity and emissivity
of the materials
d. None of the above
33. Amount of heat transferred per unit
temperature per unit length.
a. Emissivity
b. Thermal conductivity
c. Heat transfer coefficient
d. None of the above

34. Proportionality factor that represents
the property of a material through heat
conduction.
a. Thermal resistivity
b. Thermal conductivity
c. Thermal coefficient
d. None of the above
35. Which of the following is a factor
that influences thermal conductivity of a
material?
a. Chemical composition of materials
b. Temperature of materials
c. Surrounding pressure
d. All of the above
36. If the temperature surrounding the
material is reduced, the thermal
conductivity also ___.
a. changes in a decreasing manner
b. changes in an increasing manner
c. does not change
d. None of the above
37. Temperature of the surrounding air.
a. Dry-bulb temperature
b. Wet-bulb temperature
c. Ambient temperature
d. All of the above
38. Fluids with low molecular weight
have ___.
a. high thermal conductivity
b. low thermal conductivity
c. no thermal conductivity
d. None of the above
39. Basically, the thermal conductivity of
a material increases if the ___.
a. thickness is increased
b. temperature is increased
c. temperature is decreased
d. All of the above
40. If the flow of fluid is on streamline
characteristic, the fluid is at ___.
a. turbulent condition
b. laminar condition
c. eddies
d. All of the above
41. Which of the following materials has
low thermal conductivity?
a. Building brick
b. Asbestos
c. Firebrick
d. Concrete
e. None of the above
42. Which of the following statements
is true?
a. The thermal conductivity of
aluminum is higher than that of silver.
b. Silver transmits heat faster than
aluminum.
c. Aluminum and silver transfer heat at
the same rate.
d. 	All of the above
43. Device used in transferring heat.
a. Insulator
b. Heat absorber
c. Heat exchanger
d. All of the above
44. When two fluids in a heat exchanger
move in opposite direction, the device is
classified as ___.
a. parallel flow HE
b. cross flow HE
c. constant flow HE
d. None of the above
45. Ability of a material to give up or to
receive heat.
a. Resistance
b. Thermal conductance
c. All of the above
d. None of the above

46. Insulating ability or resistance of a
material to the flow of heat.
a. Thermal resistance
b. Thermal conductivity
c. Thermal insulator
d. All of the above
47. A thick-walled stainless-steel tube (k
= 19 w/m-°C, with 2 cm ID and 4 cm
OD) is covered with a 3-cm layer of
asbestos insulation (k = 0.2 w/m-°C). If
the inside wall temperature of the pipe
is maintained at 600°C and the
temperature outside of the insulation is
at 100°C, what would be the heat loss
per foot length of the tube? (Problem 7)
a. 600 w/m
b. 680 w/m
c. 720 w/m
d. None of the above
48. Ceramic material designed to be
resistant to high temperature -- i.e.,
1000° to 1800°C.
a. Refractory
b. Asbestos
c. Fiber glass
d. None of the above
49. What is the heat transfer loss per
foot of a 2in. nominal pipe (OD=2.37
in.) covered with 1in.-thick insulating
material having an average thermal
conductivity of 0.037 BTU/hr-ft-°F. The
inner and outer temperatures of the
insulation are 380° and 80°F,
respectively. (Problem 6)
a. 161 BTU/hr-ft
b. 114 BTU/hr-ft
c. 125 BTU/hr-ft
d. None of the above
50. An example of heat conductor.
a. Silica brick
b. Refractory cement
c. Asbestos fiber
d. None of the above
51. Material that is poor conductor of
heat or has low thermal conductivity.
a. Conductor
b. Insulator
c. Resistor
d. All of the above
52. Insulators used for steam lines are
classified as ___.
a. low-temperature-range insulator
b. medium-temperature-range
insulator
c. high-temperature-range insulator
d. None of the above
53. A good example of high-temperature
insulating material.
a. Iron
b. Wood
c. Asbestos
d. All of the above
54. Good example of a dual-temperature
insulator.
a. Expanded silica
b. Cellular glass
c. Vermiculite
d. All of the above
55. Form of insulants used in industrial
insulation application.
a. Flexible strips
b. Foil
c. Flexible pipe section and mattresses
d. All of the above

56. An extruded foam used for low-
temperature systems, such as
refrigeration, building and sub-zero
insulation.
a. Polystyrene foam
b. PVC foam
c. Plastic foam
d. All of the above
57. Good insulator for kiln dryers.
a. Rice husk
b. Brick
c. Concrete
d. None of the above
58. Which of the following factors
needs to be considered in selecting an
insulant?
a. Operating temperature
b. Maintenance cost
c. Ability to resist mechanical and heat
damage
d. All of the above
59. To protect the insulant from
mechanical damage, it must be
provided with ___.
a. metal sheet cladding
b. nets and asbestos cement
c. wire net and bituminous compound
d. All of the above
60. Which of the following statements
is true?
a. In insulation, heat gain is more
costly than heat loss.
b. The cost of extracting heat from a
refrigerated space is the same with the
cost of heat losses from a high-
temperature system.
c. The cost of insulating high-
temperature system is the same with
that of low temperature system.
d. 	All of the above
61. The presence of moisture in a low-
temperature insulation material may
cause ___.
a. reduction in the insulating value of
the material
a. improvement in the insulating value
of the materials
c. reduction in the cost of the
insulating materials
d. All of the above

AGRICULTURE AND
POSTHARVEST
LOSSES

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
1.Refers to product-processing and distribution
industries.
a. Agriculture
b. Farming
c. Agricultural processing
d. Agribusinesses

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
WHAT IS AGRICULTURE?
Farming – production of food and fiber
Agriculture – includes farming and farm-supply industries
(feed, seed, machinery, pharmaceuticals, etc) as well as
the product-processing and distribution industries, which
convert the raw food into the form consumers want and
move it to them (referred to as agriculturally-related
industries, or “agribusinesses”).

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
2. The following are food processing and
distribution industries, except:
a.Storage
b.Transportation
c.Machinery
d.Services

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
POSTHARVEST LOSS
Postharvest loss is the
degradation in both quantity and
quality of a food product during
the chain of interconnected
activities from the time of harvest
to the delivery of food to the
consumer (from farm to fork or
from crop to consumption).

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Post harvest flow chart
Harvesting
Pre-drying
in field
Threshing Winnowing Drying
Storage
Parboiling and drying
For milling
Processing (pre
cleaning, fine
cleaning, grading)
and fumigation
for seed
Harvesting
Packaging
Marketing	Marketing
Utilization by
consumer
Hauling

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
3. The following are causes of postharvest losses,
except:
a.Labor shortage during harvest season
b.Rough transportation
c.Unfriendly farmers
d.Limited drying facility

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
4. The following are good harvest handling
practices, except:
a.Harvest in dry and sunny weather.
b.Do not mix grain for milling with seed production.
c.Use combine if possible.
d.None of the above

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Causes of Postharvest Losses
• Inefficient harvesting and handling methods
• Labor shortage during harvest season
• Harvesting immature and overmature crops
• Poor processing techniques
• Limited drying facility
• Excess rainfall
• Lack of storage facilities
• Rough transportation/load/unload
• No or poor access to new technology
• No farmers friendly business model

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS

threshing

handling

drying

storage

Crop Consumption
Physical losses in traditional postharvest chain
Physical losses in mechanized postharvest chain
In SE Asia (2011), physical losses range from 15-25%.
Quality losses range from 10-30% (loss in value)

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
POSTHARVEST LOSS
Postharvest Losses in Rice
Based on a study conducted by PhilMech and PhilRice (2010):

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Postharvest Losses in Corn
Based on a 2009 study, an average of 7.8 percent was lost in the
corn postharvest system, of which 4.54 percent was due to drying
loss.
❖ In Isabela, the losses amounted to around 7.15 percent where
4.01 percent was measured in drying.
❖ In Bukidnon, postharvest losses obtained was 7.35 percent,
4.99 percent was also due to drying loss.
❖ While in South Cotabato, 5.98 percent was the total
postharvest losses from which 4.63 percent was incurred during
the drying operation.
POSTHARVEST LOSS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
POSTHARVEST LOSS
Losses in Maize can be of two types:
Quantity Loss Quality Loss
• Improper time of harvesting • Change in colour, smell or taste
• Inconsistent harvest technology • Contamination with toxins
• Improper drying methods • Pathogen
• Spillage during storage • Insect excreta
• Damage caused by pest
organism (Aflatoxin) • Reduction in nutritional value
• Poor handling
• Damage caused due to rodents

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
4. The following are good harvest handling
practices, except:
a.Harvest in dry and sunny weather.
b.Do not mix grain for milling with seed production.
c.Use combine if possible.
d.None of the above

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Harvest Handling
• Harvest in dry and sunny weather to avoid extra
moisture
• Harvest only in appropriate ripening stage (80-85%)
• Use combine harvester if available/possible
• Do not mix grain for milling with seed production
• Take moisture measurement after harvesting
• Avoid delays in threshing and drying after
harvesting
POSTHARVEST MANAGEMENT

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
5. The following are good field drying practices,
except:
a.Dry after threshing.
b.Allow 2-3 days in the field for panicle drying.
c.Sack after threshing.
d.Leave the cut crop in the field for sun drying.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Field Drying
POSTHARVEST MANAGEMENT
• Leaving the cut crop in the
field and exposing it to the
sun for drying
• Panicle drying, usually
farmers dry their paddy 2-3
days in the field
• For seed its better thresh
after cutting and then dry.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
6. Several grades of grain quality taken together
are called:
a.Standard
b.Grading
c.Code
d.Protocol

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRAIN QUALITY
What is a grain grade?
• A grain grade defines a specific quality of grain. There
may be several grades, which taken together are called a
standard.
• Different countries may have different standards, or in
some cases the same standards apply in several countries.
• In a quality conscious market, buyers of grain (cereals and
pulses) wish to purchase grain at a certain grade.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
7. The following are examples of organic foreign
matters in grains, except:
a.Maize cob particles
b.Foreign grains
c.Stones
d.Leaves

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRAIN QUALITY
What does high quality grain mean?
High quality grain conforms to a grade that is suitable for sale into
regional or international markets.
The following imperfections must be limited in such grain -
1. Foreign matter
This is either organic (e.g. maize cob particles,
leaves, tassels, or different types of grain, etc),
inorganic (e.g. stones, dust)
or filth (e.g. rodent dropping and dead insects).

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
8. These grains come from poor postharvest handling
especially shelling or threshing.
a.Mould-damaged
b.Insect-damaged
c.Broken
d.Rodent-damaged

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRAIN QUALITY
2. Broken grain
Most broken grain comes from poor
postharvest handling especially
shelling or threshing.
3. Insect damaged grain
Insects make holes in grains and
hollow them out.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
9. Rodents chew into grain and remove the
____________.
a.Roots
b.Starch
c.Germ
d.Endosperm

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRAIN QUALITY
4. Rodent damaged grain
Rodents chew into grain and remove
the germ.
5. Mould damaged grain
Mouldy grains have been dried too slowly
or allowed to become wet. They have
patches of mould growth on them and may
also be discoloured. Some moulds also
produce mycotoxins like aflatoxin.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
10. These grains have been dried too slowly or allowed
to become wet.
a.Rodent-damaged
b.Heat-damaged
c.Insect-damaged
d.Mouldy

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
11. Grains that have underwent grain heating,
especially stack burn.
a.Discoloured
b.Mouldy
c.Heat-damaged
d.Rodent-damaged

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRAIN QUALITY
6. Discoloured grain
Grain may be discoloured due to grain
heating, especially stack burn which may
have no connection with mould growth.
7. Grain with an unusual smell
Poor handling, especially slow drying or
contamination or storage near fertiliser or
other agrochemicals can give grain off-
odours that are unacceptable.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRAINS: MORPHOLOGY,
PROPERTIES AND
QUALITY

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
12. Also called as whole grains, these refer to the
entire seed of a plant.
a.Kernels
b.Pearled grains
c.Grits
d.Pulses

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
WHAT IS GRAIN?
Grain may be dried cereals (like maize, rice, sorghum, etc) or dried pulses
(like beans, cowpea, gram).
Cereals
Maize Sorghum	Paddy rice
Pulses
Beans Cowpe
a
Gram
• Seeds of plants in the grass family.
• All grains start life as whole grains. In their natural state growing in the fields,
whole grains are the entire seed of a plant. Industry calls this as "kernel”.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
13. Refers to the whole grain with bran layer removed.
a.Pulses
b.Pearled grains
c.Grits
d.Kernels

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
FORMS OF GRAINS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
14. It refers to the embryo which, if fertilized by pollen,
will sprout into a new plant.
a.Endosperm
b.Husk
c.Germ
d.Gran

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
STRUCTURE
Germ – is the embryo which, if
fertilized by pollen, will sprout
into a new plant
- Principal part of a seed
- It contains many B vitamins,
some protein, minerals, and
healthy fats.
- Consists of cells that are very
sensitive to heat

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
15. The largest part of the kernel and provides
essential energy to the young plant.
a.Husk
b.Germ
c.Endosperm
d.Bran

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
STRUCTURE
Endosperm – the germ’s
food supply, which
provides essential
energy to the young
plant
- It is by far the largest
portion of the kernel
- Fills the whole inner
part of the seeds
- It contains starchy
carbohydrates, proteins
and small amounts of
vitamins and minerals.
Husk – the multi-layered
outer skin of the kernel,
and is tough enough to
protect the other two
parts of the kernel from
assaults by sunlight,
pests, water, and
disease.
- It contains important
antioxidants, B
vitamins and fiber.
- It reduces the rate of
drying significantly.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• The rice grain is the ripened
ovary, with the lemma, palea,
rachilla, sterile lemmas and
the awn firmly attached to it.
• The rice hull includes the lemma
and palea and their associated
structures – the sterile lemmas,
rachilla, and awn.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
16. It is the basic unit of the inflorescence or the
panicle.
a.Pedicel
b.Sterile lemma
c.Spikelet
d.Floret

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• A spikelet is a basic
unit of the inflorescence
or the panicle.
• These spikelets are
borne on the primary
and secondary
branches.
• It consists of the pedicel
and the floret.
• The floret is borne on
the pedicel.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• The rudimentary glumes are the
laterally enlarged, cuplike apex of the
pedicel. They are the lowermost parts
of the spikelet. During threshing, the
rudimentary glumes are separated
from the rest of the spikelet.
• The sterile lemmas are small,
bractlike projections attached to the
floret.
• The rachilla is a small axis that bears
the single floret. It is between the
sterile lemmas and the floret.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
18. It is the larger protective glume covering the floret
of a rice grain.
a.Palea
b.Keel
c.Nerve
d.Lemma

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• The floret includes the
lemma, palea, and the
flower.
• The larger protective
glume covering the
floret is called the
lemma and the
smaller one is referred
to as the palea.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• Both the lemma and palea
have ridges referred to as
nerves.
• The lemma has five while
the palea has three.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
19. In some rice varieties, the keel is elongated into a
thin extension called _______.
a.Lemma
b.Palea
c.Awn
d.Nerve

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• The lemma has a
constricted structure
at its end called
the keel.
• In some varieties, the
keel is elongated into
a thin extension,
the awn.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
.
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• The dehulled rice grain
is called caryopsis,
commonly referred to
as brown rice because
of the three
brownish pericarp layer
s that envelope it.
• Next to the pericarp
layers are the
two tegmen layers and
the aleurone layers.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
• The endosperm provides
nourishment to the
germinating embryo.
• The embryo lies on the
belly side of the grain and
is enclosed by the
lemma. It is the
embryonic organ of the
seed.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
20. In the embryo of rice grain, this refers to the
embryonic leaves.
a.Pericarp
b.Caryopsis
c.Radicle
d.Plumule

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PARTS OF RICE GRAIN
The embryo
contains the
plumule (embryonic
leaves) and the
radicle (embryonic
primary root).

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
21. It refers to the ratio of surface area of sphere
having the same volume as that of the particle to the
surface area of the particle.
a.Sphericity
b.Bulk density
c.Porosity
d.Circularity

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
Sphericity – the ratio of surface area of a sphere having same
volume as that of the particle to the surface area of the
particle

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
22. It refers to the mass per unit volume of a
material excluding the void space.
a.True density
b.Porosity
c.Bulk density
d.Absolute density

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Bulk Density
True Density
- the mass per unit volume of a material excluding
the void space.
PHYSICAL PROPERTIES

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
Porosity
- the percentage of
volume of inter-grain
space to the total
volume of grain bulk.
- depends on shape,
dimensions, and
roughness of the
grain surface.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
23. It is the steepest angle of descent or dip relative to
the horizontal plane to which a material can be piled
without slumping.
a.Angle of repose
b.Normal friction
c.Coefficient of friction
d.True density

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
Coefficient of Friction – is equal to the tangent of the angle of internal friction
for the material.
- depends on grain shape, surface characteristics, and moisture content.
Angle of Repose – is the steepest
angle of descent or dip relative to
the horizontal plane to which a
material can be piled without
slumping. At this angle, the material
on the slope face is on the verge of
sliding.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
24. It measures the ability of a material to conduct
thermal energy relative to its ability to store thermal
energy.
a.Thermal diffusivity
b.Resistivity
c.Specific heat
d.Thermal conductivity

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
THERMAL PROPERTIES
Specific Heat (c) – the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of unit
mass through 1°C.
Thermal Conductivity – is the amount of heat flow through unit thickness of
material over a unit area per unit time for unit temperature difference
- For single grains, it varies from 0.3 to 0.6 kcal/(m·h °C)
- For grains in bulk, it is only about 0.10 to 0.15 kcal/(m·h °C), which is due to the
presence of air space in it
Thermal Diffusivity – is the thermal conductivity divided by density and specific
heat capacity at constant pressure. It measures the ability of a material to
conduct thermal energy relative to its ability to store thermal energy.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
AERODYNAMIC PROPERTIES
Terminal Velocity –
the air velocity at
which an object
remains
suspended in a
vertical pipe
under the action
of the air current.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
AERODYNAMIC PROPERTIES
Resistance of Grain
Bed to Air Flow
– is dependent
upon: (a) bed
thickness, (b) air
velocity, (c)
orientation of the
grains, and (d)
type of grains.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
RICE QUALITY

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DIMENSION AND STRUCTURE
The length of the paddy grain varies due to variations in the length of the awn and the
pedicel.
Types of paddy:
1.Extremely long – 80% of the whole brown rice have a length of
7.5 mm or more
2.Long – 80% of the whole brown rice have a length of 6.5 mm or
more but shorter than 7.5 mm
3.Medium – 80% of the whole brown rice have a length of ≥ 5.5
mm but < 6.5 mm
4.Short – paddy with 80% of the whole brown rice are shorter than
5.5 mm

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
25. Paddy whose whole brown rice kernel has a
length/width ratio of < 2.0.
a.Slender
b.Bold
c.Round
d.Fine

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DIMENSION AND STRUCTURE
Length/Width ratio of the whole brown rice kernel:
a.Slender: ≥3.0
b.Bold: ≥ 2.0 but < 3.0
c.Round: < 2.0

because it permits termites and
rodents to enter.
• A better base is made of stone.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
UNDERGROUND STORAGE
• This method of storage is used in dry
regions where the water table does not
endanger the contents.
• Their traditional form varies from
region to region: they are usually
cylindrical, spherical or amphoric in
shape, but other types are known.
• The entrance to the pit may be closed
either by heaping earth or sand onto a
timber cover, or by a stone sealed with
mud.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
SACKS
• At the very least, the bagged grain must be kept off
the ground to prevent spoilage by translocating water
and/or termites.
• Low platforms, tarpaulins or plastic sheeting may
serve this purpose; but if there is a risk of damage by
rodents or other animals, high platforms fitted with
rodent barriers should be used.
• Alternatively, the sacks of grain should be stacked on
dunnage or waterproof sheeting, away from walls, in
a rodentproofed barn.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
METAL OR PLASTIC DRUMS
• Drums are often used as storage containers in the
house and serve notably for the storage of cereal
seeds and pulses.
• Plastic drums are used intact or after having the
upper part cut off to facilitate loading and
unloading.
• If the lid is tight fitting and the drum is completely
filled with grain, any insects present will deplete
the oxygen in the drum and die.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
SILO
• A silo is a tall storage structure, which is nothing but
a deep bin.
• Silos often are blue or the color of concrete.
• They traditionally store silage, which is grass or
other fodder harvested green and wet, primarily to
feed dairy cattle.
• There are two types of vertical silos a) flat bottom
vertical silo and b) hopper bottom vertical silo.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
SILO

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
SILO
Flat bottom Hopper bottom

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
55. Fatter than silos.
a.Drum
b.Crib
c.Sack
d.Bin

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BINS
• Bins are vented, silver, corrugated steel structures
fatter in diameter than silos and have varying heights.
• They generally store dry corn and soybeans, which
meet domestic or export market demand for feed,
food and fuel use.
• Squat silos comes under shallow bins. A squat silo
has a wall height to diameter ratio 0.5 or even less.
• Squat silo can compete with sheds for low-cost
quality storage.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BINS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
SILO and BINS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BAG AND BULK
• Type of grain stored
• Length of storage period
• Whether a particular grain or different kinds of grains are to be
stored

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
56. Bagged storage compared to bulk storage,
except:
a.Slightly cheaper
b.More costly fumigation
c.Less storage loss
d.Cheaper handling

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
ITEM BAG BULK
Land requirement Double that of
bulk storage
Half of the bag storage
Cost of storage Slightly cheaper Comparatively costly
Maximum storage period 1-2 years 5-10 years
Feasibility of being mechanical Difficult Mechanically operated
Period of construction 12-18 months 12-18 months
Economics of handling Cheaper More costly
Fumigation More costly cheaper
Cost of jute or other bags Substantial Nil
Storage loss About 1-1.5% in 1
year storage
Up to 0.2% for a longer
storage period
BAG AND BULK

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
ITEM BAG BULK
Possible Losses:
(a)Rodents It can be made
rodent proof
Rodent proof
(a)Birds Difficult to avoid Bird proof
(a)Insect Fumigated Fumigated
(a)Effects of
humidity and
temperature
Can be
minimized
Can be
controlled by
aeration
(a)Drainage Can be
controlled
Nil
BAG AND BULK

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BAG STORAGE

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
LOSSES DURING STORAGE
Four major categories of losses occurring during storage:
• Weight Loss
• Quality Loss
• Health Risk
• Economic Loss
To reduce food loss, lower the possibility of:
• Biological damage
• Chemical damage
• Physical damage

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL CHANGES
Good storage involves
controlling the following
factors:
• Temperature
• Moisture Content
• Light
• Pests
• Hygiene
• Storage Time
• Grain Quality
• Color
• Bulk Density
• Germination
• Particle Size
Physical attributes of
grains that changes
during storage:

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL CHANGES
• Grain mass, and therefore yield, is
reduced by infestation.
• Contamination not only has direct
food hygiene implications but may
also produce toxins under certain
conditions which may lead to acute
or chronic illness.
Grain Quality
RICE
CORN

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
57. General cause of yellowing of rice grain.
a. Moisture
b. Heat
c. Milling
d. Variety

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL CHANGES
• A general yellowing of the rice
grain is a result of heat build up in
the paddy grain before drying.
• Although discoloration is a
complex biochemical process, it
can be easily avoided by timely
drying of paddy after harvest.
Color
RICE
CORN

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL CHANGES
• Bulk density can be used as a qualitative indicator
and the decrease in its value during storage may
be associated with quality losses.
• This parameter generally increases with the
decrease in moisture content of the product,
except for coffee, paddy rice and barley.
Bulk Density

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL CHANGES
• Germination can be defined as the appearance of
the first visible signs of growth or root protrusion.
• Active respiration of the grain during storage will
deplete the nutrition reserves that the seed uses to
germinate or sprout.
• Molds and diseases can also reduce the ability of
the seed to germinate.
Germination

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
58. Which is a major cause for fissuring or rice
kernels?
a.Moisture adsorption
b.Heat build up
c.Molds
d.Impact force

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL CHANGES
• A major cause for fissuring of rice kernels is the moisture adsorption of
individual dry grains with moisture contents below 16%.
• This can happen either when wet grain is mixed with dry grain (in
storage, in the dryer or after drying in a batch dryer with a resulting
moisture gradient) or when dry grain is exposed to humid ambient air.
• Fissures in rice kernels usually lead to cracking of the grain during the
milling process and thus reduce the head rice recovery.
Particle Size

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHYSICAL CHANGES
• Heat build up in the grain (above 55ºC) due to
insects, molds or high humidity will often lead to a
musty odor in rice.
• In particular, molds (fungi) that grow on rice can
produce offensive odors due to deterioration of
chemical components in the rice.
Odor

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CHEMICAL CHANGES
• Cereals are characterized by relatively low protein and
high carbohydrate contents contained in kernel.
• The germ is rich in protein, fat, sugar and minerals
whereas, the endosperm is low in protein, fat and ash
contents.
• Temperature and relative humidity varies greatly which
causes physical and biochemical changes in grains
during storage.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BIOLOGICAL CHANGES
• Although non-germinative grain can
maintain nutritional value, the grain
trade prefers germinative grain also
for food and feed purposes. This
indicates, that the grain is healthy
and well preserved.
• Germinative grain breathes. Each
kernel gets oxygen from the air and
burns food from its endosperm. This
process gives off heat, water, and
carbon dioxide. This process in grain
is called respiration.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BIOLOGICAL CHANGES
• Respiration of grain produces heat, water and carbon dioxide.
This process consumes dry matter from the grain.
• Heat and water resulting from the respiration of the grain as
well as the activity of bacteria, fungi and insects cause an
increase in moisture content and temperature, which again
increases the life activity.
• The real damage to the grain is caused by fungi, insects and
mites which thrive under warm and humid conditions.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BIOLOGICAL CHANGES
• Fungi are small plants without roots, leaves and
chlorophyll, therefore they have to live of other materials
such as grain.
• Fungi reproduce by small airborne spores which are
spread everywhere by the wind.
❖ Two Basic types of Fungi:
❑ Field Fungi-Deteriorate wet crop in the field but
die as soon as the grain is brought to the indoor
storage
❑ Storage Fungi - are found everywhere on farms,
grain stores, elevators, etc
Fungi

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
59. What is the best way to control mites in
grains?
a.Apply pesticides.
b.Dry grains to 13-14% MC.
c.Control air ventilation.
d.Control storage temperature.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BIOLOGICAL CHANGES
• Although more than 80 species of grain mites are known, these
have never received the same attention as e.g., insects,
because they are more difficult to see and they eat less grain
than insects.
• Existence of mites indicates too high grain m.c. for safe
storage. This also means that fungi is active. Even a small
number of mites can damage the grain by spreading fungi and
toxins.
• The best way to control mites is to dry the grain to 13-14% m.c.
Mites

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
BIOLOGICAL CHANGES
Insects
• Attack of insects is another major source of seed and
grain losses, especially in tropical countries.
• Under favourable conditions, temperatures are
between 28°C-38°C and grain has high moisture
content which makes the kernels soft and easy to
attack and giving an ideal food mixture of dry matter
and water for insects to thrive on - each female can
produce up to 400 eggs within a couple of months.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CONTROL STRATEGIES
Physical and Mechanical Measures
• Drying
• Cooling by aeration
• Airtight storage
• Low temperature storage
• Protective packaging
Chemical Measures
• Grain protectants
• Attractants
• Repellants
Hygienic Measures
• The entire storage is to be kept under clean and hygienic
condition.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
STANDARDS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
60. A multi-sectoral effort that aims to effectively
implement or institutionalize the national grains
standards.
a.Philippine Grains Standardization Program
b.Grading Grains Program of the Philippines
c.Philippine Grains Grading Act
d.National Rice Standardization Program

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHILIPPINE GRAIN
STANDARDIZATION PROGRAM
• A multi-sectoral effort spearheaded
by the National Food Authority that
aims to effectively implement or
institutionalize the national grains
standards through continuing
advocacy, enforcement and
monitoring activities among grains
farmers, millers, traders or retailers
and the general consuming public.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PHILIPPINE GRAIN
STANDARDIZATION PROGRAM
• It is one of the NFA major programs supplying
the rice production enhancement program of
the government.
• The NFA, by virtue of P. D. NO.4 and R.A. 7394
(Consumers Act of the Philippines) is mandated
to establish and enforce the national grains
standards in collaboration with various sectors.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
NATIONAL GRAIN STANDARD
• It is a set of official rules prescribing
standard specifications on the quality,
packaging, labelling, including test and
analysis of rice and corn and other grain
commodities to help ensure efficiency,
order and fair trade in the grains production
and marketing system.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
61. Palay whose average length of the full size palay
grain is between 8.8 to 9.8 mm.
a.Very long
b.Short
c.Intermediate
d.Long

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CLASSIFICATION
SHORT GRAINS - Palay whose average
length of the full size palay grain is
below 8.0 mm
MEDIUM GRAINS - Palay whose
average length of the full size palay
rice grain ranges from 8.0 to 8.7
mm
LONG GRAINS - Palay whose average
length of the full size palay grain is
between 8.8 to 9.8 mm.
VERY LONG GRAINS - Palay whose
average length of the full size palay
grain is 9.9 mm and above.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
VARIETY
TRADITIONAL VARIETY - Refers to
indigenous or native varieties of rice
and corn other than special rice
varieties.
SPECIAL VARIETY PALAY - This
includes glutinous, aromatic palay
varieties and those with excellent
eating and nutritive quality. Palay
varieties considered under the
classification shall include but are not
limited to the following: Dinorado,
Sigadis, Milagrosa, Sampaguita,
Sinandomeng, Kalinayan, Baysilanon

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
62. Percentage of palay grains free of foreign
materials.
a.Chalkiness
b.Cleanliness
c.Purity
d.Recovery

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
OTHER PARAMETERS
PURITY - Percentage of palay grains free of foreign materials.
FOREIGN MATTER (Palay) - All mailers other than palay grains such as
(a) sand, gravel, dirt, pebbles, stones, lumps of earth, clay, mud,
chaff, straw, and (b) other grains like weed seeds and other crop
seeds.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DEFECTIVE KERNELS
CHALKY KERNELS – Kernels, whole or broken,
one-half or more of which is white like the
color of white chalk and is brittle upon
removal of the hull for palay.
IMMATURE KERNELS – Kernels, whole or broken, which are light green and chalky with
soft texture.
DAMAGED KERNELS (Corn) - Kernels or pieces of kernels of corn which are heat
damaged, sprouted, ground damaged, weather damaged, moldy, diseased,
insect-bored or otherwise materially damaged.
DAMAGED KERNELS (Palay) - Kernels which are sprouted or distinctly damaged by
insects, water, fungi and/or any other means.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DEFECTIVE KERNELS
CONTRASTING TYPE – Palay/rice kernels of different varieties other than the
variety designated, wherein the size, shape and color differ distinctly from
the characteristics of kernels of the variety designated.
RED KERNELS – Kernels that have red bran covering, wholly or partly.
DISCOLORED KERNELS – Kernels that have changed their original color as a
result of heating and other means. This is also known as "yellow kernels" or
"fermented kernels".

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
63. Any rice and corn variety which meet the highest
grade requirements for rice and corn as set forth in the
herein prescribed national standards.
a.Premium
b.Grade No. 1
c.Grade No. 2
d.Grade No. 5

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRADE
Grade – a designation indicating the degree of quality of rice and corn.
• PREMIUM GRADE -Any rice and corn variety which meet the highest
grade requirements for rice and corn as set forth in the herein
prescribed national standards.
• GRADE NO. 1
• GRADE NO. 2
• GRADE NO. 3
• GRADE NO. 4
• GRADE NO. 5 - Any milled rice variety which meets the lowest grade
requirements for milled rice.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CLASSIFICATION
• SHORT GRAINS - Rice with 80% or more of
the whole milled rice kernels having a length
of less than 5.5 mm.
• MEDIUM GRAINS - Rice with 800% or more
of whole milled rice kernels having a length
of 5 5 to 6.3 mm.
• LONG GRAINS - Rice with 80% or more of
whole milled rice kernels having a length of
6.4 to 7.4 mm.
• VERY LONG GRAINS - Rice with 80% or
more of whole milled rice kernels having a
length of 7.5 mm and above.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DEGREE OF MILLING
• DEGREE OF MILLING - The extent in which
the bran layers and germ have been
removed in milled rice.
• OVERMILLED RICE - Rice kernel from
which the hull, the germ and the bran layers
have been completely removed.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
64. Rice kernels from which the hull, the germ, the outer bran
layers and the greater part of the inner bran layers have been
removed, but parts of the lengthwise streaks of the bran
layers shall be less than 20% of the kernels.
a. Regular milled
b. Special milled
c. Overmilled
d. Well milled

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DEGREE OF MILLING
• WELL MILLED RICE - Rice kernels from which the hull, the
germ, the outer bran layers and the greater part of the inner bran
layers have been removed, but parts of the lengthwise streaks of
the bran layers shall be less than 20% of the kernels.
• REGULAR MILLED RICE - Rice kernel from which the hull, the
germ, the outer bran layers and the greater part of the inner bran
layers have been removed but parts of the lengthwise streaks of
the bran layers shall be within the range of 20-40% of the
kernels.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
GRADE FACTOR
• BROKEN KERNELS - Pieces of kernels smaller than 7.5/10 of the
average length of the unbroken kernel.
• BREWERS - Small pieces or particles of kernels that pass through a
sieve having round perforations 1.4 millimetres in diameter. This is also
known as 'binlid' or 'chips'.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DEFECTIVE KERNELS
FOREIGN MATTER (Milled Rice) - Organic and
inorganic components other than whole or
broken rice kernels (e.g., foreign seeds, husks,
bran, sand, dust and other crop seeds.)
DAMAGED KERNELS (Milled Rice) - Kernels,
which are obviously damaged by insects, water,
diseases and/or any other means as seen by
the naked eye.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CLASSIFICATION
WHITE CORN - Corn kernels of white color with not more than
two percent (2%) of other colors. A slight tinge of other
colors, other than white, shall not affect their classification
as white corn.
YELLOW CORN - Yellow corn kernel with not more than two
percent (2%) of other colors. A slight tinge of other colors,
other than yellow, shall not affect their classification as
yellow corn.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CLASSIFICATION
DENT CORN - Corn kernels which have dent in the broad end of
the kernels causes by great shrinkage of soft starch between
the two layers of corneous and flinty starch at the end of the
endosperm.
FLINT CORN - Corn kernels with relatively large amount of hard
endosperm on the sides and the inner portion is composed of
soft starch. The color of the endosperm is either white or
yellow.
POP CORN - A type of corn which forms large flakes after the
kernels explode in response to heating (popping expansion).

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
DEFECTIVE KERNEL
MOLDY KERNELS – Kernels or pieces of kernels which
are contaminated with molds.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
QUESTION
65. Color of packaging material for special rice.
a.Sky blue
b.Black
c.Light yellow
d.Light green

GENERAL SANTOS

Postharvest Losses and Challenges
Fruits and Vegetables Physiology

5

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
POSTHARVEST
LOSSES AND
CHALLENGES

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
1. It is the study of fruits
a. Olericulture
b. Pomology
c. Entomology
d. Anthology
QUESTION

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Horticulture – includes the production of fruits,
vegetables, flowers, spices, medicinal and aromatic
plants and plantation crops
Pomology – study of fruits
Olericulture – study of vegetables
Anthology – study of flowers
Storage roots and tubers – rich in carbohydrate,
particularly starch, in amounts comparable to the cereal
crops, and can be used as staple foods
Leguminous vegetables – supply as much as 14% protein

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Vegetables and root crops – rich in minerals, carotene (Pro-vitamin A)
and vitamin C, and are reasonably good sources of trace elements such
as copper, manganese and zinc, which act as enzyme cofactors
Inappropriate post-harvest handling causes:
❑ Product losses (quality decay/
physical losses)
❑ High costs and low profits
❑ Loss of market opportunities
❑ Low competitiveness

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CAUSES OF POSTHARVEST LOSSES
A. External Factors
1. Mechanical Injury
• Fresh fruits and vegetables are highly susceptible to mechanical
injury owing to their tender texture and high moisture content.
• Poor handling, unsuitable packaging and improper packing during
transportation are the cause of bruising, cutting, breaking, impact
wounding, and other forms of injury in fresh fruits and vegetables.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
2. The following are examples of causes of impact
injuries, except:
a.Suddenly stopping a vehicle
b.Vehicles with bad shock-absorber
c.Dropping product into the back of a car
d.Excessive drops during unloading
QUESTION

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CAUSES OF POSTHARVEST LOSSES
a. Impact injuries, resulting from:
• dropping the product onto a hard surface;
• dropping the product into the back of a car;
• excessive drops during loading and unloading;
• suddenly stopping or accelerating a vehicle.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CAUSES OF POSTHARVEST LOSSES
b. Vibration or abrasion injuries result when produce is
able to move within a container because of:
• vehicles with small wheels and bad shock-absorbers;
• weak crates;
• bad roads;
• transmission vibration.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
3. Compression injuries are caused by the following,
except:
a.Too high stacking of crates
b.Improper packing
c.Excessive drops
d.Over-packing of boxes
QUESTION

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CAUSES OF POSTHARVEST LOSSES
c. Compression injuries are caused by improper
packing and inadequate package performance
resulting from:
• over-packing of crates and boxes;
• too high stacking of crates;
• weak packaging.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CAUSES OF POSTHARVEST LOSSES
d. Puncturing injuries resulting from:
• nails or splinters from the crate or box;
• fingers or nails of a person;
• other crates, fork-lifts, etc.
• hard and sharp stalks of fruit.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CAUSES OF POSTHARVEST LOSSES
2. Parasitic Diseases
• Lack of natural defense mechanisms
in the tissues of fresh produce, and
the abundance of nutrients and
moisture which supports their growth
• The number of pesticides available is
rapidly declining as consumer concern
for food safety is increasing.

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
CAUSES OF POSTHARVEST LOSSES
B. Internal Factors
1. Physiological Deterioration
• Result of mineral deficiency, low or high
temperature injury, or undesirable environmental
conditions, such as high humidity.
• Enzymatic activity

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
Key process during the postharvest life:
❑ Respiration
❑ Transpiration
❑ Ethylene production
❑ Maturity process

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
4. During post-harvest glut, what may happen?
a. Fruits rot
b. Excessive demand
c. Better infrastructure
d. More informed consumers
QUESTION

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
PROBLEMS
• The raw material producer, due to
insufficient demand, weak
infrastructure, poor transportation,
and perishable nature of the produce,
lose substantial money.
• During the post-harvest glut, the loss
is imaginable and often the fruits have
to be fed to animals or allow to rot.
• Erratic supplies

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS

MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
GENERAL SANTOS
5. Typically, a processing center or factory should
process _____ types of fruits:
a.2-3

MECHANICAL SEPARATION
• Sedimentation: Two immiscible liquids, or a liquid and a solid, differing in
density, are separated by allowing them to come to equilibrium under the
action of gravity, the heavier material falling with respect to the lighter.
• Centrifugal separation: Since sedimentation is often a slow process, it can
be speeded up by applying centrifugal forces to increase the rate of
separation.
• Filtration: It is the separation of solids from liquids, by causing the mixture
to flow through fine pores which are small enough to stop the solid particles
but large enough to allow the liquid to pass.
• Sieving: It is done by interposing a barrier through which the larger
elements cannot pass, and is often used for classification of solid particles.

when the partial pressure of water
vapor is below the saturated vapor
pressure, and drying is by desorption.
